&ge; 85 (crowded long).example: Like a cinema hall that is already 85% full, so few new people are left to come in. If the funds' net ranged from 50,000 to 250,000 contracts and now sits at 230,000, the COT index is 90.
&ge; 85 (crowded long).forYou: As a seller, when this market is crowded long, avoid selling puts close to price, because fund selling can bring a quick drop.
&ge; 85 (crowded long).goodBad: Neither. A row with few weeks is only an anecdote.
&ge; 85 (crowded long).impact: If it goes up: prices after crowded weeks have still done well, so crowded has stayed crowded. If it goes down: crowded weeks have led to weaker prices, and funds usually cut afterwards.
&ge; 85 (crowded long).readIt: When you see this row, compare it with All weeks (baseline). Weaker returns here mean crowding has worked as a warning in this market.
&ge; 85 (crowded long).simple: Weeks when the COT index was 85 or more, meaning funds held close to their biggest net long of the last three years. The row shows what price and fund positions did after such weeks.

&le; 15 (washed out).example: Like a clearance sale where almost everyone who wanted to sell has already sold. If the funds' net ranged from minus 40,000 to plus 160,000 contracts and now sits at minus 20,000, the COT index is 10.
&le; 15 (washed out).forYou: As a seller, when a market is washed out, avoid selling calls too close, because short covering can bring a sharp jump.
&le; 15 (washed out).goodBad: Neither. A row with few weeks is only an anecdote.
&le; 15 (washed out).impact: If it goes up: prices after washed-out weeks have bounced more. If it goes down: weak markets have kept falling even after funds were very short.
&le; 15 (washed out).readIt: When you see this row, compare it with All weeks (baseline). Better returns here mean a washed-out market has tended to bounce.
&le; 15 (washed out).simple: Weeks when the COT index was 15 or less, meaning funds were close to their most bearish position of the last three years. Most of the selling may already be done.

0-1 DTE share.example: Like starting a 10-day course on the last day: little time for the plan to work.
0-1 DTE share.forYou: Keep most trades away from the last day.
0-1 DTE share.goodBad: Low is good; high means heavy expiry-day risk.
0-1 DTE share.impact: If it goes up: more trades rely on the riskiest days. If it goes down: you use more time.
0-1 DTE share.readIt: When you see a high percent, many trades were very short-dated.
0-1 DTE share.simple: DTE means days to expiry. This is the share of trades opened with a day and a half or less to expiry. NIFTY sellers earn mostly overnight. Intraday option selling lost money in 2017-20.

1&sigma; coverage.example: Like a weather forecaster who says rain-free 68 days in 100: check if it really was 68. If 75 of 100 landed inside, the band was a bit wide.
1&sigma; coverage.forYou: Trust the one-sigma band only as much as this coverage supports.
1&sigma; coverage.goodBad: Near 68% is good; well below is bad for a seller.
1&sigma; coverage.impact: If it goes above 68%: bands are too wide and premium is left on the table. If below: bands are too narrow, which costs sellers money.
1&sigma; coverage.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with 68.3%, not 100%.
1&sigma; coverage.simple: How often the outcome landed inside the one-sigma band. The target is about 68.3%. A Kupiec test beside it says if any gap is more than chance.

1-sigma move.example: Like the usual range of a city's temperature this week: most days fall inside, but a heat wave can break it. Trading: forward 24,000, IV 12 percent, 30 days gives about 24,000 x 0.12 x 0.29 = 830 points.
1-sigma move.forYou: Use it to check the Shorts outside 1 sigma rule.
1-sigma move.impact: If it goes up: the expected range widens, so strikes must sit further out. If it goes down: the range narrows.
1-sigma move.readIt: When you see this number, place sold strikes at least this far from the forward.
1-sigma move.simple: This is the normal-sized move NIFTY may make up to the second expiry. It comes from the forward price, the at-the-money IV and time left. About two thirds of outcomes would land inside it. Real markets cross it more often than that.

2&sigma; adjusted.example: Like planning a trip with the real road map, not a straight-line guess. If plain is 24,200 to 25,800, adjusted may be 24,000 to 25,800.
2&sigma; adjusted.forYou: Use this band rather than the plain one for far short puts.
2&sigma; adjusted.impact: If skew deepens: the lower edge moves down. If moves are balanced: it matches the plain band.
2&sigma; adjusted.readIt: When you see this band, compare it with the gaussian band. The difference shows the hidden falling risk.
2&sigma; adjusted.simple: The two-sigma range after fixing for the real shape of moves. It leans the way NIFTY's moves lean. Usually the lower edge sits further down.

2&sigma; coverage.example: Like a school bus that is on time 95 days in 100. If it is on time only 85 days, the timetable is wrong, not unlucky.
2&sigma; coverage.forYou: If this is well below 95%, add extra distance to far short strikes.
2&sigma; coverage.goodBad: Near 95% is good; well below is bad.
2&sigma; coverage.impact: If it goes above 95%: the band is a bit wide. If it goes below: the band is too narrow and far strikes are less safe than shown.
2&sigma; coverage.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with 95.4%. Falling well short means the band is sized wrongly.
2&sigma; coverage.simple: How often the outcome landed inside the two-sigma band. The target is about 95.4%. This wider band should fail rarely.

2&sigma; gaussian.example: Like assuming a road is flat both ways. If NIFTY is 25,000 and one sigma is 400, this band is 24,200 to 25,800.
2&sigma; gaussian.forYou: Do not set put strikes from this band alone.
2&sigma; gaussian.impact: If volatility goes up: this band widens. If it goes down: it narrows.
2&sigma; gaussian.readIt: When you see this band, always compare it with the adjusted band. The plain one usually understates falls.
2&sigma; gaussian.simple: The plain two-sigma range that assumes up and down moves are equal. It is the price plus or minus two standard deviations. It is shown beside the adjusted band to show the difference.

20-day realised.example: Like checking how much your daily auto fare jumped around over the last month. If gold moves about 1% a day, the 20-day realised is about 16%, because 1% times the square root of 252 is about 16.
20-day realised.forYou: As a seller, sell when implied is well above this number, and be careful when this number is rising fast.
20-day realised.goodBad: Neither by itself. Low is calmer for sellers, but premium is usually small then too.
20-day realised.impact: If it goes up: the market has been swinging more, so sold options get tested more often. If it goes down: the market has been calm, and premium is easier to keep.
20-day realised.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with implied vol. If implied is clearly above it, options are priced for more movement than has really happened.
20-day realised.simple: How much the price actually moved over the last 20 sessions, written as a yearly percentage. It compares each day's close with the day before. A bigger number means a bumpier ride.

2008 financial crisis.example: Like a town where the biggest bank shuts and every shop slashes prices to raise cash. Crude oil was near 147 dollars a barrel in July 2008 and below 40 dollars by December 2008.
2008 financial crisis.forYou: As a seller, this row shows how much one bad window can take. Use defined-risk spreads and smaller size when a broad panic starts.
2008 financial crisis.goodBad: Bad for short puts. A smaller Worst than the baseline row means the rule handled it better.
2008 financial crisis.impact: If this happens again: prices can fall for months while option prices (implied vol) jump, so sold puts get hit again and again as each floor breaks.
2008 financial crisis.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it.
2008 financial crisis.simple: The world money panic of 2008, when the big US bank Lehman Brothers failed in September. Almost every commodity fell hard because buyers feared a deep slump. The desk replays sessions from July 2008 to March 2009.

2011 silver crash.example: Like a crowded mela stall where the owner suddenly asks for a bigger deposit and half the crowd has to leave at once. A silver option sold for Rs 100 of premium can lose many times that in a week like this.
2011 silver crash.forYou: As a seller, after a near-vertical rally in silver, sell smaller and further away, and watch for exchange margin hikes.
2011 silver crash.goodBad: Bad for sellers on both sides. Compare its Worst with the baseline row.
2011 silver crash.impact: If this happens again: a crowded rally can reverse in days, and both sides of a short strangle can be tested as price swings up and then down.
2011 silver crash.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it.
2011 silver crash.simple: In 2011 silver raced to almost 50 dollars an ounce by late April and then fell very fast in early May. The US exchange raised the money needed to hold silver futures several times in a few days, which forced many buyers out. The desk replays sessions from April to October 2011.

2013 gold crash.example: Like a jeweller's rate dropping sharply over one weekend. If gold is at Rs 30,000 per 10 grams, a 13% fall takes it to about Rs 26,100 in two days.
2013 gold crash.forYou: As a seller, do not treat gold as safe just because it moved slowly for months. Keep a stop on short puts.
2013 gold crash.goodBad: Bad for short puts on gold and silver.
2013 gold crash.impact: If this happens again: a calm, slow metal can break down all at once, so puts sold close to the price lose fast.
2013 gold crash.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it.
2013 gold crash.simple: In April 2013 gold fell about 13% in just two sessions, 12 and 15 April, one of its sharpest drops in decades. It kept sliding into June. The desk replays sessions from mid-March to mid-July 2013.

2014-16 oil crash.example: Like a sabzi mandi where farmers keep bringing more tomatoes than people can buy, so the price drops week after week. Crude at Rs 6,000 a barrel would end near Rs 2,000 after a fall that size.
2014-16 oil crash.forYou: As a seller, in a long slide do not keep selling puts just because the price looks cheap. Respect the trend and lean on the call side.
2014-16 oil crash.goodBad: Bad for short puts, kinder to short calls.
2014-16 oil crash.impact: If this happens again: a long, steady fall keeps pushing price through sold puts one expiry after another.
2014-16 oil crash.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it.
2014-16 oil crash.simple: From mid-2014 to early 2016 crude oil fell for many months because the world had more oil than it needed. In November 2014 OPEC chose not to cut its output, and Brent went from above 110 dollars to below 30 dollars. The desk replays sessions from June 2014 to February 2016.

2020 COVID (incl. negative crude).example: Like a godown so full that the owner pays you to take the goods away. A crude put sold for Rs 100 at a Rs 1,500 strike lost far more than its premium when price went to zero and below.
2020 COVID (incl. negative crude).forYou: As a seller, never hold naked short puts into a panic and an expiry together. A put spread caps the loss.
2020 COVID (incl. negative crude).goodBad: Bad, the worst kind of window for short puts.
2020 COVID (incl. negative crude).impact: If this happens again: prices can fall past levels anyone thought possible and implied vol can multiply, so a naked short put has no real floor.
2020 COVID (incl. negative crude).readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it. The Crude below zero card under it shows the exact April 2020 put cases.
2020 COVID (incl. negative crude).simple: The COVID-19 market crash of early 2020. On 20 April 2020 the US WTI crude future for May even settled below zero, at minus 37.63 dollars a barrel, and MCX settled its open April crude futures at minus Rs 2,884. The desk replays sessions from February to May 2020.

2020 palladium spike and crash.example: Like a new phone selling at double price for weeks and then nobody wanting it even at half price. A metal at Rs 2,000 rising to Rs 2,800 and then falling to Rs 1,500 within weeks is that kind of ride.
2020 palladium spike and crash.forYou: As a seller, a thin market making a record spike can turn quickly, so keep size small and use defined risk on palladium and platinum.
2020 palladium spike and crash.impact: If this happens again: both short calls and short puts can be hit in the same quarter, and implied vol can more than double.
2020 palladium spike and crash.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it. Price move can look small here because the window starts and ends at similar prices, while the ride in between was huge.
2020 palladium spike and crash.simple: Palladium hit a record near 2,800 dollars an ounce in late February 2020, then lost close to half its value within weeks in the March COVID selloff. Up first and then down fast hurt sellers on both sides. The desk replays sessions from mid-January to mid-April 2020.

2022 LME nickel squeeze.example: Like a trader who promised 100 bags of sugar he did not have, and every seller doubles the price because they know he must buy. Nickel at Rs 2,000 a kg going to Rs 4,000 in two days is that kind of move.
2022 LME nickel squeeze.forYou: As a seller, never hold naked short calls on a metal where one big player is known to be heavily short. Use spreads.
2022 LME nickel squeeze.goodBad: Bad, the worst kind of window for short calls.
2022 LME nickel squeeze.impact: If this happens again: a squeeze can blow far past every call strike, and the market may even stop trading, so you cannot get out.
2022 LME nickel squeeze.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it.
2022 LME nickel squeeze.simple: In March 2022 nickel on the London Metal Exchange more than doubled in about two days and went above 100,000 dollars a tonne intraday. A huge short position could not be covered, so the exchange cancelled trades and stopped nickel trading for days. The desk replays sessions from mid-February to April 2022.

2022 energy shock.example: Like cooking gas suddenly costing much more because one big supplier is cut off. A Rs 6,000 crude price jumping 20% to Rs 7,200 in a couple of weeks is that kind of move.
2022 energy shock.forYou: As a seller, during a war or supply shock, keep both sides far away and sell less, or use spreads.
2022 energy shock.goodBad: Bad for short calls first, then for short puts.
2022 energy shock.impact: If this happens again: prices can jump on war news, so short calls get hit first, and the later fall then hurts short puts.
2022 energy shock.readIt: When you see this row, look at Worst and Worst on 5 lakh first, then Losing. Each row sells options on every session of the window and holds to the next MCX option expiry, so it shows how the rule did if you had traded right through it.
2022 energy shock.simple: After Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022, energy prices jumped and stayed wild for months. Brent briefly went above 130 dollars a barrel in early March 2022, and gas prices in Europe hit records later that year. The desk replays sessions from February to October 2022.

25&Delta; butterfly.example: Like extra charges for a trip in a storm on both ends of the road. If wings cost 2 points more than the middle, tails are priced as fat.
25&Delta; butterfly.forYou: A rising butterfly means far strikes pay more, but the market is warning of bigger moves.
25&Delta; butterfly.impact: If it goes up: big moves are feared more, and far options pay more. If it goes down: the market sees fewer big moves.
25&Delta; butterfly.readIt: When you see this number, check if it is rising. A bigger number means more fear of large moves.
25&Delta; butterfly.simple: How much more far-away options cost than the middle option. It shows how fat the market prices the tails. Tails means very big moves either way.

25&Delta; risk reversal.example: Like flood insurance costing more than sunshine insurance, because people fear floods more. If the call is 11% and the put 14%, the reading is -3.
25&Delta; risk reversal.forYou: When it turns sharply more negative, sell puts further away.
25&Delta; risk reversal.impact: If it goes more negative: crash protection costs more, so short puts pay more but carry more risk. If it rises toward zero: fear is easing.
25&Delta; risk reversal.readIt: When you see this number, expect it to be negative. A sudden deeper negative means fear of falls is rising.
25&Delta; risk reversal.simple: The price of an out-of-the-money call minus the price of an out-of-the-money put, in volatility terms. Negative means puts cost more. That is normal for stock indexes.

25&Delta; risk reversal and butterfly.example: Before monsoon, umbrella prices rise more than sunglasses; that tilt is the risk reversal. If NIFTY's far puts cost more than far calls, risk reversal is negative, which is normal.
25&Delta; risk reversal and butterfly.forYou: As a seller, richer puts pay you more, but for a reason: the market fears a fall.
25&Delta; risk reversal and butterfly.goodBad: A sharp rise in skew or butterfly signals rising fear; flat and steady means calm.
25&Delta; risk reversal and butterfly.impact: If risk reversal goes more negative: puts are in demand, and downside fear is rising. If butterfly goes up: both tails are bid, and a big move is priced in.
25&Delta; risk reversal and butterfly.readIt: When you see these, watch changes more than levels. Negative risk reversal is normal for NIFTY. Skew getting steeper while NIFTY is calm often comes before a volatile spell.
25&Delta; risk reversal and butterfly.simple: Two numbers that show the shape of fear in option prices. Risk reversal compares a far call's IV with a far put's IV. Butterfly shows how pricey both far sides are versus the middle.

3 losses in 50.example: Like the chance of three rainy days in a row during a 50-day season.
3 losses in 50.forYou: Expect at least one such streak in many 50-trade stretches and do not quit because of it.
3 losses in 50.goodBad: Lower is easier on your nerves.
3 losses in 50.impact: If it rises: losing streaks are more common. If it falls: streaks are rarer.
3 losses in 50.readIt: When you see this, read it as how often to expect a rough patch. For the current rules it is about 35%.
3 losses in 50.simple: The chance that any run of 50 trades has at least three losses in a row. Streaks are what a seller feels first.

3-loss streak odds.example: Like a good batsman getting out cheaply three innings running: it happens to everyone over a season.
3-loss streak odds.forYou: Read it before a losing run comes, so the run does not surprise you.
3-loss streak odds.goodBad: High means streaks are expected; low means rarer, but never impossible.
3-loss streak odds.impact: If it goes up: losing runs are more likely, so size smaller. If it goes down: runs are rarer but still possible.
3-loss streak odds.readIt: When you see a high percent, expect a losing run at some point this year and plan for it.
3-loss streak odds.simple: This is the chance of three or more losing trades in a row in a year of weekly trades. It uses the backtest's loss rate. Such a run is normal for this strategy. It is not a reason to change plans or win money back.

3-year positioning percentile.example: If in a class of 100 students you rank 95th in height, you are taller than almost everyone. A 95 here means funds are more long than in almost every week.
3-year positioning percentile.forYou: A crowded reading warns you that a sharp reverse move is more possible against your position.
3-year positioning percentile.goodBad: Extremes mean crowding and higher risk of sharp reversals; middle values are ordinary.
3-year positioning percentile.impact: If it goes up: fewer new buyers remain and a story change can force selling. If it goes down: funds are light, so buying may return later.
3-year positioning percentile.readIt: When you see this number, above 90 is crowded long and below 10 is crowded short. Then check the statistics card for what price did after such weeks.
3-year positioning percentile.simple: It ranks today's fund net bet against the last 156 weekly reports, about three years. 100 is the most long, 0 the least. It shows crowding, not direction.

5%+ above the 50-day average.example: Like a runner who has sprinted far ahead of the group. If the 50-day average is 24,000, NIFTY above 25,200 turns this on.
5%+ above the 50-day average.forYou: As a seller, stretched rallies can keep going, so keep short calls at a safe distance rather than betting on a pullback.
5%+ above the 50-day average.impact: If this turns on: the rally is stretched far ahead of its average. If it turns off: price has cooled back toward its average.
5%+ above the 50-day average.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY is far above its usual path. The table shows how long it stayed stretched and how NIFTY moved afterwards.
5%+ above the 50-day average.simple: The 50-day average is NIFTY's average close over the last 50 sessions. This state is on when NIFTY closes more than 5% above that average. Price has run well ahead of its trend.

5%+ below the 50-day average.example: Like a train running far behind its timetable. If the 50-day average is 25,000, NIFTY below 23,750 turns this on.
5%+ below the 50-day average.forYou: As a seller, deep falls come with high fear and big swings, so size short puts small and keep them far away.
5%+ below the 50-day average.goodBad: Bad for open short puts; neither as a forecast.
5%+ below the 50-day average.impact: If this turns on: the fall is deep compared with the recent trend. If it turns off: price has climbed back toward its average.
5%+ below the 50-day average.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY has fallen far from its usual path. The table shows how long such spells lasted and what NIFTY did next.
5%+ below the 50-day average.simple: The 50-day average is NIFTY's average close over the last 50 sessions. This state is on when NIFTY closes more than 5% below it. Price has fallen well behind its trend.

5-session change.example: Like checking what tomatoes cost now against last Monday. If MCX crude went from Rs 6,000 to Rs 6,300 in 5 sessions, the change is +5%.
5-session change.forYou: As a seller, a big weekly push means do not sell options close to price on the side it is pushing toward.
5-session change.goodBad: Neither. It is a direction reading, not a score.
5-session change.impact: If it goes up: the recent push is upward, or implied vol has been rising. If it goes down: the recent push is downward, or implied vol has been falling.
5-session change.readIt: When you see this number, check its sign first. Plus means up over the week, minus means down, and a big size means a strong recent push.
5-session change.simple: How much something changed over the last 5 trading sessions, about one week. In the momentum readings it is the price change in percent. In the implied volatility rank card it is the change in implied vol, in points.

80% range hit rate.example: Like a guess of 25 to 30 degrees that is right only 5 days in 10: the range is too tight.
80% range hit rate.goodBad: Near 80 percent is well calibrated; far below means overconfident ranges.
80% range hit rate.impact: If it goes up toward 80 percent: your ranges are honest. If it goes down: they are too narrow.
80% range hit rate.readIt: When you see it below 65 percent, widen your ranges.
80% range hit rate.simple: This is the share of your 80 percent ranges that contained the final settlement. Far below 80 percent means your ranges are too narrow, which is the usual bias.

A measured big event ahead.example: Like knowing the market near your house always floods during Ganesh festival, from many past years. If such an event falls before Thursday's expiry, this reason turns on.
A measured big event ahead.forYou: As a seller, the side rule stands aside rather than sell into a measured event, even when premium is rich.
A measured big event ahead.goodBad: Neither; a warning to sellers, not proof that buying pays.
A measured big event ahead.impact: If this turns on: a known market-moving event sits before expiry. If it turns off: no measured event is left before expiry.
A measured big event ahead.readIt: When you see this row, it shows what buying the at-the-money straddle on such days would have earned. A reason is used only if it paid on average and at the median over at least 10 expiries.
A measured big event ahead.simple: This buy reason is present when an event before expiry has, on the desk's own data, moved NIFTY much more than an ordinary day. It needs 8 or more past cases and a median move at least 1.25 times normal.

ADX below 20 (sideways).example: Like an auto-rickshaw stuck in traffic, moving a little forward and back but going nowhere. If NIFTY stays between 24,800 and 25,100 for weeks, ADX falls below 20.
ADX below 20 (sideways).forYou: As a seller, a sideways market is usually the friendliest for range trades like strangles and iron condors, but check the table for what followed.
ADX below 20 (sideways).goodBad: Usually good for range sellers, as long as it does not end in a sudden breakout.
ADX below 20 (sideways).impact: If this turns on: the market has gone flat and directionless. If it turns off: a trend, up or down, is starting to build.
ADX below 20 (sideways).readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY has no clear direction. The table shows how long sideways spells lasted and how big the moves were afterwards.
ADX below 20 (sideways).simple: ADX measures trend strength on a 0 to 100 scale (14 days). Below 20 means there is no real trend: NIFTY is moving sideways.

ATM IV.example: Like a bus fare that tells you how bumpy the road is expected to be. If ATM IV is 12%, the market prices about 12% yearly movement.
ATM IV.forYou: Never sell just because ATM IV is high; check it against the realised forecast first.
ATM IV.impact: If it goes up: options get dearer and bands widen. If it goes down: options get cheaper and bands narrow.
ATM IV.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the realised forecast. Their ratio is the seller's edge.
ATM IV.simple: The implied volatility at the strike nearest the current price. Implied volatility is the expected yearly move baked into option prices. Every band on this desk is built from it.

ATM implied.example: Like working out a shop's profit margin from its selling price. If the ATM option implies 12%, that is the market's priced move.
ATM implied.forYou: Use it with the realised forecast to judge whether selling is paid.
ATM implied.impact: If it goes up: options are dearer. If it goes down: options are cheaper.
ATM implied.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with India VIX and with the realised forecast.
ATM implied.simple: The volatility hidden in the price of the option nearest the current price. Nobody forecast it. It is just the number that makes the option formula match the real price.

ATM straddle.example: Like an insurance premium that tells you how much damage the insurer expects. If the 25,000 call and put cost 200 together, the market expects about a 200-point move.
ATM straddle.forYou: Short strikes inside the straddle's move are in danger; place them outside.
ATM straddle.impact: If it goes up: the market expects bigger moves and sellers collect more. If it goes down: smaller moves expected, and less premium.
ATM straddle.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the sigma band. If they disagree a lot, check the volatility input.
ATM straddle.simple: The cost of buying both the call and put at the strike nearest the price. It is the move the market is charging for until expiry. No model is needed.

ATM, ITM, OTM.example: A cinema seat already booked is ITM; one you might book later is OTM. If NIFTY is 25,000, the 25,000 call is ATM, the 24,500 call is ITM, and the 25,500 call is OTM.
ATM, ITM, OTM.forYou: As a seller, OTM premium can decay to zero; selling ITM is really a direction bet.
ATM, ITM, OTM.impact: If NIFTY moves toward your OTM strike: it becomes ATM and your risk grows fast. If it moves away: your strike goes deeper OTM and decays faster.
ATM, ITM, OTM.readIt: When you see these labels, sellers mostly live in OTM strikes. Closer to ATM pays more but turns into a loss faster. Near expiry, each option is clearly one or the other.
ATM, ITM, OTM.simple: ATM (at the money) is the strike nearest spot. ITM (in the money) already has real value. OTM (out of the money) has only time value and expires worthless if nothing moves.

Above 50-DMA.example: Like how many students in a class are scoring above their own average. If 45 of 50 stocks are above, the rally is broad.
Above 50-DMA.forYou: In a quiet market with very high participation, be a little more careful with short puts.
Above 50-DMA.impact: If it goes up in a calm market: weaker sessions have tended to follow. If it goes down: fewer stocks support the move.
Above 50-DMA.readIt: When you see this number, also check if volatility is low. In the desk's study, a high count in a calm market came before softer days.
Above 50-DMA.simple: How many of NIFTY's 50 stocks closed above their own 50-day average. It shows how many stocks are joining a move. In calm markets, very strong joining was followed by weaker days.

Above the upper Bollinger band.example: Like a car going much faster than its usual speed on the same road. If NIFTY's 20-day average is 24,600 and the upper band is 25,100, a close at 25,200 is above the band.
Above the upper Bollinger band.forYou: As a seller, strong rallies can ride the upper band for days, so do not sell calls right at the band expecting a pullback.
Above the upper Bollinger band.goodBad: Neither; stretched, not necessarily ready to fall.
Above the upper Bollinger band.impact: If this turns on: price has broken above its normal range. If it turns off: price has slipped back inside the bands.
Above the upper Bollinger band.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY has stretched sharply upward. The table shows how long such stretches lasted and what NIFTY did next.
Above the upper Bollinger band.simple: The upper Bollinger band sits 2 standard deviations above NIFTY's 20-day average. Closing above it means NIFTY has run unusually far up from its recent average.

Active states: how long they last.example: Like a winning streak in cricket: how long has it run, and how long do streaks usually last? Lasts 3+ more is the share of past spells that went three more days.
Active states: how long they last.forYou: Expect a state like overbought to last a while; do not sell calls close just because RSI is high.
Active states: how long they last.impact: If today's spell is older than most: it is closer to ending. If young: it has often run longer.
Active states: how long they last.readIt: When you see this, compare today's age with the median spell length.
Active states: how long they last.simple: Each signal state on today, how many days it has run, and how long past spells lasted. A spell is a run of days in that state. A one or two day dip still counts as the same spell.

Add a leg.example: Like writing each item of a thali on the bill one by one; dal, rice and roti together make one meal.
Add a leg.forYou: Use it to copy each leg of a real trade exactly, with the price you actually got.
Add a leg.impact: If you add a bought leg next to a sold one: your worst loss gets a cap. If you remove it: the loss can become unlimited.
Add a leg.readIt: When you see this form, check the position name first. A spelling change starts a new position by mistake.
Add a leg.simple: A leg is one single option inside a trade. Here you type one option at a time: buy or sell, expiry, strike, call or put, lots and price. Legs with the same position name join into one trade.

Adherence score.example: Like a fitness habit tracker: walked on 9 of 10 planned days is 90 percent.
Adherence score.forYou: Check which trades failed and why, one by one.
Adherence score.goodBad: 90 percent or more is the target; low means your results reflect mistakes as much as the market.
Adherence score.impact: If it goes up: you follow your rules more. If it goes down: more trades break the plan.
Adherence score.readIt: When you see this number, under 90 percent means some trades broke your own rules.
Adherence score.simple: This is the share of closed trades that passed the gate without an override and exited per plan. The target is 90 percent or more.

Agri & softs.example: Like checking the wholesale mandi rate before buying at your local shop. If world sugar jumps 10% in a month, Indian sugar stocks and prices often feel it later.
Agri & softs.forYou: Food prices feed India's inflation, which feeds RBI decisions, which move NIFTY. Treat a big jump here as a background risk.
Agri & softs.goodBad: Neither; rising farm prices are good for growers and bad for buyers.
Agri & softs.impact: If these prices go up: food inflation pressure rises, which can make the RBI more careful about cutting rates. If they go down: food costs ease.
Agri & softs.readIt: When you see this group, look at the day's change and compare it with the Agri Index page for the Indian side.
Agri & softs.simple: A group of world farm prices: sugar, wheat, corn, soybean, soybean oil, cotton, coffee and rough rice. These are US futures prices. They show where world food and crop prices are heading.

Agri COT crowding.example: If 9 of 10 grain traders already bought ahead, few buyers remain.
Agri COT crowding.forYou: Crowded is not a timing signal on its own.
Agri COT crowding.goodBad: Extremes mean crowding; middle is normal.
Agri COT crowding.impact: If it goes up: crowding long increases. If it goes down: crowding short increases.
Agri COT crowding.readIt: When you see this number, above 80 or below 20 is crowded. Read the counts beside past outcomes.
Agri COT crowding.simple: How stretched funds are against their last three years. 0 is most short and 100 is most long. It also shows what price did after past extremes.

Agri COT drivers.example: Funds may buy soybeans when crude rises, because soy oil can become biofuel.
Agri COT drivers.forYou: Use it to know what usually drives funds in your crop.
Agri COT drivers.impact: If a link grows: that factor has mattered more. If it fades: less.
Agri COT drivers.readIt: When you see these correlations, check which factor has the strongest link.
Agri COT drivers.simple: Which things fund weekly changes move with: price, past trend, the dollar, crude oil. Correlation is not cause.

Agri ETF proxy chain.example: Like reading the neighbouring district's mandi board for a hint about your own.
Agri ETF proxy chain.forYou: Use it for context only; it never triggers a sale.
Agri ETF proxy chain.impact: If US holders buy more puts: fear is rising abroad. If more calls: upside chase.
Agri ETF proxy chain.readIt: When you see this chain, read the shape only. These option markets are thin, especially CANE.
Agri ETF proxy chain.simple: Option chains on US funds like WEAT for wheat, CORN, SOYB and CANE for sugar. They show skew and positioning of US holders. They are a proxy, not the contract's own options.

Agri HAR forecast.example: Like guessing next week's onion swings from yesterday, last week and last month together.
Agri HAR forecast.forYou: This is the main yardstick for agri ranges.
Agri HAR forecast.goodBad: High means big moves expected; low means quiet.
Agri HAR forecast.impact: If it goes up: the expected range widens. If it goes down: the range narrows.
Agri HAR forecast.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with implied vol if there is one.
Agri HAR forecast.simple: The desk's forecast of how much price will really move. It mixes daily, weekly and monthly moves. It sets the range when no real implied vol exists.

Agri Index.example: Think of a big mandi with three counters: one with options, one with futures, and one just showing the day's price board.
Agri Index.forYou: Focus trade planning on tier 1 items with Indian options.
Agri Index.impact: If an item moves up a tier: more tools and plans appear. If it is tier 3: you only read prices.
Agri Index.readIt: When you see this page, check the tier of each item first. Only tier 1 can have a trade plan.
Agri Index.simple: The farm page: grains, oilseeds, sugar and coffee, livestock and Indian farm contracts. Tier 1 has traded options. Tier 2 has futures only, and tier 3 has only spot or mandi prices.

Agri Indian contract.example: SEBI has paused trading in chana, mustard, soybean, wheat, paddy, palm oil and moong since 2021, now until 31 March 2027.
Agri Indian contract.forYou: Only plan agri trades on crops with listed Indian options.
Agri Indian contract.impact: If SEBI lifts a suspension: a crop may become tradable. If none listed: you can only read it.
Agri Indian contract.readIt: When you see this label, check options, futures only, or none.
Agri Indian contract.simple: Whether India lists an option, only a future, or nothing on this crop. NCDEX has options on jeera, guar seed, guar gum, turmeric and coriander. No Indian option means no rupee trade plan.

Agri NCDEX option chain.example: Like a price list where many items were never sold, so the shopkeeper wrote a fair guess.
Agri NCDEX option chain.forYou: Do not trust untraded strike prices for real fills.
Agri NCDEX option chain.impact: If volume rises: prices are more reliable. If no trades: prices are estimates.
Agri NCDEX option chain.readIt: When you see this chain, check volume first. A strike with no trades has a theoretical price.
Agri NCDEX option chain.simple: NCDEX's settlement price, volume and open interest for each listed strike. NCDEX is India's farm commodity exchange. Most strikes do not trade, so their price is the exchange's estimate.

Agri VRP.example: An insurer charging Rs 120 for Rs 100 of expected damage earns a Rs 20 premium.
Agri VRP.forYou: Never act on a proxy VRP.
Agri VRP.goodBad: High is better for sellers; low means underpaid.
Agri VRP.impact: If it goes up: sellers are paid more. If it goes down: the edge shrinks.
Agri VRP.readIt: When you see this ratio, check if implied is real or proxy.
Agri VRP.simple: The volatility risk premium: implied volatility compared with the forecast of real moves. Sellers are paid when implied is larger. A proxy gives a ratio for context only.

Agri base rates.example: If prices rose after 6 of 10 big jumps, compare with the normal rate.
Agri base rates.forYou: Do not treat it as a forecast.
Agri base rates.impact: If the gap grows: past moves like this had a lean. If small: no lean.
Agri base rates.readIt: When you see this table, compare with the normal share and check episodes.
Agri base rates.simple: What the next 5, 10 and 21 days did after every past 20-day move like today's. Windows overlap, so read the episode count.

Agri baseline and best rule.example: Mother's standard dal versus the tweaked recipe that won a family test.
Agri baseline and best rule.forYou: Prefer the plain baseline unless the best rule clearly wins on test years.
Agri baseline and best rule.impact: If the best rule beats the baseline on new years: it can be considered. If not: baseline stays.
Agri baseline and best rule.readIt: When you see both, compare their test results and gate passes.
Agri baseline and best rule.simple: The plain monthly condor a seller would start from, and the search's pick on training years. The pick is recommended only if it passes every gate.

Agri by vol regime.example: Like an umbrella seller checking sales by rainy and dry seasons.
Agri by vol regime.forYou: Use it to judge whether waiting for high vol pays here.
Agri by vol regime.impact: If high-vol trades do better: waiting for rich premium helps. If not: the filter adds little.
Agri by vol regime.readIt: When you see this table, compare results across buckets. Small buckets swing a lot.
Agri by vol regime.simple: Results split by whether model implied volatility was low, middle or high at entry. Sellers usually hope high vol pays best. Sellers usually hope high vol pays best.

Agri check yourself.example: Like a quiz after a farm lesson.
Agri check yourself.forYou: Use it to test your understanding.
Agri check yourself.impact: Nothing moves here. Questions change as data changes.
Agri check yourself.readIt: When you see the questions, answer all correctly to mark the lesson done.
Agri check yourself.simple: Graded questions from today's farm numbers. Your answers stay in this browser.

Agri contract specs.example: Like a seed packet listing weight, variety and sowing months.
Agri contract specs.forYou: Check the lot before sizing any agri trade.
Agri contract specs.impact: If the lot is large: each move costs more. If small: risk per lot is lower.
Agri contract specs.readIt: When you see this card, check the lot size and expiry rules.
Agri contract specs.simple: Lot, price unit, months and how options expire, with where each figure was checked. Unverified items are marked.

Agri crisis replays.example: Like reviewing past droughts to see how a crop insurer would have done.
Agri crisis replays.forYou: Size so that a repeat crisis does not wipe you out.
Agri crisis replays.impact: If a crisis repeats: one lot can badly hurt a small account. If you size small: damage stays survivable.
Agri crisis replays.readIt: When you see this table, look at the worst entry per lot and its share of Rs 5 lakh.
Agri crisis replays.simple: Every day of a past farm crisis used as an entry, held to the next monthly expiry. Crises include the 2012 US drought, 2022 Ukraine war and 2023-24 cocoa spike. It uses real prices.

Agri event move.example: If soybean moves Rs 50 on normal days but Rs 150 on USDA report days, the ratio is 3.
Agri event move.forYou: Avoid holding short options through high-ratio events.
Agri event move.goodBad: High means event risk; near 1 means ordinary.
Agri event move.impact: If the ratio goes up: that report brings bigger jumps. If it goes down: it matters less.
Agri event move.readIt: When you see the ratio, near 1 means little effect.
Agri event move.simple: How big the move was on each kind of report day, against a normal day. A ratio of 1.25 or more over at least 8 cases makes it a measured event.

Agri events.example: Like the monsoon forecast day that sends vegetable traders into a rush.
Agri events.forYou: Avoid holding short options through big crop reports or monsoon updates.
Agri events.impact: If a measured event is due: the desk will not sell into it. If none: the vol rule decides.
Agri events.readIt: When you see this list, look for measured events before your expiry.
Agri events.simple: Scheduled news before the next expiry: US farm reports, the Indian monsoon and policy dates. An event counts only once it has really moved this contract.

Agri evidence verdict.example: Like testing a recipe on new guests, not just family.
Agri evidence verdict.forYou: An Indian resident cannot normally trade US farm options on margin, so US edges are hypothetical.
Agri evidence verdict.goodBad: Recommended means it passed all gates; not proven means it did not.
Agri evidence verdict.impact: If every gate passes: the rule can be recommended. If one fails: it is not.
Agri evidence verdict.readIt: When you see this verdict, recommended needs every gate passed, including Indian options listed. Not proven means it failed a gate.
Agri evidence verdict.simple: Whether a monthly option-selling rule on this farm market kept earning in new years from 2018 on. Every premium is a model. No free farm implied vol index exists.

Agri exit plan.example: Like selling your crop before the cold storage lease ends.
Agri exit plan.forYou: Exit before expiry to avoid ending up with a futures position.
Agri exit plan.goodBad: Hitting the target is good; hitting the stop is a planned loss.
Agri exit plan.impact: If the trade keeps half the credit: take it. If loss hits 1.5 times credit: cut it.
Agri exit plan.readIt: When you see this plan, note the target, stop and exit date.
Agri exit plan.simple: When to take profit, when to cut, and the date to be out. NCDEX options turn into futures at expiry. So the desk never holds into the last session.

Agri expected range.example: If jeera is Rs 25,000 and 1 sigma is Rs 1,000, it should usually end between Rs 24,000 and Rs 26,000.
Agri expected range.forYou: Place short strikes outside the range and expect weather shocks to break it.
Agri expected range.goodBad: Wide means risky; narrow means calm.
Agri expected range.impact: If volatility rises: the range widens. If it falls: it narrows.
Agri expected range.readIt: When you see this range, compare it with the history band of real past moves.
Agri expected range.simple: How far the price can move by the next expiry. About 68% of outcomes fall inside 1 sigma and 95% inside 2 sigma. That holds only if the forecast is right.

Agri futures and options basics.example: A US option is like a ticket valid any day; an Indian one is valid only on the show date.
Agri futures and options basics.forYou: An Indian resident cannot normally trade US farm contracts on margin.
Agri futures and options basics.impact: If an Indian option ends in the money: it becomes a futures position. If out: it expires worthless.
Agri futures and options basics.readIt: When you see this lesson, note contract sizes, values and one-month moves.
Agri futures and options basics.simple: US farm options are options on futures, usually usable any day. Indian MCX and NCDEX options are usable only at expiry. In the money, they turn into futures.

Agri implied vol.example: Like guessing next month's tomato price swings from what traders charge for price protection.
Agri implied vol.forYou: Treat proxy numbers as context, not a trading trigger.
Agri implied vol.goodBad: High means expensive options; low means cheap and calm.
Agri implied vol.impact: If it goes up: options cost more and the market expects bigger moves. If it goes down: calmer moves are expected.
Agri implied vol.readIt: When you see this number, check its source. A US ETF number is a proxy only.
Agri implied vol.simple: What option prices say about the size of future moves, as a yearly percent. It comes from a US ETF's options or NCDEX settlements. No free agri vol index exists.

Agri implied vs realised.example: Like checking each monsoon forecast against the actual rain.
Agri implied vs realised.forYou: Use it to judge whether implied numbers are trustworthy here.
Agri implied vs realised.goodBad: Above 68% favours sellers; below means danger.
Agri implied vs realised.impact: If it goes up: implied over-priced moves, helping sellers. If it goes down: moves beat implied.
Agri implied vs realised.readIt: When you see the hit rate, compare it with 68%.
Agri implied vs realised.simple: How often the implied volatility on file covered the move that followed. A fair implied covers about 68% of windows.

Agri in sample and out of sample.example: Last year's exam paper is practice; this year's paper is the real test.
Agri in sample and out of sample.forYou: Judge rules only by test years.
Agri in sample and out of sample.impact: If test results fall far below training: the rule was overfit. If they hold: it may be real.
Agri in sample and out of sample.readIt: When you see this table, look only at the test columns.
Agri in sample and out of sample.simple: Training years were used to choose. Test years are new years. Only the test columns are evidence.

Agri instrument browser.example: Like a mandi directory listing every crop and stall.
Agri instrument browser.forYou: Use it to find tier 1 crops worth studying.
Agri instrument browser.impact: Nothing moves here. A new instrument added makes the list longer.
Agri instrument browser.readIt: When you see this list, check each item's tier before opening it.
Agri instrument browser.simple: Every farm instrument on file, by group, with its tier, last price and change. You can search by name or exchange.

Agri lesson.example: Like a closed notice on a classroom door.
Agri lesson.impact: Nothing moves here. It goes away once data loads.
Agri lesson.readIt: When you see this, the lesson's data is missing.
Agri lesson.simple: A farm lesson that could not be built from current data. It shows instead of a broken page.

Agri lessons.example: Like a short farm course with a quiz.
Agri lessons.forYou: Complete them before trading farm options.
Agri lessons.impact: Nothing moves here. The numbers update with the data.
Agri lessons.readIt: When you see the lessons, go through them in order.
Agri lessons.simple: Seven lessons on farm futures and options built from today's data. Each has graded questions.

Agri levels.example: If cotton has not gone above Rs 60,000 or below Rs 55,000 this month, those are the ceiling and floor.
Agri levels.forYou: Use them as triggers, since NCDEX open interest walls are thin.
Agri levels.impact: If price breaks a level: the plan switches branch. If it stays inside: the base plan holds.
Agri levels.readIt: When you see these levels, check their distance from today's price.
Agri levels.simple: Resistance and support on the strike grid. They come from the 20-day high and low or expected moves. The plan's branches trigger on them.

Agri momentum readings.example: Like a doctor's checklist of pulse, temperature and blood pressure.
Agri momentum readings.forYou: Use them for context, not as signals.
Agri momentum readings.impact: If ADX rises: the trend is strengthening. If RSI is extreme: price is stretched.
Agri momentum readings.readIt: When you see these readings, check ADX for trend strength and RSI for stretch.
Agri momentum readings.simple: Textbook indicators on the daily series: RSI, ADX, distance from averages, Bollinger %B. They give context for the trend read.

Agri out-of-sample equity.example: Like tracking a savings jar month by month to see if it grows.
Agri out-of-sample equity.forYou: Look at the dips too, not only the end value.
Agri out-of-sample equity.impact: If a line rises steadily: the rule held up. If it falls: it lost on new years.
Agri out-of-sample equity.readIt: When you see this chart, compare each line's ending value and its dips.
Agri out-of-sample equity.simple: Rs 10 lakh traded from January 2018 by each rule at 2% risk per trade, after costs. The walk-forward line re-chooses its rule every two years.

Agri overfitting check.example: If you try 2,000 recipes, one will taste great by chance.
Agri overfitting check.forYou: Reject rules that fail these checks.
Agri overfitting check.goodBad: Low PBO and high deflated Sharpe are good; the reverse means luck.
Agri overfitting check.impact: If PBO goes up: the rule is more likely luck. If it goes down: more likely real.
Agri overfitting check.readIt: When you see PBO, under 50% is needed. Deflated Sharpe must be above 0.95.
Agri overfitting check.simple: Overfitting means a rule fits past luck, not a real pattern. This shows tests for it: probability of overfitting, rank correlation, deflated Sharpe and walk-forward.

Agri playbook.example: Like a farmer's plan for early, normal and late rain.
Agri playbook.forYou: Use it only on NCDEX contracts with listed options, like jeera or turmeric.
Agri playbook.goodBad: No high or low; a clear plan for each branch matters.
Agri playbook.impact: If price hits a level: that branch applies. If the call is stand aside: the plan is for reference only.
Agri playbook.readIt: When you see the playbook, check the start trade and each trigger level. A credit trade is marked not-for-today unless the side call says sell.
Agri playbook.simple: The if-then plan: what to open today. Then what to do if price rallies, stalls, breaks out or breaks down. It is drawn only where an Indian option exists on NCDEX.

Agri positioning.example: Mandi arrivals would be India's version, but that data source refuses automated access.
Agri positioning.forYou: Read these as facts, not motives.
Agri positioning.impact: If fund longs go up: funds lean bullish. If open interest falls: positions are closing.
Agri positioning.readIt: When you see this card, check the fund net or the open interest trend.
Agri positioning.simple: Who holds the contract. For US contracts, the CFTC report shows funds and producers. For Indian ones, only exchange open interest is available.

Agri price.example: Wheat in Chicago is quoted in cents per bushel, while jeera at NCDEX is quoted in rupees per quintal.
Agri price.forYou: Always check the unit before comparing agri prices.
Agri price.impact: If it goes up: calls gain, puts lose. If it goes down: puts gain, calls lose.
Agri price.readIt: When you see this price, check its unit before comparing with another market.
Agri price.simple: The contract's last settlement or closing price, in the exchange's own unit. US contracts are in cents or dollars. NCDEX and MCX are in rupees.

Agri regime state.example: Like noting how long dry spells usually last in your district.
Agri regime state.impact: If a tested state turns on: it may lean the plan. If no edge: ignore it.
Agri regime state.readIt: When you see a state, check its verdict and spell count.
Agri regime state.simple: Textbook states like trend, momentum and volatility, shown as spells. It shows when they started, how long they last and what followed. A verdict needs enough spells.

Agri registry.example: Like a mandi ledger listing every crop on one page.
Agri registry.forYou: Use it to scan all farm markets quickly.
Agri registry.impact: Nothing moves here. New entries make the registry longer.
Agri registry.readIt: When you see this list, check tier and seasonal verdict first.
Agri registry.simple: Every entry with its group, tier, source, price, change, 1-year return, trend and seasonal verdict. Click a name to open it.

Agri seasonality.example: Onion prices often rise before the kharif crop arrives and fall after harvest.
Agri seasonality.forYou: Treat seasonality as a tendency, never a forecast.
Agri seasonality.goodBad: A strong, repeated pattern is useful context; a weak one is noise.
Agri seasonality.impact: If a month's up share is high: it has tended to rise. If low: it has tended to fall.
Agri seasonality.readIt: When you see the monthly bars, check how often the month rose, not just the average.
Agri seasonality.simple: Seasonality is a pattern that repeats with the calendar. This shows the average move in each month over every year. It also shows how often each month rose.

Agri side call.example: Like a crop insurer who sells cover only when the fee clearly beats expected damage, using real data.
Agri side call.forYou: Do not sell agri premium unless the call says sell on real implied vol.
Agri side call.goodBad: Sell means rich premium on real data; stand aside means no proven edge.
Agri side call.impact: If real implied rises above 1.10 times forecast with no event: it can say sell. If not: stand aside.
Agri side call.readIt: When you see the call, check if the implied vol is real or a proxy. With a proxy or none, the desk never says sell.
Agri side call.simple: The daily answer: sell option premium on this farm contract, or stand aside. Selling needs real implied volatility at least 1.10 times the forecast. A proxy never triggers a sale.

Agri smile sensitivity.example: A cake that only works at one exact oven setting is a fragile recipe.
Agri smile sensitivity.forYou: Trust rules that survive all smile versions.
Agri smile sensitivity.impact: If it flips: the result is fragile. If it holds: it is sturdier.
Agri smile sensitivity.readIt: When you see this table, check if the verdict stays the same.
Agri smile sensitivity.simple: The assumed smile is re-run with no smile and twice the skew. A verdict that flips rests on the assumption.

Agri sources.example: Like noting which shops let you check their price lists and which did not.
Agri sources.forYou: Know which data is missing before trusting a series.
Agri sources.impact: If a source is refused: its data is missing. If it works: data updates daily or weekly.
Agri sources.readIt: When you see this table, check status: worked or refused.
Agri sources.simple: Each data source tried, whether it worked, and how many entries it gives. A refused source is recorded and never worked around.

Agri stress lab.example: Like testing a dam with fake floods.
Agri stress lab.forYou: Size agri trades at or below the tail-safe size.
Agri stress lab.goodBad: Zero safe size means even one lot is too much.
Agri stress lab.impact: If tail losses grow: safe size shrinks. If they shrink: safe size grows.
Agri stress lab.readIt: When you see the tail-safe size, never trade more lots than it.
Agri stress lab.simple: Thousands of made-up two-year markets built from this market's behaviour. It measures tail losses per lot. It sets the safe size on Rs 5 and 10 lakh.

Agri track record.example: Like a new cricketer with no matches played yet.
Agri track record.forYou: Do not size up on agri until a record exists.
Agri track record.impact: If graded calls build up: the rule can be judged. If none: no trust yet.
Agri track record.readIt: When you see this card, note that no record means no proof.
Agri track record.simple: How the side rule and its signals have done on this contract. None exists yet for agri. Nothing is graded until there is a record.

Agri trend read.example: If wheat prices have climbed for three months, the trend is up.
Agri trend read.forYou: Use it to choose which side your spreads lean.
Agri trend read.impact: If the trend turns up: plans lean up. If it turns down: plans lean down.
Agri trend read.readIt: When you see this read, check the direction and the base rate for similar moves.
Agri trend read.simple: Where the trend stands and which way the desk leans. It comes from the Momentum tab. It sets which side a plan would favour.

Agri universe.example: Like a list of every mandi board you can read, even ones you cannot buy from.
Agri universe.forYou: Use it to read the market around tradable contracts.
Agri universe.impact: If a new source is added: the list grows. If a source is refused: it is recorded, not worked around.
Agri universe.readIt: When you see this list, tier 3 has no exchange contract and no trade plan.
Agri universe.simple: Every farm price the desk can get from a free, allowed source. Tier 2 is exchange futures. Tier 3 is spot or monthly reference prices.

Agri universe series.example: Like the daily price board at a mandi: useful to read, nothing to trade.
Agri universe series.forYou: Use these series to understand tradable markets better.
Agri universe series.impact: If price moves: it tells you about the market, but no plan follows.
Agri universe series.readIt: When you see this series, read it for context only.
Agri universe series.simple: A tier 2 or 3 series: a futures contract without options, or a spot or mandi price. It shows price, range, volatility and seasonality only.

Agri vol cone.example: If onion swings this week are bigger than in most past weeks, you are high in the cone.
Agri vol cone.forYou: Use it to judge if moves are unusual for this crop.
Agri vol cone.goodBad: High means wild; low means calm.
Agri vol cone.impact: If the dot rises: the market is wilder than usual. If it falls: calmer.
Agri vol cone.readIt: When you see the cone, check if today's dot is high or low.
Agri vol cone.simple: Where today's real volatility sits against every past window of the same length. High in the cone means moves are large by this contract's standards.

Agri year by year.example: Like a farmer's yield each year, not just the ten-year average.
Agri year by year.forYou: Distrust a rule whose gains come from a few lucky years.
Agri year by year.impact: If gains spread across years: the rule is sturdier. If bunched: it is fragile.
Agri year by year.readIt: When you see this table, check if gains come from only two or three years.
Agri year by year.simple: Each rule's return within each calendar year at 2% risk per trade. Test years are marked.

Alerts.example: Like a phone reminder that rings once when the milk is boiling, not every second.
Alerts.forYou: Read act alerts first, warn second, and ignore info unless you have time.
Alerts.impact: If more alerts appear: more things need checking, so look at act ones first. If none: nothing important changed.
Alerts.readIt: When you see an alert, open the matching position and check its exit rules.
Alerts.simple: Alerts are short messages about what changed. Some come from the desk, others from your own positions. Each fires once when a line is crossed. It fires again only after the condition clears.

All ten units.example: Like passing every subject, not just your favourite ones.
All ten units.forYou: Work on the weakest unit first.
All ten units.impact: If more units reach 70 percent: you get closer. If one drops: you can lose it.
All ten units.readIt: When you see where you are, it shows how many units meet 70 percent.
All ten units.simple: This badge is about the NISM exam syllabus. It needs 70 percent or better on every unit, with 3 or more answers each.

All weeks (baseline).example: Like knowing it rains on 30 of 100 days in a normal year, so 60 of 100 after dark clouds means the clouds matter. If gold rose in 55% of all 4-week stretches, that 55% is the bar to beat.
All weeks (baseline).forYou: As a seller, do not act on a crowded reading unless its row differs clearly from this one.
All weeks (baseline).impact: If it goes up: the market has had a strong upward drift overall, so every bucket tends to look good. If it goes down: the overall drift was weaker.
All weeks (baseline).readIt: When you see this row, compare its price change and % up with the crowded long and washed out rows. Only a clear gap means the extreme reading told you something.
All weeks (baseline).simple: Every week in the stored history, with no filter. It shows what price normally did over the next 4 and 12 weeks. The crowded rows are only useful when compared with this row.

Always 1-sigma condor.example: Like a simple rule a beginner follows: always bat the same way.
Always 1-sigma condor.forYou: Use it as the bar to beat.
Always 1-sigma condor.impact: If you beat it on process: your extra rules add value. If not: simpler is better.
Always 1-sigma condor.readIt: When you see it beating your process, simplify your approach.
Always 1-sigma condor.simple: This is a benchmark. It always sells the 1-sigma iron condor on the expiry nearest 5 days. It exits at 50 percent profit or a loss of 1.5 times credit.

Annualised carry.example: Like paying extra rent to buy a scooter later instead of now. If the yearly rate is 7% when loans cost 7%, it is normal.
Annualised carry.forYou: A very high carry means a crowded long that could unwind; keep that in mind for short puts.
Annualised carry.impact: If it goes well above interest rates: buyers are crowded on borrowed money. If it goes below or negative: short-side pressure or a dividend.
Annualised carry.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with interest rates, not zero. The desk hides it when expiry is too close.
Annualised carry.simple: The futures premium over spot, written as a yearly rate. Normally it is close to the cost of borrowing money. Far above means crowded buyers; below or negative means sellers are pushing.

Answered right.example: Like scoring 8 out of 12 in a test with a pass mark of 8.
Answered right.forYou: Retake the test after studying weak levels.
Answered right.impact: If it goes up: you pass more levels. If it goes down: start lower on the path.
Answered right.readIt: When you see a score just under two-thirds, a little revision may pass the level.
Answered right.simple: This is how many questions you got right at this level in your last placement test. Two-thirds or better passes the level.

Back up and restore.example: Like copying your phone photos to a pen drive before a reset.
Back up and restore.impact: If you export often: little can be lost. If you never export: one browser clean-up erases months.
Back up and restore.readIt: When you see reset, know it erases all learning data after a second click.
Back up and restore.simple: This saves every learning record in this browser to a file, loads one back, or resets. Use export before clearing browser data or changing device. Nothing leaves the browser except your own file.

Backtest breakdowns.example: Like splitting your exam marks by subject. But if one subject had only two tests, its average means little.
Backtest breakdowns.forYou: It hints when the rules work and when they do not, if the groups are big enough.
Backtest breakdowns.goodBad: Treat any group under about 20 trades as a hint, not a rule.
Backtest breakdowns.impact: If a group shows a clear loss with many trades: avoid that condition. If few trades: wait for more data.
Backtest breakdowns.readIt: When you see these splits, check the trade count first. On the sample, VIX under 11.5 averaged minus Rs 1,420 a trade, but from only 10 trades.
Backtest breakdowns.simple: The rules' trades split into groups. Groups are how they closed, the side rule, India VIX on entry and the trend bias. Small groups swing a lot, so a group of five says very little.

Backtest summary.example: Like a student checking answers on a test he already studied from. A good score is not proof he will pass a new test.
Backtest summary.forYou: The desk's own rules lost money here, so a high win rate alone must not make you confident.
Backtest summary.goodBad: Above zero expectancy is needed; this sample is in-sample and small.
Backtest summary.impact: If expectancy turns positive as more sessions are stored: the rules may have an edge. If it stays negative: the rules lose money despite winning often.
Backtest summary.readIt: When you see this, read win rate, expectancy and drawdown together. From Aug-2025 to Nov-2026: 39 trades, 77% won, but average result minus Rs 437 and total minus Rs 17,026.
Backtest summary.simple: What the desk's own selling rules would have earned on its stored sessions, one lot, after all costs. Every figure is in-sample. That means the rules were made by people who had seen this period.

Backtest trades.example: Like a shop's sales register showing each sale, its price and its profit.
Backtest trades.forYou: Reading real trades teaches you more than the average does.
Backtest trades.goodBad: Credit is the mid price in points before slippage.
Backtest trades.impact: If losses cluster in the same conditions: there may be a pattern to avoid. If spread out: they may just be bad luck.
Backtest trades.readIt: When you see this list, look at the losing trades. See how big they were next to the winners.
Backtest trades.simple: The last 30 trades the rules took. It shows dates, strikes, credit, profit after costs and why each closed. S means sold and B means bought.

Badge.example: Like a certificate that must be renewed by keeping up your skill.
Badge.forYou: Aim for the badge by better decisions, not more trades.
Badge.impact: If your figures meet the condition: the badge is earned. If they slip: it goes back to not yet.
Badge.readIt: When you see not yet, read what it takes and where you are.
Badge.simple: A badge is a skill milestone. It is earned by quality over a minimum sample, never by trades, rupees or time. It can be lost if recent figures fall.

Band factor.example: Like a tailor who keeps finding his shirts 10% too tight: he should multiply sizes by 1.1. A factor of 0.60 once came from three bugs, not real cheapness.
Band factor.forYou: If the factor moves far from 1, question the volatility inputs before trading.
Band factor.goodBad: Near 1 is good; far from 1 means the model needs fixing.
Band factor.impact: If it goes above 1: bands are too narrow and strikes are riskier than shown. If below 1: bands are too wide.
Band factor.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with 1. A factor drifting far from 1 is a warning sign.
Band factor.simple: A multiplier the range would need to hit its promised coverage. It is learned from the desk's own record. Above 1 means bands are too narrow; below 1, too wide.

Base metals and China.example: When China builds more houses and cars, it buys more copper wire and zinc.
Base metals and China.forYou: Watch China PMI dates when holding copper or zinc options.
Base metals and China.goodBad: A high ratio means China data moves the metal a lot.
Base metals and China.impact: If China's factory data rises: base metals often get support. If it falls: they often weaken.
Base metals and China.readIt: When you see the China PMI ratio, above 1 means PMI day moves the metal more than normal.
Base metals and China.simple: Copper, aluminium, zinc, lead and nickel are base metals. Factories buy them, about half in China by a common estimate. MCX lists options on copper and zinc only.

Base rate.example: Like knowing it rains in Mumbai on 80% of July days. A forecaster saying 80% every July day adds nothing.
Base rate.forYou: Ignore any signal that does not beat its base rate.
Base rate.impact: If it goes up: the event is more common, so a forecast must say more. If it goes down: the event is rarer.
Base rate.readIt: When you see this number, compare the desk's forecast with it.
Base rate.simple: How often the thing being forecast happened in the past. It is the simplest guess there is. Any forecast must beat it to be useful.

Baseline.example: To prove a lucky pen helps, compare marks with the same student using a normal pen.
Baseline.forYou: It stops you from trusting a signal that is right only because the market rarely moves far.
Baseline.goodBad: Beating the baseline with a small p-value is the only pass.
Baseline.impact: If the edge over baseline grows: the signal adds value. If it is zero or negative: it adds nothing.
Baseline.readIt: When you see a baseline, look at the edge over it, not the signal's hit rate alone.
Baseline.simple: A fair stand-in a signal must beat to count. For a wall, it is any level the same distance away. Only the gap between the signal and the baseline is evidence.

Baseline and best rule.example: The baseline is your mother's standard dal. The best rule is the tweaked recipe that won the family taste test.
Baseline and best rule.forYou: Prefer the plain baseline unless the best rule clearly wins on test years.
Baseline and best rule.goodBad: A best rule that wins out of sample is useful; one that only wins in training is luck.
Baseline and best rule.impact: If the best rule beats the baseline out of sample: it can be recommended. If not: the baseline stays the reference.
Baseline and best rule.readIt: When you see both, compare their test-year results. The best rule counts only if it beats the baseline on new years.
Baseline and best rule.simple: The baseline is a plain monthly condor sold when implied is 10% above forecast. A condor sells a call and a put with protection beyond. The best rule is the search's pick from training years.

Basis.example: Like the extra Rs 5 for home delivery that disappears when you collect in person. If forward is 25,040 and spot 25,000, basis is +40.
Basis.forYou: Treat a large stubborn basis near expiry as a hint about crowded positions.
Basis.impact: If it goes up: buyers are paying more for futures. If it goes down or negative: selling pressure or a dividend.
Basis.readIt: When you see this number, check whether it is shrinking as expiry nears. A stubborn premium near expiry is traders, not cost.
Basis.simple: Forward price minus today's price. It should shrink to zero by expiry. A gap that stays high into expiry shows positioning.

Below the lower Bollinger band.example: Like a temperature dropping far below the normal for that month. If NIFTY's 20-day average is 25,000 and the lower band is 24,500, a close at 24,400 is below the band.
Below the lower Bollinger band.forYou: As a seller, this is when put premium is fat but falls can keep going, so sell puts only with room and a wing.
Below the lower Bollinger band.goodBad: Bad for open short puts; neither as a forecast.
Below the lower Bollinger band.impact: If this turns on: price has broken below its normal range, often with fear rising. If it turns off: price is back inside the bands.
Below the lower Bollinger band.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY has stretched sharply downward. The table shows spell lengths and how NIFTY moved over the next sessions.
Below the lower Bollinger band.simple: The lower Bollinger band sits 2 standard deviations below NIFTY's 20-day average. Closing below it means NIFTY has fallen unusually far from its recent average.

Bid / Ask.example: At the mandi, a buyer offers Rs 39 and the seller asks Rs 45. If a NIFTY call shows Rs 42 but bid is 39, you get 39 when you sell.
Bid / Ask.forYou: As a seller, count your credit at the bid, not at the last price.
Bid / Ask.goodBad: A narrow spread means a liquid strike; a wide one means hidden cost.
Bid / Ask.impact: If the spread goes up: your cost to enter and exit rises. If it goes down: you keep more of the quoted premium.
Bid / Ask.readIt: When you see bid and ask, check the gap. A small gap means easy trading. A wide gap on far strikes can eat all the premium, which the illiquid tag warns about.
Bid / Ask.simple: Bid is the best price a buyer will pay now. Ask is the best price a seller will accept now. The gap between them is the spread, a cost you pay in and out.

BoJ policy decision.example: Like a moneylender who suddenly raises his rate, forcing borrowers in other towns to sell things to pay him back. NIFTY reacts on the next Indian session after the decision.
BoJ policy decision.forYou: As a seller, only an event that counts changes the side rule; otherwise it is background news.
BoJ policy decision.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: Japan's decisions have been rippling into NIFTY more. If it goes down: NIFTY has treated them like any other day.
BoJ policy decision.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with an ordinary day's move and check Cases and Counts.
BoJ policy decision.simple: The Bank of Japan sets Japan's interest rates. Japan's rates matter worldwide because many traders borrow cheaply in yen to invest elsewhere.

Bollinger squeeze (narrowest 10% of the.example: Like a pressure cooker sitting silent before the whistle. If NIFTY's bands shrink from 1,200 points wide to just 500 points wide, that is a squeeze.
Bollinger squeeze (narrowest 10% of the.forYou: As a seller, quiet markets pay thin premium and can break out, so do not sell closer strikes just because recent moves were small.
Bollinger squeeze (narrowest 10% of the.goodBad: Neither; calm now, but calm does not last forever.
Bollinger squeeze (narrowest 10% of the.impact: If this turns on: price has coiled into a very tight range. If it turns off: the bands are widening again, often because a bigger move has started.
Bollinger squeeze (narrowest 10% of the.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY is calmer than almost any time in the last year. The table shows how long squeezes lasted and whether moves after them were larger than normal.
Bollinger squeeze (narrowest 10% of the.simple: Bollinger bands sit 2 standard deviations above and below NIFTY's 20-day average. A squeeze means the gap between the bands is in its narrowest 10% of the past year. The market has gone unusually quiet.

Book cap.example: Like a lift's weight limit: each person is fine, but too many together and the lift will not move.
Book cap.forYou: Close or shrink a trade before adding one when you are near the cap.
Book cap.impact: If the book's total goes up: you get close to the cap. If it goes down: there is room for another trade.
Book cap.readIt: When you see the book near its cap, the next trade will likely be blocked.
Book cap.simple: This is the most all open trades together may lose if gapped through. The default is 6 percent of capital. A new trade that would push the book past it is blocked.

Bootstrap.example: Like shuffling past weeks of auto fares to see the full spread of a month's cost. If this band is much wider than the other bands, history is warning the models are too calm.
Bootstrap.forYou: When the bootstrap band is far wider, trust it and keep short strikes further away.
Bootstrap.impact: If it is much wider than the others: real history has been rougher than the models say. If close to them: the models match history.
Bootstrap.readIt: When you see this band, compare it with the formula bands. It is usually the widest, and that is expected.
Bootstrap.simple: A range built by replaying real past NIFTY moves thousands of times. It uses blocks of 5 days in a row, because jumpy days come in bunches. No formula is assumed.

Bootstrap band.example: Like drawing random 5-ball overs from past matches to guess a total score. If the four model bands say plus or minus 300 and the bootstrap says 450, real history was rougher than the models.
Bootstrap band.forYou: As a seller, when this band is much wider, move strikes out or trade smaller.
Bootstrap band.impact: If it goes up versus the others: real history shows bigger moves than models expect. If it is close to them: models and history agree.
Bootstrap band.readIt: When you see this band, compare it with the four model bands. If it sits far outside them, trust history over the maths. Blocks of five keep wild weeks intact.
Bootstrap band.simple: A range made by reshuffling real past NIFTY days in blocks of five, 20,000 times. No formula is used. It is usually the widest of the five bands.

Breached.example: Like a cricket bowler who is expected to give a few boundaries. A band that never breaches is too wide.
Breached.forYou: If breaches run above the promise, widen your short strikes.
Breached.impact: If it goes up beyond the promise: bands are too narrow and strikes are riskier. If it is near the promise: bands are honest.
Breached.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with what the band promises. Too many breaches means the band is too narrow.
Breached.simple: Sessions where the outcome fell outside the stated band. Some breaches are expected. A 68% band should fail about three times in ten.
