Breakeven.example: Like a stall's breakeven sale count: sell 50 cups and you cover costs; more is profit. Trading: sold 24,000 put for 60 points, breakeven 23,940.
Breakeven.forYou: Remember costs push the true breakeven a little further out.
Breakeven.impact: If NIFTY ends beyond a breakeven: you lose. If inside: you keep part or all of the credit.
Breakeven.readIt: When you see breakevens, compare them with the expected range.
Breakeven.simple: The breakeven is where a trade neither makes nor loses money at expiry. For sellers it is the sold put minus credit below and sold call plus credit above. Between them you keep money.

Breakevens.example: Like a shopkeeper who can absorb a Rs 50 discount before he starts losing. If you sell the 24,500 put for 60 points, breakeven is 24,440.
Breakevens.forYou: Watch NIFTY against these breakevens, not just the strikes.
Breakevens.impact: If the credit goes up: breakevens move further out, more cushion. If it goes down: less cushion.
Breakevens.readIt: When you see these numbers, compare them with the range bands. Touching a strike is not yet a loss.
Breakevens.simple: The prices where the trade stops making money at expiry. For the put side it is the short strike minus the credit. For the call side it is the short strike plus the credit.

Brent.example: Like two mandis selling the same onion at slightly different prices. If Brent is $80 and WTI is $76, a Brent headline overstates what MCX crude did.
Brent.forYou: Use Brent to judge India's economy, but use WTI to judge your MCX crude position.
Brent.impact: If it goes up: India's oil bill rises, which can hurt the rupee and NIFTY. If it goes down: India's costs ease.
Brent.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with WTI. When the two disagree, a news headline about oil may mislead you.
Brent.simple: Brent is the world's main crude oil price, from the North Sea, in dollars. India's import bill follows Brent. MCX crude follows WTI instead, so the two can differ.

Brent crude.example: Like the national average rate that many cities follow. If Brent rises from 80 to 88 dollars, that is a 10% jump in the cost of a barrel.
Brent crude.forYou: As a seller of MCX crude options, read it with WTI. If both are crowded the same way, a sharp reversal is more likely.
Brent crude.goodBad: Neither. It is a market, not a score.
Brent crude.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish on global oil. If it goes down: they are cutting longs or adding shorts on global oil.
Brent crude.readIt: When you see this row, compare it with WTI. When both show funds buying, the oil view is broad, not just a US story.
Brent crude.simple: The world's main crude oil benchmark, from the North Sea, traded on ICE in London in lots of 1,000 barrels. Much of the world's oil, including much of what India imports, is priced against it.

Brent&ndash;WTI spread.example: Like two bus routes to the same place with different fares. If Brent is $80 and WTI $75, the spread is $5.
Brent&ndash;WTI spread.forYou: When trading MCX crude, judge moves by WTI, and use this spread to discount Brent headlines.
Brent&ndash;WTI spread.impact: If it goes up: Brent news exaggerates what MCX crude is doing. If it goes down: the two crudes move more alike.
Brent&ndash;WTI spread.readIt: When you see this number, check its rank over the past year. A wide spread means Brent news overstates the move in your MCX crude.
Brent&ndash;WTI spread.simple: Brent's price minus WTI's price, in dollars a barrel. MCX crude follows WTI, so this gap is what a Brent headline does not tell you. It does not vote.

Brier score.example: Like a weatherman who said 90% rain but it stayed dry: he loses many points. One who said 60% loses fewer.
Brier score.forYou: Trust a probability on the page more when its Brier score is well below 0.25.
Brier score.goodBad: Lower is better; 0 is perfect and 0.25 is coin-flip level.
Brier score.impact: If it goes up: the forecasts are less accurate. If it goes down: forecasts are better.
Brier score.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with 0.25. Lower is better.
Brier score.simple: Measures how close stated chances were to what happened. Zero is perfect. Saying 50% to everything scores 0.25.

Brier skill.example: Like a new coach who must win more than the old team's normal 60%. Skill 0.1 means a bit better; -0.1 means worse.
Brier skill.forYou: Ignore a forecast whose skill is zero or negative.
Brier skill.goodBad: Above 0 is good; below 0 means the forecast added nothing.
Brier skill.impact: If it goes up above zero: forecasts add real information. If it goes below zero: the simple base rate did better.
Brier skill.readIt: When you see this number, check its sign first.
Brier skill.simple: Compares the desk's Brier score with simply quoting the usual historical rate. Above zero means the desk beat that simple answer. Below zero means it did worse.

Brokerage.example: Like an auto driver's fixed fare per trip, whether the trip is short or long.
Brokerage.forYou: On small credits, Rs 20 per order is a big share, so avoid needless orders.
Brokerage.goodBad: Rs 20 per order; the biggest cost in the worked example.
Brokerage.impact: If you add legs or close early: brokerage grows. If you hold to expiry: you skip exit orders.
Brokerage.readIt: When you see brokerage, count orders. It is the largest part of costs on a small condor.
Brokerage.simple: The fee your broker charges per order, Rs 20 here. A four-leg condor opened and closed is 8 orders, so Rs 160.

Build-up (the four quadrants).example: At the mandi, more crates arriving with prices falling means sellers are piling in. If the NIFTY 25,500 call's premium falls while OI rises, writers are building a wall there.
Build-up (the four quadrants).forYou: As a seller, short covering near your strike is an early warning to act.
Build-up (the four quadrants).impact: If short build-up grows near your strike: more writers defend it, which helps you. If short covering appears there: the wall is going away, and price may break through.
Build-up (the four quadrants).readIt: When you see the action label, focus on the walls and strikes near yours. Short build-up above spot creates resistance. Short covering at that strike means the defence is failing.
Build-up (the four quadrants).simple: Price and open interest moving together show if positions are opening or closing. Price up with OI up is long build-up. Price down with OI up is short build-up. Price up with OI down is short covering; both down is long unwinding.

Builder vs best scanner row.example: Like comparing your home-cooked dal with the best restaurant dal on taste, price and time.
Builder vs best scanner row.forYou: It stops you from trading a weaker idea just because it is yours.
Builder vs best scanner row.impact: If your build's EV per risk rises above the scanner's: your idea is better on the desk's numbers. If it stays lower: use the scanner row or skip.
Builder vs best scanner row.readIt: When you see this table, check EV per risk first. If yours is lower, the scanner has a better use of the same risk.
Builder vs best scanner row.simple: Your built position next to the best-ranked scanner trade on the same expiry, measure by measure. It shows if your idea beats the scanner's best.

Buy or sell today.example: Like an umbrella seller who sells only when his price beats the usual rain cost by 10%. If implied is 13% and forecast 11%, the ratio is 1.18, so selling is allowed.
Buy or sell today.forYou: Follow the rule's answer, and treat standing aside as a real decision, not a missed chance.
Buy or sell today.goodBad: The ratio must be at least 1.10 for a sell; below that the rule does not sell.
Buy or sell today.impact: If the ratio rises above 1.10 with no measured event: the rule says sell. If it falls below 1.10 and no tested buy reason exists: it says stand aside.
Buy or sell today.readIt: When you see this, read the ratio against 1.10 and the count of events and buy reasons. Buying needs a reason that has paid buyers in at least 10 past expiries.
Buy or sell today.simple: A written rule that says sell options, buy them, or do nothing this expiry. Selling needs implied volatility at least 1.10 times the forecast of real moves. It also needs no event before expiry that has truly moved NIFTY.

By VIX regime.example: Like an umbrella seller's profit split by how cloudy it was when he stocked up.
By VIX regime.forYou: It tells you in which kind of market your rules make or lose money.
By VIX regime.goodBad: Buckets: under 12, 12-16, 16-20, 20-30, 30 and up. Small buckets swing a lot.
By VIX regime.impact: If a bucket loses with many trades: avoid selling in that regime. If it has few trades: wait for more data.
By VIX regime.readIt: When you see this table, check which VIX bucket loses. Note how many trades each bucket has.
By VIX regime.simple: Expectancy and win rate split by India VIX on the day each trade opened. India VIX is the market's fear gauge. Sellers usually earn most when VIX is high and lose most when a low VIX jumps.

By vol regime.example: An umbrella seller earns most in the rainy season. This checks whether that is true for him.
By vol regime.forYou: Use it to judge whether waiting for rich premium has paid in this commodity.
By vol regime.goodBad: Better results in high vol support the seller's rule; no difference means vol level did not matter.
By vol regime.impact: If high-vol trades earn more: waiting for high vol helps. If not: the vol filter adds little.
By vol regime.readIt: When you see this table, compare expectancy across low, middle and high. Small buckets swing a lot.
By vol regime.simple: Results split by whether implied volatility was low, middle or high when the trade opened. Sellers usually do best when it is high. This checks if the commodity agrees.

CAGR.example: If Rs 10 lakh became Rs 11 lakh in about 6.8 years, the CAGR is about 1.5% a year.
CAGR.forYou: These rules, at a 2% risk cap, grew money slower than a bank deposit on the model's prices.
CAGR.goodBad: Higher is better; compare with a safe deposit rate.
CAGR.impact: If CAGR rises: money grows faster. If it falls below zero: money shrinks.
CAGR.readIt: When you see CAGR, compare it with a bank deposit. Recommended rule: about 1.5% a year since 2020; current rules about 0.7%.
CAGR.simple: CAGR is compound annual growth rate. It is the steady yearly growth that turns start money into end money. It counts profits being reinvested.

CE IV.example: Like a price tag that shows how worried buyers are about a rise.
CE IV.forYou: Compare call and put IV to see which side the market fears.
CE IV.impact: If it goes up: calls are dearer. If it goes down: calls are cheaper.
CE IV.readIt: When you see it, compare with put IV at the same distance.
CE IV.simple: This is the implied volatility of the call, the fear level in its price. It is shown on out-of-the-money strikes, those above NIFTY.

CE OI (L).example: Like a crowd of shopkeepers all promising the same price ceiling.
CE OI (L).forYou: Use it as context, not as a forecast.
CE OI (L).impact: If it goes up: more sellers at that level. If it goes down: they are leaving.
CE OI (L).readIt: When you see a big number, many call sellers sit at that strike.
CE OI (L).simple: CE means call option. OI means open interest, the number of contracts still open. This is call open interest at that strike, in lakh shares. Large call OI marks where sellers are committed.

CE and PE.example: A call is like booking a cinema seat at today's price; a put is like insurance on your scooter. If you sell the NIFTY 25,500 CE, you lose if NIFTY rises above 25,500.
CE and PE.forYou: As a seller, you write both sides, and the put side is where damage usually arrives fastest.
CE and PE.impact: If NIFTY goes up: calls get pricier, hurting short calls. If NIFTY goes down: puts get pricier, hurting short puts, and falls tend to be faster.
CE and PE.readIt: When you see the chain, read both sides together. Short calls lose when NIFTY rises through the strike. Short puts lose when it falls through.
CE and PE.simple: CE is a call: the right to buy at the strike. PE is a put: the right to sell at the strike. Every contract has a buyer who paid and a writer who got paid.

CE price.example: Like the closing rate of a vegetable on that day.
CE price.impact: If it goes up after you sell: you lose. If it goes down: you gain.
CE price.readIt: When you see it, remember your fill will be a little worse.
CE price.simple: This is the call's price at that day's close. It is its last trade if it traded, else NSE's settlement price. Fills add or subtract slippage.

CFTC positioning.example: Like a weekly class attendance sheet handed in a few days late. It does not cover the rupee spot market at all.
CFTC positioning.forYou: Use it for background on world markets, not for timing NIFTY trades.
CFTC positioning.impact: If positions shift a lot: big groups changed their lean last week. If unchanged: no new lean is shown.
CFTC positioning.readIt: When you see this table, check the observation date. A blank row means no data, not zero.
CFTC positioning.simple: Selected official US reports of futures positions by trader groups. They show Tuesday positions, usually released Friday. They are delayed and do not cover every market.

CFTC trader category.example: Like a school reporting marks by section, not by student name. Managed Money net long 50,000 means that group as a whole is long.
CFTC trader category.forYou: Use categories for background on world futures, not for NIFTY trades directly.
CFTC trader category.impact: If the group's net rises: the group became more long. If it falls: it became less long or more short.
CFTC trader category.readIt: When you see a category, remember it is a group total. A Producer position may be a hedge, but the report does not prove it.
CFTC trader category.simple: A group the US regulator, the CFTC, uses to bundle reported futures traders. Examples are Asset Manager or Managed Money. It shows the group's total, not any one trader or their reason.

CFTC trader groups.example: At a grain mandi, the farmer selling ahead to lock a price is the producer. A trader buying for profit is like a fund. Every sale needs a buyer, so when one group buys, another sells.
CFTC trader groups.forYou: Know that a big producer short is normal hedging, not a bearish bet.
CFTC trader groups.goodBad: No group's size is good or bad alone; watch how it changes against its usual role.
CFTC trader groups.impact: If producers sell more: miners are locking in prices, often near highs. If funds buy more: someone else, usually producers or banks, is selling to them.
CFTC trader groups.readIt: When you see the groups, look for who sits opposite the funds. A strongly negative correlation with funds marks the usual other side. Producers are usually net short because they hedge.
CFTC trader groups.simple: The CFTC sorts big futures traders into four groups. Producers and merchants are miners and users who protect their business. Swap dealers are banks; managed money is funds; the rest are other big traders.

COT index.example: If a family's monthly gold buying over three years ranged from 0 to 100 grams, buying 80 grams now scores 80. That is high for this family, even if another family buys far more.
COT index.forYou: Read an extreme as a crowding warning, not a timing signal; crowds can stay crowded for months.
COT index.goodBad: Near 100 risks a sharp drop if the story changes; near 0 risks a sharp bounce.
COT index.impact: If it goes up: funds are more crowded long, so fewer new buyers are left. If it goes down: funds are more bearish, so there is room for buying later.
COT index.readIt: When you see this number, above 80 means crowded long and below 20 means washed out. Middle values say little. Then check the forward-return table to see what followed such readings before.
COT index.simple: It shows where the funds' net bet sits inside its own three-year range. The scale runs from 0 to 100. 100 is the most bullish in three years; 0 is the most bearish.

COT trader group.example: A refinery that sells diesel ahead to lock its price is a hedger. A fund buying crude for profit is a speculator. One's sale is the other's purchase.
COT trader group.forYou: Know who takes the other side before calling a fund move bullish or bearish.
COT trader group.goodBad: No level is good or bad on its own; changes against the usual pattern matter.
COT trader group.impact: If one group adds net longs: other groups must have reduced theirs. If producers sell more: they are locking prices, often after a rally.
COT trader group.readIt: When you see this table, read net and net as share of open interest. Producers are usually net short. All group nets add up to zero.
COT trader group.simple: The Commitments of Traders (COT) report sorts big traders by their main business. Oil companies and refiners hedge; banks are swap dealers; funds are managed money. Small traders are non-reportable.

CVaR 99 per trade.example: Out of 100 monsoons, take the single worst flood and measure its damage. That average worst damage is CVaR 99.
CVaR 99 per trade.forYou: This is the loss you must be able to take calmly, several times in a career.
CVaR 99 per trade.goodBad: Closer to zero is better. CVaR 95 is the same idea using the worst 5%.
CVaR 99 per trade.impact: If it grows more negative: one bad trade can erase many good ones. If it moves toward zero: the tail is thinner.
CVaR 99 per trade.readIt: When you see CVaR 99, compare it with your typical win. For the current rules it is about minus Rs 11,800 per lot, against a typical win near Rs 1,700.
CVaR 99 per trade.simple: CVaR means conditional value at risk. It is the average of the worst 1% of trades. It tells you how much a really bad trade costs, not just where bad starts.

CVaR-adjusted return.example: Like comparing two jobs by pay per risk of injury. A safe job that pays a little can beat a risky one.
CVaR-adjusted return.forYou: A negative number means you are taking crash risk without being paid for it.
CVaR-adjusted return.goodBad: Above zero is needed; negative means losing on average under these models.
CVaR-adjusted return.impact: If it rises above zero: the rule pays for its tail risk. If it is below zero: you carry a tail and lose on average too.
CVaR-adjusted return.readIt: When you see this, check the sign first. The current rules show about minus 0.03: a small loss for a big tail.
CVaR-adjusted return.simple: Expectancy divided by the size of the worst 1% loss. It says how much a trade earns for each rupee of bad-day loss it carries.

Calib. error.example: Like a friend who says he is 80% sure of 10 things: 8 should come true. If only 6 do, he is overconfident.
Calib. error.forYou: Discount the desk's percentages when this error is large.
Calib. error.goodBad: Lower is better; near 0 means honest probabilities.
Calib. error.impact: If it goes up: stated chances are less honest. If it goes down: they match reality better.
Calib. error.readIt: When you see this number, smaller is better. It is in percentage points.
Calib. error.simple: Checks whether the desk's stated chances come true that often. For example, does an 80% call happen 80% of the time? It is the average gap, weighted by how many calls were made.

Calibrated.example: Like a forecaster whose rain calls and temperature ranges both hold up over a month.
Calibrated.forYou: Earn it with honest forecasts, not cautious ones.
Calibrated.impact: If both reach target: you earn it. If either slips: you can lose it.
Calibrated.readIt: When you see where you are, check both the Brier score and the range hit rate.
Calibrated.simple: This badge needs a Brier score of 0.20 or lower over at least 10 profit forecasts. Your 80 percent ranges must also be right 65 to 95 percent of the time, over at least 10.

Calibration (Brier).example: Like a weather forecaster: if she says 70 percent rain, it should rain on about 7 of 10 such days.
Calibration (Brier).forYou: Write a real confidence on every trade so this has data.
Calibration (Brier).goodBad: Lower than the reference bar shows real skill. Higher means guessing your win rate would do better.
Calibration (Brier).impact: If it goes down: your confidence fits reality better. If it goes up: you are more over- or under-confident.
Calibration (Brier).readIt: When you see this score, lower is better; compare it with the guess-your-win-rate bar shown beside it.
Calibration (Brier).simple: Calibration means your stated confidence matches what really happens. The Brier score measures this. Zero is perfect. The bar to beat is always guessing your own win rate.

Calibration (ECE).example: A weather app says 80% chance of rain on 10 days, and it rains on only 6. It is overconfident. If the desk says a NIFTY range holds 80% but it holds 65%, every trade is sized too big.
Calibration (ECE).forYou: As a seller, you size trades from stated probabilities, so an overconfident desk quietly makes every trade too big.
Calibration (ECE).goodBad: Low ECE means honest confidence; high ECE means the stated chances cannot be trusted as written.
Calibration (ECE).impact: If it goes up: the stated probabilities are less honest, and your trade sizes may be too large. If it goes down: the probabilities can be trusted more for sizing.
Calibration (ECE).readIt: When you see this number, smaller is better; a low ECE means stated chances match reality. Check whether the misses are mostly overconfident. If so, the calibration haircut should shrink the probabilities.
Calibration (ECE).simple: It checks if the desk's confidence is honest. When it says 70%, does it happen about 70% of the time? ECE (expected calibration error) is the average gap between said and real.

Calibration Brier.example: Like a weather forecaster's error score: saying 90 percent and being wrong costs more than saying 60 percent and being wrong.
Calibration Brier.forYou: Write an honest chance on every replay.
Calibration Brier.goodBad: Lower is better; near 0.25 or above means no better than saying 50 percent.
Calibration Brier.impact: If it goes down: your sense of odds improves. If it goes up: you are more overconfident or underconfident.
Calibration Brier.readIt: When you see a value, compare it with 0.25; under 0.20 over 10 forecasts helps earn the Calibrated badge.
Calibration Brier.simple: This scores your chance-of-profit forecasts. It is the average squared gap between your chance and what happened, 1 for profit, 0 for loss. Zero is perfect, 0.25 is always saying 50 percent. Lower is better.

Calibration trainer.example: Like a weather forecaster saying 70 percent rain today and checking tomorrow if it rained.
Calibration trainer.forYou: Lock a forecast every day; under 100 forecasts the score is mostly noise.
Calibration trainer.impact: If your score improves: your sense of odds is getting sharper. If it worsens: you may be overconfident.
Calibration trainer.readIt: When you see the lock button, decide your number before looking at anything else.
Calibration trainer.simple: This asks a few market questions each day. You lock a probability before the next session opens. Then the desk's number and the base rate are shown. Later closes score your answer automatically.

Call OI.example: Like counting how many rented bicycles are still out at night, not how many rides happened. If call OI is 120 lakh, that many call contracts are open.
Call OI.forYou: Look at which strikes hold the most call OI to find the call wall.
Call OI.impact: If it goes up: more call positions are being opened, often by sellers capping the upside. If it goes down: call positions are closing.
Call OI.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with put OI and check where it is piled up by strike.
Call OI.simple: The total number of call contracts still open across all strikes. It counts positions that stayed open, not trades made today. It is shown in lakhs.

Call wall.example: Like a strong boundary wall that rarely gets climbed. If the call wall is 25,500 and NIFTY is 25,000, it acts as a ceiling.
Call wall.forYou: Consider selling calls at or beyond the call wall, not below it.
Call wall.impact: If the call wall moves up: the ceiling rises and there is more room above. If it moves down: the ceiling is closer.
Call wall.readIt: When you see this strike, note how far it is from the price. It is the desk's strongest graded claim.
Call wall.simple: The strike with the most call contracts open. Call sellers lose money above it, so they defend it. The desk found it held on 92.9% of graded sessions.

Call wall holds.example: Like a goalkeeper who says no ball will cross the line this match. After the match you check if he was right. Over many matches you learn how often he keeps his word.
Call wall holds.forYou: As a seller, a call wall that usually holds is a sensible place to keep your short calls beyond, never a guarantee.
Call wall holds.goodBad: Higher is better, but only if it beats the same-distance baseline on the Track record tab.
Call wall holds.impact: If the hit rate goes up: the call wall has been a more reliable ceiling. If it goes down: rallies have been breaking through it more often.
Call wall holds.readIt: When you see this claim's hit rate, compare it with how often any level that far away would hold. Only a clearly higher rate means the wall really helps.
Call wall holds.simple: Each day the desk writes down that NIFTY will not close above the call wall by expiry. The call wall is the call strike where sellers hold the most contracts. Later it checks if that came true.

Call wall test.example: Like checking if a famous wall stops floods better than any wall of the same height.
Call wall test.forYou: Do not sell calls just above the call wall thinking it is extra safe.
Call wall test.impact: If the call wall beat the baseline: it would be a useful ceiling. Since it did not: it is just a level.
Call wall test.readIt: When you see this test, compare hold rates. Call wall held 78% of 67 expiries; any level held 83%; p = 0.94.
Call wall test.simple: Did NIFTY close below the strike with the most call open interest on every session until expiry? It is compared with any level the same number of sigma above spot.

Carry.example: Like booking a train ticket a month ahead and paying a small booking fee for the wait. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the one-month future is 25,150, carry is about 0.6% for the month, roughly 7% a year.
Carry.forYou: Use carry to spot mood: a sudden drop in carry while NIFTY is flat often means quiet selling pressure, so keep short puts a bit further away.
Carry.goodBad: Near the interest rate is normal; far above or below it is a signal worth checking.
Carry.impact: If it goes up: traders are paying more to hold long positions, usually a sign of bullish demand. If it goes down (or turns negative): the future is cheap, often because traders expect a fall or a dividend is coming.
Carry.readIt: When you see carry, compare it with the bank interest rate (about 6 to 7% a year). Close to that rate is normal.
Carry.simple: How much extra a future costs compared with the index today, turned into a yearly percentage. It is mostly the interest you save by buying later instead of paying now. The desk hides it when a contract has no open interest, because then the price is not real.

Case study: crude below zero.example: Like a godown so full that the owner pays people to take goods away.
Case study: crude below zero.forYou: Use defined-risk spreads in crude and exit before expiry.
Case study: crude below zero.impact: If you hold short puts to expiry without protection: losses can be unlimited in practice. If protected: loss is capped.
Case study: crude below zero.readIt: When you see this case, compare the capped condor loss with the huge naked put loss.
Case study: crude below zero.simple: On 20 April 2020, US May crude settled at minus 37.63 dollars. MCX April crude settled at minus Rs 2,884. It shows the seller's maths for a turned-into-futures put and a condor.

Case study: gold 2013 and silver 2011.example: Like reviewing a past flood to see how much damage your house would suffer.
Case study: gold 2013 and silver 2011.forYou: Size gold and silver trades so a repeat crash does not wipe you out.
Case study: gold 2013 and silver 2011.impact: If a crash repeats: one lot can take a big bite of a small account. If you size small: the damage stays survivable.
Case study: gold 2013 and silver 2011.readIt: When you see this table, look at the worst per lot and worst on Rs 5 lakh.
Case study: gold 2013 and silver 2011.simple: Two metal crashes replayed on real prices for the baseline condor. It shows losing share, the worst loss per lot, and the worst on Rs 5 lakh.

Chance of a 30% drawdown.example: If 8 out of 100 farmers using a method lost a third of their savings, that method is risky.
Chance of a 30% drawdown.forYou: At the current size this is above the desk's own limit, a reason to size down.
Chance of a 30% drawdown.goodBad: Under 5% passes; the current rules are about 8% at the current size.
Chance of a 30% drawdown.impact: If it rises: your size is too big for the rule's tail. If it falls under 5%: the size passes the desk's test.
Chance of a 30% drawdown.readIt: When you see this, compare with 5%. At the current size the current rules show about 8%, above the line.
Chance of a 30% drawdown.simple: The share of simulated two-year paths where the account fell 30% or more from a high. The desk's sizing keeps this under 5%.

Change in OI.example: Like counting how many new umbrella orders came in today, and how many were cancelled. If the NIFTY 25,500 call added 20 lakh OI today, that level was built up.
Change in OI.forYou: As a seller, check it daily near your strikes to spot a wall fading before it breaks.
Change in OI.goodBad: Rising OI at your nearby wall is supportive; falling OI there is a warning.
Change in OI.impact: If it goes up at a strike: the level is being built, so it may hold better. If it goes down: writers are leaving, and the level may break.
Change in OI.readIt: When you see this, read it with the price change at that strike. A wall that grew is stronger. A wall that shrank while premium rose is being abandoned.
Change in OI.simple: How much open interest at a strike grew or shrank today. Positive means new positions opened. Negative means positions closed.

Channel into India.example: Like a recipe: wheat prices matter because food is a big part of your monthly kitchen bill. Food is about 46% of India's price index.
Channel into India.forYou: Use channels to understand why a world move might reach NIFTY before you adjust strikes.
Channel into India.impact: If a channel stays valid: its driver deserves weight. If the link breaks: ignore that driver's push.
Channel into India.readIt: When you see a channel, ask if the reason makes sense to you. If not, do not trust that driver's contribution.
Channel into India.simple: The written reason a world market affects India. For example, crude matters because India imports most of its oil. It is written out so you can disagree with it.

Check yourself.example: Like a short quiz at the end of a school chapter.
Check yourself.forYou: Use it to test whether you understood the lesson.
Check yourself.impact: Nothing moves up or down. As data changes, the questions change too.
Check yourself.readIt: When you see the questions, answer all correctly to mark the lesson done.
Check yourself.simple: Graded questions built from today's commodity numbers. Your answers stay in this browser.

Checked.example: Like news marked confirmed, partly confirmed or rumour.
Checked.forYou: Always confirm on the exchange before relying on any row.
Checked.impact: If a row moves to verified: you can trust it more. If it stays unverified: treat it with care.
Checked.readIt: When you see partial or unverified, check the exchange before acting.
Checked.simple: This shows how well a rule-change row was confirmed. Verified means the official SEBI or NSE document says it. Partial means a detail rests on another source. Unverified means only news or snippets.

Checklist item.example: Like ticking boxes on a safety checklist before using a gas cylinder.
Checklist item.forYou: Aim for all five every time.
Checklist item.impact: If more items pass: your process score rises. If fewer: it falls.
Checklist item.readIt: When you see an unticked item, it costs a process point.
Checklist item.simple: This is one of five process points. They are plan, defined risk, budget, right conditions, and exit as planned. Each one kept adds one point to your process score.

China NBS PMI.example: Like asking shop owners in a market whether business is better or worse than last month. It often lands on a weekend, so NIFTY reacts on the next open.
China NBS PMI.forYou: As a seller, an event that counts and falls before your expiry makes the side rule stand aside.
China NBS PMI.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: China's factory news has been moving NIFTY more. If it goes down: NIFTY has been ignoring it.
China NBS PMI.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with an ordinary day's move and check whether Counts says yes.
China NBS PMI.simple: This is China's official monthly survey of factory managers, released on the last day of each month. Above 50 means factories are growing, below 50 means shrinking.

Claims.example: Like writing your match prediction in a notebook before the toss, then marking it after. NIFTY range claims score high; direction claims score near 50%.
Claims.forYou: As a seller, trust only the parts of the desk that have a graded record.
Claims.goodBad: A high hit rate means a claim you can lean on; near 50% means a coin flip.
Claims.impact: If a claim's hit rate goes up: it deserves more trust. If it goes down: rely on it less and find what broke.
Claims.readIt: When you see the claims table, read each row's hit rate. Trust the high scorers like ranges and walls. The best and worst claims differ by nearly 50 points.
Claims.simple: Every prediction the desk makes is written down on the day. Later, each one is scored right or wrong. Each type is scored separately, so you see what works.

Classic pivots.example: Like everyone agreeing to meet at the big clock tower, just because everyone knows it. If NIFTY's pivot is 25,000 and R1 is 25,150, many traders place orders near 25,150.
Classic pivots.forYou: As a seller, trust OI walls over pivots, because walls have money committed behind them.
Classic pivots.impact: If price breaks above R1 or below S1: some traders react, so moves can speed up briefly. If price stays between: the crowd sees a normal day.
Classic pivots.readIt: When you see pivots, check if one lines up with an OI wall. If it does, respect that level. If not, it is just arithmetic with no money behind it.
Classic pivots.simple: Support and resistance levels made from yesterday's high, low and close. The pivot is their average; R1 to R3 sit above and S1 to S3 below. They only work because many people watch them.

Clean.example: Like a day when every answer in your test was right. If 60 of 100 sessions were clean, the desk was fully right 60% of the time.
Clean.forYou: Use it as an overall honesty check on the desk, not for a single trade.
Clean.impact: If it goes up: more sessions had every claim right. If it goes down: more sessions had at least one miss.
Clean.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the scored count.
Clean.simple: Sessions where every graded claim was correct. It is a strict measure. One wrong claim makes the session not clean.

Close.example: Like the final score of a cricket match, not the score at tea. If NIFTY closed at 25,000, that is the number used for all calculations.
Close.forYou: Measure your short strikes' distance from this official close.
Close.impact: If it goes up: every band shifts up with it. If it goes down: every band shifts down.
Close.readIt: When you see this number, use it as the base for every range and strike distance.
Close.simple: The final settled price of NIFTY for the day. The desk takes it from the exchange's official closing file, not the live feed. A live price during the day is just a tick.

Close &minus; low.example: Like a kite that dipped low but was pulled back up high. If the low was 24,900 and close 25,050, this is 150.
Close &minus; low.forYou: A close near the high means calls deserve more care the next day.
Close &minus; low.impact: If it goes up: buyers had control at the close. If it goes down: the close was near the low, sellers in control.
Close &minus; low.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with high minus close. If this is larger, the day closed near its high.
Close &minus; low.simple: How far the close is above the day's low. A big number means buyers lifted the price off the bottom. It and high minus close together make the day's range.

Close &minus; open.example: Like a cricket team's runs in the second innings only. If NIFTY opened 25,150 and closed 25,050, this is -100.
Close &minus; open.forYou: If gaps keep fading during the day, they may not threaten your strikes much.
Close &minus; open.impact: If it goes up: Indian traders pushed prices higher during the day. If it goes down: they pushed lower.
Close &minus; open.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the overnight gap. Same sign means conviction; opposite sign means the gap faded.
Close &minus; open.simple: The close minus the open. It is the move during Indian trading hours only, with the overnight gap removed. It shows whether India itself pushed the price.

Close in journal.example: Like writing in a match diary after the game: score, how you got out, and how you felt.
Close in journal.forYou: Fill it for every close, winners and losers alike.
Close in journal.impact: If you fill it honestly: your metrics show your real habits. If you skip it: the discipline numbers go wrong.
Close in journal.readIt: When you see this form, fill it right after closing, while the memory is fresh.
Close in journal.simple: This records how a trade ended. You enter why, the profit or loss, costs and how you felt. The exit is then marked per plan or not.

Combined POP.example: Like the chance that it neither floods nor droughts this season. If calls fail 10% and puts 15%, combined POP is 75%.
Combined POP.forYou: Do not chase a high POP alone; check the loss size too.
Combined POP.impact: If it goes up: the trade wins more often, usually with less premium. If it goes down: it wins less often.
Combined POP.readIt: When you see this number, also check expected shortfall. A high POP can hide a big loss.
Combined POP.simple: The model's chance that both short legs of a trade expire worthless. Worthless means the seller keeps all the premium. It is 1 minus the chance of each side being crossed.

Commodity HAR forecast.example: To guess next week's onion price swings, you look at yesterday, last week and last month. Recent days count, but so does the longer picture.
Commodity HAR forecast.forYou: This is the yardstick the desk uses to judge whether option premium is worth selling.
Commodity HAR forecast.goodBad: High means big moves are expected; low means a quiet market is expected.
Commodity HAR forecast.impact: If it goes up: the expected range widens and selling looks less attractive. If it goes down: the range narrows and selling edge can improve.
Commodity HAR forecast.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with implied vol. Where no implied vol exists, this number sets the expected range.
Commodity HAR forecast.simple: A forecast of how much the price will really move. It mixes recent daily, weekly and monthly moves. The weights come from this commodity's own history.

Commodity IV rank.example: If tomatoes cost Rs 20 to Rs 100 this year and cost Rs 80 today, the rank is 75. That is pricey for tomatoes.
Commodity IV rank.forYou: Use it as background only, because the side rule still compares implied with the forecast.
Commodity IV rank.goodBad: High rank means rich premium; low rank means cheap premium.
Commodity IV rank.impact: If it goes up: premium is richer than usual. If it goes down: premium is cheaper than usual.
Commodity IV rank.readIt: When you see this number, above 70 means premium is rich against history. Below 30 means cheap. Percentile is usually more useful than rank.
Commodity IV rank.simple: It shows where today's implied volatility sits in its own past year. 0 is the year's low and 100 the year's high. Percentile is the share of past days below today.

Commodity MCX price.example: Gold in Mumbai costs more than gold in London times the rupee, because of import duty and a local premium. That gap is steady, so percent moves are the same.
Commodity MCX price.forYou: All your MCX strikes and ranges are measured from this number.
Commodity MCX price.goodBad: The level itself is neither good nor bad; what matters is how it moves against your strikes.
Commodity MCX price.impact: If it goes up: calls gain and puts lose value. If it goes down: puts gain and calls lose.
Commodity MCX price.readIt: When you see this price, know it is the underlying for every MCX option strike. Compare it with the world price times the rupee rate to see the local premium.
Commodity MCX price.simple: The settlement price of the nearest MCX futures contract, in rupees. MCX is India's commodity exchange. This is the price India trades.

Commodity VRP.example: An insurer charges Rs 120 for a risk he expects to cost Rs 100. The extra Rs 20 is his premium for surprises.
Commodity VRP.forYou: Without implied vol there is no VRP, so silver, copper and gas never pass this test.
Commodity VRP.goodBad: High is better for sellers; low or negative means selling is underpaid.
Commodity VRP.impact: If it goes up: sellers are paid more for risk. If it goes down: the edge for sellers shrinks.
Commodity VRP.readIt: When you see this ratio, the side rule sells only at 1.10 or more. Also compare it with the ratio against the last 21 sessions.
Commodity VRP.simple: VRP means volatility risk premium. It is implied volatility minus the volatility expected to follow. Positive is normal, as payment for rare big moves.

Commodity base rates.example: If prices rose after 6 of 10 big Diwali weeks, versus 5 of 10 normal weeks, the edge is small.
Commodity base rates.forYou: Do not read a base rate as a forecast for this week.
Commodity base rates.goodBad: A big gap with many episodes is meaningful; small gaps are noise.
Commodity base rates.impact: If the gap from any day grows: past moves like today's have had a lean. If the gap is small: there is no lean.
Commodity base rates.readIt: When you see this table, compare closed higher with on any day. Also read the episode count. With few dozen episodes, a 5-point gap is noise.
Commodity base rates.simple: It shows what happened after past 20-day moves as big as today's. How often did price close higher 5, 10 and 21 days later. It is set beside any day's share.

Commodity data preview.example: Like a sample plate at a sweet shop before the full box is packed.
Commodity data preview.impact: Nothing goes up or down here. When the engine loads, this preview disappears.
Commodity data preview.readIt: When you see this preview, treat it as a placeholder. The full cards will replace it.
Commodity data preview.simple: A temporary preview of commodity data cards. It shows only until the main engine places them on the page.

Commodity event calendar.example: Like a school calendar with exam dates marked, so you know which days are tense.
Commodity event calendar.forYou: Check this before opening any option that spans an event date.
Commodity event calendar.goodBad: Many events before expiry mean more jump risk; few mean a quieter window.
Commodity event calendar.impact: If a big event falls before expiry: risk of a jump rises. If none: fewer scheduled jumps.
Commodity event calendar.readIt: When you see this list, check the days away for your expiry. Dates derived from a rule are marked unverified.
Commodity event calendar.simple: Scheduled news that moves commodities. It includes EIA oil stocks, OPEC+ meetings, US Fed decisions, US inflation and jobs, and China factory data. OPEC+ is the oil producers' group.

Commodity events.example: If onion prices always jump on the day of the export policy news, that day is a real event. Other days with talk but no jump do not count.
Commodity events.forYou: Plan to close or halve before any measured event inside your option's life.
Commodity events.goodBad: A high event ratio means big event-day moves and more risk; near 1 means it hardly matters.
Commodity events.impact: If a measured event appears before expiry: the side call becomes stand aside. If none: selling is allowed if the vol rule passes.
Commodity events.readIt: When you see this list, look for events marked as moving the market. Those stop the desk from selling premium. Weekly inventory reports do not block.
Commodity events.simple: Scheduled news before expiry, and whether each has really moved this commodity before. An event counts if it has 8 or more past cases. Its median move must be at least 1.25 times a normal day.

Commodity evidence verdict.example: Like testing a recipe on new guests, not just on family who already liked it.
Commodity evidence verdict.forYou: Never trade a rule the verdict does not recommend, and remember premiums are estimates.
Commodity evidence verdict.goodBad: Recommended means it survived new years; not recommended means it did not.
Commodity evidence verdict.impact: If test-year results turn positive and pass the checks: the rule earns trust. If they fail: the rule is not recommended.
Commodity evidence verdict.readIt: When you see this verdict, check if the test years were positive. Then check the overfitting tests and the tail-safe size.
Commodity evidence verdict.simple: Whether a monthly option-selling rule kept earning in years the search never saw, from 2018 on. It also shows overfitting tests and safe size. Every premium is a model, as MCX chains are not stored.

Commodity exit plan.example: If you rent a godown, you plan to empty it before the lease ends, or you get stuck with the goods. Options are the same.
Commodity exit plan.forYou: Always exit before expiry day to avoid being turned into a futures or gold delivery position.
Commodity exit plan.goodBad: Hitting the target early is good; hitting the stop is a planned, limited loss.
Commodity exit plan.impact: If the trade earns half its credit: take it. If losses hit 1.5 times the credit: cut it.
Commodity exit plan.readIt: When you see the plan, note the profit target, the stop and the exit date. Credit spreads: buy back at half the credit, stop at 1.5 times credit lost.
Commodity exit plan.simple: It says when to take profit, when to cut a loss, and the date to be out. MCX options in the money at expiry turn into futures. So the plan never holds into the last session.

Commodity expected range.example: If gold is Rs 70,000 and the 1 sigma range is Rs 2,000, gold should usually end between Rs 68,000 and Rs 72,000.
Commodity expected range.forYou: Keep short strikes outside 1 sigma, and expect shocks to break it more than 32% of the time.
Commodity expected range.goodBad: A wide range means more risk; a narrow range means a calmer market expected.
Commodity expected range.impact: If volatility goes up: the range widens and short strikes inside it carry more risk. If it goes down: the range narrows.
Commodity expected range.readIt: When you see this range, compare it with the history band of real past moves. Commodities have fat tails, so the 2 sigma line matters.
Commodity expected range.simple: How far the MCX price can move by the next option expiry. One sigma covers about 68% of outcomes. Two sigma covers about 95%, if the volatility is right.

Commodity futures curve.example: Rice stored in a godown for a year costs rent and interest, so rice for next year is priced higher: contango. If rice is scarce today, today's rice costs more: backwardation.
Commodity futures curve.forYou: Each MCX option sits on one futures month, so check that month's price on the curve.
Commodity futures curve.goodBad: Mild contango is normal for stored metal; steep backwardation signals a tight, nervous market.
Commodity futures curve.impact: If the curve steepens upward: holding the commodity costs more, a sign of plenty. If it turns downward: buyers pay up for now, a sign of shortage.
Commodity futures curve.readIt: When you see the curve, check if it slopes up or down. Read the carry a year figure, the yearly cost of the slope. Then compare MCX months with the world curve.
Commodity futures curve.simple: It shows the futures prices for later months of the same commodity. If later months cost more, it is contango. If they cost less, it is backwardation.

Commodity implied vol.example: If a godown owner charges a high fee to insure onions, he expects big price swings. A high option price means the market expects big moves.
Commodity implied vol.forYou: Know that the MCX options you trade may be priced differently from this US-based number.
Commodity implied vol.goodBad: High means options are expensive and the market is nervous; low means calm and cheap options.
Commodity implied vol.impact: If it goes up: options cost more and sellers get paid more for more risk. If it goes down: options get cheaper.
Commodity implied vol.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the forecast of real moves. Remember it is not the MCX option chain. Every option price here is an estimate.
Commodity implied vol.simple: Implied volatility is the size of moves that option prices assume, as a yearly percent. For commodities it is free only for crude (OVX) and gold (GVZ). These are US indexes, converted into rupees.

Commodity implied vs realised.example: Like checking each weather forecast against the rain that actually fell.
Commodity implied vs realised.forYou: Check this before trusting that implied vol is too high in your commodity.
Commodity implied vs realised.goodBad: Well above 68% favours sellers; below it means moves often beat the forecast.
Commodity implied vs realised.impact: If the hit rate goes up: implied has been over-pricing moves, helping sellers. If it goes down: implied has been too low, hurting sellers.
Commodity implied vs realised.readIt: When you see inside 1 sigma, about 68% is fair. Higher means implied was usually generous. Check the average premium in vol points.
Commodity implied vs realised.simple: For each past day, it compares implied volatility with the move that followed in 21 sessions. It shows how often implied covered the move. It shows how often a seller was paid.

Commodity lesson.example: Like a closed notice on a classroom door.
Commodity lesson.forYou: Check back later when the data is updated.
Commodity lesson.impact: Nothing moves here. It disappears once the data loads.
Commodity lesson.readIt: When you see this, the data for the lesson is missing.
Commodity lesson.simple: A lesson that could not be built from current data. It shows instead of a broken page.

Commodity lessons.example: Like a short course with exercises using today's market.
Commodity lessons.forYou: Complete them to understand commodity options before trading.
Commodity lessons.impact: Nothing moves up or down. As data changes, the lesson numbers update.
Commodity lessons.readIt: When you see the lessons, go through them in order and answer the questions.
Commodity lessons.simple: Seven lessons on commodity options, built from today's data. Each has graded questions.

Commodity levels.example: If onions have not gone above Rs 40 or below Rs 30 this month, those are the ceiling and floor traders watch.
Commodity levels.forYou: Use these levels as your strike and trigger guide since MCX open interest walls are not available.
Commodity levels.goodBad: Levels close to price mean a trigger may come soon; far levels mean room to move.
Commodity levels.impact: If price breaks above resistance: the plan moves to its breakout branch. If it breaks below support: it moves to its breakdown branch.
Commodity levels.readIt: When you see these levels, read the distance in percent from today. Resistance 1 and Support 1 are nearest. The plan's branches trigger on them.
Commodity levels.simple: Resistance is a price where rises may stall. Support is where falls may stall. Here they come from the 20-day high and low and expected moves, rounded to strikes.

Commodity momentum readings.example: Like a cricket scorecard showing run rate, wickets and required rate together, these numbers describe today's price game.
Commodity momentum readings.forYou: These decide which side your spreads lean, so glance at them before picking strikes.
Commodity momentum readings.goodBad: Strong trend readings warn against selling on the trend's side; neutral readings suit two-sided selling.
Commodity momentum readings.impact: If the trend gets stronger: the plan sells spreads only on the side against the trend. If there is no trend: it sells both sides.
Commodity momentum readings.readIt: When you see these readings, check ADX first. Above 25 means a strong trend. Then check RSI for stretch.
Commodity momentum readings.simple: Today's values of textbook indicators. RSI and stochastic show momentum; ADX shows trend strength. Distance from averages and Bollinger %B show stretch.

Commodity option expiries.example: Like the use-by dates on milk packets in a fridge, each option has its own date. Gold futures expire every two months, but MCX lists monthly options in between, so there are no gaps.
Commodity option expiries.forYou: Choose your expiry from this ladder and check its likely range before placing strikes.
Commodity option expiries.goodBad: A wide range means big possible moves and more risk; a narrow range means a calm market expected.
Commodity option expiries.impact: If volatility goes up: every range on the ladder widens. If time to expiry shrinks: the range for that expiry narrows.
Commodity option expiries.readIt: When you see this ladder, pick the expiry you trade. Read its 1 sigma range, which covers about 68% of outcomes. Farther dates have wider ranges.
Commodity option expiries.simple: An expiry is the last day an option lives. This lists every coming MCX option expiry for the commodity. It also shows how far price could move by each date.

Commodity playbook.example: Like a farmer's plan: if rain comes early, sow paddy; if late, sow pulses. You decide each branch before the weather arrives.
Commodity playbook.forYou: Gold's big lot often risks more than Rs 20,000, so expect 0 lots and look at the mini contract.
Commodity playbook.goodBad: There is no high or low here; a clear plan for each branch is what matters.
Commodity playbook.impact: If price hits a trigger level: the plan's branch for that case applies. If the side call is stand aside: credit spreads are shown for reference, not as today's trade.
Commodity playbook.readIt: When you see the playbook, find today's starting position and each trigger level. Check the lots figure: Rs 20,000 divided by one lot's max loss. If it shows 0, use the mini contract figure.
Commodity playbook.simple: A plan for every session until expiry, not just one trade. It gives a starting position and steps if price stalls, breaks out, pulls back or breaks down. Premiums are estimates because MCX option chains are not free.

Commodity positioning link.example: Like checking the trader list for your own mandi, not the whole state.
Commodity positioning link.forYou: It describes crowding; it does not time trades.
Commodity positioning link.goodBad: Extreme z-scores mean crowding; near 0 is ordinary.
Commodity positioning link.impact: If the net goes up: funds lean more long. If it goes down: funds lean more short.
Commodity positioning link.readIt: When you see this number, read net as a share of open interest and its z-score. A z-score above 2 or below -2 means crowded.
Commodity positioning link.simple: This instrument's line from the weekly fund-positioning report. It shows what funds hold in the matching futures contract. Some markets have no free report.

Commodity reads.example: Like reading the weather forecast for a city you are not visiting: useful to know, but no action.
Commodity reads.forYou: Use it to understand markets you cannot trade through options.
Commodity reads.impact: If price crosses a level: the read changes branch. No trade follows from it.
Commodity reads.readIt: When you see this card, read the levels and the expected move. For futures-only metals, see what one move is worth on one lot.
Commodity reads.simple: The if-then tree without a trade, for a market with no Indian option. It shows levels and what a stall, breakout, pullback or breakdown would mean. The desk does not trade futures.

Commodity regime state.example: If monsoon spells usually last two weeks, you plan around that. Here, a state like overbought has its own usual length.
Commodity regime state.forYou: Most textbook signals show no edge, so do not trade them on faith.
Commodity regime state.goodBad: A tested edge is useful; no edge means the signal is just noise here.
Commodity regime state.impact: If a state with a proven edge turns on: the plan may lean with it. If it says no edge: ignore it for direction.
Commodity regime state.readIt: When you see a state, check its verdict. A verdict needs 15 or more spells and the same sign in both halves of history. Otherwise it says too few or no edge.
Commodity regime state.simple: Common chart signals like RSI, Bollinger bands and ADX, studied on this commodity's past. For each signal it shows how long spells last. It shows what price did 10 days after.

Commodity side call.example: A shop sells rain insurance only if the price is clearly above the expected rain damage. If the price is too low, it does not sell. Same idea here.
Commodity side call.forYou: Treat stand aside as the default, and never sell just because premium looks big.
Commodity side call.goodBad: Sell means options are priced above likely moves; stand aside means the edge is thin or unknown.
Commodity side call.impact: If the ratio goes up past 1.10: the call can turn to sell. If it drops below, or a measured event appears: the call turns to stand aside.
Commodity side call.readIt: When you see the call, check the implied over forecast ratio. Below 1.10 means stand aside. For silver, copper and gas there is no implied vol, so the desk never says sell.
Commodity side call.simple: The desk's daily answer: sell option premium on this commodity, or stand aside. Selling needs implied volatility at least 1.10 times the forecast. It also needs no event that has moved this market before expiry.

Commodity track record.example: Like a weather office counting how many rain forecasts came true, after the day has passed.
Commodity track record.forYou: Do not size up on a short record; no rule is proven yet.
Commodity track record.goodBad: A high hit rate over many calls is encouraging; a short record proves nothing.
Commodity track record.impact: If the hit rate goes up over many calls: the rule has been working. If it goes down: the rule's edge is in doubt.
Commodity track record.readIt: When you see this record, count the graded calls first. Few calls mean little. Until it fills, check implied against realised instead.
Commodity track record.simple: How the desk's commodity calls did once their expiry passed. Sell calls are graded against the straddle's breakevens. Stand aside is not graded.

Commodity vol cone.example: If daily onion price swings over one week have ranged from Rs 1 to Rs 10, and today's is Rs 8, you are near the top of the cone.
Commodity vol cone.forYou: Use it to judge whether option prices are high or low by this commodity's own standards.
Commodity vol cone.goodBad: Near the top means wild moves; near the bottom means calm moves.
Commodity vol cone.impact: If today's dot rises in the cone: markets are moving more than usual. If it falls: markets are calmer than usual.
Commodity vol cone.readIt: When you see the cone, check if today's dot is near the top or bottom. Then see where implied vol sits on it.
Commodity vol cone.simple: Realised volatility is how much the price actually moved. The cone shows its lowest, middle and highest values for windows of 5 to 63 days. It also shows where today sits.

Commodity world benchmark.example: Like checking the London gold rate to understand the Mumbai jeweller's price.
Commodity world benchmark.forYou: Use it for context on markets you cannot trade in India.
Commodity world benchmark.goodBad: The level is neither good nor bad; it is a reference.
Commodity world benchmark.impact: If it goes up: the Indian price usually follows, adjusted for the rupee. If it goes down: the Indian price usually falls too.
Commodity world benchmark.readIt: When you see this price, note its unit and date. For zinc, lead and nickel it is an exchange-traded stand-in, which drifts a little.
Commodity world benchmark.simple: The main world futures contract for a commodity, in its own unit like dollars an ounce or a barrel. It is used when no Indian contract exists. It also builds the long rupee history.

Conditional base rate.example: Like knowing your team wins 57% of home matches anyway. A pundit who is right 57% of the time has told you nothing new.
Conditional base rate.forYou: Before trusting any lean, check that it beats this base rate.
Conditional base rate.impact: If it goes up: past days like today more often ended higher. If it goes down: they more often ended lower; it is history, not a promise.
Conditional base rate.readIt: When you see this number, also read the episode count. A rate built on about 11 separate episodes is a hint, not a fact.
Conditional base rate.simple: How often the price was higher on the target date, starting from past days like today. It is the score any lean must beat. A lean that only matches it adds nothing.

Cone verdict claim.example: Like predicting a shop profits on days its prices are marked high.
Cone verdict claim.forYou: Do not sell only because the cone says rich until this record proves it.
Cone verdict claim.impact: If it proves right over time: the cone helps you time selling. If not: ignore the label.
Cone verdict claim.readIt: When you see this claim, check its graded record against chance.
Cone verdict claim.simple: A forward claim: when premium is rich, the at-the-money straddle is kept to expiry. When thin or cheap, it is not.

Cone verdict test.example: Like checking if umbrellas sold on 'expensive' days really make more profit than on 'cheap' days.
Cone verdict test.forYou: Do not sell just because the cone says rich.
Cone verdict test.impact: If rich days kept more: the verdict would help. Here they kept fewer, so it did not.
Cone verdict test.readIt: When you see this test, compare the two rates. Rich side kept 45% of 20; other side 51% of 47; p = 0.76.
Cone verdict test.simple: When the cone calls premium rich, does a sold straddle survive to expiry more often? Rich and fair-to-rich days are compared with thin and cheap days.

Confidence.example: Like 6 of 10 friends recommending a film: they lean, but do not insist. 60% confidence argues for the smaller of two trade sizes.
Confidence.forYou: Use the smaller size when confidence is around 60% or lower.
Confidence.impact: If it goes up: more inputs agree, so a fuller size is reasonable. If it goes down: inputs are split, so trade smaller.
Confidence.readIt: When you see this number, use it for size, not direction. The claims ledger shows if it has earned trust.
Confidence.simple: How much of the evidence points the same way. It is not the chance of being right. Each input votes, and this is the share agreeing.

Contango, backwardation and the roll.example: Storing wheat in a godown costs rent, so next season's wheat is pricier: contango. In a shortage, today's wheat costs more: backwardation.
Contango, backwardation and the roll.forYou: Ignore roll-day jumps on charts and check which month your option is on.
Contango, backwardation and the roll.goodBad: Mild contango is normal; deep backwardation signals tightness.
Contango, backwardation and the roll.impact: If contango widens: holding costs more and supply is ample. If backwardation deepens: supply is tight now.
Contango, backwardation and the roll.readIt: When you see a jump on a continuous chart at roll day, it is not a real move. Check the gap between months.
Contango, backwardation and the roll.simple: Contango means later futures months cost more than the nearest. Backwardation means they cost less. The roll is switching from an expiring contract to the next.

Contribution to bias.example: Like one loud student making the whole class seem noisy. A -30 from one driver differs from a -30 that six drivers agree on.
Contribution to bias.forYou: Trust a strong world reading only when several drivers agree.
Contribution to bias.impact: If one driver's share grows: the reading depends on one source and is weaker. If many share it: the reading is broader.
Contribution to bias.readIt: When you see this column, check if the total came from one driver or many. Many agreeing is stronger evidence.
Contribution to bias.simple: How much of the day's world number came from this one driver. Each driver is capped at 1.5 times its normal big move. This stops one bad price from taking over.

Cooling-off.example: Like counting to ten before replying to an angry message.
Cooling-off.forYou: Use the pause to write what happened in the stopped trade.
Cooling-off.impact: If it is longer: less chance of a revenge trade, fewer trades. If shorter: less protection after a loss.
Cooling-off.readIt: When you see cooling-off active, wait it out; read your journal instead.
Cooling-off.simple: This is a pause on new trades after any stop. Exits stay allowed. The default is 24 hours. It is experimental: no trading study has tested it directly.

Cornish-Fisher.example: Like a road that is steeper going down than up: brakes matter more on the way down. If the plain lower edge is 24,200, the fixed one might be 24,000.
Cornish-Fisher.forYou: Place short puts using this lower edge, not the plain bell-curve one.
Cornish-Fisher.impact: If skew gets more negative: the lower edge moves further down. If returns look more balanced: the fix shrinks.
Cornish-Fisher.readIt: When you see this band, compare its lower edge with the plain band. The gap shows how much falling risk the plain band hides.
Cornish-Fisher.simple: A fix to the normal bell-curve range using the real shape of NIFTY's moves. NIFTY falls faster than it rises. So this fix pushes the lower edge further down.

Cost of impatience.example: Like buying snacks every time you feel bored: Rs 50 here and there adds up to Rs 1,500 a month.
Cost of impatience.forYou: Use it as a reminder that skipping a trade is a valid choice.
Cost of impatience.goodBad: Negative means waiting would have saved money; positive means no-edge days happened to pay in this sample.
Cost of impatience.impact: If it goes more negative: impatience cost more. If it moves toward zero or positive: waiting mattered less in this sample.
Cost of impatience.readIt: When you see a negative number, read it as the price of not waiting in the backtest.
Cost of impatience.simple: This is the total the backtest made or lost on trades taken when the filter said stand aside. Standing aside would have made zero. A negative figure is money given away by not waiting.

Costliest habits.example: Like listing household leaks by water wasted: fix the biggest leak first.
Costliest habits.forYou: Work on the top habit first each week.
Costliest habits.impact: If a habit's rupees go up: it is your biggest leak. If it falls: you are fixing it.
Costliest habits.readIt: When you see the top habit, open the lesson linked to it.
Costliest habits.simple: This groups your logged mistakes into habits and ranks them by the rupees they cost. Ties are broken by how often they happen. The top habits get their review cards moved to the front.

Costs per trade.example: Like selling mangoes for Rs 100 but paying Rs 15 for the cart, the market fee and the transport. You keep Rs 85.
Costs per trade.forYou: Costs are certain while profit is not, so they matter most on small credits.
Costs per trade.goodBad: Lower is better. Lower is better. Now: Rs 20 brokerage an order, STT 0.15% on sells, NSE 0.03553%, GST 18%.
Costs per trade.impact: If costs rise: your edge shrinks and some trades turn negative. If they fall: more trades become worth it.
Costs per trade.readIt: When you see costs, compare them with the credit. If costs are a big share of the credit, the trade needs a lot of luck.
Costs per trade.simple: Everything a trade pays on the way in and out. That is brokerage, taxes, exchange fees, stamp duty, GST and slippage. Slippage is the gap between the fair price and the price you really get. On cheap far-away spreads, costs can eat the whole edge.

Costs share.example: Like a delivery fee that eats into a small online order: Rs 40 fee on a Rs 200 order is 20 percent.
Costs share.forYou: Trade less often to keep it low.
Costs share.goodBad: Low is good; high means trading too often for the size of the gains.
Costs share.impact: If it goes up: costs take more of your gains. If it goes down: more of the profit stays with you.
Costs share.readIt: When you see this percent, a high figure means costs eat much of what you earn.
Costs share.simple: Costs are brokerage, taxes and fees you entered. This shows them as a share of your gross profit. Every extra entry and exit adds to it.

Coverage.example: Like a forecaster who says the temperature will be 25 to 30: if it is in that range only half the time, her range is too narrow.
Coverage.forYou: Check coverage before trusting any range.
Coverage.goodBad: Close to target is good; far below means ranges are too tight.
Coverage.impact: If it goes down: strikes placed at the band edge get hit more. If it goes up: premium was left on the table.
Coverage.readIt: When you see coverage, compare it with the band's target, like 68 percent.
Coverage.simple: Coverage is the share of outcomes that landed inside a stated range. A one-sigma band should cover about 68 percent. Too low means the band is too narrow.

Coverage and source.example: Like the label on a food packet showing who made it and when.
Coverage and source.forYou: Check coverage before trusting a pattern.
Coverage and source.impact: If coverage is long: statistics are more reliable. If short: less.
Coverage and source.readIt: When you see this card, check the start date and any gaps.
Coverage and source.simple: Where the series comes from, how far back it goes, and what is missing. Follow the link to the publisher's page.

Coverage and the Kupiec test.example: A bus app promises the bus comes within 10 minutes 2 times in 3. If it is late much more often, the app is wrong. A NIFTY one-sigma band should be broken on about 1 day in 3; holding 67% against 68% is honest.
Coverage and the Kupiec test.forYou: As a seller, this check tells you if the ranges you sell outside can be believed.
Coverage and the Kupiec test.goodBad: Coverage near the promise with Kupiec passing is good; a failed test means the band size is wrong.
Coverage and the Kupiec test.impact: If coverage goes up far above the promise: bands are too wide, and premium goes to others. If it goes down below: bands are too narrow, and your strikes are too close.
Coverage and the Kupiec test.readIt: When you see coverage, compare it with the promised rate, like 68% for one sigma. Then check if Kupiec passes. Passing means the gap is just luck; failing means the band is truly too wide or too narrow.
Coverage and the Kupiec test.simple: Coverage is how often the real close landed inside the band. The Kupiec test checks if the gap from the promise is bigger than luck. Too few misses is also a problem, not a win.

Crack spread.example: If a sugarcane crusher pays Rs 100 for cane and sells the sugar for Rs 130, his margin is Rs 30. Refiners have the same kind of margin.
Crack spread.forYou: A wide crack can support crude demand, which matters for your crude view.
Crack spread.goodBad: A wide crack means strong refining margins; a thin one means weak fuel demand.
Crack spread.impact: If it goes up: refiners run harder, adding fuel supply later. If it goes down: refiners cut runs.
Crack spread.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with its 5-year median and its 1-year percentile.
Crack spread.simple: What a refinery earns turning a barrel of crude into a fuel like petrol or diesel. It is fuel price times 42 gallons minus the crude price. 42 gallons make one barrel.

Credit and margin.example: You earn Rs 100 renting your bike, but must leave Rs 5,000 as deposit. If a NIFTY strangle pays Rs 3,000 but blocks Rs 1.5 lakh, that is a 2% return on locked money.
Credit and margin.forYou: As a seller, what usually ruins you is being forced out of a trade, more than the loss itself.
Credit and margin.impact: If margin goes up during a bad move: you may be forced to close at a poor price. If credit goes up for the same margin: the trade uses capital better.
Credit and margin.readIt: When you see these, check margin before credit. Spreads with wings block about their maximum loss; naked shorts block more. Keep the desk's 40% cash buffer free.
Credit and margin.simple: Credit is the premium you receive when you sell. Margin is money the exchange locks up against your risk. Neither means much alone; compare them.

Credit received.example: Like advance money a tailor takes for an order: Rs 1,000 in hand now, but he must still deliver. Trading: sell an option for 80 and buy a wing for 20, credit is 60 points.
Credit received.forYou: Use it as the measuring stick for both your target and your stop.
Credit received.goodBad: A larger credit pays more but almost always means strikes closer to the market, so more risk.
Credit received.impact: If it is bigger: the target is bigger but you usually took more risk. If it is smaller: less to gain, so check the risk is small too.
Credit received.readIt: When you see this number, halve it for the profit target. Multiply it by 1.5 for the stop.
Credit received.simple: Credit is the money you collect when you sell options. This is what you took in when you opened the trade. Money paid for bought options is taken off. The exit rules are measured against this number.

Credit worth the risk.example: Like refusing a job that pays Rs 100 but risks Rs 1,000 of damage. Trading: a 100-point spread needs at least 15 points credit.
Credit worth the risk.impact: If credit goes up: the rule passes. If it goes down: the rule fails.
Credit worth the risk.readIt: When you see this rule missed, the reward is too small for the risk.
Credit worth the risk.simple: This rule says the credit must be at least 15 percent of the spread width. Thin credit with cheap wings makes the risk lopsided.

Crisis literate.example: Like a fire-safety certificate earned by passing 5 different drills.
Crisis literate.forYou: Practise crisis days with the same rules as calm days.
Crisis literate.impact: If you pass more crisis days: you get closer. If your process slips on them: they do not count.
Crisis literate.readIt: When you see where you are, it shows how many crisis days you have passed.
Crisis literate.simple: This badge is about crisis practice. It needs 5 different synthetic crisis days debriefed with process 70 percent or more.

Crisis replays.example: Like testing a house design against the worst real earthquakes on record, not just average ones.
Crisis replays.forYou: These have happened before and will again, so size for them.
Crisis replays.goodBad: Smaller worst losses and drawdowns are better.
Crisis replays.impact: If a crisis cell shows a loss bigger than your comfort: your size is too big. If small: the rule survives that crisis.
Crisis replays.readIt: When you see this table, read the worst single trade. In the 2008 replay the current rules' worst trade lost about Rs 27,000 at the desk's size.
Crisis replays.simple: The rules replayed on the worst real periods: 2008, election days, demonetisation, COVID, June 2022. It also tests a made-up 8% overnight gap. Each cell gives the worst trade and worst drawdown.

Crude below zero.example: Imagine milk so plentiful that dairies pay you to take it away. That happened to crude.
Crude below zero.forYou: Always use defined-risk spreads and exit before expiry in crude.
Crude below zero.goodBad: There is no good side; it shows the worst case for unprotected sellers.
Crude below zero.impact: If you hold a naked short put into expiry: losses can be huge. If you use a defined-risk spread: loss is capped at the width.
Crude below zero.readIt: When you see this case, compare the condor's capped loss with the naked put's loss of several lakh.
Crude below zero.simple: In April 2020, US crude prices went below zero. MCX options expired on 16 April. Options in the money turned into futures that settled at minus Rs 2,884 on 20 April.

Crude oil (MCX).example: Like auto-rickshaw fares that change with petrol prices. If WTI oil jumps $3, MCX crude jumps too, converted to rupees.
Crude oil (MCX).forYou: If you sell crude options, use wide strikes and small size, because crude is the loudest market here.
Crude oil (MCX).impact: If it goes up: long crude gains, short calls lose fast. If it goes down: short puts lose fast; crude moves are large either way.
Crude oil (MCX).readIt: When you see this number, check WTI and the term structure row. A one-week range of about 7% either way is normal for crude.
Crude oil (MCX).simple: The price of crude oil in India on MCX, in rupees per barrel. It follows the American WTI oil price. It is the most jumpy of the five markets on the page.

Currency futures position.example: Like one shop's sales figures, not the whole market's. A net long in Yen futures shows one group's lean in that contract.
Currency futures position.forYou: Treat it as delayed context, not proof of any investor's view.
Currency futures position.impact: If the net goes up: the group leans more toward that currency. If it goes down: less.
Currency futures position.readIt: When you see this row, check the date and category before reading a shift.
Currency futures position.simple: A reported group position in a named currency futures market, like Euro or Yen. It does not cover all currency trading. It also does not cover the rupee spot market.

Current vs recommended.example: Like a report card comparing two students in every subject, on both practice tests and final exams.
Current vs recommended.forYou: It shows whether the suggested rule beat yours on years nobody used to pick it.
Current vs recommended.goodBad: Look for higher expectancy and Sharpe with a smaller drawdown out-of-sample.
Current vs recommended.impact: If the recommended line keeps leading out-of-sample: the change looks justified. If the lines converge: the change may not matter.
Current vs recommended.readIt: When you see this table, focus on the out-of-sample columns. Recommended: Sharpe 0.96 and Rs 674 a trade; current: Sharpe 0.07 and Rs 32.
Current vs recommended.simple: Trades, win rate, average win and loss, expectancy, CAGR, drawdown, worst month and the tail for every rule line. It shows them in-sample and out-of-sample. CAGR and drawdown use Rs 10 lakh with each trade sized to its risk cap.

Curriculum.example: Like solving a maths problem before looking at the answer key; peeking first teaches little.
Curriculum.forYou: Answer first, then check; never the other way round.
