Curriculum.impact: If more lessons reach mastered: the skills are more likely to stick. If many stay started: come back after a gap.
Curriculum.readIt: When you see status new, started, done or mastered, mastered means right on three separate days without help.
Curriculum.simple: This is the full list of 34 lessons in six levels. Each lesson names a common wrong belief, shows a live example, and ends in questions. Answer before opening the worked example. Answers after peeking do not count.

Daily loss limit.example: Like leaving the mela once you have spent your Rs 500 budget for the day.
Daily loss limit.forYou: Respect it; the next trade after a bad day is often the worst one.
Daily loss limit.impact: If you hit it: no new entries today. If you stay under: trading stays open.
Daily loss limit.readIt: When you see this hit, stop opening trades for the day.
Daily loss limit.simple: Once your booked losses today reach this, new trades are locked until tomorrow. The default is 1 percent of capital. Exits are never locked.

Dated cost table.example: Like a bus fare chart with old and new prices and the date each started.
Dated cost table.forYou: It shows exactly what each order costs you today.
Dated cost table.goodBad: Current STT on sold options is 0.15% of premium, from April 2026.
Dated cost table.impact: If a rate rises: every trade costs more and thin trades may turn unprofitable. If it falls: trading gets cheaper.
Dated cost table.readIt: When you see this table, read the current rate and its start date for each charge.
Dated cost table.simple: Each charge is kept as a list of dates and rates. A trade pays the rate in force on its own date. STT on sold premium went 0.0625% to 0.1% to 0.15%.

Dealer and writer gamma.example: Like shopkeepers who buy when prices fall and sell when they rise, which keeps prices steady; or panicked ones who do the opposite and make swings bigger. Near a big OI strike like 25,000, hedging can pin NIFTY.
Dealer and writer gamma.forYou: As a seller, short gamma at spot means bigger swings, so keep strikes further and wings on.
Dealer and writer gamma.goodBad: Long gamma is friendlier for sellers; short gamma is riskier.
Dealer and writer gamma.impact: If gamma at spot goes up (more long): hedging tends to dampen moves. If it goes down (more short): hedging tends to make moves bigger.
Dealer and writer gamma.readIt: When you see this section, look for whether gamma at spot is long (calming) or short (amplifying), and where the flip level sits.
Dealer and writer gamma.simple: This section shows how the people who sold options must hedge as NIFTY moves. Their hedging can calm price down near some strikes and push it harder near others.

Decisions ahead.example: Like the exam timetable pinned on a school board: you know which days need extra preparation. If the RBI meets on 5 Dec, that week NIFTY may move more than usual.
Decisions ahead.forYou: Avoid selling tight strikes just before a big decision; either widen the strikes or wait until after.
Decisions ahead.impact: If a decision falls before your expiry: option premiums are usually higher, and the risk of a sudden move is too. If it falls after: your trade avoids that event.
Decisions ahead.readIt: When you see a date here, check if it falls before your option's expiry.
Decisions ahead.simple: A list of upcoming central-bank meetings and big data releases, with dates. Each date says whether it was confirmed by more than one source. These are the days markets often move most.

Defined risk.example: Like a safety net under a trapeze artist.
Defined risk.impact: If you keep it: the worst case is capped. If you break it: one gap can be huge.
Defined risk.readIt: When you see this rule missed, a leg is unprotected.
Defined risk.simple: This rule says every sold option needs a bought option behind it, so the worst loss is known. A sold option alone can lose far more than its credit.

Deflated Sharpe.example: If 11,000 people toss coins, someone gets 15 heads in a row. You would need far more than 15 before calling him skilled.
Deflated Sharpe.forYou: It is a strong warning against trusting the best backtest too much.
Deflated Sharpe.goodBad: Above 0.95 is the desk's proof bar elsewhere; 0.03 means not proven.
Deflated Sharpe.impact: If it rises toward 0.95 or more: the edge is likely real. If it stays near zero: the winner may just be the luckiest.
Deflated Sharpe.readIt: When you see deflated Sharpe, read it as a probability from 0 to 1. Here it is 0.03 after 11,030 trials: the training Sharpe 0.52 is below the 0.76 luck alone could give.
Deflated Sharpe.simple: The winner's Sharpe ratio after allowing for how many rules were tried. With many tries, some rule will look great by luck. Deflated Sharpe is the probability the winner beats the best that luck alone would give.

Delivery.example: Like buying a house versus just visiting a house open day. If 70% of volume is delivered, real owners changed; at 25%, it was mostly churn.
Delivery.forYou: If a big fall comes with high delivery, give short puts more room.
Delivery.impact: If it goes up: moves are backed by real buyers or sellers and may last. If it goes down: moves are churn and may reverse.
Delivery.readIt: When you see this number, look at it on big move days. High delivery on a fall means real stock was sold.
Delivery.simple: The share of traded shares that actually changed owners, not bought and sold the same day. It is compared with its 20-day average. It separates real buying from quick trading.

Delivery percentage.example: At the mandi, 100 crates changed hands, but 70 were taken home and 30 were resold the same day. A big NIFTY stock rising on only 25% delivery is weaker than one rising on 70%.
Delivery percentage.forYou: As a seller, a big NIFTY move on thin delivery may fade, which matters when it nears your strike.
Delivery percentage.goodBad: High delivery means real ownership change; low delivery means same-day churn.
Delivery percentage.impact: If it goes up on a move: the move has real buyers and may last. If it goes down on a move: the move may reverse when traders unwind.
Delivery percentage.readIt: When you see this number, compare it on big moves in heavy stocks. A rally on thin delivery is often traders' positions that must be closed later. Heavy delivery means buyers already paid.
Delivery percentage.simple: The share of a stock's trading where shares truly changed owners. The rest was bought and sold the same day. High delivery shows real conviction; low delivery shows churn.

Delta.example: Like a kite string: a tight string (high delta) moves the kite a lot when you pull. A loose string (low delta) moves it a little.
Delta.forYou: Selling low-delta strikes means more often right but smaller premium; the research tested 10, 15 and 20 delta strikes.
Delta.goodBad: Near zero is neutral; a big number means you are betting on direction.
Delta.impact: If NIFTY moves toward a short strike: that leg's delta grows and the position leans against the move. If it moves away: delta shrinks.
Delta.readIt: When you see a position delta, read it as your lean. Positive gains if NIFTY rises; negative gains if it falls; near zero is neutral.
Delta.simple: Delta is how much an option's price moves when NIFTY moves 1 point. It is also a rough chance of the option ending in the money. A 20 delta option has about a 20% chance.

Density sd.example: Like the usual spread of marks around the class average. If density sd is 400, a normal move to expiry is about 400 points.
Density sd.forYou: Keep short strikes at least one, ideally more, of these away from spot.
Density sd.impact: If it goes up: wider expected moves. If it goes down: narrower expected moves.
Density sd.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with your strike distances. Also check how many strikes were used.
Density sd.simple: The standard deviation of the range of outcomes priced by options. Standard deviation is the normal size of a move. It is measured in NIFTY points.

Desk backtest trade.example: Like an answer key written after the exam was graded.
Desk backtest trade.forYou: Learn from its exit, not its money.
Desk backtest trade.impact: If its result is good: it may still be hindsight. If bad: it shows the risk.
Desk backtest trade.readIt: When you see it, treat it as an example, not proof.
Desk backtest trade.simple: This is the trade the desk's backtest made that day, with its exit and rupee result. It is in-sample: the rules were written after seeing the period.

Desk side rule.example: Like a weather rule deciding fishing or no fishing.
Desk side rule.impact: If it said sell: the conditions suited sellers. If it said stand aside: trading was against the rule.
Desk side rule.readIt: When you see stand aside, ask why you traded if you did.
Desk side rule.simple: This says whether the desk's rule said sell premium or stand aside that day, and why. It used only that day's data.

Desk stance.example: Like a friend's hunch about the match: interesting, but not a reason to bet.
Desk stance.forYou: Read it last, after the rules.
Desk stance.impact: If it changes: it is just context. If it stays: nothing changes for your rules.
Desk stance.readIt: When you see it, do not base your trade on it.
Desk stance.simple: This is the desk model's market view stored for that day. Its own grading says its direction calls are no better than a coin flip. Treat it as context only.

Digital asset.example: Like the price tag on a phone, which says nothing about how many were sold. If Bitcoin is $60,000, that is only its price.
Digital asset.forYou: Treat crypto moves as rough mood background only.
Digital asset.impact: If it goes up: risk appetite may be strong. If it goes down sharply: risk mood may sour; the price alone does not prove why.
Digital asset.readIt: When you see this price, check its source and date.
Digital asset.simple: A digital token price, like Bitcoin or Ethereum, from a named source. A spot price is just a price. It does not show positions, forced sales or flows.

Directional probability.example: Like bookies' odds before a match: win, lose or draw. If NIFTY is 25,000, the numbers might read 16% above, 16% below and 68% inside the range.
Directional probability.forYou: As a seller, the inside number is roughly your chance the short strangle expires worthless.
Directional probability.goodBad: A high inside number is calmer pricing; a low one means the market expects a breakout.
Directional probability.impact: If the inside number goes up: the market prices a calmer finish. If it goes down: a break out of the range is priced as more likely.
Directional probability.readIt: When you see these three, read the inside number as the chance your range holds. All three come from IV. If IV is wrong, all three are wrong together.
Directional probability.simple: Three chances: NIFTY ends above, below or inside the expected range at expiry. They come from today's option prices, not a forecast. For a seller, the middle one matters most.

Directional stance.example: Calling the coin toss before a cricket match: even experts get it right about half the time. If the desk says NIFTY at 25,000 will close higher tomorrow, its record says that is right only about 49% of the time.
Directional stance.forYou: As a seller, this reminds you to trade ranges, never bets on which way NIFTY goes.
Directional stance.goodBad: Near 50% means no skill at direction; a steady figure well above 50% over many sessions would be unusual.
Directional stance.impact: If it stays well above 50% for a long time: there may be some skill. Check the sample size first. If it stays near 50%: direction is a guess. Never turn a range trade into a direction bet.
Directional stance.readIt: When you see this hit rate, expect it near 50%, which is a coin flip. That is the point: range calls work, direction calls do not. Use the range claims, not this, for your trades.
Directional stance.simple: A claim about whether NIFTY closes up or down next session. The desk makes it only when positions look strongly one-sided. It is published to show how hard direction is to guess.

Discipline.example: Like a fitness diary: it does not measure the weather, it measures whether you went for the walk you planned.
Discipline.forYou: Visit it weekly to check habits, not daily to chase numbers.
Discipline.impact: If your rule-following goes up: your results rely less on luck. If it goes down: mistakes, not the market, start to drive losses.
Discipline.readIt: When you see this page, start with the adherence score, then the guard rails, then the patience meter.
Discipline.simple: This page is about how you trade, not what the market does. It covers when to wait, how big to trade, when to stop, and whether you kept your own rules. Desk numbers come from its backtest, a test of the rules on past data. Your own data stays in this browser.

Discipline metrics.example: Like a student checking homework done on time, not just exam marks: habits show up sooner than marks.
Discipline metrics.forYou: Pick one weak metric a week to work on.
Discipline metrics.impact: If they improve: your trading depends less on luck. If they slip: habits, not the market, are driving results.
Discipline metrics.readIt: When you see these numbers, look for the one furthest from its target.
Discipline metrics.simple: These numbers show how closely you follow your rules, taken from your own journal. Process numbers show change quickly. Profit numbers need many trades before they mean anything.

Do the agri signals work?.example: Like checking whether folk weather sayings really predict rain.
Do the agri signals work?.forYou: Do not trade on anything that is not works.
Do the agri signals work?.goodBad: Works is evidence; anything else is not proven.
Do the agri signals work?.impact: If a signal moves to works: it can be used as evidence. If not: ignore it.
Do the agri signals work?.readIt: When you see the verdict, works means right direction and p under 5%. Weak means maybe luck.
Do the agri signals work?.simple: Fund extremes, WASDE changes, seasonal direction, seasonal volatility and the cone verdict, each tested against a baseline. Each gets a one-word verdict.

Do the signals work?.example: Like checking whether the old saying about red sky predicts rain, by counting real days.
Do the signals work?.forYou: Do not trade on a signal unless it says works.
Do the signals work?.goodBad: Works means it beat the baseline and was unlikely to be luck; anything else is not proven.
Do the signals work?.impact: If a signal moves to works: it can be used as evidence. If it drops to does not work: ignore it.
Do the signals work?.readIt: When you see the verdict, trust only works. Weak means maybe luck.
Do the signals work?.simple: Fund extremes, EIA surprises and the cone verdict, each tested against a plain baseline. Each gets a one-word verdict: works, weak, does not work, or too few.

Dollar index.example: Like a strong rupee making foreign goods cheaper for us but our exports dearer. At the 70th percentile or higher, this row votes -1 for all five markets.
Dollar index.forYou: If the dollar is surging, take extra care with short puts on gold.
Dollar index.impact: If the dollar goes up: gold, silver and oil tend to face pressure. If it goes down: they tend to get support.
Dollar index.readIt: When you see this row, read the 20-day move and its percentile. 70 or above votes down; 30 or below votes up.
Dollar index.simple: The US dollar against six big world currencies. A strong dollar makes commodities priced in dollars costlier for others, which pushes them down. Gold feels it most, crude least.

Downside difference.example: Like a map that forgets a steep slope on one side of the hill. If the plain edge is 24,200 and the adjusted is 24,000, the gap is 200 points.
Downside difference.forYou: Add this distance to your put strike buffer.
Downside difference.impact: If it goes up: the plain band understates falls more. If it goes down: up and down risks are more balanced.
Downside difference.readIt: When you see this number, a big value means put strikes need extra room.
Downside difference.simple: How far the skew-adjusted lower edge sits below the plain bell-curve lower edge. A large gap means the plain band hides falling risk.

Drawdown distribution.example: Like a chart showing how many years the river rose 1 metre, 2 metres or 3 metres.
Drawdown distribution.forYou: It shows the full range of pain, not just the average.
Drawdown distribution.goodBad: Bars further right mean deeper falls to sit through.
Drawdown distribution.impact: If bars shift right: deeper falls are more common. If they shift left: the rule is gentler.
Drawdown distribution.readIt: When you see the bars, look at how far right they reach. Those are the deep falls.
Drawdown distribution.simple: A bar chart of how often each size of two-year drawdown happened across the simulated paths. It covers the current rules and the safest variants.

Drawdown recovery.example: Like a broken arm: it takes a minute to break and weeks to heal. Rs 100 falling to Rs 80 needs Rs 20 more, which is 25 percent of Rs 80.
Drawdown recovery.forYou: Use it to choose a size that you could sit through without breaking rules.
Drawdown recovery.goodBad: Short recovery is easier to live with; long recovery tests patience and often leads to revenge trades.
Drawdown recovery.impact: If recovery times go up: losses take longer to repair, so size smaller. If they go down: the strategy healed faster in this sample.
Drawdown recovery.readIt: When you see this, read the time in weeks, and imagine sitting through it calmly.
Drawdown recovery.simple: Drawdown means a fall from your highest account value. This shows how long the backtest took to climb back to its old high. Recovery needs a bigger gain than the loss. A 20 percent fall needs 25 percent to get back.

Drawdown, 99th percentile.example: Like planning for the worst monsoon in a hundred years when building a house.
Drawdown, 99th percentile.forYou: Ask yourself if you could live through this fall without quitting.
Drawdown, 99th percentile.goodBad: Lower is safer; above 30% is a serious hit.
Drawdown, 99th percentile.impact: If it rises: your account can fall further in a bad stretch. If it falls: the rule is gentler.
Drawdown, 99th percentile.readIt: When you see this, read it as a share of capital. For the current rules it is about 42%.
Drawdown, 99th percentile.simple: The two-year drawdown that only 1 path in 100 is worse than. It is the bad-luck case to prepare for. It is measured on Rs 5 lakh at the rule's size.

Driver correlation.example: If umbrella sales rise most weeks when it rains, their correlation is high. Rain does not tell you which shopkeeper sold how many. In gold, funds often buy when the dollar falls.
Driver correlation.forYou: Use it to know which news, like dollar moves, has tended to push fund flows in your metal.
Driver correlation.goodBad: A strong link shows a past habit; a weak link means that factor has not mattered.
Driver correlation.impact: If it goes up towards +1: funds have tended to move with that factor. If it goes down towards -1: they have tended to move against it.
Driver correlation.readIt: When you see this number, near 0 means no link. Beyond 0.5 either way means a strong link. Also read the same-direction share: 50% is a coin flip. Check how many weeks it uses.
Driver correlation.simple: Correlation is a number from -1 to +1 that shows how two things move together. Here it links fund buying with things like price, the dollar and US yields. It shows habit, not cause.

Dubai 1st line.example: Like checking the rate at the nearest big mandi when your own village has no rate board. India buys a lot of Gulf crude, so this market matters for Indian refiners.
Dubai 1st line.forYou: As a seller, it is background only, since no Indian option trades on it.
Dubai 1st line.goodBad: Neither. It is a proxy market.
Dubai 1st line.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish on Middle East crude. If it goes down: they are less bullish or adding shorts.
Dubai 1st line.readIt: When you see this row, read only the positioning numbers. No price line is drawn for it.
Dubai 1st line.simple: An ICE future that tracks Middle East sour crude, the kind of oil that comes from the Gulf. The desk uses its positioning as the closest published proxy for the Murban and Dubai crude that Asia buys, but it is not Murban itself. No price series is stored for it.

Due now.example: Like library books that are due back today. If 12 cards show here, those 12 are ready to be checked again; the page caps reviews at 15 a day.
Due now.forYou: As a seller, short daily reviews keep rules like stop levels and position sizing fresh in your mind.
Due now.goodBad: Lower is better, but zero only matters if you reviewed honestly.
Due now.impact: If it goes up: more cards are waiting, maybe because you skipped days. If it goes down: you are keeping up.
Due now.readIt: When you see this number, clear it a little each day rather than all at once.
Due now.simple: This is the number of review cards whose next review date has arrived. You review each card at growing gaps of 1, 3, 7, 16, 35 and 80 days; a miss sends it back to 1 day.

E1.example: Like working out how far a cyclist usually rides in 5 days from his daily average. Trading: NIFTY 24,000, IV 12 percent, 5 sessions gives about 24,000 x 0.12 x 0.14 = 400 points.
E1.forYou: Practise until you can do it in your head roughly.
E1.impact: If your error goes down: you can size ranges quickly. If it stays high: redo the lesson on ranges.
E1.readIt: When you see your answer marked close, check you used trading sessions, not calendar days.
E1.simple: Exercise 1: build the one-sigma range, the normal expected move, to an expiry. Use spot times implied volatility times the square root of sessions over 252. Within 3 percent counts as right.

E10.example: Like working out flood damage to a house at three water levels.
E10.forYou: Use it to feel what a gap costs before it happens.
E10.impact: If you value gaps accurately: you size better. If not: revisit max loss and wings.
E10.readIt: When you see a big loss at minus 5 percent, remember a stop cannot help in a gap.
E10.simple: Exercise 10: value today's one-sigma condor after three gaps. The gaps are minus 3, minus 5 and plus 3 percent, held to expiry. Within 10 percent counts.

E2.example: Like placing fielders just outside where the batsman usually hits.
E2.forYou: Use it to learn where strikes belong, not as a trade tip.
E2.impact: If your picks match more often: you place strikes well. If shorts land inside the range: you take ordinary moves as risk.
E2.readIt: When you see half credit, your strikes were outside the range but not at the desk width.
E2.simple: Exercise 2: pick the sold put, sold call and wing width of a one-sigma iron condor from today's prices. An iron condor sells a put and a call with protective wings. Full credit for the first strikes outside the expected range.

E3.example: Like guessing a bowler's chance of a wicket this over, then checking the record.
E3.forYou: Remember POP ignores how big the loss is.
E3.impact: If your error goes down: your feel for odds improves. If it stays large: practise with delta as a guide.
E3.readIt: When you see your guess far from the model, compare with one minus delta as a quick check.
E3.simple: Exercise 3: estimate the chance of profit, POP, for a sold strike with a slider. Then see the model's POP and how often the desk's strikes really survived. Within 5 points counts.

E4.example: Like working out a shop's profit per crate and then per rupee invested. Trading: 20 points x 65 per lot = Rs 1,300.
E4.forYou: Always convert points to rupees before deciding.
E4.impact: If your accuracy goes up: rupee maths becomes automatic. If not: re-check lot size first.
E4.readIt: When you see ROM under 0.80 percent, the desk would reject the trade.
E4.simple: Exercise 4: turn an option price into rupees per lot, then into return on margin, ROM. Margin is the money the broker blocks. Exact to one rupee for the credit, within 3 percent for ROM.

E5.example: Like reading a crowd: more people arriving and prices rising means buyers are rushing in.
E5.forYou: Remember build-up describes flows; it is weak as a forecast.
E5.impact: If your accuracy rises: you read flows correctly. If not: revisit the build-up lesson.
E5.readIt: When you see a leg marked wrong, re-check which way price and open interest moved.
E5.simple: Exercise 5: sort three legs into four build-up types from price change and open interest change. Open interest is the number of contracts still open. Each leg is graded on its own.

E6.example: Like an insurer checking if the premium is more than the claims it usually pays.
E6.forYou: Check this ratio before any selling trade.
E6.impact: If the ratio goes up: sellers are paid more for the risk. If it goes down: selling pays less than it costs.
E6.readIt: When you see a ratio between 0.95 and 1.10, the case is unclear.
E6.simple: Exercise 6: decide whether today's price pays the seller. Compare implied volatility with forecast realised volatility, the move NIFTY actually makes. Above 1.10 pays; below 0.95 does not.

E7.example: Like checking if a box of 10 mangoes is priced about the same as 10 single mangoes.
E7.forYou: Use it as a quick sanity check on option prices.
E7.impact: If the ratio goes up: options are dearer than the formula says. If it goes down: they are cheaper.
E7.readIt: When you see a result far above 0.8, the straddle is rich compared with the formula.
E7.simple: Exercise 7: divide an expiry's at-the-money straddle by its one-sigma move. A straddle is a call plus a put at the same strike. Theory says about 0.8. Within 5 percent counts.

E8.example: Like a stall: 8 of 10 days earn Rs 500, 2 days lose Rs 2,500, average is Rs 400 minus Rs 500, a Rs 100 loss a day.
E8.forYou: Do this sum for any strategy before trusting its win rate.
E8.impact: If expectancy goes up: the strategy pays on average. If it goes negative: it loses despite many wins.
E8.readIt: When you see a high win rate with negative expectancy, that is the desk's own record.
E8.simple: Exercise 8: work out expectancy, the average result per trade, from win rate, average win and average loss. Within Rs 25 counts.

E9.example: Like a tipster right 60 percent of the time when just guessing the favourite is right 65 percent: no skill.
E9.impact: If you spot signals correctly more often: you resist false claims better. If not: practise asking for the base rate.
E9.readIt: When you see a high hit rate below its base rate, it is worse than useless.
E9.simple: Exercise 9: given a study's hit rate and its base rate, decide if it is a real signal. Signal means above its base rate with a p-value under 0.05, meaning chance alone rarely gives that result.

ECB rate decision.example: Like the RBI, but for Europe. NIFTY reacts on the next Indian session after the decision.
ECB rate decision.forYou: As a seller, only an event that counts changes the side rule.
ECB rate decision.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: Europe's rate days have been moving NIFTY more. If it goes down: they have been quiet for NIFTY.
ECB rate decision.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with an ordinary day's move and check Cases and Counts.
ECB rate decision.simple: The European Central Bank sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro. Its decisions move the euro and world bond markets.

EIA weekly inventories vs seasonal norm.example: If a godown usually loses 10 bags in Diwali week but lost 30 this year, demand is strong. Crude stocks falling more than normal works the same way.
EIA weekly inventories vs seasonal norm.forYou: Know that weekly EIA reports move crude every week, so expect them inside any option you hold.
EIA weekly inventories vs seasonal norm.goodBad: A bigger-than-normal draw means tightness; a bigger-than-normal build means surplus.
EIA weekly inventories vs seasonal norm.impact: If stocks fall more than normal: crude prices tend to get support. If they rise more than normal: prices tend to come under pressure.
EIA weekly inventories vs seasonal norm.readIt: When you see this number, a draw bigger than normal points to a tight market. A build bigger than normal points to a loose one. Oil data comes Wednesday, gas on Thursday.
EIA weekly inventories vs seasonal norm.simple: The EIA is the US energy data office. Each week it reports how much crude, petrol, diesel and gas is stored. This compares the change with the usual change for that week over five years.

ETF spot.example: If one share of a gold fund is worth about one tenth of an ounce, the share price times 10 gives the ounce price.
ETF spot.forYou: Use the ratio to map US ETF strikes to the commodity price you follow.
ETF spot.impact: If it goes up: the commodity price in dollars has risen. If it goes down: it has fallen.
ETF spot.readIt: When you see this price, use the ratio to turn ETF strikes into commodity prices.
ETF spot.simple: The ETF's last closing price, and its ratio to the US futures price. Gold is roughly GLD divided by that ratio.

EV after costs.example: A shopkeeper earns Rs 100 on 9 days and loses Rs 1,000 on 1 day. His average day is minus Rs 10. That minus Rs 10 is his EV.
EV after costs.forYou: Only a positive EV after costs means the trade is paid on the desk's numbers. It is an average, not a promise.
EV after costs.goodBad: Above zero is paid; below zero loses on average. The desk takes the worse of two history versions to stay cautious.
EV after costs.impact: If EV goes up: the trade pays more on average. If it falls below zero: the trade loses on average, even if it wins often.
EV after costs.readIt: When you see EV after costs, check its sign first. Then see how big it is next to the maximum loss.
EV after costs.simple: EV is expected value: the average profit if you could take the same trade many, many times. This one is after all charges and slippage, per lot, held to expiry. It uses NIFTY's real moves since 2007, scaled to today's volatility.

EV per risk.example: Two lemonade stalls: one earns Rs 10 on Rs 100 spent, another Rs 30 on Rs 1,000. The first is better per rupee.
EV per risk.forYou: It helps you pick the trade that uses your margin best.
EV per risk.goodBad: Higher is better; below zero is a losing trade on average.
EV per risk.impact: If it rises: each rupee of risk is better paid. If it falls below zero: you are paying to take risk.
EV per risk.readIt: When you see EV per risk, compare it across rows, not alone. A small trade with a good number beats a big trade with a thin one.
EV per risk.simple: EV after costs divided by the most the trade can lose. It tells you how many rupees you earn, on average, for each rupee you risk. It is the key used to rank trades.

Edge.example: Like a shop knowing why customers come: lower price, better quality, or closer location.
Edge.forYou: Write one clear edge before every trade.
Edge.impact: If you name a clear edge: you can later check if that edge works. If you leave it vague: you learn nothing.
Edge.readIt: When you see a blank or vague edge, the trade was likely a guess.
Edge.simple: Edge is the reason a trade should pay over many tries. Here you name it: rich volatility, event premium, range and walls, or other. A trade with no named edge is a guess.

Edge filter.example: Like a calendar marking good and bad weather days for fishing.
Edge filter.forYou: Match your trading days to the sell colour.
Edge filter.impact: If sell days go up: more chances to trade. If they go down: more waiting.
Edge filter.readIt: When you see a long run of stand-aside days, expect to wait.
Edge filter.simple: This strip colours each recent session by what the side rule said. The colours are sell or stand aside.

Effective.example: Like a new train timetable announced in May but starting in June.
Effective.forYou: Check the date before using any rule in a trade plan.
Effective.impact: If the date has passed: the new rule applies. If it is ahead: plan for the change.
Effective.readIt: When you see a future date, the old rule still applies until then.
Effective.simple: This is the date the rule took effect for NIFTY contracts. It is not the date the circular was issued. Lot changes hit new contracts first.

Emotion.example: Like noting you shopped while hungry: you often buy more than planned.
Emotion.forYou: If you rate 4 or 5, wait before saving the trade.
Emotion.impact: If strong-emotion entries go up: more decisions are made in heat. If they go down: calmer decisions.
Emotion.readIt: When you see strong emotions often, check those trades' results.
Emotion.simple: This records how you felt at entry and how strongly, from 1 to 5. Strong emotion, 4 or 5, is flagged at the gate.

Energy.example: Like the petrol price at your pump, but at the world wholesale level. If Brent rises from 70 to 80 dollars a barrel, India's import bill and inflation go up.
Energy.forYou: A sharp crude spike is a reason to give short calls less weight and short puts more room.
Energy.goodBad: For India, falling energy prices are usually good and rising ones bad.
Energy.impact: If energy prices go up: bad for India's inflation and the rupee, often a drag on NIFTY. If they go down: good for India's import bill and usually supportive for NIFTY.
Energy.readIt: When you see this group, watch crude first: it moves the rupee, inflation and oil-company stocks.
Energy.simple: A group of world fuel prices: WTI crude, Brent crude, natural gas, gasoline, heating oil and coal. India imports most of its oil, so these prices matter a lot for India. They are US and European futures prices.

Energy positioning primer.example: Like reading the rules before a cricket match, this tells you who is who on the energy field.
Energy positioning primer.forYou: Read it once so the crude and natural gas positioning tables make sense to you.
Energy positioning primer.impact: Nothing here moves up or down. Knowing the groups changes how you read every energy table that follows.
Energy positioning primer.readIt: When you see this guide, note that data is measured on Tuesday and published Friday. So it is three sessions old when it appears.
Energy positioning primer.simple: A short guide to the weekly fund-positioning reports for oil, fuels and gas. It explains the trader groups and when data is measured. Read it once before the energy tables.

Entries after losses.example: Like a gambler doubling his bet after losing to win it back.
Entries after losses.forYou: After a loss, wait and journal before the next trade.
Entries after losses.goodBad: Low is good; high suggests revenge trading.
Entries after losses.impact: If it goes up: you trade more after losses, which is risky. If it goes down: you handle losses better.
Entries after losses.readIt: When you see this count, check whether those trades were bigger or worse than usual.
Entries after losses.simple: These are trades opened within 72 hours of a losing close. Taking more risk after a loss is the best-known way traders give money back.

Equity curve.example: Like a graph of your piggy bank's balance after each week. You see the steady climbs and the sudden drops.
Equity curve.forYou: The few big drops decide your result, so look at those first.
Equity curve.goodBad: A rising line is good; deep sudden drops show tail risk.
Equity curve.impact: If the curve climbs over time: the rule earned. If it slides: losses outweigh wins.
Equity curve.readIt: When you see the curve, look for many small steps up and a few big steps down. That shape is typical of option selling.
Equity curve.simple: A line showing running total profit, one lot after costs, trade by trade. The solid line is the desk's weekly rules; dashed lines are benchmarks. Green dots are wins and red dots are losses.

Equity since 2008.example: Like a student's marks over many years where the early years were practice papers he had already seen.
Equity since 2008.forYou: Do not be impressed by the left side; it was chosen to look good.
Equity since 2008.goodBad: Weekly trades before February 2019 are hypothetical, as NIFTY had no weekly options then.
Equity since 2008.impact: If a line soars on the left but stalls on the right: it was fitted to the past. If it rises on both sides: it is more believable.
Equity since 2008.readIt: When you see this chart, look only to the right of the dashed line for proof.
Equity since 2008.simple: The same lines over all years from 2008. A dashed line marks where the test years begin. Only the right side of that line is evidence.

Event check.example: Like not planning a picnic on the day of a cyclone warning.
Event check.forYou: Check the event calendar before every trade.
Event check.impact: If an event falls in the trade: gap risk rises. If none: the rule passes.
Event check.readIt: When you see this rule missed, an event sat inside your trade.
Event check.simple: This rule says no big scheduled event inside the trade's life, or a deliberate stand-aside because of one. Events are priced in, but gap risk is outside a daily stop.

Event impact on NIFTY.example: Like checking if your shop is really busier on festival days or just feels busier. An event counts only with 8 or more past cases and a median move 1.25 times a normal day.
Event impact on NIFTY.forYou: Avoid fresh short positions just before events that count here.
Event impact on NIFTY.impact: If an event's multiple rises past 1.25: it starts to block the sell rule. If it falls below: it is treated as an ordinary day.
Event impact on NIFTY.readIt: When you see this, read which event types count and their multiple. A multiple of 1.5 means moves 50% bigger than normal.
Event impact on NIFTY.simple: How much NIFTY really moved after each kind of scheduled release, compared with a normal day. Calendars call many events high impact. Most barely move NIFTY.

Event inside.example: Like planning a picnic on the day of a cricket final. Traffic may be fine, or it may be very bad.
Event inside.forYou: An event inside your trade is a jump risk that a normal range does not cover.
Event inside.goodBad: More measured event days inside means a wider range; the multiple comes from the desk's event study.
Event inside.impact: If a big event falls inside: the range widens and losses on a jump can be large. If no event is inside: normal ranges apply.
Event inside.readIt: When you see this flag, check the event premium on the Positioning tab. Ask if you are paid for the jump.
Event inside.simple: A scheduled event, like an RBI decision or US data, falls before the trade expires. Such events can make NIFTY jump. The desk widens its expected range for events it has measured as bigger than a normal day.

Event premium.example: Like a caterer charging extra for a wedding day. If past weddings needed only a little extra food, the charge is rich.
Event premium.forYou: Sell through an event only when it is priced rich, and still keep size small.
Event premium.goodBad: 1.25 or more = rich, 0.80 or less = cheap, between = fair. The method tends to read a bit rich.
Event premium.impact: If the premium rises above history: sellers are paid more for the event. If it falls below: the event is underpriced and risky to sell.
Event premium.readIt: When you see the ratio, compare it with 1.25 (rich) and 0.80 (cheap). The 4-Dec-2026 RBI was 1.19, fair.
Event premium.simple: How big a one-day NIFTY move options charge for an event like RBI, US CPI or the Budget. It is compared with how much NIFTY really moved on past such days. Rich means sellers are paid more than history says.

Event premium track record.example: Like checking a weather man's past forecasts before trusting today's.
Event premium track record.forYou: It tells you if selling event premium has been paid in the past.
Event premium track record.goodBad: About 68% inside and a median move about 0.67 of the priced move means fair pricing.
Event premium track record.impact: If more than 68% land inside: events were overpriced, good for sellers. If fewer: events were underpriced.
Event premium track record.readIt: When you see this, look at how many events landed inside one priced move. If priced fairly, about 68% should.
Event premium track record.simple: The same event-premium estimate run on past events, against what NIFTY really did. It checks if the estimate was right in the past.

Event-day move.example: If onion prices move Rs 2 on normal days but Rs 5 on export-ban news days, the ratio is 2.5.
Event-day move.forYou: Avoid holding short options through events with a high ratio.
Event-day move.goodBad: High ratio means event risk; near 1 means ordinary.
Event-day move.impact: If the ratio goes up: that event has bigger jumps. If it goes down: it matters less.
Event-day move.readIt: When you see this ratio, near 1 means little effect. Above 1.25 with 8 or more cases makes it a measured event.
Event-day move.simple: The size of the price move on each event day, compared with normal days. A ratio above 1 means the event moved price more than usual.

Event-day move history.example: Like noting how much the traffic grew on each past festival, compared with a normal Monday.
Event-day move history.forYou: It tells you which events deserve respect when you hold short options.
Event-day move history.goodBad: Higher multiples of an ordinary day mean a bigger jump risk.
Event-day move history.impact: If an event's typical move is big: sell less or skip through it. If small: it may be safe to hold through.
Event-day move history.readIt: When you see this table, read the times an ordinary day column. Above 1 means the event moves NIFTY more than usual.
Event-day move history.simple: How much NIFTY moved on each past RBI decision, FOMC decision, US CPI day and Budget. It is compared with an ordinary day. It shows which events really move NIFTY.

Every expiry.example: Like comparing train fares for this week, next week and next month before booking. A weekly might pay little while the monthly pays well.
Every expiry.forYou: As a seller, when the front week is cheap, check here whether a later expiry pays better.
Every expiry.goodBad: Neither; a menu, not a recommendation by itself.
Every expiry.impact: If an expiry's premium goes up: it may be the better one to sell. If it goes down: that expiry is paying less for the same risk.
Every expiry.readIt: When you see this section, pick an expiry and compare its spread and range with the others.
Every expiry.simple: This section lines up each NIFTY expiry from this week to next month. For each one it shows the best-paying spread, how far NIFTY can go, and the open-interest walls.

Every state since 2007.example: Like testing every old saying about rain against 18 years of weather records. A signal is reliable only with 15 or more spells and a strong test score.
Every state since 2007.forYou: Use signals here for move size, and ignore direction calls that are not marked reliable.
Every state since 2007.impact: If a signal's moves-after number goes up: bigger moves tend to follow it. If its up-after matches normal: it says nothing about direction.
Every state since 2007.readIt: When you see this table, read up-after against the bracketed normal rate. Reliable signals must also agree before and after 2017.
Every state since 2007.simple: A scorecard of every popular chart signal: what NIFTY did after each, compared with a normal day. Most popular signals say little about direction. Several say a lot about how big the next move is.

Evidence behind this tab.example: Like a medicine label listing which claims are tested and which are just tradition.
Evidence behind this tab.forYou: Read it once so you know which rules are proven and which are trials.
Evidence behind this tab.impact: If evidence grades go up: you can trust a feature more. If they are weak: test it on yourself.
Evidence behind this tab.readIt: When you see experimental, treat the feature as a trial your own journal must judge.
Evidence behind this tab.simple: This lists every study the discipline features rest on, with a grade for how strong it is. Features without solid trading evidence are labelled experimental.

Evidence interpretation.example: Like saying many umbrellas were sold today, without knowing if rain was coming or a sale was on. Rising price with rising OI is a label, not proof of who bought.
Evidence interpretation.forYou: Do not trade on a story about why a move happened unless a dated source supports it.
Evidence interpretation.impact: If new data arrives: the reading changes to fit it. If a cause is not proven by a report: the desk leaves it unexplained.
Evidence interpretation.readIt: When you see a reading, treat it as a label for the data. Look for a dated news report before naming a cause.
Evidence interpretation.simple: A short reading of market data using a stated rule. It organises facts. It cannot prove why someone traded or what caused a move.

Exam practice.example: Like a mock board exam before the real one.
Exam practice.forYou: Take full mock sets under time pressure.
Exam practice.impact: If it goes up: you are closer to passing. If it goes down: revise weak units.
Exam practice.readIt: When you see your score, compare it with 60 percent.
Exam practice.simple: These are practice sets marked like the NISM exam. A right answer gets 1 mark, a wrong answer loses a quarter mark, a blank gets 0. 60 percent passes the real exam.

Exam score.example: Like a quiz where wrong guesses cost a little.
Exam score.impact: If it goes up: you are safer. If it goes down: more revision needed.
Exam score.readIt: When you see it near 60 percent, you are on the edge.
Exam score.simple: This is right answers minus a quarter for each wrong one. It is shown against the 60 percent pass mark.

Excess kurtosis.example: Like a road with more potholes than the map says. If excess kurtosis is 2, big shocks are more likely than a bell curve suggests.
Excess kurtosis.forYou: When it is high, use wings and smaller size.
Excess kurtosis.impact: If it goes up: big moves are more likely, a danger for sellers. If it goes down: moves are closer to normal.
Excess kurtosis.readIt: When you see this number, positive values mean you should expect surprise moves more often.
Excess kurtosis.simple: How fat the tails of expected moves are compared with a normal bell curve. Tails means very big moves. Zero means normal; positive means big moves are more common than normal.

Exercise accuracy.example: Like a batsman's average over his last 10 innings, not his whole career.
Exercise accuracy.goodBad: High means fluent arithmetic; it says nothing about trading profit.
Exercise accuracy.impact: If it goes up: your current calculation is sharper. If it goes down: practise the weak exercise.
Exercise accuracy.readIt: When you see it dip after mixed sets, that is normal; mixing is harder.
Exercise accuracy.simple: This is the share of your last 50 exercise answers that were right. Close answers count half. It shows your current skill, not your early tries.

Exercise record.example: Like a cricketer's net-session log: balls faced, clean hits, and how far off the bad ones were.
Exercise record.forYou: Focus on the exercise with the worst first-try accuracy.
Exercise record.impact: If accuracy goes up: you calculate better. If error rises: revisit that exercise's lesson.
Exercise record.readIt: When you see median error falling, your calculation is getting more precise.
Exercise record.simple: This shows each of the ten exercises: attempts, accuracy, first-try accuracy and median error. Close answers count half. Falling error on range, chance and straddle exercises is the goal.

Exit.example: Like a reason column in a shop's returns diary: damaged, wrong size, or changed mind.
Exit.forYou: Aim for every exit to be a planned one.
Exit.impact: If planned exits go up: your adherence improves. If own-choice or rolled exits go up: decisions are made on the fly.
Exit.readIt: When you see many discretionary or rolled exits, your plan is not running the trades.
Exit.simple: This says why and when a trade closed. Reasons are take profit, stop, planned time, gap, expiry, your own choice, or a roll. In replays, exits are checked only at each day's close.

Exit arithmetic.example: Like a shop that earns Rs 50 on each good sale but loses Rs 150 on each bad one: it needs 3 good sales for every bad one to break even.
Exit arithmetic.forYou: Use it to see why a high win rate alone is not enough.
Exit arithmetic.impact: If your win rate goes up: each trade earns more on average. If it goes down below about 75 percent: the rules lose money.
Exit arithmetic.readIt: When you see the rows for 70, 75, 80 and 85 percent win rates, check which ones are positive.
Exit arithmetic.simple: This shows what the take-profit and stop rules mean for the win rate you need. Wins are capped at half the credit. Losses stop at 1.5 times the credit. So you must win about 3 trades in 4 just to break even.

Exit plan.example: Like deciding when to leave a party: by 10 pm, or earlier if it gets rowdy.
Exit plan.forYou: Set it before committing, not after.
Exit plan.impact: If you widen the stop: losses can grow bigger. If you tighten it: you get stopped more often.
Exit plan.readIt: When you see the defaults, change them only for a written reason.
Exit plan.simple: This holds your profit target, your stop and your time exit. Target and stop are measured against the credit. Defaults are the desk's rules: 50 percent and 1.5 times.

Exit plan set.example: Like booking your return ticket before you leave.
Exit plan set.impact: If you set it: exits are calm. If you skip it: exits are emotional.
Exit plan set.readIt: When you see this rule missed, you had no plan to get out.
Exit plan set.simple: This rule says you set a profit target and a stop. Or you chose to hold a defined-risk trade to expiry. Deciding exits before entry makes them easier to follow.

Exit reason.example: Like a reason code on a return slip at a shop: damaged, wrong size, changed mind.
Exit reason.forYou: One stop wiped out about five take-profits in this sample, so size for the stop, not the win.
Exit reason.goodBad: Checked on daily closes only, so an intraday touch of the stop is not seen.
Exit reason.impact: If stops become more common: losses pile up fast. If take-profits dominate: small wins add up, but one stop can erase five of them.
Exit reason.readIt: When you see exit reasons, count how many stops there were and how much they cost. On the sample, 27 take-profits won Rs 1,349 each on average; 6 stops lost Rs 6,681 each.
Exit reason.simple: Why a backtest trade closed. Take profit at half the credit, stop at 1.5x the credit lost, or held to expiry. Open means it is still running.

Exit rules.example: Like a cricket team's rule to declare at 300 and to change plans if 5 wickets fall early: decided before the match, not in the heat of it.
Exit rules.forYou: Follow them every time; they stop one bad week wiping out many good ones.
Exit rules.impact: If a rule fires: the plan says close or decide now. If nothing fires: hold and wait for the next check.
Exit rules.readIt: When you see a rule marked close or hit, follow it before checking anything else.
Exit rules.simple: These are the playbook's three reasons to close a trade. Take profit at half the credit, and stop at 1.5 times it. Act when a sold strike is tested. They are rules, not forecasts.

Exit rules on real chains.example: Like replaying the same cricket innings with different declaring rules: declare at 300, or bat on. Same batting, different finish.
Exit rules on real chains.forYou: It shows that holding to expiry did worse than taking profit early on this real sample.
Exit rules on real chains.goodBad: Small, mostly low-VIX sample: treat differences as hints, not proof.
Exit rules on real chains.impact: If a different exit shows better numbers here and elsewhere: the desk may switch. If only here: it may be luck in a small sample.
Exit rules on real chains.readIt: When you see this table, compare expectancy and max drawdown across rows. Every exit lost money on this sample. The current one (take profit 50%, stop 1.5x) lost least, about Rs 437 a trade.
Exit rules on real chains.simple: The desk's real past trades, same entries, replayed with different exits. It tries taking profit at half the credit or holding to expiry. Stops at 1x, 1.5x, 2x the credit or none are tried too. A rule changes only if this, the rule research and the stress test all agree.

Expectancy per trade.example: You win Rs 1,400 on 8 days and lose Rs 6,600 on 2 days. The total is minus Rs 2,000 over 10 days. Expectancy is minus Rs 200 a day.
Expectancy per trade.forYou: A seller can win 8 times in 10 and still lose overall; this number catches that.
Expectancy per trade.goodBad: Positive is good; negative means losing on average. It says nothing certain about the next trade.
Expectancy per trade.impact: If it rises above zero: the rules earned on average. If it stays below zero: each trade costs you money on average, however often it wins.
Expectancy per trade.readIt: When you see expectancy, check its sign before the win rate. The desk's weekly rules show minus Rs 437 per trade on 39 trades.
Expectancy per trade.simple: The average rupee result of one trade, one lot, after all costs. Winners and losers are added together and divided by the number of trades. It is the most honest single number.

Expected P&amp;L.example: Like an umbrella seller's average earnings over many days of rain and sun. If he earns Rs 100 on 9 days and loses Rs 500 on 1, the average is Rs 40.
Expected P&amp;L.forYou: Only sell when this is positive, and still check the tail risk.
Expected P&amp;L.impact: If it goes up: the trade has more edge on average. If it goes down or negative: no edge, so skip it.
Expected P&amp;L.readIt: When you see this number, check it is positive. A negative number means the trade loses on average.
Expected P&amp;L.simple: The average profit or loss over all possible outcomes, weighted by their chance. The desk uses the forecast of real moves, not option prices. Otherwise every trade looks exactly fair.

Expected shortfall.example: Like knowing a shop has 5 bad days a year, and they lose Rs 5,000 on average. Size your trade to this number.
Expected shortfall.forYou: Size your lots so this loss would not hurt your account badly.
Expected shortfall.impact: If it goes up: the bad days hurt more, so trade smaller. If it goes down: tail losses are smaller.
Expected shortfall.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with what you can afford to lose. It is the figure a seller should size against.
Expected shortfall.simple: The average loss on the worst days, beyond the VaR line. VaR says where the cliff edge is. Expected shortfall says how far down the fall goes.

Expected value a trade.example: Like a tea stall's average profit per cup: some cups earn Rs 5, some are spilled, average maybe Rs 3. Trading: at 80 percent wins, 0.8 x 0.5 minus 0.2 x 1.5 = 0.1 credit a trade.
Expected value a trade.forYou: Use it to check a strategy pays before costs, then subtract costs.
Expected value a trade.goodBad: Positive means a small average gain per trade; negative means a steady average loss.
Expected value a trade.impact: If it goes up: each trade is worth more on average. If it goes down or negative: the rules lose money at that win rate.
Expected value a trade.readIt: When you see this number, multiply by your credit to get rupees, then remember costs come off.
Expected value a trade.simple: Expected value is the average result of one trade over many trades. Here it is counted in units of the credit, before costs. Positive means the rules make money over many trades at that win rate.

Expiries scanned.example: Like a list of trains to a city, with travel time, stops and the best fare.
Expiries scanned.forYou: It helps you choose which expiry to sell, not just which strike.
Expiries scanned.goodBad: An expiry with nothing scanned had no strike pair liquid enough.
Expiries scanned.impact: If an event falls inside an expiry: its range widens and risk rises. If an expiry has no liquid pair: it cannot be traded safely.
Expiries scanned.readIt: When you see this table, pick the expiry and check its events and expected move first.
Expiries scanned.simple: Each expiry the scanner looked at. It shows the expected move, the open-interest walls and the gamma flip. It also shows events inside and the best edge found. An empty expiry had no liquid strikes to trade.

Expiry.example: Like a cinema ticket that is useless after the show starts. If your NIFTY option expires Tuesday, by then it is worth either something real or zero.
Expiry.forYou: As a seller, close before expiry day, because the last day's risk is not worth its small premium.
Expiry.impact: If expiry gets closer: premium melts faster, but risk per rupee gets much higher. If it is far: decay is slow and moves have more time to reach you.
Expiry.readIt: When you see days to expiry, remember: more days means more premium and more time for trouble. Fewer days means fast decay but fast-changing risk. This desk exits before expiry day.
Expiry.simple: The date an option contract ends and settles. NIFTY has weekly expiries on Tuesday. Time value melts slowly at first, then very fast at the end.

Expiry range 1&sigma;.example: Like a weather forecaster who says tomorrow will be between 28 and 34 degrees and should be right about 2 days in 3. If he is right only half the time, his bands are too narrow.
Expiry range 1&sigma;.forYou: As a seller, trust the band only as much as this hit rate stays near 68%.
Expiry range 1&sigma;.goodBad: Near 68% is good; well below 68% means the band underestimates risk.
Expiry range 1&sigma;.impact: If it goes up well above 68%: the bands have been too wide, so premium was safer than it looked. If it goes down well below: moves have been bigger, so short strikes need more room.
Expiry range 1&sigma;.readIt: When you see this hit rate, compare it with 68%. Close to 68% means the band is honest. Far below means real moves are bigger than the desk expects.
Expiry range 1&sigma;.simple: Each day the desk writes down a price band it expects NIFTY to finish inside at expiry. The 1-sigma band should catch the expiry price about 68 times out of 100. Later it checks how often it really did.

Expiry range 2&sigma;.example: Like saying tomorrow will be between 25 and 37 degrees: almost always right. If that wide band is still wrong 1 day in 10, the weather is wilder than you think.
Expiry range 2&sigma;.forYou: As a seller, short strikes near the 2-sigma line still get hit sometimes, so always keep a protective wing.
Expiry range 2&sigma;.goodBad: Near 95% is good; clearly below 95% means fat tails, so size smaller.
Expiry range 2&sigma;.impact: If it goes down: big moves outside the wide band are more common, so tail risk is higher. If it stays near 95%: the wide band has been a fair guide to the worst cases.
Expiry range 2&sigma;.readIt: When you see this hit rate, compare it with 95%. A few points below 95% means big surprise moves happen more often than the model assumes.
Expiry range 2&sigma;.simple: This is the wider version of the expiry band. It should catch the expiry price about 95 times out of 100. Later the desk checks how often it really did.

Expiry range claim.example: Like promising your mother you will be home between 6 and 8, and being right most days. If the one-sigma claim held 73%, bands were slightly wide.
Expiry range claim.forYou: This is the claim your short strangles live on, so watch its hit rate closely.
Expiry range claim.goodBad: Near 68% for one sigma is good; well below is bad.
Expiry range claim.impact: If it goes above target: bands are wide and premium is left uncollected. If below: bands are too narrow, which costs sellers money.
Expiry range claim.readIt: When you see the hit rate, compare it with 68% or 95%, not 100%.
Expiry range claim.simple: A claim made on the day that NIFTY will settle inside a range at expiry. The one-sigma version should be right about 68% of the time. The two-sigma version about 95%.

Expiry weekday.example: Like a weekly market day that moved from Thursday to Tuesday.
Expiry weekday.forYou: Your weekly trades now end on Tuesdays.
Expiry weekday.impact: If the weekday changes: your trading calendar and old backtests must shift. If not: your routine stays the same.
Expiry weekday.readIt: When you see this, plan entries and exits around Tuesday. Holidays can shift an expiry.
Expiry weekday.simple: The weekday NIFTY options expire. It was Thursday until August 2025. From 1-Sep-2025 it is Tuesday; the monthly is the last Tuesday of the month.

Expiry-day margin.example: Like a landlord asking for an extra deposit on the last day of your lease.
Expiry-day margin.forYou: Keep extra cash ready, or close before expiry day.
Expiry-day margin.goodBad: Extra 2% of notional on expiry day, on top of the base 2%.
Expiry-day margin.impact: If you hold shorts into expiry day: margin jumps and must be covered. If you exit before: you avoid it.
Expiry-day margin.readIt: When you see this, keep spare cash for expiry day. The desk halves size on expiry day for gamma.
Expiry-day margin.simple: On its own expiry day, a short index option needs an extra 2% of its value as margin. Expiring legs also get no margin benefit from a hedge in a later expiry.

FII and DII cash flows.example: Two strong boys pulling a rope from opposite ends: it stays still. If both pull one way, it moves fast.
FII and DII cash flows.forYou: Opposite flows suit range selling; same-side flows warn of a trend.
FII and DII cash flows.goodBad: Sums cover only the sessions the desk has stored.
FII and DII cash flows.impact: If both buy or both sell: NIFTY tends to trend, risky for a range seller. If they offset: NIFTY tends to range.
FII and DII cash flows.readIt: When you see these flows, check if the two groups agree. Agreement over 5 to 20 sessions hints at a trend.
FII and DII cash flows.simple: How much foreign (FII) and Indian (DII) institutions bought or sold in shares, net, in rupees crore. When they are on opposite sides, the index usually ranges. When on the same side, it tends to trend.

FII long share.example: Like a class vote: if only 35 of 100 children say yes, most are against. If that is unusual for this class, watch for a change.
FII long share.forYou: Extremes warn you that a fast move may be near, which threatens short strikes.
FII long share.goodBad: Where it sits against its own history matters more than the level. Extremes tend to unwind.
FII long share.impact: If it falls to an extreme low: heavy shorts may buy back and spark a fast rally. If it rises to an extreme high: a fast fall is possible when they sell.
FII long share.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with its own history, not with 50%. On 13-Nov-2026 it was 35%, about the 52nd percentile since 2021.
FII long share.simple: The share of foreign institutions' index futures that are long (betting on a rise). 50% is balanced. Low means they are mostly short; high means mostly long.

FOMC rate decision.example: Like the RBI setting home-loan rates, but for America. The decision comes out late at night India time, so NIFTY reacts on the next Indian session.
FOMC rate decision.forYou: As a seller, an event that counts makes the side rule stand aside instead of selling; one that does not count is treated like a normal day.
FOMC rate decision.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: this event has been shaking NIFTY more. If it goes down: NIFTY has been treating it like any other day.
FOMC rate decision.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with the normal day's move. The desk counts an event only with 8 or more past cases and a median move at least 1.25 times an ordinary day.
FOMC rate decision.simple: The FOMC is the US central bank committee that sets US interest rates, about eight times a year. Its decision can move the dollar, US bond yields and world markets.

FX & rates.example: Like the exchange counter at an airport showing how many rupees one dollar costs. If USD/INR goes from 84 to 86, the rupee has weakened.
FX & rates.forYou: When the dollar and US yields jump together, expect bigger NIFTY moves and keep your short strikes wider.
FX & rates.goodBad: Neither on its own; it is the weather report for global money.
FX & rates.impact: If US yields and the dollar go up: foreign investors may pull money out of India, a headwind for NIFTY. If they go down: money tends to flow back to markets like India.
FX & rates.readIt: When you see this group, check the rupee and the US 10-year yield first. A weak rupee plus rising US yields often means foreign selling in India.
FX & rates.simple: A group of currency rates and interest rates: the rupee against the dollar, the dollar index, US Treasury yields, the US fear index VIX, and other currencies. Money flows between countries follow these numbers. They show whether foreign money may come into India or leave.

Fail-day result.example: Like playing a match on a waterlogged pitch: on average your team scores less, so you would rather not play.
Fail-day result.forYou: Remember this number when you feel tempted on a stand-aside day.
Fail-day result.goodBad: Below zero means no-edge trades lost money in the test; near the pass-day number means the filter added little.
Fail-day result.impact: If it goes down: trading on no-edge days hurts more. If it goes up toward or above zero: the filter matters less in this sample.
Fail-day result.readIt: When you see a negative number, it is the average cost of trading without the filter's OK.
Fail-day result.simple: This is what the same trade made when entered on a day the filter said stand aside. If it is below zero, each such trade is like paying a tax.

Feature impact.example: Like changing one ingredient in a recipe at a time to see which one really improves the taste.
Feature impact.forYou: It shows which single tweak most protects you.
Feature impact.goodBad: Cuts the tail = smaller 1% tail without a higher chance of a 30% drawdown.
Feature impact.impact: If a change cuts the tail: the rule gets safer. If it only helps when VIX is low: it may hurt when VIX is high.
Feature impact.readIt: When you see this table, look for rows marked cuts the tail. Those shrink the worst losses without raising drawdown risk.
Feature impact.simple: Each rule change tried on its own, compared with the current rules at the same maximum loss. It says which changes cut the tail and which only help in calm times.

Fetch pipeline.example: Like checking whether the milk, sugar and tea all arrived before blaming the cook. If the NIFTY close looks strange, a skipped step or old date usually explains it.
Fetch pipeline.forYou: As a seller, check this before acting on a surprising number, so you do not trade on stale data.
Fetch pipeline.impact: If a step fails or is stale: numbers built on it may be wrong or old. If all steps are fresh: you can trust the page is built on today's data.
Fetch pipeline.readIt: When you see this panel, check each step's status and date. A stale date means old data. A surprising figure is more often a data issue than a real market move.
Fetch pipeline.simple: The list of data steps that ran to build this page. Each step says done, skipped or waiting. Check it first when a number looks odd.

Field.example: Like the left column of a mobile plan card: Data, Calls, Validity. For example the Lot size row might read 100 barrels for CRUDEOIL and 10 barrels for CRUDEOILM.
Field.forYou: As a seller, check lot size, tick value and option expiry here before every new contract. Brokers can ask for more margin than the exchange minimum shown.
Field.goodBad: Neither. It is a label for the rows.
Field.impact: If this happens again: when MCX changes a rule, like the lot size, the row changes and your profit or loss per point changes with it.
Field.readIt: When you see this column, read across each row to compare contracts. Check Lot size and Tick value before you work out your rupee risk.
Field.simple: The first column of the MCX contract specifications table. Each row names one rule of the contract, such as lot size, tick size or option expiry. The other columns give that rule for each MCX contract.

Fill.example: Like paying a little extra to an agent: the shelf price is Rs 100, you pay Rs 101.
Fill.forYou: Count slippage in every trade plan.
Fill.impact: If slippage goes up: each trade costs more. If it goes down: fills are closer to marks.
Fill.readIt: When you see the fill, it is slightly worse than the mark.
Fill.simple: This is the price assumed for your order. It is the mark minus slippage when selling, plus slippage when buying. Slippage is a small extra cost standing in for the gap between buy and sell prices.

Filter pass rate.example: Like a farmer counting rainy days: if only 3 of 10 days bring rain, he plans for 3 sowing days, not 10.
Filter pass rate.forYou: Set your trade count to match it, not your mood.
Filter pass rate.goodBad: High means many good days for sellers; low means the market is rarely paying, so stand aside more.
Filter pass rate.impact: If it goes up: more days suit selling. If it goes down: fewer good days, so expect to wait more.
Filter pass rate.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with how often you trade. Trading more often means some trades had no edge.
Filter pass rate.simple: This is the share of recent sessions when the side rule said sell. The side rule is the desk's buy, sell or stand-aside call. It tells how often the market actually pays a seller.

Fired.example: Like a smoke detector light: on or off.
Fired.forYou: Glance at it to understand today's market mood.
Fired.impact: If a trigger turns to fired: it may pick the lesson. If it stays off: it is ignored today.
Fired.readIt: When you see fired on several triggers, only the top one chose the lesson.
Fired.simple: This says whether the trigger's condition is true in today's data. Only the first trigger that fires picks the lesson. The rest are shown so you can check the choice.

First-try accuracy.example: Like a surprise test versus a test after studying the same paper twice.
First-try accuracy.forYou: Judge yourself by this number, not overall accuracy.
First-try accuracy.goodBad: High means real fluency; low means you rely on retries.
First-try accuracy.impact: If it goes up: you know the skill cold. If it goes down: the skill fades between sessions.
First-try accuracy.readIt: When you see it lower than overall accuracy, retries are flattering your score.
First-try accuracy.simple: This is the share of right answers on your first answer of each day for an exercise. Retries make overall accuracy look better than it is. First tries show what you really know.

Flip side holds.example: Like predicting a cow stays on its side of the river for five days.
Flip side holds.forYou: A high hit rate alone means little because NIFTY often stays on one side anyway.
Flip side holds.impact: If it beats the baseline over time: the flip is useful. If not: it is not.
Flip side holds.readIt: When you see this claim, compare its hit rate with how often any level would hold.
Flip side holds.simple: A forward claim: five sessions later NIFTY is still on the same side of the gamma flip. It is graded after five sessions.

Forecast.example: Like scoring both your winner pick and your run-range guess.
Forecast.impact: If both score well: your forecasting is sound. If one is poor: work on that kind.
Forecast.readIt: When you see the row, check which forecast it is.
Forecast.simple: This says which of your two forecasts the row scores. Your chance of profit is scored by Brier. Your range is scored by whether it held the final settlement.

Forecast calibration.example: Like a forecaster whose 70 percent rain days see rain about 7 times in 10.
Forecast calibration.forYou: Read it over many replays, not one.
Forecast calibration.impact: If it improves: your sense of odds is sharper. If it worsens: you are overconfident.
Forecast calibration.readIt: When you see it, look at the all-replays figures more than this one.
Forecast calibration.simple: This compares your stated chances with what happened, for this replay and all replays. Calibrated means your 70 percent calls come true about 70 percent of the time.

Forecast log.example: Like a diary of your match predictions with the final scores filled in.
Forecast log.forYou: Read back your misses to see what you got wrong.
Forecast log.impact: If more entries resolve: your score becomes more reliable. If many wait: scores are still early.
Forecast log.readIt: When you see an outcome blank, the question has not resolved yet.
Forecast log.simple: This lists your latest 30 forecasts: date, question, your answer, the desk's number and the outcome. Each entry shows when it was locked, so nothing can be changed later.

Forecast realised.example: Like predicting next week's crowd from yesterday, last week and last month. If the forecast is 11% and ATM implied is 13%, the ratio is 1.18.
Forecast realised.forYou: Check that implied is at least 1.10 times this forecast before selling.
Forecast realised.impact: If it goes up: real moves are expected to be larger, so selling gets less attractive. If it goes down: selling looks better paid.
Forecast realised.readIt: When you see this number, divide ATM implied by it. That is the IV/RV ratio.
Forecast realised.simple: The desk's forecast of how much NIFTY will truly move, from daily, weekly and monthly moves. It is the realised volatility forecast. Compared with implied, it decides whether selling is paid.

Forecasts resolved.example: Like a new forecaster with 5 predictions checked: too few to judge her.
Forecasts resolved.impact: If it goes up: your score becomes more trustworthy. If it stays low: keep forecasting.
Forecasts resolved.readIt: When you see a small count, treat your Brier score as a rough early guess.
Forecasts resolved.simple: This counts your forecasts whose outcome is now known. Below it is the number still waiting. Scores mean little until this reaches many dozens.

Foreign exchange pair.example: Like saying 1 dollar buys 100 yen: USD/JPY = 100. If it rises to 105, the dollar got stronger.
Foreign exchange pair.forYou: For India, watch USD/INR rising, which means a weaker rupee.
Foreign exchange pair.impact: If the number goes up: the first currency got stronger. If it goes down: the first currency got weaker.
Foreign exchange pair.readIt: When you see a pair, check which currency comes first before saying which strengthened.
Foreign exchange pair.simple: An exchange rate between two currencies. The first is the base, the second is the quote. The order tells you which currency got stronger when the number moves.

Forward and basis.example: Booking a cinema ticket for next week may cost a bit more than today's show. If NIFTY spot is 25,000 and the forward is 25,060, the basis is 60 points.
Forward and basis.forYou: As a seller, remember your strike distance in the model is measured from the forward, not the screen spot.
Forward and basis.impact: If the basis goes up: futures trade richer than spot, often from longs paying up. If it goes down near expiry: it is behaving normally.
Forward and basis.readIt: When you see this number, the basis should shrink toward zero near expiry. A gap that stays near settlement means positioning, not normal cost. The desk also uses it to check the chain is fresh.
Forward and basis.simple: The forward is the fair price of NIFTY for a future date. The basis is the gap between that and today's spot price. Options are priced from the forward, not spot.

Forward claims on the new signals.example: Like writing your exam predictions in a sealed envelope before results come out.
Forward claims on the new signals.forYou: This is the honest live record to watch over the coming months.
Forward claims on the new signals.goodBad: Needs many graded cases before it means much.
Forward claims on the new signals.impact: If the graded hit rate beats the baseline over many cases: the signal earns trust. If not: it stays unproven.
Forward claims on the new signals.readIt: When you see this table, check how many claims are graded and pending. Most new signal claims started on 13-Nov-2026.
Forward claims on the new signals.simple: From now on, each signal is written down every session and graded later. This record cannot be adjusted after the fact. Trust it more as it grows.

Forward returns after positioning extrem.example: If it rained after 3 of 4 cloudy mornings, that is too few mornings to trust. Read how many mornings first.
Forward returns after positioning extrem.forYou: Use it to check whether a crowded fund position has actually mattered for your market in the past.
Forward returns after positioning extrem.goodBad: A big gap from baseline with many weeks is meaningful; a gap with few weeks is noise.
Forward returns after positioning extrem.impact: If a row's return is well above baseline: that situation has been followed by rises. If below: it has been followed by falls, but only in the past.
Forward returns after positioning extrem.readIt: When you see this table, read the Weeks column first. Then compare the average return and percent up with the any-week row.
Forward returns after positioning extrem.simple: This shows what price did in the 4 weeks after each kind of fund situation. Any week is the baseline to compare with. A row built on few weeks is just a story.

From spot.example: Like the distance in kilometres between you and a toll gate: 200 km away is far, 5 km is near. Trading: NIFTY 24,000 and a 24,500 sold call is 500 points from spot.
From spot.forYou: Use it with sigma away; points tell distance, sigma tells how big that distance is today.
From spot.goodBad: Large positive is safe for a short leg; small or negative is danger.
From spot.impact: If it goes up: the short leg is safer. If it goes down or turns negative: the strike is being crossed and losses grow.
From spot.readIt: When you see a small or negative number on a short leg, that leg is the one at risk.
From spot.simple: Spot is NIFTY's current level. This is the number of points between spot and the strike. It is positive while the option is out of the money. That means it would expire worthless right now.

Front ATM IV.example: Like today's rain chance compared with this week's: today's can jump around more.
Front ATM IV.forYou: Always read it alongside Next ATM IV.
Front ATM IV.impact: If it goes up: options are dearer and sellers get paid more for more risk. If it goes down: premiums shrink.
Front ATM IV.readIt: When you see it much higher than the next expiry, something soon is worrying the market.
Front ATM IV.simple: This is implied volatility, the fear level priced in, for the nearest expiry at the strike closest to NIFTY. Very short expiries have the noisiest IV. Compare it with the next expiry.

Front expiry.example: Like the bus leaving first from the stand: it is the one most people are rushing to catch. If today is Monday 17 Nov and options end on Thursday, Thursday is the front expiry.
Front expiry.forYou: As a seller, the front expiry pays the fastest decay but also carries the sharpest risk on the last day. Size it smaller than a longer expiry.
Front expiry.goodBad: Neither good nor bad; it is simply the clock your nearest options run on.
Front expiry.impact: If it goes up (more days left): premium is bigger and decays slowly. If it goes down (fewer days left): premium melts quickly but a sudden move can hurt sellers fast.
