Front expiry.readIt: When you see the front expiry date, count the sessions left. Fewer sessions means premium melts faster and small moves matter more.
Front expiry.simple: The nearest date on which NIFTY options end. Options for this date have the least time left, so they react fastest to every move. Most of the desk's levels are worked out for this date.

Fund behaviour statistics.example: A shopkeeper notes that buyers come more on salary week. That is a habit, not a rule for any one buyer.
Fund behaviour statistics.forYou: Use these habits to know what usually drives funds in crude or gas, not to predict any one week.
Fund behaviour statistics.goodBad: A strong figure with many weeks is a solid habit; a weak one is not useful.
Fund behaviour statistics.impact: If a correlation grows stronger: that habit has been more reliable. If it weakens: the habit has faded.
Fund behaviour statistics.readIt: When you see a correlation, below 0.1 is negligible and above 0.5 is strong. Check n, the number of weeks behind it.
Fund behaviour statistics.simple: Measured habits of funds in this market over all stored weeks. Do they follow price, do they predict next month, who takes the other side. These are correlations, not reasons.

Fund breadth.example: If onion prices rise because 50 small traders each buy a little, the demand is broad. If one big trader buys a whole truck, it is narrow and can vanish if he changes his mind.
Fund breadth.forYou: Be more careful selling premium against a move that rests on a handful of big funds.
Fund breadth.goodBad: A high and rising count means broad support; a falling count means the bet is thinning out.
Fund breadth.impact: If the count goes up: more funds share the view, so the move is sturdier. If it goes down: fewer funds hold it, so a sudden reversal is more likely.
Fund breadth.readIt: When you see these counts, compare them with the change in contracts. Rising longs with rising trader count is broad buying. Rising longs with a flat count is concentration.
Fund breadth.simple: This counts how many separate funds hold long bets and how many hold short bets. It shows whether a move is broad or narrow. Many funds joining is broad; a few big funds is narrow.

Futures build-up.example: Like more shops opening on a busy street: new money is coming in. If crude rises 1% and open contracts rise 5%, that is a long build-up and votes +1.
Futures build-up.forYou: Treat a short build-up as a reason to keep short puts further away.
Futures build-up.impact: If new long positions build: the vote is up. If new short positions build: the vote is down; exits count for nothing.
Futures build-up.readIt: When you see this row, find which of four boxes it falls in. Long build-up votes +1, short build-up -1; short covering and long unwinding vote 0. Roll days vote 0.
Futures build-up.simple: Reads price change together with the change in open contracts. Price up and contracts up means new buyers. Price down and contracts up means new sellers.

Futures contract.example: Like booking a train seat on a fixed train: a different train has a different fare. MCX crude and Brent crude can differ by several dollars.
Futures contract.forYou: Make sure the contract you watch is the one your trade depends on.
Futures contract.impact: If the contract changes: price and positions belong to the new one. If you compare two contracts: expect gaps between them.
Futures contract.readIt: When you see a futures row, read its contract name and source.
Futures contract.simple: A standard agreement traded on an exchange for one named market and terms. Different contracts for the same thing can have different prices. WTI, Brent and MCX crude are not the same series.

GARCH(1,1).example: After a heavy rain day, you expect more rain for a few days, slowly fading. After a 400-point NIFTY day, GARCH raises the forecast, then lowers it over the following weeks.
GARCH(1,1).forYou: As a seller, when GARCH and HAR-RV disagree, use wider strikes or smaller size.
GARCH(1,1).goodBad: A high forecast means rough days ahead; a low one means calmer days.
GARCH(1,1).impact: If it goes up: bigger moves are expected soon. If it goes down: calmer days are expected.
GARCH(1,1).readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the HAR-RV forecast. It is a cross-check, not the main forecast. If the two disagree a lot, widen your band.
GARCH(1,1).simple: A model that guesses tomorrow's market movement. It blends a long-run average, yesterday's guess and yesterday's actual move. It captures that wild days tend to come in groups.

GST.example: Like GST added to a restaurant's service charge, not to the bill for food you take home.
GST.forYou: Fewer orders means less brokerage and less GST.
GST.goodBad: 18% on brokerage, exchange charge and SEBI fee.
GST.impact: If brokerage rises: GST rises with it. If you trade fewer orders: GST falls.
GST.readIt: When you see GST, read it as 18% extra on your broker and exchange fees.
GST.simple: Goods and Services Tax, 18%, added on brokerage, the exchange charge and the SEBI fee. It is not charged on the premium itself.

Gamma by expiry.example: Like checking which class in a school is the noisiest. The headmaster watches that class most.
Gamma by expiry.forYou: It tells you which expiry's strikes to watch for your trade.
Gamma by expiry.goodBad: Net is the desk's estimate under its assumption. Gross treats every contract as hedged, so it is an upper bound.
Gamma by expiry.impact: If one expiry's gamma grows: its strikes matter more for price this week. If it falls: that expiry stops steering NIFTY.
Gamma by expiry.readIt: When you see this table, look at which expiry has the largest net number at spot. That expiry drives the pinning or the pushing this week.
Gamma by expiry.simple: The same gamma numbers split by expiry date. It shows which expiry carries the most hedging pressure. Net counts only the sellers' share; Gross counts all open contracts.

Gamma flip.example: Like the line on a slope where a ball stops rolling back and starts rolling away. On 13-Nov-2026 the flip was 25,589 with NIFTY at 25,144.
Gamma flip.forYou: Keep your short strikes in mind against this level, but do not treat it as a wall.
Gamma flip.goodBad: The desk's test: NIFTY stayed on its side of the flip 83% of the time. A random level held 85%, so the flip did not beat chance.
Gamma flip.impact: If spot moves toward the flip: the calming effect weakens. If spot crosses it: moves may grow faster, so wide short strikes matter more.
Gamma flip.readIt: When you see the flip number, compare it with spot. A flip 400-plus points away gives room; a flip close to spot means the mood can change soon.
Gamma flip.simple: The NIFTY level where option sellers switch from calming the market to speeding it up. Above or below it, their hedging works in opposite ways. The desk finds it on a grid within 7% of spot.

Gamma flip test.example: Like checking if a line painted on a road really stops cars better than a line nobody painted.
Gamma flip test.forYou: Do not rely on the flip as a barrier for your strikes.
Gamma flip test.impact: If the flip beat the mirror: it would act as a barrier. Since it did not: it is not a barrier.
Gamma flip test.readIt: When you see this test, compare rates. Flip: 83% of 53 windows; mirror level: 85%; p = 0.69.
Gamma flip test.simple: Five sessions later, is NIFTY still on the same side of the gamma flip? It is compared with a level the same distance on the other side.

Gamma profile as spot moves.example: Like a road that is flat up to a village and then turns downhill. Below the village a cycle rolls slowly; past it, it speeds up.
Gamma profile as spot moves.forYou: It shows how far NIFTY can travel before the market's mood can change from calm to fast.
Gamma profile as spot moves.goodBad: It is a snapshot: each strike keeps today's IV and open interest, which change in a real move.
Gamma profile as spot moves.impact: If NIFTY moves toward the zero crossing: the calming effect fades. If it moves past it: hedging may add speed to the move.
Gamma profile as spot moves.readIt: When you see this line, find where it crosses zero and how far that is from today's NIFTY. Then check if your short strikes sit on the calm side or the fast side.
Gamma profile as spot moves.simple: A line showing the sellers' total gamma if NIFTY were at a different level today. Where the line crosses zero is the gamma flip. On one side moves are calmed, on the other side they spread.

Gamma regime claim.example: Like predicting the river stays calm while the dam is strong.
Gamma regime claim.forYou: It is the most promising of the new signals, but still unproven.
Gamma regime claim.impact: If it keeps being right: calm gamma days favour sellers. If not: the regime does not matter.
Gamma regime claim.readIt: When you see this claim, track its graded hit rate as cases build up.
Gamma regime claim.simple: A forward claim: when sellers are long gamma, real volatility over five sessions stays under front implied volatility. When short, it does not.

Gamma regime test.example: Like testing if a strong dam calms a river more than a weak one. There was always some dam.
Gamma regime test.forYou: It is the only signal with a weak hint of working, so use it lightly.
Gamma regime test.goodBad: Verdict: weak (p under 0.25 but not under 0.05).
Gamma regime test.impact: If the gap grows with more data: the regime signal helps. If it shrinks: it is noise.
Gamma regime test.readIt: When you see this test, read the two medians. Strong long gamma: 9.1% vol; weaker: 10.6%; p = 0.15.
Gamma regime test.simple: Is real volatility over the next five sessions lower when option sellers are long gamma? Sellers were long gamma on 313 of 315 days. So the test compares strong against weaker long gamma.

Gap move.example: Like a fire drill: imagine the alarm rings at 3 percent, 5 percent and 8 percent and see what you would lose.
Gap move.forYou: Look at the worst column before every new trade.
Gap move.impact: If the loss in these columns grows: you hold more crash risk. If it shrinks: the book can absorb shocks better.
Gap move.readIt: When you see the minus 5 or minus 8 percent column, remember it is the hopeful crash case.
Gap move.simple: This shows the position valued as if NIFTY opened that many percent up or down. It uses today's volatility. In a real fall fear usually rises, so the real down-gap loss can be worse.

Gap scenarios.example: You plan to sell mangoes at Rs 50, but the mandi opens with everyone at Rs 80. You never got a chance at Rs 50. If NIFTY closed at 25,000 and opens at 25,600 after budget news, your 25,500 short call is already in loss.
Gap scenarios.forYou: As a seller, size your trade so the worst gap on this table is a loss you can survive.
Gap scenarios.goodBad: A large gap loss means the trade is too big or unprotected; a small one is survivable.
Gap scenarios.impact: If the gap loss goes up: you need a smaller trade or a wing to cap it. If it goes down: the trade can survive a bad open more easily.
Gap scenarios.readIt: When you see this table, look at the worst gap row first, not the best. Ask: could I live with this loss? If not, the trade is too big, whatever the probability of profit says.
Gap scenarios.simple: What your trade is worth if NIFTY opens far away from yesterday's close. A stop loss cannot help here, because no trading happens in between. This number should decide how big your trade is.

Gasoline.example: Like the wholesale price of petrol before taxes are added at your local pump. If gasoline is 2.10 dollars a gallon and rises to 2.40, petrol is getting costlier worldwide.
Gasoline.forYou: It matters for Indian refiners and oil-marketing stocks, and through fuel prices, for inflation.
Gasoline.goodBad: Neither; good for refiners when high, bad for consumers.
Gasoline.impact: If it goes up: fuel inflation rises and refining margins usually improve. If it goes down: fuel gets cheaper and refiners may earn less.
Gasoline.readIt: When you see the gasoline price, compare its move with crude. Gasoline rising faster than crude means refiners are earning more.
Gasoline.simple: The world price of petrol, from the RBOB gasoline future traded in New York, in US dollars per gallon. It shows what refiners earn from turning crude into petrol. It moves with crude but also with driving season.

Gate.example: Like a school register mark: present, late with a note, or not recorded.
Gate.forYou: Compare overridden trades with passed ones each month.
Gate.impact: If overridden trades go up: more trades break your own rules. If passed trades go up: your entries follow the rules.
Gate.readIt: When you see overridden, read the reason you wrote and how that trade ended.
Gate.simple: This shows how a trade got through the pre-trade gate. Passed means all hard rules held. Overridden means a hard rule failed and you wrote why. Not gated means it was added from before the gate existed.

Generator validation.example: Like checking a flight simulator flies like a real plane before trusting a pilot trained on it.
Generator validation.forYou: It tells you how far you can trust the stress test.
Generator validation.goodBad: Closer to the real NIFTY row is better.
Generator validation.impact: If a model matches the real numbers: its results are more believable. If it misses fat tails or gaps: its tail numbers are too kind.
Generator validation.readIt: When you see this table, compare each model's row with the real NIFTY row. Big gaps mean that model is less trustworthy.
Generator validation.simple: Checks that each model's fake NIFTY behaves like the real one. It compares swings, fat tails, wild spells, gaps and VIX. A model that misses these would make the stress test too gentle.

Global bias.example: Before a cricket match, you check the weather: clouds mean the game may be choppy, but clouds do not tell you who wins. If crude oil jumped 3% overnight, NIFTY at 25,000 may open with a gap, even if the option chain looked calm yesterday.
Global bias.forYou: As a seller, a strongly negative reading means keep your put further away, not bet on a fall.
Global bias.goodBad: A big number either way means a rougher day; near zero means a quiet night abroad.
Global bias.impact: If it moves far from 0 either way: a big opening gap is more likely. Short strikes near spot then carry more risk. If it stays near 0: the world gave little push, and the usual range is more likely to hold.
Global bias.readIt: When you see this number, read its size first. Near 0 is a quiet night; near -60 or +60 is a big one. Then check whether today's expected range is wide enough to cover a gap. If too little data came in, the page hides the number instead of showing a fake calm 0.
Global bias.simple: One number from -100 to +100 for what the world did to India overnight. It adds up crude oil, the dollar, US interest rates, metals and food prices. Negative means a headwind, positive means a tailwind. It tells you how big a day may be, not which way it goes.

Global context.example: Like checking the weather in nearby cities before deciding whether to carry an umbrella. If US stocks fell 2% overnight and crude jumped, NIFTY may open weak.
Global context.forYou: As a seller, a weak world tape means more overnight gap risk for short puts.
Global context.goodBad: Neither; it is background, not a trade signal.
Global context.impact: If the global tone turns up: India tends to open with support. If it goes down: gap-down risk rises for the next open.
Global context.readIt: When you see this section, read the overall bias it gives for India first, then the details behind it.
Global context.simple: This section shows what markets around the world did and what that suggests for India today. It covers things like US stocks, the dollar, crude oil and bond yields.

Global tape &rarr; India read.example: Like hearing the weather on the road before your auto ride: heavy rain means a slower trip. A reading of -30 means a rough overnight world for India.
Global tape &rarr; India read.forYou: On a strongly negative day, give short puts more room; this number has not been graded for direction.
Global tape &rarr; India read.impact: If it goes up: the world helped India overnight. If it goes down: the world hurt; respect a bigger downside, but do not short on it alone.
Global tape &rarr; India read.readIt: When you see this number, use it for how big the day may be, not which way. No number is shown when reporting drivers cover under 66% of the total weight.
Global tape &rarr; India read.simple: One number from -100 to +100 for what the world did to India overnight. It adds up oil, the dollar, US rates, metals and food prices. Negative is a headwind, positive a tailwind.

Glossary.example: Like a dictionary that also tells you when a word does not matter.
Glossary.forYou: Look terms up here; practise them in the lessons.
Glossary.impact: If you look things up here first: lessons go faster. If you skip it: lessons may feel confusing.
Glossary.readIt: When you see a Practise this link, follow it to the lesson that drills the term.
Glossary.simple: This explains every core term on the desk in plain words, with today's numbers. Each entry shows what it is, what it changes about a decision, and when it is noise.

Gold (MCX).example: Like buying imported mangoes: the price depends on the foreign price, the exchange rate, and the import tax. If world gold is flat but the rupee weakens 1%, MCX gold rises about 1%.
Gold (MCX).forYou: Before selling gold options, check both the dollar gold price and the rupee, since either can move your strikes.
Gold (MCX).impact: If it goes up: long gold positions gain and short calls lose. If it goes down: the reverse, and short puts get closer to danger.
Gold (MCX).readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the world price row. Check whether today's move came from gold itself or from the rupee.
Gold (MCX).simple: The price of gold as traded in India on MCX, in rupees per 10 grams. It moves with the world gold price, the rupee, and a local extra charge. A rupee move alone can change it on a quiet world day.

Gold, real yields and the dollar.example: When fixed deposit rates rise, people may buy less gold. When the rupee weakens, gold in India costs more.
Gold, real yields and the dollar.forYou: Watch the rupee too, because it moves your MCX gold position.
Gold, real yields and the dollar.goodBad: A strong negative link means gold reacts to the dollar; a weak link means it is not reacting now.
Gold, real yields and the dollar.impact: If the dollar or yields go up: gold often faces pressure. If the rupee weakens: MCX gold rises even if world gold is flat.
Gold, real yields and the dollar.readIt: When you see the yearly correlations, check if the link is strong this year. It is unstable.
Gold, real yields and the dollar.simple: Gold often falls when the dollar or US bond yields rise. The link is real on average but changes year to year. MCX gold also depends on the dollar-rupee rate.

Gold/silver ratio.example: Like how many kilos of onions one kilo of almonds buys. If the ratio is 90, silver looks cheap; at 65, it looks dear.
Gold/silver ratio.forYou: Use it to choose between gold and silver before trading, not to time a trade.
Gold/silver ratio.impact: If it goes up: silver is getting cheaper against gold. If it goes down: silver is getting dearer.
Gold/silver ratio.readIt: When you see this number, check its rank over one year and ten years. It does not vote.
Gold/silver ratio.simple: How many ounces of silver one ounce of gold buys. High means silver is cheap against gold. It has mostly stayed between 65 and 90 for a decade.

Gross longs.example: Like counting how many people in your colony bought umbrellas expecting rain. If funds hold 180,000 long gold contracts and 40,000 short, gross longs are 180,000 and the net is 140,000.
Gross longs.forYou: As a seller, a rally with rising gross longs has more fuel, so do not sell calls too close.
Gross longs.goodBad: Neither by itself. Very high gross longs can mean a crowded trade.
Gross longs.impact: If it goes up: funds are adding new bets on a rise, a stronger sign than short covering. If it goes down: funds are selling longs, often after losses or to lock in profit.
Gross longs.readIt: When you see this line, ask whether the net is moving because funds are buying or because shorts are being covered. A rise in gross longs is fresh buying.
Gross longs.simple: The total number of contracts that managed money funds hold betting on a rise. It counts only the buying side, before taking away the shorts. The net position is gross longs minus gross shorts.

Gross shorts.example: Like shopkeepers who sold rice they do not yet have, hoping to buy it cheaper later. If funds hold 60,000 short copper contracts, a sudden rise forces many of them to buy back.
Gross shorts.forYou: As a seller, very high gross shorts mean a sudden rally (a squeeze) is possible, so keep short calls further away.
Gross shorts.goodBad: Neither by itself. A big short pile is fuel for a sharp rally.
Gross shorts.impact: If it goes up: funds are adding bets on a fall. If it goes down: funds are buying back shorts, which pushes price up for a while.
Gross shorts.readIt: When you see this line, check whether a rise in net comes from falling gross shorts. That is short covering, which can be sharp but often fades.
Gross shorts.simple: The total number of contracts that managed money funds hold betting on a fall. It counts only the selling side, before taking it away from the longs. Shorts that are bought back are called short covering.

Guard rails.example: Like a monthly spending limit you set on your card: once set, you cannot raise it on a whim.
Guard rails.forYou: Set them on a calm day and leave them alone for the week.
Guard rails.impact: If limits are tight: you lose less on bad days but may trade less. If they are loose: they protect less.
Guard rails.readIt: When you see a lock active, new entries wait; exits are always allowed.
Guard rails.simple: These are your own loss limits, cooling-off after a stop, and smaller size after losses. You set them once and they lock for a week. They are experimental. Your journal measures whether they help.

HAR-RV forecast.example: Guessing tomorrow's mango price from yesterday's, last week's and last month's prices together. For NIFTY, a wild day raises the forecast, and calm weeks pull it back down.
HAR-RV forecast.forYou: As a seller, it lets you judge today's option price against a real forecast instead of against itself.
HAR-RV forecast.goodBad: A high forecast means bigger moves expected; a low one means calmer days expected.
HAR-RV forecast.impact: If it goes up: expected future moves are bigger, so IV / RV falls and selling is less attractive. If it goes down: IV / RV rises and selling looks better paid.
HAR-RV forecast.readIt: When you see this number, use it as the RV side of the IV / RV ratio. Check its R-squared, which shows how well it fits. It is slow to spot sudden breaks.
HAR-RV forecast.simple: A forecast of coming market movement. It mixes three time spans: yesterday, last week and last month. Each gets its own weight.

Habit.example: Like a batsman who keeps getting out to the same shot; the shot needs fixing, not the player's worth.
Habit.forYou: Fix one habit at a time.
Habit.impact: If a habit appears more: it costs more over time. If less: the rule is working.
Habit.readIt: When you see a habit named, read the rule that prevents it.
Habit.simple: A habit is a mistake that keeps coming back. Examples: selling cheap premium, skipping the stop, trading too big. Each habit names the rule that prevents it. The habit is graded, never the person.

Habits.example: Like ticking reasons a dish went wrong: too much salt, too little time.
Habits.forYou: Tick honestly; hidden habits cannot be fixed.
Habits.impact: If more habits are ticked: more mistakes were made. If fewer: cleaner trades.
Habits.readIt: When you see habits ticked, check if the same ones repeat across trades.
Habits.simple: These are the habits ticked in a paper trade's review. They are pre-filled from the checklist. Each one goes to the mistake log with an even share of any loss.

Hard rules (a failed rule blocks unless.example: Like the rules at a petrol pump: no smoking, engine off. Break one and you are stopped unless there is a real emergency.
Hard rules (a failed rule blocks unless.forYou: Treat a failed hard rule as a stop sign, not a speed bump.
Hard rules (a failed rule blocks unless.impact: If one fails and you override: the trade is counted as an override and compared later. If all pass: the trade is compliant.
Hard rules (a failed rule blocks unless.readIt: When you see a red hard rule, read its detail line; it says exactly what failed.
Hard rules (a failed rule blocks unless.simple: These are must-pass checks in the pre-trade gate. They are: side rule says sell, defined risk, per-trade cap, book cap, no lock, exit plan written. A failed one blocks the trade unless you type a reason.

Heating oil.example: Like the diesel price that decides truck freight in India. If heating oil goes from 2.30 to 2.60 dollars a gallon, transport costs rise worldwide.
Heating oil.forYou: High diesel prices push up Indian inflation, which can delay RBI rate cuts and weigh on NIFTY.
Heating oil.goodBad: For India, lower is usually better.
Heating oil.impact: If it goes up: freight and inflation pressure rise. If it goes down: transport gets cheaper and inflation pressure eases.
Heating oil.readIt: When you see heating oil, compare it with crude. Diesel rising faster than crude points to strong industrial demand or tight supply.
Heating oil.simple: The world price of diesel-type fuel, from the NYMEX heating oil (ULSD) future, in US dollars per gallon. Trucks, ships, farm machines and factories run on this fuel. It is a good gauge of real economic activity.

Heavy short gamma.example: Like a crowd that runs the same way as soon as a few people start running. If NIFTY falls 100 points and hedgers must sell more futures, the fall can grow.
Heavy short gamma.forYou: As a seller, short-gamma days are when big moves happen faster, so keep wings on.
Heavy short gamma.impact: If this turns on: dealer hedging is making moves bigger. If it turns off: hedging is neutral or calming again.
Heavy short gamma.readIt: When you see this row, it shows what buying the at-the-money straddle on such days would have earned, held to expiry.
Heavy short gamma.simple: This buy reason is present when option writers are short gamma at today's spot. Their hedging then pushes price further in the direction it is already moving.

Held, wide.example: Like carrying an umbrella every day in a dry month. If NIFTY moved 50 points inside a 400 point band, it held, wide.
Held, wide.forYou: If this count is high, you may be able to sell a little closer, carefully.
Held, wide.impact: If it goes up: bands are too wide, and premium is left for others. If it goes down: bands are tighter.
Held, wide.readIt: When you see this number, a high count means the bands may be too cautious.
Held, wide.simple: The outcome stayed inside the band with lots of room to spare. It suggests the band was wider than needed. Too many of these means the desk quotes ranges that cannot be wrong.

High &minus; close.example: Like a ball thrown high that falls back down. If the high was 25,200 and close 25,050, this is 150.
High &minus; close.forYou: A rally that gets sold often eases pressure on short calls.
High &minus; close.impact: If it goes up: sellers took control by the close. If it goes down: the close held near the high.
High &minus; close.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with close minus low. If this is bigger, the day closed in its lower half.
High &minus; close.simple: How far the close is below the day's high. A big number means sellers pushed the price down from the top. It shows whether a rally was sold.

History band.example: Like checking ten years of monsoon records, not just last month's weather. Say the cone is Rs 68,600 to Rs 71,400 for gold. If history says Rs 67,500 to Rs 72,500, expect bigger moves.
History band.forYou: Place strikes outside whichever is wider, the cone or the history band.
History band.impact: If it is wider than the cone: size your trade to the wider range. If narrower: recent times are noisier than usual.
History band.readIt: When you see this band, compare it with the cone. If the band is wider, recent calm may not last.
History band.simple: What moves of the same length actually did over the last ten years. It covers the same middle share of moves as the one-sigma cone. It includes big crisis years, so it shows fat tails.

History breach.example: Like checking how often a river crossed the danger mark in 18 monsoons, not just the forecast.
History breach.forYou: It is a reality check on the market's odds for your short strike.
History breach.goodBad: Lower is safer. Overlapping windows mean the cases are not fully independent.
History breach.impact: If the breach rate rises: past data says your strike is more often crossed. If it falls: history supports the strike.
History breach.readIt: When you see history breach, compare it with POP. If history breaches more often than the smile says, be careful.
History breach.simple: It counts how often NIFTY closed beyond a strike this far away, in the same number of sessions. It uses daily closes since 2007. It checks the market's odds against what really happened. Closes only, so intraday touches are more common.

History depth.example: Judging a new batsman after 3 matches tells you little; after 50 you know him. An IV rank from 30 NIFTY sessions means almost nothing.
History depth.forYou: As a seller, do not lean on a rank or percentile that only just has enough history.
History depth.goodBad: Deep history means ranked numbers are meaningful; shallow history means they are thin and unreliable.
History depth.impact: If it goes up: more numbers become reliable and get shown. If it is low: percentiles and rankings stay hidden or should be trusted less.
History depth.readIt: When you see this number, check if it is above the usable window. When a hidden number appears for the first time, it only just crossed the line. Treat those early readings with extra care.
History depth.simple: How many past sessions are stored, compared with how many are needed. Ranks and percentiles need enough history to mean anything. Too little, and the desk hides the number.

Hold vs plan.example: Like staying at a party long after you said you would leave; the trouble often starts late.
Hold vs plan.forYou: Close on the planned day unless the plan itself says otherwise.
Hold vs plan.goodBad: Zero overstays is good; many means time exits are being ignored.
Hold vs plan.impact: If overstays go up: more risk in the last days near expiry. If they go down: you keep to time exits.
Hold vs plan.readIt: When you see trades held past plan, look at what made you stay.
Hold vs plan.simple: This shows how long trades were held, and how many stayed past the time exit in your plan. Holding to expiry is where most of the March 2020 losses sat.

Horizon.example: Like asking how far a train goes in 1 day versus 1 week. A one-week range for crude is much smaller than a two-month range.
Horizon.forYou: Pick the horizon that ends on your option's expiry and read only that row.
Horizon.impact: If the horizon is longer: the range is wider, growing with the square root of time. If shorter: the range is narrower.
Horizon.readIt: When you see a horizon, match it to how long your trade will live. A two-month range is no help for a one-week trade.
Horizon.simple: The future date a range is drawn to, counted in trading days. The page uses 5, 10, 22 and 44 trading days, plus the contract's expiry. Holidays are not counted, so the real date can be a day later.

How MCX options work.example: Like a cinema ticket that is only valid on the show date.
How MCX options work.forYou: Know that metals can go to delivery, so exit before expiry.
How MCX options work.goodBad: There is no high or low; it explains the mechanics.
How MCX options work.impact: If an option ends in the money: it becomes a futures position. If out of the money: it expires worthless.
How MCX options work.readIt: When you see this lesson, note lot sizes. Gold is 1 kg, silver 30 kg, crude 100 barrels.
How MCX options work.simple: MCX options are European, so they can only be used at expiry. They are options on futures. In the money at expiry, they turn into futures at the strike.

How a range is built.example: Like measuring a trip in school days, not including Sundays. If NIFTY is 25,000 with 12% implied and 4 trading days left, the band is about 380 points.
How a range is built.forYou: Make sure your short strikes clear the trading-day range, not a calendar-day one.
How a range is built.impact: If implied volatility goes up: the range widens. If time left goes down: the range narrows.
How a range is built.readIt: When you see a range, check it used trading days. Calendar days would make strikes look safer than they are.
How a range is built.simple: The range is the price times implied volatility, scaled by the square root of time left. Time is counted in trading days, not calendar days. Using calendar days makes the band about 18% too wide on a 4-day expiry.

How far can NIFTY go?.example: Like asking how often the river rose 2 metres in past monsoons. If 500 points lower happened in 8% of cases, that strike was reached 8 times in 100.
How far can NIFTY go?.forYou: Choose short strikes where the reach chance is small enough for you.
How far can NIFTY go?.impact: If volatility goes up: the chances of big moves rise. If it goes down: they fall.
How far can NIFTY go?.readIt: When you see this table, find your strike's distance and read the chance. History since 2007 includes the 2008 and 2020 crashes.
How far can NIFTY go?.simple: How often, in past cases, NIFTY ended that many points lower or higher. It counts over the same number of sessions. Past moves are resized to today's volatility. The larger of resized and raw counts is shown.

ICE Gasoil.example: Like the diesel rate at a big port that many smaller towns copy. Indian refiners export diesel, so this market affects what they earn.
ICE Gasoil.forYou: As a seller, it is background only, since no Indian option trades on it.
ICE Gasoil.goodBad: Neither. It is a market, not a score.
ICE Gasoil.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish on European diesel. If it goes down: they are less bullish or adding shorts.
ICE Gasoil.readIt: When you see this row, compare it with ULSD / heating oil. If both show fund buying, the diesel view is broad.
ICE Gasoil.simple: The European diesel future on ICE in London, low-sulphur gasoil in lots of 100 tonnes. It is the main diesel benchmark for Europe. No price series is stored for it on this page.

IV / RV.example: Like an umbrella seller charging Rs 110 when rain usually costs him Rs 100. A ratio of 1.10 means 10% extra pay for the risk.
IV / RV.forYou: Sell only when this is at least 1.10; between 0.95 and 1.10 the edge is thin.
IV / RV.goodBad: Higher is better for sellers; the desk wants at least 1.10, and stands aside below 0.95.
IV / RV.impact: If it goes up: sellers are paid more for the risk. If it goes down: premium is too cheap to sell.
IV / RV.readIt: When you see this number, above 1.10 means selling is paid. Below 0.95 the desk stands aside.
IV / RV.simple: Implied volatility divided by the forecast of real movement. It shows if options are priced above the risk they usually carry. This is the seller's edge.

IV / RV &mdash; the seller&rsquo;s edge.example: An insurer charges Rs 110 for risks that cost Rs 100; the ratio is 1.10. If NIFTY IV is 13 and forecast RV is 11, the ratio is about 1.18.
IV / RV &mdash; the seller&rsquo;s edge.forYou: As a seller, this is the main gate on whether to sell at all today.
IV / RV &mdash; the seller&rsquo;s edge.goodBad: Above 1.10 is a fair price for selling; below 0.95 is underpaid risk.
IV / RV &mdash; the seller&rsquo;s edge.impact: If it goes up: sellers are paid more for the risk. If it goes down below 1: stand aside, because a smaller bad trade is still a bad trade.
IV / RV &mdash; the seller&rsquo;s edge.readIt: When you see this ratio, above about 1.10 means selling is paid. Below 0.95 means it is not. In between, be careful.
IV / RV &mdash; the seller&rsquo;s edge.simple: IV divided by forecast realised volatility. Above 1 means options charge more than moves have cost. Below 1 means they charge less.

IV percentile.example: Like being taller than 80 of 100 children in your school. If IV percentile is 80, options are dear compared with most days.
IV percentile.forYou: Use it with the IV/RV ratio; a high percentile alone does not mean selling is paid.
IV percentile.impact: If it goes up: options cost more than usual, a better time for sellers if the edge holds. If it goes down: premiums are thin.
IV percentile.readIt: When you see this number, use it to judge if premium is unusually rich or cheap today.
IV percentile.simple: The share of past days that had lower implied volatility than today. 80 means today is higher than 80% of days. It is harder to fool than IV rank.

IV percentile test.example: Like checking if fruit sold when prices are high leaves more profit after spoilage.
IV percentile test.forYou: It leans the right way but is not proven, so do not lean on it.
IV percentile test.impact: If the gap holds with more data: high IV would be a useful sell signal. For now it is not proven.
IV percentile test.readIt: When you see this test, compare rates. High IV: 57% of 46; low IV: 44% of 16; p = 0.28.
IV percentile test.simple: When front implied volatility is high against its own history, does a sold straddle survive more often? Percentile 50 or more is compared with under 50.

IV rank.example: Like your marks placed between your worst and best test this year. If one test was a freak 99, every other mark looks low.
IV rank.forYou: Prefer IV percentile when deciding whether today's option prices are unusual.
IV rank.impact: If it goes up: options are priced richer than usual this year. If it goes down: they are cheaper.
IV rank.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with IV percentile. If they disagree, one spike is distorting the rank.
IV rank.simple: Where today's implied volatility sits between this year's lowest and highest. 0 means at the low, 100 at the high. One spike can stretch the range and fool it.

IV rank and percentile.example: In a class of 100, percentile 68 means you scored more than 68 children. Rank 25 means your score is a quarter of the way from lowest to highest mark.
IV rank and percentile.forYou: Sellers are paid most when both are high, so it shows quickly how well you are paid.
IV rank and percentile.goodBad: Higher is better for a seller; both high together is the strongest sign. The desk's test of IV percentile 50 or more did not beat chance.
IV rank and percentile.impact: If both rise: you collect more premium for the same risk. If both fall: premium is thin, so the same risk pays less.
IV rank and percentile.readIt: When you see these two numbers, look for both high together. On 13-Nov-2026 front IV rank was 25 and percentile 68: mixed, not clearly rich.
IV rank and percentile.simple: Two ways to say if option prices are high or low against their own past. Rank puts today between the year's lowest and highest. Percentile counts how many past days were lower.

IV rank vs IV percentile.example: If one day hit 45 degrees, a 35-degree day ranks low on the scale but hotter than most days. If NIFTY IV rank is 20 but percentile is 50, one old spike is stretching the scale.
IV rank vs IV percentile.forYou: As a seller, trust the percentile when deciding if premium is rich enough today.
IV rank vs IV percentile.goodBad: High percentile means rich premium versus history; low means cheap premium.
IV rank vs IV percentile.impact: If both go up: options are rich versus the past, and selling is paid more. If both go down: options are cheap, and selling is paid less.
IV rank vs IV percentile.readIt: When you see both, prefer percentile to judge if today is unusual. Use rank only for distance from the extremes. A big gap between them means one outlier is distorting rank.
IV rank vs IV percentile.simple: IV rank shows where today's IV sits between the year's lowest and highest. IV percentile shows what share of days had lower IV than today. One wild spike can make them disagree.

IV term structure.example: Like an umbrella seller who charges more for a whole month of cover than for one day. If he charges more for tomorrow, he expects a storm tomorrow.
IV term structure.forYou: It shows if the expiry you plan to sell is priced for calm or for a storm.
IV term structure.goodBad: Back above front is the normal calm shape; front above back (inverted) signals near-term fear.
IV term structure.impact: If near-term IV rises above far IV: fear is near, premium is rich but risk is high. If near IV falls below far IV: the normal calm shape returns.
IV term structure.readIt: When you see near IV above far IV (inverted), the market fears the next few days. Check the events calendar next.
IV term structure.simple: IV, or implied volatility, is the market's guess of how much NIFTY will swing, built into option prices. This chart shows that guess for each expiry. Normally far expiries have a higher guess than near ones.

IV-implied.example: Like a taxi meter quote for the whole trip before you start. Say NIFTY is 25,000, implied volatility is 12%, and 5 trading days remain. The range is about plus or minus 420 points.
IV-implied.forYou: Check that your short strikes sit outside this band before selling.
IV-implied.impact: If implied volatility goes up: the band widens and options cost more. If it goes down: the band narrows and premiums shrink.
IV-implied.readIt: When you see this band, treat it as the market's own number. It assumes up and down moves are equal in size, which is not true.
IV-implied.simple: The range the option market itself is pricing until expiry. It is the price times the implied volatility, scaled by the square root of trading days left. It uses no history at all.

IV-implied band.example: Like a taxi fare quote based only on today's meter rate. If NIFTY is 25,000, IV is 13% and 4 trading days remain, the band is roughly plus or minus 400 points.
IV-implied band.forYou: As a seller, this is the market's own range, a starting point before the other four checks.
IV-implied band.impact: If IV goes up: this band widens. If IV goes down: it narrows.
IV-implied band.readIt: When you see this band, compare it with the four others. It assumes up and down moves are equal, which is not true. If it is wider than the skew-corrected band, that is the reason.
IV-implied band.simple: A range made only from the at-the-money IV. It is spot times IV, scaled by the square root of trading days left. It uses no past data at all.

IV/RV gate.example: A trader sells umbrellas only if the price is at least 10% above what rain usually costs him.
IV/RV gate.forYou: It keeps you out when premium is cheap against the expected moves.
IV/RV gate.goodBad: Higher gate = fewer but better-paid trades.
IV/RV gate.impact: If the gate is raised: fewer trades, each better paid. If removed: more trades, some underpaid.
IV/RV gate.readIt: When you see gate rows, compare 'no gate', '1.10' and 'as a size scaler' on test results.
IV/RV gate.simple: IV/RV means implied volatility divided by the desk's forecast of real volatility. The gate sells only when implied is high enough versus the forecast. The current rules need at least 1.10.

If-then exit plan.example: Like deciding before a road trip: if it rains we stop at the dhaba, if we are late we skip the temple.
If-then exit plan.forYou: Write each exit in rupees or points so there is nothing to argue with later.
If-then exit plan.impact: If you write it clearly: exits are easier to follow under stress. If you skip it: decisions get made in panic.
If-then exit plan.readIt: When you see unticked boxes, the gate blocks until all four exits are confirmed.
If-then exit plan.simple: This is a plan you write before the trade. It says what you do at the target, at the stop, at a set time, and after a gap. All four must be confirmed.

If-then playbook.example: Like a cricket captain's plan: if the pitch turns, bring the spinner; if it rains, defend. If NIFTY closes above the 25,500 ceiling, the plan says which spread to roll.
If-then playbook.forYou: Decide your actions in advance from the branches, so you are not deciding in a panic.
If-then playbook.impact: If NIFTY reaches a ceiling or floor: follow that branch. If it breaks through: the plan says add, roll or exit.
If-then playbook.readIt: When you see the playbook, read the starting position first, then the branches. Each branch is based on the daily close.
If-then playbook.simple: A plan for the next few sessions, not one single trade. It has a starting position and branches. Branches cover a drift, a run to a ceiling, a break above it, or a fall to a floor.

Implied event move.example: If insurers charge extra for one stormy day, that extra shows how big a storm they expect.
Implied event move.forYou: Compare it with the real past move to see if event risk is fairly priced.
Implied event move.goodBad: Larger than past moves means event premium is rich; smaller means cheap.
Implied event move.impact: If it goes up: options price a bigger event jump. If it goes down: a smaller one.
Implied event move.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the past event-day move. If n/a, no index exists.
Implied event move.simple: The one-day move that the option market prices for an event. It comes from OVX for crude or GVZ for gold. Silver, copper and gas have none.

Implied forward.example: Like a mango booked today for delivery next week, with a small storage charge added. If NIFTY is 25,000, the forward might be 25,040.
Implied forward.forYou: Measure strike distances from the forward, not just spot, near expiry.
Implied forward.impact: If it goes up versus spot: futures demand or carry cost is higher. If it goes down: there is pressure from sellers or a dividend.
Implied forward.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with spot. The gap is the basis.
Implied forward.simple: The price the option market says NIFTY trades at for delivery on expiry day. It is worked out from many call and put pairs, not assumed. It is usually a little above today's price.

Implied volatility.example: Like insurance prices for crops no insurer covers.
Implied volatility.forYou: No option selling is possible without implied vol.
Implied volatility.impact: Nothing to compare here. If a series gets options: implied vol becomes available.
Implied volatility.readIt: When you see this card, note that no implied vol means no premium to measure.
Implied volatility.simple: What the option market prices for future movement. None is stored for these series. Tier 1 contracts with options have it.

Implied volatility (IV).example: Like insurance prices going up before monsoon; the price itself tells you the fear. If NIFTY IV jumps from 12 to 16, every option gets dearer, even if NIFTY does not move.
Implied volatility (IV).forYou: As a seller, high IV pays you more per risk, but that does not mean it pays you enough.
Implied volatility (IV).goodBad: High IV means rich premium and a nervous market; low IV means thin premium and calm.
Implied volatility (IV).impact: If IV goes up: option prices rise, so a seller loses even if NIFTY stays still. If IV goes down: option prices fall, helping a seller.
Implied volatility (IV).readIt: When you see IV, watch the change more than the level. A 15% one-day jump in VIX is this desk's signal to cut size. Compare IV with RV to see if selling is paid.
Implied volatility (IV).simple: IV is how much movement the option price is charging for. It is worked out backwards from the price people pay. It is not a forecast anyone made.

Implied vs realised move.example: Like a weather forecaster saying 50 mm of rain. If only 30 mm falls, umbrella sellers were overpaid. If 80 mm falls, they were underpaid.
Implied vs realised move.forYou: It tells you if selling straddles has actually paid in this market lately.
Implied vs realised move.goodBad: Above 50% hit rate and a positive edge favour sellers. Recently the last 20 cases kept only 40%, a warning.
Implied vs realised move.impact: If real moves come in smaller than implied: sellers keep money. If they come in bigger: buyers win and sellers lose.
Implied vs realised move.readIt: When you see this chart, read the hit rate and the average edge together. Over 311 stored cases the hit rate was 53% and the average edge was about minus 4 points.
Implied vs realised move.simple: Every day, the at-the-money straddle price says how far NIFTY may move by expiry. This chart compares that guess with the real move. It shows if sellers were paid enough.

In sample.example: Like a student's score on the practice paper she already saw.
In sample.forYou: Do not judge the model by this number alone.
In sample.impact: If the gap to out of sample grows: the model overfits more. If it shrinks: it is more honest.
In sample.readIt: When you see it much lower than out of sample, the model is flattered by its own data.
In sample.simple: This is the error on the days the price model was fitted on. It is shown only to compare with the out-of-sample figure.

In sample and out of sample.example: Practising on last year's exam paper is in sample. This year's new paper is out of sample.
In sample and out of sample.forYou: Judge any rule only by its test columns.
In sample and out of sample.goodBad: Strong test results are encouraging; strong training results alone prove nothing.
In sample and out of sample.impact: If test results drop far below training: the rule was overfit. If they hold up: the rule may be real.
In sample and out of sample.readIt: When you see this table, look only at the test columns. Check expectancy per lot, win rate and the worst trade.
In sample and out of sample.simple: In sample means the years used to choose the rule. Out of sample means new years it never saw. Only the out-of-sample columns are evidence.

Index Price/Earnings.example: Paying Rs 2,000 for a shop that earns Rs 100 a year is a P/E of 20. If NIFTY's P/E is in its top 10% of history, it is expensive, but that says nothing about tomorrow.
Index Price/Earnings.forYou: As a weekly seller, this barely affects tomorrow, but extremes hint how hard a shock could hit.
Index Price/Earnings.goodBad: Very high means expensive, with more to unwind in a shock; low means cheap, not safe.
Index Price/Earnings.impact: If it goes up into the top range: a shock could cause a bigger fall. If it goes down to the bottom range: prices are cheaper, but that is about years, not days.
Index Price/Earnings.readIt: When you see this number, look at its percentile, not just the level. It matters only at extremes. A very high reading tells you how far a shock could drag prices.
Index Price/Earnings.simple: The index level divided by the total profit of its companies over the past year. It shows how costly the market is. The desk ranks today against every stored day.

Index futures.example: Like booking a fixed price with a vegetable seller for next month's supply. If BANK NIFTY is 56,000 and its future is 56,200, buyers are paying 200 points to wait a month.
Index futures.forYou: Use the other indices to confirm NIFTY: if BANK NIFTY futures turn cheap while NIFTY is calm, banks may pull NIFTY down later.
Index futures.goodBad: Neither; liquid rows are trustworthy, untraded rows are not.
Index futures.impact: If basis goes up: buyers are keen to hold longs. If it goes down: the future is cheap against the index, often a sign of caution.
Index futures.readIt: When you see an index futures table, read the rows marked liquid first and compare basis across expiries.
Index futures.simple: A future is a deal to buy or sell an index on a set date at a price agreed today. NSE lists futures on several indices, not only NIFTY. This tab shows each one's price, basis, carry, open interest and volume by expiry.

Index points.example: In a cricket team total of 100, you check how many runs each batsman scored. If NIFTY rose 100 points and one bank added 40, it carried much of the day.
Index points.forYou: As a seller, a NIFTY move carried by one or two stocks can reverse more easily.
Index points.impact: If one stock's points go up: that stock is driving NIFTY. If points are spread thin across many: the move is broad, not one stock's story.
Index points.readIt: When you see this column, look for the few stocks with the biggest numbers. On a near-flat day, the desk may hide it, because stocks cancel each other out.
Index points.simple: How many NIFTY points one stock added or removed today. It is the stock's move times its weight. It shows real movers, not just loud ones.

India CPI.example: Like checking how much more your household spends on vegetables, milk and rent than last year. It comes out after the market closes, so the move shows on the next open.
India CPI.forYou: As a seller, an after-close release means overnight gap risk for open shorts.
India CPI.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: inflation data has been moving NIFTY more. If it goes down: NIFTY has been calm on these days.
India CPI.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with an ordinary day's move and check whether Counts says yes.
India CPI.simple: India CPI is the monthly measure of how fast prices are rising in India. Food is a big part of it, and it shapes what the RBI does with rates.

India VIX.example: Like an insurance premium that rises when floods are forecast. A high VIX pays you more because the market expects to hurt you more.
India VIX.forYou: Check the IV/RV ratio, not the VIX level, to decide if selling is paid; below 12.5 always buy wings.
India VIX.impact: If it goes up: premiums rise, ranges widen, and every short strike carries more risk. If it goes down: premium is thin; below 12.5 the desk wants wings.
India VIX.readIt: When you see this number, check its change and level. A VIX of 12 is calm; 20 is jumpy (a rough rule of thumb, not a desk number).
India VIX.simple: The market's own estimate of how much NIFTY may move over the next month, as a yearly percent. Rising VIX means bigger moves are priced. Below 12.5, the desk makes protective wings compulsory.

India VIX in the bottom 20% of its year.example: Like a quiet weekday morning on a highway with almost no traffic. If VIX ranged 11 to 20 over the year and sits at 11.5 today, this is on.
India VIX in the bottom 20% of its year.forYou: As a seller, low VIX pays little, and a sudden VIX rise from here hurts, so do not sell closer or bigger to make up for it.
India VIX in the bottom 20% of its year.goodBad: Calm for now, but thin pay for the risk.
India VIX in the bottom 20% of its year.impact: If this turns on: the market is calm and premium is thin. If it turns off: VIX has risen back toward normal.
India VIX in the bottom 20% of its year.readIt: When you see this state ON, options are cheap compared with their own year. The table shows how NIFTY moved after such calm spells.
India VIX in the bottom 20% of its year.simple: This is on when India VIX is lower than on 80% of days in the past year. The market is calm and option prices are cheap.

India VIX in the top 20% of its year.example: Like hotel rates in Goa during Christmas week: higher than almost any other time of year. If VIX ranged 11 to 20 over the year and sits at 19 today, this is on.
India VIX in the top 20% of its year.forYou: As a seller, you collect more premium, but the market is also moving more, so wings and size matter more than usual.
India VIX in the top 20% of its year.goodBad: Good for premium collected, bad for the size of moves.
India VIX in the top 20% of its year.impact: If this turns on: fear is high and premium is rich. If it turns off: VIX has fallen back toward normal.
India VIX in the top 20% of its year.readIt: When you see this state ON, options are expensive compared with their own year. The table shows how long such spells lasted and how big NIFTY's moves were afterwards.
India VIX in the top 20% of its year.simple: This is on when India VIX is higher than on 80% of days in the past year (252 sessions). Fear and option prices are high compared with recent history.

Indian contract.example: Some vegetables are sold at your local mandi; others only in big city markets. If it is not sold locally, you cannot buy it here.
Indian contract.forYou: Only plan trades on markets where MCX lists options.
Indian contract.goodBad: Options listed means tradable; none means read-only.
Indian contract.impact: If MCX adds options: the market can get a trade plan. If there is no contract: there is nothing to trade here.
Indian contract.readIt: When you see this label, check options, futures only, or none. With no Indian contract, the desk always stands aside.
Indian contract.simple: Whether this market trades in India at all. MCX lists options on gold, silver, copper, zinc, crude and gas. Aluminium, lead and nickel have futures only.

Iron condor / short strangle.example: Betting the score stays between 150 and 200; the condor version also buys insurance past each side. If NIFTY is 25,000, sell 25,500 CE and 24,500 PE, and the condor also buys 25,700 CE and 24,300 PE.
Iron condor / short strangle.forYou: As a seller, the condor turns a possible account-ending day into a known, bad but survivable loss.
Iron condor / short strangle.impact: If NIFTY stays in the range: both earn premium as time passes. If NIFTY moves fast through one side: the strangle's loss has no limit, while the condor's is capped.
Iron condor / short strangle.readIt: When you see which one is suggested, check India VIX. This desk uses a condor below VIX 12.5. Above that, a strangle can be justified.
Iron condor / short strangle.simple: A short strangle sells a call above NIFTY and a put below it. It wins if NIFTY stays between them. An iron condor adds bought protection beyond each, capping the loss.

Is premium rich.example: Like checking if a mango seller is charging 100 rupees a kilo when last month it was 60. If options price a 1% daily move and NIFTY actually moves 0.7%, premium is rich.
Is premium rich.forYou: As a seller, sell when premium is rich and sell less or wait when it is cheap.
Is premium rich.impact: If it goes up (richer): sellers are paid more for the risk. If it goes down (cheaper): sellers are paid too little.
Is premium rich.readIt: When you see this section, check IV rank and percentile, the volatility cone and implied versus realised moves. The side rule sells only when implied is at least 1.10 times forecast realised volatility.
Is premium rich.simple: This section asks whether options are expensive compared with their own past and with how much NIFTY actually moves. Sellers want rich premium: paid more than the moves usually cost.

Journal an existing position.example: Like adding last month's bills to a new expense app so your total is complete.
Journal an existing position.forYou: Use it once for each older trade so nothing is missing.
Journal an existing position.impact: If you journal old trades: your metrics become complete. If you skip them: the record has gaps.
Journal an existing position.readIt: When you see not gated on a trade, it was added this way and skipped the checklist.
Journal an existing position.simple: This adds a diary entry for a trade opened before the gate existed. Then its exit can still be scored. The entry is marked as not gated.

Kelly fraction.example: A coin pays Rs 2 on heads and costs Rs 1 on tails. Kelly says bet a quarter of your money. If the coin pays nothing extra, bet nothing.
Kelly fraction.forYou: Never size above half of Kelly. With Kelly at zero, the desk's numbers show no edge to size up.
Kelly fraction.goodBad: Zero means no edge; the desk caps size at half of Kelly.
Kelly fraction.impact: If Kelly rises: the rule has a bigger edge. If it is zero: there is no edge to size up.
Kelly fraction.readIt: When you see Kelly, read it as a ceiling, not a target. For the current rules it is 0, so the desk recommends no size.
Kelly fraction.simple: Kelly is a formula for the share of capital to risk that grows money fastest in theory. It uses the win rate and the size of wins and losses. If a rule loses on average, Kelly says risk zero.

Kupiec test.example: Like checking if a coin that landed heads 55 times in 100 is really unfair, or just lucky.
Kupiec test.forYou: Trust it more as the number of cases grows.
Kupiec test.impact: If p goes down below 0.05: the band likely misses its target. If p goes up: no evidence of a problem.
Kupiec test.readIt: When you see p above 0.05, the band is not proven wrong; it is not proven right either.
Kupiec test.simple: This test checks whether a band's coverage differs from its target by more than chance. A p-value above 0.05 means the record cannot reject the band. It is weak with under 100 cases.

LTP and premium.example: Like the price of the last mango sold, which may be an hour old. If the NIFTY 25,500 call's LTP is Rs 40 but nobody has traded for hours, you may not get Rs 40.
LTP and premium.forYou: As a seller, premium is pay for risk, not profit; take it only when IV / RV is fair.
LTP and premium.impact: If premium goes up after you sell: your trade is losing. If it goes down: your trade is gaining.
LTP and premium.readIt: When you see LTP, check the volume and bid-ask too. At busy strikes near spot, LTP is reliable. Far strikes can show a stale LTP.
LTP and premium.simple: LTP is the last traded price of an option. Premium is the price of the option. For a seller, it is the money you receive when you sell.

Ladder replay.example: Like checking if a recipe's promised taste matched the real dish, every day for months. If it won 75% with an average of Rs 400, the quotes held up.
Ladder replay.forYou: Trust the ladder's expected profits only as far as the replay supports them.
Ladder replay.impact: If replay results go up: the ladder's quotes have been earned. If they go down: the quotes are too hopeful.
Ladder replay.readIt: When you see this, read trades, expiries, win rate and average rupees. The expiry count is the honest sample size.
Ladder replay.simple: Every stored day is run through the same expiry ladder and held to expiry. Only what was known that day is used. It checks whether the quoted expected profits were really earned.

Largest leg.example: If a shop's net stock rises by 10 bags, it matters whether 10 new bags came in or 10 sold bags got returned.
Largest leg.forYou: Before selling calls into a crude rally, check whether it is driven by short covering that may fade.
Largest leg.goodBad: New positions show conviction; exits show pressure that usually passes.
Largest leg.impact: If fresh buying leads: the move is backed by new money. If short covering leads: the rally may stop once sellers finish buying back.
Largest leg.readIt: When you see this label, fresh buying means conviction. Short covering is often fear and can fade fast. Check the second tag, like de-risking, which reads both legs together.
Largest leg.simple: It shows which side of fund bets moved more this week. It could be fresh buying, buyers quitting, sellers buying back, or fresh selling. The same net change can mean different things.

Largest move.example: Like a flood measured against normal river levels: 3 times normal is rare but happens.
Largest move.forYou: Note how your plan handled the biggest day.
Largest move.impact: If it goes up: the path had wild days. If it goes down: the path was calm.
Largest move.readIt: When you see 3 or more, that day would have tested any short strike.
Largest move.simple: This is the biggest one-day move in the revealed path. It is measured in sigmas, using the previous day's India VIX. A 3-sigma day should be rare, but markets make them far more often.

Lean.example: Like a class vote where toppers' votes count double. If the total is +4 and the threshold is 3, the lean is up.
Lean.forYou: Use the lean only to choose which side of the range to defend more carefully, never as a forecast.
Lean.impact: If the score goes up past the threshold: the lean turns up. If it falls below the negative threshold: the lean turns down; in between it is none.
Lean.readIt: When you see a lean, check its score against the threshold of about 3. Also check its graded record; no hit rate is quoted until 20 leans have resolved.
Lean.simple: The desk's tilt on direction for one market. Each evidence row votes up, down or nothing, with a weight, and the votes are added. Past the threshold it says up or down; inside it, none.

Learning days.example: Like counting the days you went to the gym this year, not how many days in a row.
Learning days.forYou: Study a little on many days rather than a lot on a few.
Learning days.impact: If it goes up: more spaced practice. If it stays flat: you have not studied recently, with no penalty.
Learning days.readIt: When you see this number grow, your practice is spread over many days, which helps memory.
Learning days.simple: This counts the separate days on which you studied. Any question, forecast, case, replay debrief or exam set counts. It is not a streak. Missing a day costs nothing.

Learning levels.example: Like school classes 1 to 6: you can sit in class 5, but class 3 maths helps.
Learning levels.forYou: Work roughly in order; skip ahead only if you can answer unaided.
Learning levels.impact: If a bar goes up: you have finished more of that level. If it stays low: that level needs time.
Learning levels.readIt: When you see the bar under a level, it shows the share of its lessons done.
Learning levels.simple: The course has six levels, from basics to professional. They cover base rates, contracts and rupees, pricing, selling and risk, evidence, and sizing, rules and tax. Later levels assume the earlier ones.

Learning section.example: Like a driving school with a simulator: it builds skill and judgement, but it cannot promise you will never crash.
Learning section.forYou: Spend short, regular sessions here rather than long, rare ones.
Learning section.impact: If your scores here go up: your arithmetic and judgement of odds improve. If they go down: revisit the weak lessons.
Learning section.readIt: When you see this section, start with Your next step if you have ten minutes.
Learning section.simple: This is a course for option sellers built on the desk's own data. It has lessons, exercises, a forecast trainer, case studies and myth cards. It trains skills you can measure. It does not measure or promise trading profit.

Lesson.example: Like a chapter in a textbook with a short test at the end.
Lesson.forYou: Use New questions to practise again with fresh numbers.
Lesson.impact: If your answers become right more often: the skill is forming. If misses repeat: they show on the progress tab.
Lesson.readIt: When you see close on an answer, your method was right but the arithmetic slipped.
Lesson.simple: One lesson has a goal, a wrong belief it fixes, references, a live example and two or three questions. The worked example stays hidden until you ask. That keeps your first try honest.

Lesson trigger.example: Like a school bell schedule: the first bell that rings decides the next class.
Lesson trigger.forYou: Use it to learn which market conditions matter most to a seller.
Lesson trigger.impact: If a market condition becomes true: its lesson takes over. If none do: the lesson follows your habit.
Lesson trigger.readIt: When you see the trigger list, the first one marked fired picked the lesson.
Lesson trigger.simple: A trigger is a market condition that chooses today's lesson. Triggers are checked in a fixed order; the first true one wins. The last one always fires and points to your costliest habit.

Lessons done.example: Like finishing a chapter once versus being able to explain it on three different days.
Lessons done.forYou: Aim for mastered, not just done.
Lessons done.impact: If done goes up: you have covered more ground. If mastered goes up: the skills are sticking.
Lessons done.readIt: When you see done much higher than mastered, come back to those lessons after a gap.
Lessons done.simple: This counts lessons whose questions you answered right at least once, out of all lessons. Underneath is the number mastered. Mastered means every question right, without help, on three different days.

Livestock cycles.example: Like milk, which cannot be stored for long, so each month has its own price.
Livestock cycles.forYou: Read for context, as there are no Indian livestock options.
Livestock cycles.impact: If a disease hits: supply falls and prices jump. If supply grows: prices ease.
Livestock cycles.readIt: When you see this lesson, note the seasonal pattern and the shock replay.
Livestock cycles.simple: Hog prices have seasons and cattle have multi-year cycles. Livestock cannot be stored, so each month is priced on its own supply. It also replays the 2014 hog disease shock.

Long leg.example: Like a helmet: it costs Rs 1,000 and you hope never to use it, but it limits how bad a fall can be.
Long leg.forYou: Keep one behind every short leg so a gap cannot sink the account.
Long leg.impact: If you remove it: the worst loss can become unlimited. If you move it closer: the cap gets tighter but it costs more.
Long leg.readIt: When you see a long leg, check it sits behind each short leg on the same side and expiry.
Long leg.simple: A long leg is an option you bought. It costs money but it caps the loss of a short leg next to it. In a spread it is the wing that turns unlimited risk into a known worst case.

Long share.example: If 8 of 10 neighbours expect onion prices to rise, the long share is 80%. Few are left to turn buyers.
Long share.forYou: Use it to compare crowding across energy markets of different contract sizes.
Long share.goodBad: Very high or very low means one-sided crowding; near half means a balanced market.
Long share.impact: If it goes up: funds are more one-sided long, so a sharp drop on bad news is likelier. If it goes down: more funds are betting on a fall.
Long share.readIt: When you see this percent, near 50% means funds disagree. Near 80% or 20% means strong agreement. It is unit-free, so you can compare crude with petrol.
Long share.simple: It is fund longs divided by all fund longs plus shorts. 50% means evenly split; 80% means four longs for each short. It shows how one-sided the funds are.

Longest losing streak.example: A batsman out for low scores five matches in a row may be dropped, even if he is good. Streaks test patience.
Longest losing streak.forYou: Prepare for longer streaks than any backtest shows. The stress test puts 3 losses in a row within 50 trades at 35%.
Longest losing streak.goodBad: Shorter is easier; a trade at exactly zero after costs is not a loss.
Longest losing streak.impact: If streaks get longer: confidence and capital get tested harder. If shorter: the rule is easier to follow.
Longest losing streak.readIt: When you see this number, plan for a longer one in real life. In the small stored sample it was only 1 loss in a row.
Longest losing streak.simple: The most losing trades in a row in the sample. Long streaks make sellers quit a rule at the worst moment.

Lookback window.example: Judging a batsman on 5 innings is quick but jumpy; on 50 it is steady but slow. If NIFTY's 10-day volatility is far above its 63-day volatility, something new has started.
Lookback window.forYou: As a seller, when short-window volatility jumps, widen your strikes instead of chasing the higher premium.
Lookback window.impact: If the short window goes up above the long one: risk is rising now, so widen strikes. If it goes down below: things are calming.
Lookback window.readIt: When you see several windows, check if they agree. When short is far above long, the market is changing. When they agree, the reading is steadier.
Lookback window.simple: How many past days a number is calculated from: 10, 21 or 63 days. 21 is about a month and 63 about three months. Short windows react fast; long ones are steady.

Looks today.example: Like counting how often you checked your phone in an hour.
Looks today.forYou: Aim for only your planned looks.
Looks today.goodBad: Low is calm; high often comes with nervous exits.
Looks today.impact: If it goes up: more chances to react emotionally. If it goes down: calmer days.
Looks today.readIt: When you see a high count, ask whether any look led to a useful action.
Looks today.simple: This counts how many times you opened My positions today. It counts only this browser.

Losing trades, one at a time.example: Like a quiz show where you lock your answer before the reveal, so you cannot pretend you knew.
Losing trades, one at a time.forYou: Lock your choice first every time.
Losing trades, one at a time.impact: If you judge well before the reveal: your decision skill improves. If you only judge after: hindsight fools you.
Losing trades, one at a time.readIt: When you see a case, judge the decision on what was known at entry, not on the result.
Losing trades, one at a time.simple: Each losing backtest trade is a case, mixed with winners so you cannot guess the ending. You see the entry, decide, then see what happened. Then you ask which rule would have changed it.

Lot size.example: Like mangoes sold only in boxes of 65. You cannot buy just 10.
Lot size.forYou: Your risk per lot depends on it, so recheck sizing when it changes.
Lot size.impact: If the lot size rises: each lot's gain and loss grow. If it falls: they shrink.
Lot size.readIt: When you see lot size, multiply points by 65 for rupees. A 20-point gain is Rs 1,300 per lot.
Lot size.simple: The number of NIFTY units in one contract. It is 65 since January 2026; it was 75 before. Profit per lot is points times lot size.

Lots.example: Like eggs sold only by the tray of 30, never one at a time. Trading: a 10-point move on 2 lots of 65 is Rs 1,300.
Lots.forYou: Pick lots from your risk budget, never from your mood.
Lots.impact: If lots go up: every point moves more rupees, both ways. If lots go down: gains and losses both shrink.
Lots.readIt: When you see this number, multiply by the lot size to get units per point.
Lots.simple: A lot is the fixed bundle size the exchange sets for each option. This shows how many lots the leg holds. Rupee P&L equals price change times lots times lot size.

Lower 1 sigma.example: Like a forecast that the night will probably not drop below 22 degrees. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the 1-sigma move to expiry is 500 points, the lower 1 sigma is 24,500.
Lower 1 sigma.forYou: As a seller, short puts at or beyond this line are a common starting point, but give puts a little extra room.
Lower 1 sigma.goodBad: Neither; a guide for where to place short puts.
Lower 1 sigma.impact: If it goes up: NIFTY has risen or expected moves have shrunk. If it goes down: NIFTY has fallen or options are charging for bigger moves.
Lower 1 sigma.readIt: When you see this level, read it as a floor that holds about 2 times in 3. Real falls come faster than rises, so it gets tested more.
Lower 1 sigma.simple: This is the bottom edge of the range NIFTY is expected to stay inside by expiry about 68 times out of 100. It comes from today's implied volatility.

Lower 2 sigma.example: Like a dam built for the worst flood in 20 years. If NIFTY is 25,000 and 1 sigma is 500 points, the lower 2 sigma is 24,000.
Lower 2 sigma.forYou: As a seller, keep a protective long put near here so a crash cannot wipe out many months of premium.
Lower 2 sigma.goodBad: Neither; an outer guide, not a guarantee.
Lower 2 sigma.impact: If it goes up: NIFTY has risen or the market expects calmer moves. If it goes down: NIFTY has fallen or options are pricing bigger possible falls.
Lower 2 sigma.readIt: When you see this level, read it as the outer floor. Crashes cross it more often than the normal model says.
Lower 2 sigma.simple: This is the bottom edge of the wider range NIFTY should stay inside by expiry about 95 times out of 100. It is twice the 1-sigma distance below spot.

MACD above its signal line.example: Like a cyclist who has been speeding up for the last few days compared with his usual pace. If NIFTY climbs from 24,600 to 25,000 in a week, MACD usually moves above its signal line.
MACD above its signal line.forYou: As a seller, this alone is a weak, very common signal, so do not move strikes just because it flipped. Check the table's verdict first.
MACD above its signal line.goodBad: Neither; it is on roughly half of all days, so it carries little news by itself.
MACD above its signal line.impact: If this turns on: short-term momentum has turned up. If it turns off: the upward push has faded, which often happens without any big fall.
MACD above its signal line.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY's recent push is up. The table shows how long such spells lasted and how NIFTY behaved over the next 5, 10 and 21 sessions compared with an ordinary day.
MACD above its signal line.simple: MACD compares a fast average of NIFTY (12 days) with a slow one (26 days). The signal line is a 9-day average of MACD itself. When MACD is above it, short-term push is upward.

MACD below its signal line.example: Like a car that is slowing down compared with how it drove last week. If NIFTY slips from 25,000 to 24,700 over a week, MACD usually drops below its signal line.
MACD below its signal line.forYou: As a seller, treat this as background, not a reason to panic out of short puts. Only the table's verdict tells you if it ever mattered.
MACD below its signal line.goodBad: Neither; it is a common, mild state.
MACD below its signal line.impact: If this turns on: short-term momentum has turned down. If it turns off: the selling push has faded.
MACD below its signal line.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY's recent push is down. The table shows spell lengths and how NIFTY moved over the next 5, 10 and 21 sessions against an ordinary day.
MACD below its signal line.simple: MACD compares a fast average of NIFTY (12 days) with a slow one (26 days). The signal line is a 9-day average of MACD. When MACD is below it, short-term push is downward.

MCX close-to-close 21.example: Like checking prices at your own local market, not just the city average. If MCX crude moves about 2% a day, this reads about 32%, because 2% times the square root of 252 is about 32.
MCX close-to-close 21.forYou: As a seller, if this is well above the forecast, the forecast may be too low for MCX, so ask for more premium.
MCX close-to-close 21.goodBad: Neither by itself. It matters only against implied vol and the forecast.
MCX close-to-close 21.impact: If it goes up: the MCX contract has been jumpier, so sold MCX options are riskier. If it goes down: the MCX contract has been calmer.
MCX close-to-close 21.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the 21-day realised on the world price. If MCX moves clearly more, the rupee or local trading is adding extra movement.
MCX close-to-close 21.simple: How much the MCX contract itself moved over its last 21 sessions, written as a yearly percentage. It compares each MCX close with the one before. The other vol numbers on this card use the world price, so this one checks them against the Indian contract.
