MCX contract.example: Like changing from this month's bus pass to next month's: the fare difference is not a real price rise. Without this fix, a 4% gap between crude months would look like a 4% crash.
MCX contract.forYou: Make sure the contract you trade matches the one the page is analysing.
MCX contract.impact: If the contract rolls: the shown price switches to next month's contract. The desk rolls 3 days before expiry.
MCX contract.readIt: When you see a contract date, check it is the one your options are on. A step on the chart at a roll is not a real move.
MCX contract.simple: Each futures price belongs to one expiry month. The page shows the nearest contract more than 3 days from expiry. When it switches to the next month, the small price jump is removed from calculations.

MCX contract specifications.example: Like the rules on a ration card: how much, at what price unit, and on which days.
MCX contract specifications.forYou: Always check lot size and tick value before trading, especially in gold.
MCX contract specifications.goodBad: Big lots mean big risk per trade; small lots give finer control.
MCX contract specifications.impact: If the lot is large: each tick costs more and risk per trade grows. If you use a mini: risk per lot is smaller.
MCX contract specifications.readIt: When you see this table, check lot, tick value and margin. Gold is quoted per 10 grams but one lot is 1 kg.
MCX contract specifications.simple: The rules for each MCX contract: lot size, quote unit, tick, expiry, trading hours, margin and settlement. A tick is the smallest price step. Tick value is what one tick is worth on one lot.

MCX option contract.example: Like a bus pass that says route, fare and validity date, this tells you what one option covers and when it ends.
MCX option contract.forYou: Check rupees per point before sizing, because gold's 1 kg lot moves a lot of money.
MCX option contract.goodBad: A large lot means bigger risk per trade; a mini lot keeps risk smaller.
MCX option contract.impact: If rupees per point is high: each price move hits your account harder. If you use a mini contract: the risk per lot is smaller.
MCX option contract.readIt: When you see this card, check rupees per point. It is what one lot gains or loses per 1-point move. Then check the next expiry date.
MCX option contract.simple: The terms of an MCX option: lot size, strike gaps and expiry date. MCX options are on the futures contract. They expire a few business days before the future.

MCX option costs.example: Like the GST, packing and delivery charges added to a food bill.
MCX option costs.forYou: Include all costs before deciding a small premium is worth selling.
MCX option costs.goodBad: Low costs help; high costs eat small edges.
MCX option costs.impact: If costs go up: thin trades become unprofitable. If they go down: more trades make sense.
MCX option costs.readIt: When you see this table, add the charges to your expected profit. Rows marked secondary come from broker copies.
MCX option costs.simple: Every charge on an MCX option order, with its rate. CTT is a tax: 0.05% of premium on sells. MCX charges Rs 41.80 per lakh of premium since October 2024.

MCX parity.example: If gold costs Rs 60,000 abroad and duty adds Rs 6,000, fair Indian gold is Rs 66,000. If Mumbai sells at Rs 66,500, the extra Rs 500 is the premium.
MCX parity.forYou: Use it to see if MCX gold is pricey or cheap against the world price.
MCX parity.goodBad: A big premium means strong local demand; a discount means weak demand.
MCX parity.impact: If the premium goes up: local demand or a later expiry's carry is adding to price. If it goes down: local demand is weak.
MCX parity.readIt: When you see this figure, check MCX premium to parity. A steady small gap is normal. A sudden change is worth a look.
MCX parity.simple: Parity is the world price converted into MCX units using today's dollar-rupee rate. Import duty is added where MCX quotes include it. MCX above parity shows a local premium.

MCX premium.example: Like a sweet shop in a festival week charging Rs 10 more than the factory price. If world gold converts to Rs 66,000 and MCX is Rs 70,000, the premium is about 6%.
MCX premium.forYou: If the premium jumps suddenly, expect MCX gold to move even when world gold is calm.
MCX premium.impact: If it goes up: MCX gets dearer than the world, often on duty or demand. If it goes down: the local extra fades.
MCX premium.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with past days. A premium that changes fast is news: a duty change or a demand rush.
MCX premium.simple: How far the Indian MCX price is above or below the world price converted to rupees. For gold it is import duty plus local demand. For crude it is near zero.

Macro driver.example: Like a cricket team where each player has a different role. A 1% day in gold is ordinary, but a 1% day in the dollar is big.
Macro driver.forYou: Look at which drivers moved most before the open, and check if they touch your strikes' risk.
Macro driver.impact: If a driver moves a lot: it adds more to the day's overall world reading. If it is quiet: it adds little.
Macro driver.readIt: When you see a driver, read its move against its own normal size. A driver with stale data scores nothing.
Macro driver.simple: One world market the desk tracks because it can reach India. There are 14, like crude, the dollar, US rates, metals and food items. Each has a weight and a normal big-day size.

Managed money across energy.example: Like a board at the petrol pump listing petrol, diesel and CNG prices side by side, this lists fund bets in each fuel.
Managed money across energy.forYou: Use it to see if a fund move in crude is alone or part of a wider energy move.
Managed money across energy.goodBad: Broad agreement across markets is a stronger message than one market moving alone.
Managed money across energy.impact: If funds add net longs across many energy markets: there is broad bullish money in oil. If they cut across many: energy prices face wide pressure.
Managed money across energy.readIt: When you see this table, compare markets by percentile, not raw contracts, because contract sizes differ. Then click your market for its charts and log.
Managed money across energy.simple: One row for each energy futures market, like crude, petrol and gas. It shows what funds hold and how that changed this week. Click a row to see more.

Managed money action.example: At a cold-storage godown, new traders booking potatoes is new longs. Traders who sold ahead now buying back to close is short covering. The same net rise can come from either.
Managed money action.forYou: Treat short covering rallies with more caution than new-longs rallies before selling premium on the downside.
Managed money action.goodBad: Fresh positions mean real conviction; exits mean pressure that usually passes once they finish.
Managed money action.impact: If the label changes from new longs to long liquidation: support from funds is leaving and prices can slip. If it changes to short covering: a quick bounce is possible but may not last.
Managed money action.readIt: When you see this label, ask whether it is a fresh bet or an exit. New longs or new shorts show conviction. Covering and liquidation are exits, often forced, and can fade quickly.
Managed money action.simple: A one-word label for what funds did this week. New longs means fresh buying; short covering means sellers buying back. Long liquidation means buyers quitting; new shorts means fresh selling.

Managed money net position.example: Picture 100 traders at the Lasalgaon onion mandi. 70 have booked to buy later and 30 to sell later. Their net is +40, so the crowd leans towards higher onion prices. In gold, funds holding 150,000 long and 50,000 short contracts are net +100,000.
Managed money net position.forYou: Use it to see where big money leans in gold or silver, not as an MCX trade signal.
Managed money net position.goodBad: Very high means a crowded long bet that can unwind fast; very low means selling may be tired.
Managed money net position.impact: If it goes up: more fund money is betting on a rise, which often comes with rising prices. If it goes down: funds are cutting bets or turning short, and prices often soften.
Managed money net position.readIt: When you see this number, first check its sign: plus means funds lean long, minus means short. Then compare it with its own past using the COT index. A raw number alone means little.
Managed money net position.simple: Managed money means big hedge funds that trade futures for profit. The US regulator, the CFTC, counts their bets every week. Net position is their buy bets minus their sell bets. Above zero means funds bet on a rise; below zero, on a fall.

Margin (est.).example: Like a deposit for renting a hall. If margin is Rs 1,00,000, that money cannot be used elsewhere until you close.
Margin (est.).forYou: Keep spare margin beyond this so a bad day does not force you out.
Margin (est.).impact: If it goes up: more capital is tied up and return on margin falls. If it goes down: capital is freed.
Margin (est.).readIt: When you see this number, compare it with your free capital and with the credit.
Margin (est.).simple: The money the broker blocks for the trade. For spreads with wings it is about the max loss. For naked sales it is only an estimate; the exchange sets the real figure.

Margin at risk.example: Like the deposit a landlord holds. It is the most he can keep if things go wrong.
Margin at risk.forYou: It is the number to size against, not the premium you collect.
Margin at risk.goodBad: Lower relative to capital is safer; EV per risk divides by this number.
Margin at risk.impact: If it rises: one bad trade costs more of your capital. If it falls: the trade is smaller and safer.
Margin at risk.readIt: When you see margin at risk, compare it with your capital. The desk sizes trades so one full loss is about Rs 20,000.
Margin at risk.simple: The rupees a position can lose. For a spread or condor it is the maximum loss at expiry plus costs. For a naked short leg it is a margin estimate.

Margin buffer.example: You keep Rs 400 spare in your wallet on a Rs 1,000 trip in case the taxi fare jumps. If Rs 10 lakh is your capital and the trade blocks Rs 6 lakh, your buffer is Rs 4 lakh, or 40%.
Margin buffer.forYou: As a seller, a trade that only fits with no buffer does not fit at all.
Margin buffer.goodBad: A large buffer lets you survive a bad day; a thin one lets the broker close you first.
Margin buffer.impact: If it goes up: you can ride out a bad move without being forced out. If it goes down: one adverse move can force you to close at the worst moment.
Margin buffer.readIt: When you see this number, check it is still near the desk's 40% rule. If it is small, a move against you can trigger a margin call. Next, check how much margin would rise in the gap scenarios.
Margin buffer.simple: The spare money left unused after your trade is on. Margin (money the broker blocks) grows fast when a trade goes wrong. The buffer stops the broker from closing you out at the worst price.

Mark.example: Like the rate board at a vegetable market: today onions are Rs 40 a kilo, whatever you paid last week.
Mark.forYou: Use it to see what each leg would cost to close today.
Mark.impact: If the mark of a sold option goes up: you are losing. If it goes down: you are gaining.
Mark.readIt: When you see est next to a mark, treat that price as a rough estimate, not a real trade.
Mark.simple: The mark is what an option is worth right now. It is the last traded price for that strike. If no price exists, the page estimates one and shows est. In a replay, it is the closing or settlement price that day.

Market analysis.example: Like a doctor saying: 70% of your fever is from the cold, 30% we do not know yet. If NIFTY fell 200 points and the usual causes explain 120, then 80 points are unexplained.
Market analysis.forYou: Before selling options, check whether a big unexplained move is sitting near your strikes.
Market analysis.impact: If the explained share goes up: the move came from known causes and is easier to trust. If it goes down: something unknown moved the market, so look at the news before selling.
Market analysis.readIt: When you see this reading, look at the unexplained part and the headlines together. A price older than 4 days is marked stale. So is a CFTC report past 10 days, or news past 48 hours.
Market analysis.simple: One reading per market. It says how big today's move was and how much the usual causes explain. It also says what is coming next. The part nobody can explain is shown openly, not hidden with a story.

Market benchmark.example: Like the official mandi rate for onions in one city. Gold per ounce in dollars is not the same as MCX gold per 10 grams in rupees.
Market benchmark.forYou: Compare benchmarks only when their dates and units match.
Market benchmark.impact: If it goes up: that reference price rose. If it goes down: it fell; the move alone does not give a cause.
Market benchmark.readIt: When you see a benchmark move, check its unit, currency and date before comparing.
Market benchmark.simple: A named reference price for one product, unit and market. Gold is often per ounce, copper per pound, crude per barrel. Benchmarks can differ by contract, currency and time.

Market breadth.example: If the team scores 200 but only two batsmen scored, the win is fragile. If NIFTY rises 100 points but 35 of 50 stocks fell, the rise is narrow.
Market breadth.forYou: As a seller, a rally with narrow breadth may not travel as far toward your call strike.
Market breadth.goodBad: Broad breadth means many stocks agree; narrow breadth means a few names carry the index.
Market breadth.impact: If breadth goes up with the index: the move is broad and better supported. If breadth goes down while the index rises: a few heavy stocks are carrying it.
Market breadth.readIt: When you see breadth, compare it with the index move. Narrow breadth makes a move fragile. In calm markets, very broad up days were followed by weaker sessions, in the desk's study.
Market breadth.simple: How many of the 50 NIFTY stocks rose and how many fell. It also counts how many sit above their 50-day average. It shows if a move is broad or carried by a few.

Market coverage.example: Asking 50 shops for tomato prices gives a better average than asking 5.
Market coverage.forYou: Check coverage before trusting a retail price move.
Market coverage.impact: If coverage rises: the median is more reliable. If it falls: noisier.
Market coverage.readIt: When you see this count, distrust months with few markets.
Market coverage.simple: How many markets reported a price each month. The national median is taken across them. Few markets make a noisier median.

Market horizon.example: Like comparing your height today with last year's mark on the wall. If gold was Rs 65,000 a month ago and is Rs 70,000 now, the 1M move is about +7.7%.
Market horizon.forYou: Use horizons to see how stretched a market is, not as a signal to trade.
Market horizon.impact: If the window gets longer: moves usually look bigger. If shorter: they look smaller; it never predicts the next move.
Market horizon.readIt: When you see this column, check the source date. A blank means not enough history, not zero movement.
Market horizon.simple: A comparison of the latest stored value with an earlier one. Labels like 1D, 1W, 1M, 6M and 1Y name the look-back window. It shows how far a market moved, not a forecast.

Market region.example: Like rainfall reports by state: a missing report does not mean no rain. The US yield curve here has 6 points.
Market region.forYou: Do not assume calm in a region just because its data is unavailable.
Market region.impact: If a region's data updates: the comparison is current. If it is missing: treat it as unknown, not unchanged.
Market region.readIt: When you see a region, check its source and date.
Market region.simple: The country or area a rate, currency or business measure belongs to. Each region needs its own reliable source. Missing data does not mean the market stood still.

Market section.example: Like the vegetable section and fruit section in a shop. The sign is not for sale; the mangoes under it are.
Market section.forYou: Use the section to find the right market quickly, then check the date before trusting any number.
Market section.impact: If data under it updates: the section shows newer values. If a feed fails: the value shows as unavailable, not as zero.
Market section.readIt: When you see a section, look at the dates next to each value. An old or missing date means that number may not be current.
Market section.simple: A page heading that groups related markets together. It is just a label, not a price. Each value under it shows its date, and missing data is shown as missing.

Max drawdown.example: A farmer's savings go from Rs 50,000 to Rs 23,000 in a bad season before recovering. The Rs 27,000 fall is his drawdown.
Max drawdown.forYou: Size so that a drawdown twice this big would still not make you quit or break the account.
Max drawdown.goodBad: Smaller is better. The stress test treats a 30% fall of capital as the line to stay under.
Max drawdown.impact: If it grows: you need more capital and patience to survive the rule. If it shrinks: the rule is easier to live with.
Max drawdown.readIt: When you see max drawdown, compare it with your capital and your nerve. The weekly rules' worst fall was about Rs 26,700 on one lot.
Max drawdown.simple: The biggest fall in your running profit from a high point to a later low, in rupees. It is the pain you sit through before things recover. It often decides if you can stick with a rule.

Max loss.example: Like a fixed excess on car insurance: you know your worst bill. A 100 point spread with 30 credit and lot 75 can lose Rs 5,250.
Max loss.forYou: Prefer trades with wings so this number is real and known.
Max loss.impact: If spread width goes up: max loss grows. If credit goes up: max loss shrinks.
Max loss.readIt: When you see this number, ask if you can afford to lose it. Unlimited means no wing.
Max loss.simple: The most the trade can lose. With wings it is the spread width minus the credit, times the lot size. Without wings it is unlimited, and the desk says so.

Max loss if gapped.example: Like the full price of a car you lend a friend: the worst case is losing the whole car, not just a scratch. Trading: 100-point width, 20 credit, 1 lot of 65 means 80 x 65 = Rs 5,200.
Max loss if gapped.forYou: Size every trade from this number, not from margin.
Max loss if gapped.goodBad: Low relative to capital is safe; high means one trade could hurt a lot.
Max loss if gapped.impact: If it goes up: the worst case is bigger, so the trade may break the cap. If it goes down: the worst case is smaller.
Max loss if gapped.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with your per-trade cap.
Max loss if gapped.simple: This is the worst the position can lose at expiry. It is what a gap straight through your strikes costs, whatever your stop says. For a spread it is the width minus the credit, times lots and lot size.

Max pain.example: Like a popular belief that rain comes every time you wash your car: tested, it is just chance. If max pain is 25,100, do not expect NIFTY to go there.
Max pain.forYou: Ignore max pain when choosing strikes.
Max pain.impact: If max pain moves: nothing changes for your trade, since it has not predicted anything here. Its pull has not worked better than chance in the stored data.
Max pain.readIt: When you see this number, treat it as background only. The desk never sizes a trade on it.
Max pain.simple: The strike where option buyers would lose the most at expiry. Some believe price drifts there before expiry. The desk tested it: right on 50.2% of 255 sessions, a coin flip.

Max pain pull claim.example: Some fans think a team always wins at its home ground, but the records show about half and half. If max pain is 25,000 and NIFTY is at 25,300, the belief says it falls to 25,000; the record says that is a coin flip.
Max pain pull claim.forYou: As a seller, never pick strikes or size trades on max pain; the record shows no real pull.
Max pain pull claim.goodBad: Near 50% means it is folklore; a steady high score would be needed before trusting it.
Max pain pull claim.impact: If it rose well above 50% for a long time: the pull might be real, but it has not. If it stays near 50%: never size a trade on max pain.
Max pain pull claim.readIt: When you see this result, expect about 50%, which is no better than chance. Treat max pain as background only. For real levels, look at the OI walls instead.
Max pain pull claim.simple: Max pain is the strike where option buyers would lose the most at expiry. Many people believe NIFTY drifts toward it. The desk tested this belief, and it works only about half the time.

Max profit.example: Like the full fee a tutor earns if the student finishes the whole course. Trading: sell a condor for Rs 4,000 credit and Rs 4,000 is the most you can make.
Max profit.forYou: Plan to take about half of it, not all of it.
Max profit.impact: If it goes up: the best case is bigger, usually with more risk. If it goes down: the best case shrinks.
Max profit.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with max loss to see how lopsided the trade is.
Max profit.simple: This is the most the trade can make if held to expiry, at the best NIFTY level. For a credit spread or condor it equals the credit received. If profit keeps rising past every strike, it shows unlimited.

Measure.example: Like a teacher reporting both the class's middle mark and the bottom tenth's marks.
Measure.forYou: Read the out-of-sample column for the honest error.
Measure.impact: If the error goes up: trust synthetic prices less. If it goes down: trust them more.
Measure.readIt: When you see the 90th percentile row, that is how wrong the worst strikes are.
Measure.simple: This names the error number in the row. Price errors are in points. IV errors are in volatility points. The median shows a typical strike, the 90th percentile the worst tenth.

Median.example: Like the middle child in a line of children sorted by height. If the median is 25,020, half the outcomes are above.
Median.forYou: Use it as the centre when judging if your strikes are balanced.
Median.impact: If it goes up: the middle of priced outcomes moves up. If it goes down: it moves down.
Median.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with spot and the forward.
Median.simple: The middle level of the range of outcomes the option market is pricing. Half the outcomes are above it, half below. The desk rejects a range whose average does not match the forward price.

Median answer error.example: Like an archer's typical distance from the bullseye in centimetres.
Median answer error.forYou: Track it on range and straddle exercises especially.
Median answer error.goodBad: Small is precise; large means your estimates are often far off.
Median answer error.impact: If it goes down: you are more precise. If it goes up: your method or arithmetic is slipping.
Median answer error.readIt: When you see it fall over weeks, your estimates are getting tighter.
Median answer error.simple: This is your typical distance from the right answer in an exercise. Median means the middle value when errors are lined up. It is in percent, points or rupees depending on the exercise.

Metals and oil.example: Like a weather page for five cities: today's heat, next week's likely range, and a rain guess. Gold at Rs 70,000 might be shown with a next-week range of Rs 68,500 to Rs 71,500.
Metals and oil.forYou: If you sell options on MCX, place strikes outside the range, not just on the side of the lean.
Metals and oil.impact: If a range gets wider: the market is more jumpy and positions need more room. If it gets narrower: the market is calmer, but calm can end.
Metals and oil.readIt: When you see this page, read the range before the lean. The range is what a position must survive. The lean is still being graded and may not be proven yet.
Metals and oil.simple: The page for gold, silver and crude oil on MCX in rupees, plus WTI and Brent oil in dollars. It shows where each price is and where it may be by five dates. It also shows which way the facts lean.

Mistake log.example: Like a diary of wrong turns on a trip, so you do not take them again.
Mistake log.forYou: Log every mistake you notice, big or small.
Mistake log.impact: If you log honestly: your costliest habits become clear. If you hide mistakes: the habits stay hidden too.
Mistake log.readIt: When you see the log, look for repeated items.
Mistake log.simple: This records every mistake in this browser: missed questions, paper-trade review tags and anything you log from real trades. Logging is private and not scored. The goal is honest entries, not few entries.

Mock exam pass.example: Like scoring above the pass mark in a mock to be safe on the real day.
Mock exam pass.forYou: Aim for a margin above the real pass mark.
Mock exam pass.impact: If your best rises past 70 percent: you earn it. If it stays under: keep practising.
Mock exam pass.readIt: When you see your best mock, compare it with 70 percent.
Mock exam pass.simple: This badge needs 70 percent or more, after wrong-answer penalties, on a 50-question mock exam. The real pass mark is 60 percent.

Mode.forYou: Keep it on during busy days.
Mode.impact: If you turn it on: fewer looks. If off: live numbers all the time.
Mode.readIt: When you see on, live P&L is hidden between checks.
Mode.simple: This says whether scheduled-check mode is on or off. When on, live P&L hides between check times.

Model stack.example: A recipe card that lists every step, so anyone can check how the dish was made. For NIFTY, it goes from each strike's IV to the probability, then shrinks that probability if past ones were too confident.
Model stack.forYou: As a seller, this lets you check that every number you trade on comes from a named method.
Model stack.impact: If the haircut goes up: the desk trusts its raw probabilities less, so sizes shrink. If it goes down: the record supports the raw numbers more.
Model stack.readIt: When you see this list, use it to trace where any number came from. Pay most attention to the last step, the calibration haircut. It is fitted from the record, not from guesswork.
Model stack.simple: The list of methods the desk uses, in order, to get its numbers. It starts with option prices and ends with a correction. That last correction comes from the desk's own past hit rate.

Momentum.example: Like a runner whose last lap beat 65% of all his past laps: he is moving well. But at the very top, near the 95th, he often tires.
Momentum.forYou: If momentum is strong one way, give more room to short strikes on that side.
Momentum.impact: If it goes up: a stronger up push that often lasts one to three months. If it goes down: a stronger down push; at extremes it can reverse.
Momentum.readIt: When you see this row, read the percentile. Above 65 votes up, below 35 votes down, in between votes nothing.
Momentum.simple: The last 20 days' move, ranked against every 20-day move in ten years. At the 65th percentile or higher it votes up. At the 35th or lower it votes down.

Moneyness.example: Like how far a shop is from a bus stop. Near shops get more customers; far ones get fewer.
Moneyness.forYou: It tells you which row of the pricer check applies to your strikes.
Moneyness.goodBad: Further out means cheaper and safer options, with a larger model error at short tenors.
Moneyness.impact: If the strike moves closer to spot: more premium and more risk. If further: less premium and less risk.
Moneyness.readIt: When you see moneyness rows, find where your short strike sits, like put 1 to 2 sigma.
Moneyness.simple: How far a strike is from the current NIFTY level, measured in sigma here. At the money is near spot; out of the money is away from spot.

Monthly loss limit.example: Like a monthly data pack: once used up, you wait for the new month.
Monthly loss limit.forYou: Use the pause to find which habit cost the most.
Monthly loss limit.impact: If you hit it: no new entries until the 1st. If you stay under: trading stays open.
Monthly loss limit.readIt: When you see this hit, stop new trades and review the month.
Monthly loss limit.simple: Once your booked losses this month reach this, new trades are locked until the 1st. The default is 5 percent of capital.

Morning brief.example: Like a cricket captain's team talk before a match: yesterday's score, today's pitch, and the plan. If NIFTY is 25,000, the brief shows the range NIFTY will likely stay in tomorrow.
Morning brief.forYou: Read it before placing any option sale, and check the NIFTY range against your short strikes.
Morning brief.impact: If more signals agree: the brief makes a firmer lean. If signals are few or mixed: it shows no lean, and you should trade smaller or wait.
Morning brief.readIt: When you see this page, read the stories first, then the decision table. Check yesterday's graded call to see if the desk was right. A lean needs 3 of up to 9 signals before it makes a call.
Morning brief.simple: The first page to read each day. It says why each market moved, what the desk would do today, and how yesterday's call turned out. Blue tags are the desk's own numbers. Grey tags are news headlines you can click.

Moving average.example: Like your average cricket score over the last 20 innings. If NIFTY is 25,000 and its 200-day average is 24,000, it is above its long-term line.
Moving average.forYou: As a seller, NIFTY sitting just a few points above its average is noise, not a signal.
Moving average.impact: If NIFTY crosses above the line: trend followers may buy. If it crosses below: they may sell, sometimes speeding the move.
Moving average.readIt: When you see a moving average, check if NIFTY is above or below it. More useful is how many of the 50 stocks sit above their own average. That is breadth.
Moving average.simple: The average closing price over the last 20, 50 or 200 days. It is recalculated each evening. It is a slow line that many people watch.

My positions.example: Like a shop's own diary of stock on the shelf: it lists what you hold today and what it would fetch if you sold now.
My positions.forYou: Open it at your planned check times to see where each trade stands against its exit rules.
My positions.impact: If you add more positions: more of your money is at risk at once. If you close positions: the page shrinks and so does your risk.
My positions.readIt: When you see this page, read each position's P&L now first. Then check the exit rules for anything near a stop or target.
My positions.simple: This page shows the option trades you really hold. It says what each one is worth now and what you made or lost. It also shows what happens if NIFTY moves. Everything stays in this browser only.

Myth vs measurement.example: Like hearing a tea seller claims his stall is lucky; you ask: lucky compared with what?
Myth vs measurement.forYou: Practise asking compared with what before trusting any claim.
Myth vs measurement.impact: If the hit rate beats the base rate clearly: the claim may be real. If not: the claim is noise.
Myth vs measurement.readIt: When you see a high hit rate, wait for the base rate before believing it.
Myth vs measurement.simple: Each card shows a popular market claim with the hit rate the desk measured. It also shows the base rate to beat, the sample size and a p-value. A p-value says how likely pure chance is. First decide from the hit rate, then see the base rate.

NIFTY 50.example: Like a class average where top students' marks count more. NIFTY can rise even when most of its 50 stocks fall, if a few heavy ones jump.
NIFTY 50.forYou: As a seller, every strike you sell is a bet on where this one number ends.
NIFTY 50.impact: If NIFTY goes up: short calls get closer to their strikes. If it goes down: short puts get closer.
NIFTY 50.readIt: When you see the NIFTY level, also check breadth and each stock's points. A move by two heavy stocks is different from one by forty. Members change about twice a year.
NIFTY 50.simple: India's main stock index of 50 large companies. Bigger companies count more. This desk trades its options.

NIFTY and RSI, six months.example: Like a growth chart showing when a child had a growth spurt. Above 70 is overbought, below 30 oversold.
NIFTY and RSI, six months.forYou: Use the chart for context, and check the states table before acting on RSI.
NIFTY and RSI, six months.impact: If RSI goes above 70: NIFTY is stretched up. If it goes below 30: stretched down; neither alone predicts a turn.
NIFTY and RSI, six months.readIt: When you see this chart, find where the current spell started.
NIFTY and RSI, six months.simple: A chart of NIFTY and its RSI over six months. RSI is a 0 to 100 gauge of recent up versus down moves. The shaded band is 30 to 70.

NIFTY close.example: Like the starting point marked on a map before a hike.
NIFTY close.forYou: Use it as the anchor for every distance in the replay.
NIFTY close.impact: If you pick a day with a very different close: all distances and strikes shift. If similar: the setup looks alike.
NIFTY close.readIt: When you see it, measure your strikes' distance from it.
NIFTY close.simple: This is NIFTY's closing level on the replay day. Every strike and every sigma on the page is measured from it or from the forward price.

NIFTY up and VIX up over 5 sessions.example: Like people buying umbrellas while the sun is still shining. If NIFTY goes from 24,700 to 25,000 in a week and VIX goes from 13 to 13.8, this turns on.
NIFTY up and VIX up over 5 sessions.forYou: As a seller, rising VIX makes option prices dearer, which can hurt open shorts even when NIFTY is going your way.
NIFTY up and VIX up over 5 sessions.goodBad: Neither; a warning sign worth checking, not a forecast.
NIFTY up and VIX up over 5 sessions.impact: If this turns on: traders are hedging into a rise. If it turns off: either the rally stalled or the fear cooled.
NIFTY up and VIX up over 5 sessions.readIt: When you see this state ON, buyers are paying up for protection during a rally. The table shows how NIFTY moved after such weeks.
NIFTY up and VIX up over 5 sessions.simple: This is on when NIFTY rose more than 1% over the last 5 sessions and India VIX rose more than 5% over the same 5 sessions. Normally VIX falls when NIFTY rises, so this is unusual.

NISM Series VIII map.example: Like a syllabus chart for a school exam, with chapter page numbers.
NISM Series VIII map.forYou: Cover all ten units, especially 6 to 10.
NISM Series VIII map.impact: If your unit accuracy goes up: you are closer to exam-ready. If not: revise that unit.
NISM Series VIII map.readIt: When you see a unit with low accuracy, practise that unit next.
NISM Series VIII map.simple: NISM Series VIII is the equity derivatives certificate exam in India. This map lists its ten units, where the desk covers each, and the practice questions per unit. Units 6 to 10 are not visible on the live desk, so they get more questions.

NSE transaction charge.example: Like a mandi fee charged on every sale and purchase in the market yard.
NSE transaction charge.forYou: It rarely changes a decision, but it is part of the cost stack.
NSE transaction charge.goodBad: 0.03553% of premium since October 2024, down from about 0.05%.
NSE transaction charge.impact: If it rises: costs grow slightly. If it falls: costs shrink slightly.
NSE transaction charge.readIt: When you see this, note it is small. Brokerage and slippage are much bigger.
NSE transaction charge.simple: The exchange's fee on premium turnover, charged on both buys and sells. GST of 18% is added. On cheap options it is only a few paise.

NSE volume 50%+ above its 20-day average.example: Like a railway station on Diwali eve, far more crowded than a normal day. If average volume is 200 million shares and today is 310 million, this turns on.
NSE volume 50%+ above its 20-day average.forYou: As a seller, heavy volume often comes with news and bigger moves, so check what caused it before adding new shorts.
NSE volume 50%+ above its 20-day average.goodBad: Neither; it tells you the market is busy, not which way it will go.
NSE volume 50%+ above its 20-day average.impact: If this turns on: something has drawn a crowd into the market. If it turns off: trading has returned to normal levels.
NSE volume 50%+ above its 20-day average.readIt: When you see this state ON, participation is unusually heavy. This uses the desk's own stored data, so it has a shorter history than the price-based states.
NSE volume 50%+ above its 20-day average.simple: This is on when NIFTY's traded volume today is more than 1.5 times its average of the last 20 sessions. Many more people are trading than usual.

Natural gas.example: Like gas demand jumping in a cold winter. If Henry Hub goes from 3.00 to 3.60 dollars, that is a 20% move, and MCX natural gas moves about the same.
Natural gas.forYou: As a seller of MCX natural gas options, expect big moves. Sell smaller and further away than on crude.
Natural gas.goodBad: Neither. It is a market, not a score.
Natural gas.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish or are covering shorts. If it goes down: they are adding shorts or selling longs.
Natural gas.readIt: When you see this row, check the 3-year percentile and the weekly change. When funds are heavily short gas, short covering can bring sharp rallies.
Natural gas.simple: The US Henry Hub natural gas future on NYMEX, in lots of 10,000 MMBtu. MCX natural gas is priced from it. It is one of the wildest-moving energy markets, driven by weather and storage.

Net P&L.example: Like a stall's takings minus the cost of stock and rent at the end of the day.
Net P&L.forYou: Read it alongside the adherence score, never alone.
Net P&L.impact: If it goes up: you kept more after costs. If it goes down: losses or costs grew.
Net P&L.readIt: When you see this number, remember costs are already subtracted.
Net P&L.simple: This is your booked profit or loss on closed trades. The costs you entered are already taken off.

Net credit.example: Like a shopkeeper getting Rs 100 advance and spending Rs 30 on a guard. If you sell for 60 points, buy wings for 20, and lot is 75, credit is Rs 3,000.
Net credit.forYou: Check credit against max loss before entering any spread.
Net credit.impact: If it goes up: more income and a bigger cushion. If it goes down: less income for the same risk.
Net credit.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with max loss and margin.
Net credit.simple: Premium received minus premium paid, times the lot size. It is what you collect at the start. It is also the most you can make.

Net delta.example: Like a boat in a river: delta near zero means the boat stays in place whichever way the current pushes. Trading: delta of minus 50 means a 100-point NIFTY rise costs about Rs 5,000.
Net delta.forYou: Check it after big NIFTY moves, because a seller's delta grows as the market runs.
Net delta.goodBad: Close to zero means little direction risk. A large plus or minus means you carry a direction bet.
Net delta.impact: If it goes up (more positive): you gain more when NIFTY rises and lose more when it falls. If it goes down (more negative): the reverse.
Net delta.readIt: When you see this number, multiply it by 100 to see the rupee change for a 100-point move.
Net delta.simple: Delta tells how much the trade gains or loses when NIFTY moves one point. Net means all legs added together. Near zero means you are not betting on a direction.

Net futures position.example: Like 12 people wanting to buy and 5 wanting to sell: net 7 buyers. 12 long minus 5 short is 7 net long.
Net futures position.forYou: Treat it as slow background on how big players lean, not a trade signal.
Net futures position.impact: If it goes up: the group is more long. If it goes down: it is less long or more short.
Net futures position.readIt: When you see this number, check its sign and date. Large longs and shorts can cancel into a small net.
Net futures position.simple: Long contracts minus short contracts for one group in one market. Positive means net long, negative means net short. It is a weekly, delayed snapshot.

Net gamma.example: Like a cycle going downhill: the further it rolls, the faster it goes. A small push is easy to stop; a long slope is not.
Net gamma.forYou: Use it to judge how jumpy the trade will be, especially near expiry when gamma grows.
Net gamma.goodBad: Small means the trade changes slowly; large negative means a big move hurts fast.
Net gamma.impact: If it goes more negative: losses speed up on big moves, so watch closer. If it moves toward zero: the trade is calmer.
Net gamma.readIt: When you see a large negative number, expect delta to swing fast on a big move. Check your short strikes.
Net gamma.simple: Gamma tells how fast delta changes when NIFTY moves. Sellers usually have negative gamma. That means the trade turns against them faster the further NIFTY travels.

Net index futures by group.example: Like seeing which neighbours are betting on rain and which on sunshine, every day of the monsoon.
Net index futures by group.forYou: A squeeze can carry NIFTY through a short call quickly, so watch heavy net shorts.
Net index futures by group.goodBad: Large net short positions are fuel for short-covering rallies.
Net index futures by group.impact: If a heavy net short grows and NIFTY rises: short covering can push it up fast. If shorts shrink: that fuel is used up.
Net index futures by group.readIt: When you see a big net short group, remember they must buy back if the index rises fast.
Net index futures by group.simple: Each group's index futures long minus short, day by day. It shows who is betting on direction and how that bet is changing.

Net position change.example: Your weight on one day can jump from a big meal. The four-week trend tells you the real direction.
Net position change.forYou: Trust the four-week number more than a single noisy week.
Net position change.goodBad: Large changes show strong action; small ones mean little happened.
Net position change.impact: If it goes up: the group is adding net longs. If it goes down: the group is adding shorts or cutting longs.
Net position change.readIt: When you see both numbers, check if they agree. If one week is down but four weeks is up, it may be a pause or a turn. Watch the decision log.
Net position change.simple: How much a group's net bet changed over one week or four weeks. One week shows the latest decision. Four weeks shows the direction of travel.

Net premium.example: Like the money left after selling one item and buying another: sell for Rs 80, buy for Rs 20, net Rs 60.
Net premium.forYou: Check it against the spread width; it should be at least 15 percent.
Net premium.impact: If it goes up: the reward is bigger, usually with more risk. If it goes down: less reward for the same structure.
Net premium.readIt: When you see a positive number, you collected money; negative means you paid.
Net premium.simple: This is the credit received, or debit paid, across all legs. It is in points per unit at the marks. After slippage it becomes your fill, and times the lot it becomes rupees.

Net theta.example: Like rent a shopkeeper earns daily for letting someone use his space: Rs 500 a day comes in as long as nothing goes wrong.
Net theta.forYou: Compare it with the possible loss on a big day so you see the trade-off clearly.
Net theta.goodBad: Positive is the seller's daily pay; it is earned only if NIFTY stays calm.
Net theta.impact: If it goes up: each quiet day pays more, but usually the risk is higher too. If it goes down: less daily pay.
Net theta.readIt: When you see this number, remember it is pay for carrying risk. It is not free money.
Net theta.simple: Theta is how much the trade earns or loses from one day passing. Option prices shrink as expiry comes closer. Sellers usually have positive theta: time pays them for carrying risk.

Net to open interest.example: Like 10 extra buyers among 100 shoppers: 10%. 10 net out of 100 open contracts is 10%.
Net to open interest.forYou: A very large reading is a hint of crowding in that world market.
Net to open interest.impact: If it goes up: the group's lean is bigger relative to the market. If it goes down: smaller, or total contracts grew.
Net to open interest.readIt: When you see this percent, a large value means the group leans heavily in that market.
Net to open interest.simple: The net position divided by all open contracts in that market, as a percent. It puts the net size in context. It is not a share of all market risk.

Net vega.example: Like an umbrella seller who sold forward at a fixed price: if a storm warning comes, umbrellas get dearer and his deal looks worse. Trading: vega of minus Rs 2,000 loses Rs 2,000 if IV rises one point.
Net vega.forYou: Check it before events and after sharp falls, when fear usually rises.
Net vega.goodBad: Near zero means little exposure to fear changes; large negative means a fear spike can hurt a lot.
Net vega.impact: If it goes more negative: a fear spike costs you more. If it moves toward zero: fear changes matter less.
Net vega.readIt: When you see this number, check the event calendar: results, RBI or budget days can push fear up.
Net vega.simple: Implied volatility is the market's fear level priced into options. Vega tells how much the trade gains or loses when it rises one point. Sellers usually have negative vega. A jump in fear hurts them even if NIFTY does not move.

Never stand aside.example: Like a fisherman going out every day, even when the weather board says stay home. Comparing his catch tells you if the board helps.
Never stand aside.forYou: On this sample standing aside helped, so respect the stand-aside call.
Never stand aside.goodBad: Worse than the rules means the side gate added value.
Never stand aside.impact: If this line does better than the rules: standing aside cost money. If worse: standing aside saved money.
Never stand aside.readIt: When you see this line, compare it with the rules. It lost Rs 29,526 over 55 trades, worse than the rules' Rs 17,026 over 39.
Never stand aside.simple: The desk's weekly trade taken every time it was flat, ignoring the side rule's stand-aside call. It shows if standing aside saved money.

New today.example: Like learning 5 new English words a day instead of 50. If it shows 3 / 5, you can start 2 more new cards today.
New today.forYou: As a seller, slow and steady learning sticks better than cramming before a trade.
New today.goodBad: Neither; any number up to 5 is fine.
New today.impact: If it goes up: you started more new material today. If it goes down: a fresh day has begun or you are focusing on reviews.
New today.readIt: When you see this, treat the limit as a guard against overloading yourself.
New today.simple: This shows how many new cards you have started today out of the daily limit of 5. New cards are added slowly so reviews do not pile up.

Next ATM IV.example: Like the weekly weather outlook that sets your travel plan.
Next ATM IV.forYou: Use it to place strikes outside 1 sigma.
Next ATM IV.impact: If it goes up: the expected move is wider, so strikes move further out. If it goes down: the range narrows.
Next ATM IV.readIt: When you see it, it decides how far out the strikes need to be.
Next ATM IV.simple: This is implied volatility at the strike closest to NIFTY for the second expiry. Its sigma sets the one-sigma move used in the templates and the process check.

Next gap.example: Like a friend you meet often at first, then less often as you get to know them well.
Next gap.forYou: Do not worry about box 0; it is where learning happens.
Next gap.impact: If cards move to higher boxes: you remember them well. If they drop to box 0: they need more practice.
Next gap.readIt: When you see many cards in box 0, those are your weak spots.
Next gap.simple: This is how many days a card in this box waits before coming back after a correct recall. Box 0 holds missed cards; they return tomorrow. Higher boxes come back less often.

Next-session cap.example: Like expecting tomorrow's auto fare to be at most 10 rupees more than today's. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the one-session 1-sigma move is 160 points, the cap is 25,160.
Next-session cap.forYou: As a seller, a close above this cap tells you the day was bigger than normal; check your short calls.
Next-session cap.impact: If it goes up: NIFTY rose or the market expects bigger daily swings. If it goes down: NIFTY fell or daily swings are expected to be smaller.
Next-session cap.readIt: When you see this level, read it as where tomorrow's rise would normally stop about 5 days in 6.
Next-session cap.simple: This is NIFTY's spot plus a 1-sigma move for just the next trading session, worked out from implied volatility. It is the upper edge of tomorrow's expected range.

Next-session range.example: Like expecting tomorrow's auto fare to be between Rs 90 and Rs 110 on most days. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the band is 24,800 to 25,200, a close of 25,350 would be outside it.
Next-session range.forYou: Keep short strikes well outside tomorrow's band, especially on expiry day.
Next-session range.goodBad: Neither good nor bad; a wide band means more risk and usually more premium.
Next-session range.impact: If the band gets wider: options expect bigger moves, so short strikes need more room. If it gets narrower: the market expects a calm day.
Next-session range.readIt: When you see this band, treat the edges as normal moves, not shocks. A close outside it happens about 1 day in 3.
Next-session range.simple: The price band the desk expects NIFTY to close inside tomorrow. About 68 days out of 100 the close should land inside it. The width comes from how much options say NIFTY will move.

Next-session range claim.example: Like a daily class test instead of a yearly exam: problems show up sooner. If NIFTY is 25,000 with 12% implied, the band is about 190 points.
Next-session range claim.forYou: Use it as an early warning before trusting expiry ranges.
Next-session range claim.goodBad: Near 68% is good; a steady fall below is a warning.
Next-session range claim.impact: If its hit rate rises above 68%: bands are getting wide. If it falls below: bands are getting too narrow.
Next-session range claim.readIt: When you see its hit rate, compare it with 68%. Drift away from 68% warns that bands are going off.
Next-session range claim.simple: A claim that tomorrow's close lands inside a band from today's implied volatility. It resolves every day. So it gathers results much faster than expiry claims.

No reason (always buy).example: Like buying a lottery ticket every week whether or not you have a tip. Any real buy reason should beat this row to be worth using.
No reason (always buy).forYou: As a seller, this row is roughly your trade turned upside down: what the buyer loses, the seller keeps, before costs.
No reason (always buy).impact: If its average goes up: plain buying has paid more over the period. If it goes down: sellers have been collecting more on average.
No reason (always buy).readIt: When you see this row, compare each buy reason against it. A reason that is not better than always buying adds nothing.
No reason (always buy).simple: This row is the plain comparison: buying the at-the-money straddle on every stored session, with no reason at all. It shows what a buyer gets by default.

No-edge entries.example: Like going fishing after the forecast said no fish today.
No-edge entries.goodBad: Zero is the goal; a high count means impatience.
No-edge entries.impact: If it goes up: more trades without an edge. If it goes down: you wait better.
No-edge entries.readIt: When you see this count above zero, look at how those trades did.
No-edge entries.simple: These are selling trades you opened while the side rule said stand aside. They had no edge behind them.

OI direction signals.example: Like testing an old saying, such as red sky means rain, against a weather diary. PCR above 1.2 reads bullish, but here it has to prove it.
OI direction signals.forYou: Do not trade on PCR, max pain or OI flow unless this test says they passed.
OI direction signals.impact: If a signal's hit rate rises above 58% with enough samples: the desk may use it. If it stays lower: it is ignored.
OI direction signals.readIt: When you see this, check whether each signal passed. Most popular readings have not passed in the stored data.
OI direction signals.simple: Popular ways of reading open interest to guess direction, tested against real results. A reading is used only once it has been right often enough. It needs 58% or better over 40 sessions and 8 expiries.

OI walls.example: Like two fences around a playground. If the call wall is 25,500 and the put wall 24,500, NIFTY usually stays between.
OI walls.forYou: Place short strikes at or beyond the walls, with extra room on the put side.
OI walls.impact: If the walls move apart: the expected range widens. If they move closer: the range narrows.
OI walls.readIt: When you see these strikes, note the distance from spot. The lower wall breaks more often, on panic days.
OI walls.simple: The two strikes with the most open contracts: the biggest call strike above, the biggest put strike below. Sellers defend these, so they act as range edges. Call wall held 92.9%, put wall 80.0%.

Observation date.example: Like a school report card dated March but handed out in April. A CFTC position shown today may be 3 days old.
Observation date.forYou: Always check this date before acting on any number on the market pages.
Observation date.impact: If the date is recent: the value is current. If it is old: the market may have moved since.
Observation date.readIt: When you see this date, compare it with today. An old date means the number may not reflect now.
Observation date.simple: The date the source says a value describes. It is not always the day it was published or downloaded. CFTC reports describe Tuesday but come out about Friday.

Of capital.example: Like saying Rs 5,000 lost is 5 percent of your Rs 1,00,000 savings.
Of capital.forYou: Use it to make paper losses feel real.
Of capital.impact: If it goes up: the trade gained more of your capital. If it goes down: the loss bites deeper.
Of capital.readIt: When you see a large percent loss, imagine it with real money.
Of capital.simple: This is the paper trade's net P&L as a share of the capital you declared in the plan. A loss in percent is harder to ignore than a number on a practice screen.

One change at a time.example: Like a doctor changing one medicine at a time to see which one really helps.
One change at a time.forYou: It shows which single change in your trading would have helped most.
One change at a time.goodBad: Better test expectancy and smaller drawdown than 'as is' means the change helped.
One change at a time.impact: If a change improves the test numbers: that setting matters. If not: it is safe to ignore.
One change at a time.readIt: When you see this table, compare each row's test results with the 'as is' row.
One change at a time.simple: Each row changes just one setting of the rule. Examples are entry time, stop type, holding to expiry or strike choice. It tests specific claims directly instead of hiding them in one combined rule.

One-sigma range, five ways.example: Five friends guess a cricket score using different clues. If all say 160 to 180, you believe it. If the five NIFTY bands all land near 24,700 to 25,300, that range is solid.
One-sigma range, five ways.forYou: As a seller, size down when the five bands disagree.
One-sigma range, five ways.goodBad: Close agreement means a trustworthy range; wide disagreement means take less risk.
One-sigma range, five ways.impact: If the bands spread apart: uncertainty is high, so cut size. If they come together: the range is better supported.
One-sigma range, five ways.readIt: When you see the five bands, check if they agree. When they spread apart, the honest move is a smaller trade. Never pick the band that says what you want.
One-sigma range, five ways.simple: Five different methods answer one question: how far might NIFTY move? They share almost no assumptions. Agreement is strong evidence; disagreement means real uncertainty.

Open &minus; prev close.example: Like finding your street flooded in the morning after night rain. If NIFTY closed 25,000 and opened 25,150, the gap is +150.
Open &minus; prev close.forYou: Overnight gaps can skip your stop loss, so keep strikes far enough to survive a normal gap.
Open &minus; prev close.impact: If it goes up: a bigger gap up, which can jump past short calls. If it goes down: a gap down, which can jump past short puts.
Open &minus; prev close.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with close minus open. A gap that the day reverses means the gap faded.
Open &minus; prev close.simple: Today's opening price minus yesterday's close. It is the overnight gap from news and world markets. Positive means a gap up.

Open interest (OI).example: Volume is how many people walked through the mandi today; OI is how many still hold unpaid orders. If the NIFTY 25,500 call has huge OI, many writers will defend that level.
Open interest (OI).forYou: As a seller, short strikes beyond heavy OI walls have other writers defending the same level.
Open interest (OI).goodBad: High OI at one strike means a strong level; low OI means few people care about it.
Open interest (OI).impact: If OI at a strike goes up: more positions are opened, so that level matters more. If it goes down: positions are closing, so the level may weaken.
Open interest (OI).readIt: When you see OI, look for strikes with much more OI than their neighbours. These are walls. Total OI tells little; OI piled at one strike tells a lot.
Open interest (OI).simple: The number of option contracts still open at a strike. Volume counts today's trades, but OI keeps adding up over days. It shows where money is really committed.

Open interest and volume.example: If more traders keep onion deals open as prices rise, new buyers are entering.
Open interest and volume.forYou: Use it to tell real buying from short covering.
Open interest and volume.goodBad: Rising open interest means new money; falling means exits.
Open interest and volume.impact: If open interest rises with price falling: fresh selling. If it falls: positions are closing.
Open interest and volume.readIt: When you see this chart, read price and open interest together.
Open interest and volume.simple: Open interest is contracts still open. Volume is contracts traded. Price up with open interest up is fresh buying.

Option chain fetch.example: Like the full menu card at a restaurant; without it you cannot order. For NIFTY, about 120 strikes are pulled for the nearest expiry.
Option chain fetch.forYou: As a seller, every strike you choose depends on this fetch, so check its strike count first.
Option chain fetch.impact: If the strike count falls to zero: the exchange gave an empty reply, and the session stops. If it is normal: PCR, walls, bands and probabilities are all built from fresh data.
Option chain fetch.readIt: When you see this step, check the strike count. Around 120 is normal. Zero strikes means the fetch silently failed, so nothing on the page is fresh.
Option chain fetch.simple: The live list of every option strike, pulled from the exchange. It has price, open interest, volume and IV for calls and puts. Almost every number on the desk comes from it.

Option chain on the day.example: Like a price list at a market stall for that day.
Option chain on the day.forYou: Build trades from the chain, then check the rules.
Option chain on the day.impact: If you pick strikes closer to NIFTY: more credit, more risk. If further: less credit, less risk.
Option chain on the day.readIt: When you see the chain, find strikes about 1 sigma away first.
Option chain on the day.simple: This table lists strikes within about 10 percent of NIFTY for the two nearest expiries. Prices are that day's. S sells and B buys that strike into your trade.

Out of sample.example: Like testing a student on new questions, not the ones she practised.
Out of sample.impact: If it goes up: the model is less trustworthy. If it goes down: more trustworthy.
Out of sample.readIt: When you see it, trust it over the in-sample number.
Out of sample.simple: This is the error measured on days the price model was not fitted on. It is the honest number. Error on fitted days always looks better.

Out-of-sample equity.example: Like tasting a new recipe only on guests who never tasted the test batches.
Out-of-sample equity.forYou: It is the fairest test of any rule the desk offers you.
Out-of-sample equity.goodBad: Higher end value with shallow dips is better.
Out-of-sample equity.impact: If a line keeps rising in these years: the rule held up on unseen data. If it falls: its earlier success was likely luck.
Out-of-sample equity.readIt: When you see these lines, compare the end values and the dips on the way.
Out-of-sample equity.simple: Rs 10 lakh traded from January 2020 by each rule line, growing month by month after costs. These years were never used to choose any rule. It is the closest thing to a live record the model can give.

Outcome.example: Like the result of one cricket match: a strong team can still lose one game.
Outcome.forYou: Judge outcomes only over many replays.
Outcome.impact: If it goes up: the trade made money, which may be luck. If it goes down: it lost, which may also be luck.
Outcome.readIt: When you see it, read the process score first, then this.
Outcome.simple: This is the rupee profit or loss of the replayed trade after slippage and charges. One replay's outcome is mostly noise. Good process loses on some days and bad process wins on some.

Overfitting check.example: Toss 1,000 coins ten times each; one will land heads 9 times. That coin is not special, just lucky.
Overfitting check.forYou: It tells you how much of the research's best result might be luck.
Overfitting check.goodBad: The search ranks hold up, but the winner's Sharpe is not proven beyond luck after 11,030 trials.
Overfitting check.impact: If PBO rises or rank correlation falls: the search is fitting noise. If deflated Sharpe rises toward 1: the winner's edge is more likely real.
Overfitting check.readIt: When you see this card, read the three numbers together. PBO is 5.7% (good), rank correlation 0.68 (good), deflated Sharpe 0.03 (not proven).
Overfitting check.simple: Overfitting means a rule learned the noise of the past instead of a real pattern. This card runs three tests: PBO, rank correlation and deflated Sharpe, plus a walk-forward test. With thousands of rules tried, the best one looks good partly by luck.

Overrides.example: Like a list of times you ate sweets despite your diet, with your excuse beside each.
Overrides.forYou: Read your own reasons back; patterns show quickly.
Overrides.goodBad: Few is good; many means the rules are not really running your trading.
Overrides.impact: If it goes up: you bend rules more often. If it goes down: you trust the rules more.
Overrides.readIt: When you see this count, compare override results with compliant results.
Overrides.simple: These are trades saved even though a hard rule failed, with the reason you typed. Their results are compared with trades that followed the rules.

P&L.example: An umbrella seller earns the same Rs 100 on any normal day, but a flood can cost him the whole shop. If you sold a 25,500 call and 24,500 put for Rs 50 total, you keep about Rs 50 anywhere between them, and lose beyond them.
P&L.forYou: As a seller, your profit is capped at the credit, so the loss edges decide your risk.
P&L.goodBad: A wide flat top gives room to be wrong; steep edges with no wing mean unlimited losses.
P&L.impact: If NIFTY moves toward your short strike: your P&L drops, slowly at first then fast. If NIFTY stays in the middle and time passes: your P&L slowly rises toward the full credit.
P&L.readIt: When you see the P&L chart, look at the edges, not the peak. The maximum profit is known from the start and barely changes. The loss on the edges is what changes, so study where it starts and how steep it is.
P&L.simple: Profit and loss: what your trade makes or loses at a given NIFTY level on a given day. It is the premium you collected minus what it costs to buy back. For a seller, the top is flat and the edges fall.

P&L now.example: Like checking what your scooter would sell for today against what you paid: bought for Rs 50,000, sells for Rs 45,000, so P&L is minus Rs 5,000. Trading: sold an option at 100, now 60, one lot of 65, P&L is plus Rs 2,600.
P&L now.forYou: Read it against the exit rules on the same row, and act only when a rule fires.
P&L now.goodBad: Positive is money in hand if you close now; negative is money you would lose. One trade says little about skill.
P&L now.impact: If it goes up: you are closer to the take-profit target. If it goes down: you are closer to the stop, and the rule may say exit.
P&L now.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the take-profit target and the stop level, not with your feelings.
P&L now.simple: P&L means profit and loss. This is what the trade has made or lost if you closed it at today's prices. Plus means profit, minus means loss.

P&L pts.example: Like profit counted in kilos before converting to rupees.
P&L pts.forYou: Check it against the target and stop.
P&L pts.impact: If it goes up: you are in more profit. If it goes down: you are losing.
P&L pts.readIt: When you see it, multiply by lot size to get rough rupees.
P&L pts.simple: This is the entry credit minus the position value, in points per unit. It is before slippage and charges. The debrief shows rupees after both.

P(profit).example: Like an insurer who wins 95 of 100 policies but loses big on 5. If P(profit) is 85%, you lose about 15 times in 100.
P(profit).forYou: Do not pick a trade only because P(profit) is high; check the size of the losses too.
P(profit).impact: If it goes up: the trade wins more often but usually earns less. If it goes down: it wins less often.
P(profit).readIt: When you see this number, check expected shortfall right beside it. High chance plus big tail means win often, lose badly.
P(profit).simple: The model's chance that the position ends in profit. A high number can still hide a big rare loss. Read it with expected shortfall, never alone.

P/E.example: Like paying Rs 22 for every Re 1 a shop earns in a year. A very high P/E means a lot of hope is already in the price.
P/E.forYou: Do not change today's trade on P/E; just remember a very high reading means shocks can hit harder.
P/E.impact: If it goes up: the market is pricier and a shock could cause a bigger fall. If it goes down: the market is cheaper.
P/E.readIt: When you see this number, read its rank against past days. It matters only at extremes.
P/E.simple: NIFTY's level divided by its companies' yearly profits. It shows whether the index is cheap or expensive. It says almost nothing about tomorrow.

PAPER.example: Like a practice exam at home: it feels easier than the real hall.
PAPER.forYou: Use paper to learn rules, and expect real trading to be harder.
PAPER.impact: If you follow stops on paper: good start, but real trades test more. If you skip them even on paper: real trades will be worse.
PAPER.readIt: When you see PAPER, remember real money will feel harder.
PAPER.simple: This badge marks a practice position with no real money. Paper positions are kept apart from real ones. Paper trading overstates real discipline, especially at the stop, because a fake loss hurts less.

PCR (put-call ratio).example: Like counting raincoats versus sunhats in a shop: it does not decide the weather. A PCR of 0.7 means the call side is crowded.
PCR (put-call ratio).forYou: Never place or skip a trade because of PCR alone.
PCR (put-call ratio).impact: If it goes up: the put side gets more crowded. If it goes down: the call side does; neither has predicted direction here.
PCR (put-call ratio).readIt: When you see this number, above 1.2 suggests support below, below 0.8 suggests resistance above. Treat both as context only.
PCR (put-call ratio).simple: Put contracts open divided by call contracts open. Above 1 means more puts, below 1 more calls. As a direction signal it has been a coin flip on this desk.

PCR above 1.2.example: Like a shop where 12 customers ask for umbrellas for every 10 who ask for sunglasses. If put OI is 1.3 crore and call OI is 1 crore, PCR is 1.3.
PCR above 1.2.forYou: As a seller, heavy put writing is often read as support below, but a floor built by sellers can break if the market falls hard.
PCR above 1.2.goodBad: Neither; a description of positioning, not a forecast.
PCR above 1.2.impact: If this turns on: sellers have built a big floor of puts below the market. If it turns off: the put side has thinned or calls have grown.
PCR above 1.2.readIt: When you see this state ON, put writing is heavy. This uses the desk's own data, which covers only about 15 months, so the table has few cases.
PCR above 1.2.simple: PCR is the put-call ratio: open puts divided by open calls on NIFTY options. Above 1.2 means there are far more puts open than calls, usually because many people are selling puts.

PCR and VIX both rising over 5 sessions.example: Like shopkeepers selling more flood insurance just as the rain gets heavier. If PCR goes from 0.95 to 1.10 and VIX from 13 to 14 in a week, this turns on.
PCR and VIX both rising over 5 sessions.forYou: As a seller, you are on the same side as this crowd, so make sure your puts have room if the fear turns into a real fall.
PCR and VIX both rising over 5 sessions.goodBad: Neither; a positioning clue with a short history.
PCR and VIX both rising over 5 sessions.impact: If this turns on: sellers are adding puts while option prices climb. If it turns off: one of the two has stopped rising.
PCR and VIX both rising over 5 sessions.readIt: When you see this state ON, puts are being written into rising fear. This uses the desk's own data, about 15 months, so the table has few cases.
PCR and VIX both rising over 5 sessions.simple: This is on when PCR rose by more than 0.1 over 5 sessions and India VIX rose more than 5% over the same 5 sessions. People are writing more puts while fear is going up.

PCR below 0.8.example: Like a shop where only 7 customers ask for umbrellas for every 10 asking for sunglasses. If put OI is 70 lakh and call OI is 1 crore, PCR is 0.7.
PCR below 0.8.forYou: As a seller, heavy call writing is often read as a ceiling, but ceilings can break in a sharp rally.
PCR below 0.8.goodBad: Neither; a description of positioning, not a forecast.
PCR below 0.8.impact: If this turns on: sellers have built a heavy ceiling of calls above the market. If it turns off: call writing has eased or puts have grown.
PCR below 0.8.readIt: When you see this state ON, call writing is heavy. This uses the desk's own data, about 15 months, so the table has few cases.
PCR below 0.8.simple: PCR is the put-call ratio: open puts divided by open calls on NIFTY options. Below 0.8 means far more calls are open than puts, usually because many people are selling calls.

PE IV.example: Like insurance against a fall costing more than insurance against a rise.
PE IV.forYou: Expect put IV higher; worry only if the gap is unusual.
PE IV.impact: If it goes up: puts are dearer and falls are feared more. If it goes down: less fear.
PE IV.readIt: When you see put IV well above call IV, the market fears a fall.
PE IV.simple: This is the implied volatility of the put, shown on out-of-the-money strikes, those below NIFTY. Put IV above call IV at the same distance is normal. It is called put skew.

PE OI (L).example: Like many people promising to buy if price falls to a certain level.
PE OI (L).forYou: Use it as context, not as a forecast.
PE OI (L).impact: If it goes up: more sellers at that level. If it goes down: they are leaving.
PE OI (L).readIt: When you see a big number, many put sellers sit at that strike.
PE OI (L).simple: PE means put option. This is put open interest, the number of open put contracts, at that strike in lakh shares. Large put OI marks where sellers are committed.

PE price.example: Like the closing rate of a vegetable on that day.
PE price.impact: If it goes up after you sell: you lose. If it goes down: you gain.
PE price.readIt: When you see it, remember your fill will be a little worse.
PE price.simple: This is the put's price at that day's close. It is its last trade if it traded, else NSE's settlement price. Fills add or subtract slippage.

PGMs and autocatalysts.example: Petrol cars use palladium and diesel cars use platinum. More electric cars need neither.
PGMs and autocatalysts.forYou: Read it for context only, as there is no Indian contract.
PGMs and autocatalysts.goodBad: There is no good or bad level; it is context.
PGMs and autocatalysts.impact: If petrol car sales rise: palladium tends to get support. If diesel or electric cars rise: demand shifts.
PGMs and autocatalysts.readIt: When you see this card, compare palladium's price with platinum's. A wide gap pushes makers to switch metals.
PGMs and autocatalysts.simple: Platinum and palladium are the two traded platinum-group metals, PGMs. Most demand is from car exhaust parts called catalytic converters. Neither trades in India.

POP (probability of profit).example: A bet that wins Rs 10 on 85 days and loses Rs 200 on 15 days. If a NIFTY strike shows 85% POP, it wins small often and loses big rarely.
POP (probability of profit).forYou: As a seller, never treat a high POP as safety; pair it with the size of the possible loss.
POP (probability of profit).goodBad: Higher POP means more frequent small wins, not less risk of a big loss.
POP (probability of profit).impact: If POP goes up: the strike is further away and wins more often, with less premium. If it goes down: more premium, more chance of a loss.
POP (probability of profit).readIt: When you see POP, use it to compare strikes, not as a safety score. Next, check expected shortfall. Real gaps are bigger than the model allows.
POP (probability of profit).simple: The model's chance that your short option expires worthless. It comes from today's option prices. It says nothing about how big the loss is when you are wrong.

POP (smile).example: Like a bookie's odds that a team wins. They tell you what the crowd believes, not what will happen.
POP (smile).forYou: A high POP feels safe but does not mean profit; check EV and max loss too.
POP (smile).goodBad: Higher means more frequent wins, not more money. POP (history) asks the same question of past moves.
POP (smile).impact: If POP rises: the trade wins more often, usually with a smaller payout. If it falls: fewer wins, usually bigger ones.
POP (smile).readIt: When you see POP, remember a high POP often comes with a small win and a big loss. Always read it next to EV.
POP (smile).simple: POP is probability of profit: the chance the trade makes money at expiry after costs. This one is read from today's option prices, including the smile. It is the market's own odds, not the desk's forecast.

Paper trade.example: Like a label on a practice notebook so it is not mixed with the exam paper.
Paper trade.forYou: Give each paper trade a short, clear name.
Paper trade.impact: If you name trades clearly: reviews are easier. If not: records get confusing.
Paper trade.readIt: When you see the name, it links the trade to its plan and review.
Paper trade.simple: This is the name you gave the paper position in its pre-trade check. Paper positions are stored separately and never appear among real ones.

Paper trade record.example: Like a practice-match log listing runs and how well you followed the coach's plan.
Paper trade record.forYou: Read the process column before the P&L column.
Paper trade record.impact: If good-process trades grow: your habits are improving. If weak-process wins grow: luck is teaching bad habits.
Paper trade record.readIt: When you see trades in the weak-process win box, treat them as warnings.
Paper trade record.simple: This lists closed paper trades with process score, net P&L after costs and habits tagged. A grid compares process against outcome. Weak process with a win is the dangerous box, because it teaches the wrong lesson.

Parameter heatmaps.example: Like testing a cake recipe with a little more or less sugar and flour. If all versions taste good, the recipe is sturdy.
Parameter heatmaps.forYou: A sturdy rule forgives small mistakes in how you trade it.
Parameter heatmaps.goodBad: A broad patch is good; a lone bright cell suggests luck. A dash means too few trades.
Parameter heatmaps.impact: If nearby cells are also good: small changes will not break the rule. If they are bad: the rule is fragile.
Parameter heatmaps.readIt: When you see a heatmap, look at the cells around the outlined one. Green all around is good; a lone bright cell is a warning.
Parameter heatmaps.simple: The recommended rule with two settings changed at a time, scored in training and testing. The outlined cell is the recommendation. A broad green patch around it means the rule does not rely on one lucky setting.

Participant-wise open interest.example: Like a list of who has bought and who has sold tickets for a match. Every ticket sold has a buyer.
Participant-wise open interest.forYou: It is the only free view of who sits on the other side of your trade.
Participant-wise open interest.goodBad: Longs always equal shorts across the four groups; Net is long minus short.
Participant-wise open interest.impact: If one group builds a big one-sided position: it may have to unwind fast later. If positions shrink: less stored-up pressure.
Participant-wise open interest.readIt: When you see this table, look at net positions and the day change. A big change shows who just moved.
Participant-wise open interest.simple: Open interest is the number of contracts still open. NSE shows it for four groups. They are foreign institutions (FII), brokers (Pro), retail and companies (Client), and Indian institutions (DII). It covers every index together, not NIFTY alone.

Pass-day result.example: Like a batsman's average on good pitches: 45 runs on average, but sometimes 5 and sometimes 90.
Pass-day result.forYou: Compare it with the fail-day result to see what waiting is worth.
Pass-day result.goodBad: Higher than the fail-day result means the filter helped in the backtest. It is no promise for the future.
Pass-day result.impact: If it goes up: trading on good days has paid better in the test. If it goes down: even good days paid less.
Pass-day result.readIt: When you see this number, look at its range too. A wide range means a small or noisy sample.
Pass-day result.simple: This is what the backtest's weekly trade made on average when entered on a day the filter said sell. It is for one lot, after costs. A 90 percent range shows how much it varied.

Passes.example: Like a traffic light: green, red, or not yet showing.
Passes.forYou: Fix the no if you can before trading.
Passes.impact: If more items pass: the process score rises. If a no appears: one point is lost.
Passes.readIt: When you see no, you can still trade, but you lose that point.
Passes.simple: This shows whether a checklist item holds right now: yes, no, or later. Later means it can be judged only after legs exist or at review. A no is information, not a ban.

Path level.example: Like belt colours in karate: you earn them one after another.
Path level.forYou: Do not rush levels; the later ones need the earlier ones.
