Path level.impact: If you pass a level: the next opens for fast-track. If you fail one: you start there.
Path level.readIt: When you see your level, start your lessons there.
Path level.simple: This is a rung of the learning path: foundations, pricing and volatility, selling and risk, edge and evidence, professional. A level passes at two-thirds correct. Levels pass in order.

Patience meter.example: Like a fisherman who goes out only when the forecast says fish are biting: staying home on bad days is part of the job. Trading: if the filter said sell on 40 of 100 days, trading the other 60 is where money leaks.
Patience meter.forYou: Use it on days you feel the urge to trade without the filter's OK.
Patience meter.impact: If fail-day results go down: trading without the filter's OK costs more. If they go up: the cost of impatience shrinks, but check the sample size.
Patience meter.readIt: When you see this card, read the pass rate first, then compare pass-day and fail-day results.
Patience meter.simple: This shows how often the desk's edge filter said sell, and what trading anyway has cost. The edge filter is the desk's test for whether options are priced well for a seller. Waiting is part of the plan, not time lost.

Payoff.example: Like a chart of a farmer's income for different rainfall amounts. Too little or too much rain both hurt.
Payoff.forYou: It shows where you make and lose money at a glance.
Payoff.goodBad: The gap between the dashed and solid lines is time value still in the trade.
Payoff.impact: If NIFTY moves past a breakeven: you start losing. If it stays between them: time works for you.
Payoff.readIt: When you see the payoff, find the breakevens and the flat loss level. That is how far NIFTY can go and what it costs beyond.
Payoff.simple: A picture of what your position is worth at different NIFTY levels. The solid line is on expiry day; the dashed line is if NIFTY jumped there today. Ticks on the axis are the breakevens.

Payoff at expiry.example: Like a movie ticket after the show: only worth something if you actually used the seat.
Payoff at expiry.forYou: Use it to see the worst and best case of a trade at a glance.
Payoff at expiry.impact: If NIFTY ends further past a sold strike: the loss grows point for point, up to the wing. If it ends inside: you keep the credit.
Payoff at expiry.readIt: When you see the payoff line, find where it crosses zero; those are the breakevens.
Payoff at expiry.simple: At expiry an option is worth only its intrinsic value, how far it is past its strike. A sold call loses one point for each point above its strike. A sold put loses one for each point below.

Payoff ratio.example: If you win Rs 1,700 and lose Rs 7,700, the ratio is about 0.22. You need to win about 4 out of 5 times just to break even.
Payoff ratio.forYou: As a seller your wins are small, so a few extra losses can sink you.
Payoff ratio.goodBad: Higher is better; around 0.2 needs over 80% wins to break even.
Payoff ratio.impact: If it rises: each win covers more of each loss. If it falls: you need an even higher win rate.
Payoff ratio.readIt: When you see payoff ratio, compare it with the win rate. The current rules have about 0.22 with an 80% win rate.
Payoff ratio.simple: Average win divided by average loss, ignoring the sign. Option sellers usually have a small payoff ratio. That means they need a high win rate.

Per 10 paper trades.example: Like counting how many times you forgot your helmet for every 10 bike rides. If you logged 4 paper-trade habits over 20 closed paper trades, this shows 2.0.
Per 10 paper trades.forYou: As a seller, bring this down on paper before you trade the same setup with real money.
Per 10 paper trades.goodBad: Lower is better, as long as you log honestly.
Per 10 paper trades.impact: If it goes up: bad habits are showing up more often in paper trades. If it goes down: your practice is getting cleaner.
Per 10 paper trades.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with earlier weeks; a falling number means fewer bad habits in practice.
Per 10 paper trades.simple: This is how many habit mistakes you tagged in paper-trade reviews for every 10 closed paper trades. It shows how often bad habits show up in practice.

Per plan.example: Like a diet diary marking each meal as on plan or off plan.
Per plan.forYou: Aim for every exit to be per plan.
Per plan.impact: If per plan exits go up: your adherence improves. If they go down: more decisions are made on the fly.
Per plan.readIt: When you see not per plan, read the exit reason to find the habit behind it.
Per plan.simple: This says whether the exit followed your written plan. Per plan means take profit near target, stop kept within a day, or a planned time exit.

Per-trade cap.example: Like a rule to never lend more than Rs 2,000 of your Rs 1,00,000 savings to one friend.
Per-trade cap.forYou: Let it decide your size, not your confidence.
Per-trade cap.impact: If you raise it: each trade can hurt more. If it halves after losses: you trade smaller until things settle.
Per-trade cap.readIt: When you see the cap, compare it with each trade's share of capital.
Per-trade cap.simple: This is the most one trade may lose if gapped through, as a share of your capital. The default is 2 percent. It halves after two stops in a row or a 5 percent drawdown.

Pin strike.example: Like a magnet under a table pulling a marble. If the magnet is real, the marble ends near it.
Pin strike.forYou: Treat the pin as an idea to watch, not a reason to place strikes.
Pin strike.goodBad: Verdict on stored data: does not work (p = 0.40).
Pin strike.impact: If NIFTY drifts toward the pin: a short strangle around it does well. If it ignores the pin: there is no extra safety.
Pin strike.readIt: When you see the pin strike, note it, but do not rely on it. The desk's test: NIFTY settled nearer the pin 52% of the time, a mirror strike 48%. That is not better than chance.
Pin strike.simple: The strike near spot (within 5%) where option sellers hold the most gamma. The idea is that hedging pulls NIFTY toward it by expiry. The desk tests this idea and reports honestly.

Pin strike pulls.example: Like writing down 'the marble will roll to the magnet' and checking later.
Pin strike pulls.forYou: Watch it, but do not trade on it yet.
Pin strike pulls.impact: If hits pile up above chance: the pin may work after all. If not: it confirms the study's 'does not work'.
Pin strike pulls.readIt: When you see this claim, check how many are graded and the hit rate.
Pin strike pulls.simple: A forward claim: the front expiry settles nearer the pin strike than to spot on the claim day. It is graded when that expiry settles.

Pin strike test.example: To test a magnet, put a second fake magnet on the other side. If the marble does not prefer the real one, the magnet does nothing.
Pin strike test.forYou: Do not place strikes around the pin expecting a pull.
Pin strike test.impact: If the gap grows with more expiries: the pin may be real. If it stays small: the pin is noise.
Pin strike test.readIt: When you see this test, read hit vs baseline. Pin: 52% of 67 expiries; mirror: 48%; p = 0.40.
Pin strike test.simple: Does NIFTY settle nearer the pin strike than to where it was when the pin was read? It is compared with a mirror strike the same distance on the other side.

Placement result.example: Like a placement letter saying: skip class 1 and 2, start in class 3.
Placement result.forYou: Trust it and start where it says.
Placement result.impact: If more levels are fast-tracked: you skip more basics. If fewer: you start earlier.
Placement result.readIt: When you see start here, begin your lessons at that level.
Placement result.simple: This says whether a level was fast-tracked, is where you start, or lies ahead. Fast-tracking stops at the first level that does not pass.

Placement test.example: Like an entrance test that puts you in the right class.
Placement test.forYou: Take it honestly, without help, so the placement fits.
Placement test.impact: If you pass more levels: you skip ahead. If you pass fewer: you start earlier, which is fine.
Placement test.readIt: When you see a level fast-tracked, its review cards start at a 3-day gap.
Placement test.simple: This is twelve mixed questions across five levels, built from today's numbers. It places you on the path and fast-tracks what you already know. Passing says nothing about trading results.

Plan followed.example: Like leaving the party at 10 pm as promised.
Plan followed.forYou: Follow the plan, then question it in the debrief.
Plan followed.impact: If you follow it: your process score rises. If not: it falls, even if you made money.
Plan followed.readIt: When you see this rule missed, you broke your own plan.
Plan followed.simple: This rule says you exited when your rule fired and did not close outside the plan. Overrides need a written reason and still count as a miss.

Playbook and alerts.example: Like a fire drill card on a school wall: if smoke, go to gate 2. If NIFTY falls below a planned level, the playbook branch tells you to close or adjust a leg.
Playbook and alerts.forYou: As a seller, follow the branch you wrote in advance rather than deciding in the heat of a move.
Playbook and alerts.goodBad: Neither; a fired alert is information, not panic.
Playbook and alerts.impact: If this turns on (an alert fires): price has reached a level your plan cares about. If it turns off: price is back inside the calm branch.
Playbook and alerts.readIt: When you see this section, find the live branch first, then read any alert that fired since your last look.
Playbook and alerts.simple: This section shows which if-then branch of the playbook is live right now, and which alerts have fired. It tells you what your plan says to do at today's price.

Playbook branch.example: Like a train route with stations: if you reach station A do this, if station B do that.
Playbook branch.forYou: Use it to follow a plan made in calm, not to react in the moment.
Playbook branch.impact: If NIFTY moves into a new branch: the playbook's advice changes. If it stays: the current plan holds.
Playbook branch.readIt: When you see the branch change, read its action line and compare it with your positions.
Playbook branch.simple: The playbook is a set of if-then plans. This shows which plan matches where NIFTY is now: sideways, testing a level, or through it. Its action line says what to hold, close or add.

Playbook level.example: Like lines on a cricket pitch: crossing the crease changes what the batsman can do.
Playbook level.forYou: Use it to know in advance where your plan changes.
Playbook level.impact: If NIFTY crosses it: a new scenario and its action line apply. If it holds: the current plan stays.
Playbook level.readIt: When you see NIFTY near this level, check the playbook branch and your short strikes.
Playbook level.simple: This is a support or resistance level the playbook watches. Support is a level where falls have often stopped; resistance is where rises have often stopped. Crossing the first level starts a scenario. The second is a warning.

Playbook levels.example: Like checking how often a ball hit the boundary after a fast start, versus in any over. If a ceiling was reached 40% after similar moves but 20% normally, it is a likely target.
Playbook levels.forYou: Do not sell calls at a ceiling that similar moves often reach.
Playbook levels.impact: If call OI rises at a ceiling: sellers are defending it. If it falls as price nears: they are leaving, which often comes before a breakout.
Playbook levels.readIt: When you see these levels, compare the two percentages. The first much higher means this kind of move tends to reach it.
Playbook levels.simple: The ceilings and floors where option sellers hold the most open contracts. Each shows how often NIFTY reached it after moves like today's, and normally. Both use closing prices.

Position.example: Like one order at a restaurant: dal, rice and roti on one bill, judged together.
Position.forYou: Give each trade its own clear name so the legs stay together.
Position.impact: If you add legs to it: its risk and payoff change together. If you close legs: only what remains is tracked.
Position.readIt: When you see a position, read its P&L now, then its exit-rule status on the same card.
Position.simple: A position is one named trade made of one or more legs. The page shows its P&L now, its risk if NIFTY moves, its payoff at expiry and its exit rules. Profit and loss are in rupees for all lots together.

Position gamma.example: Like a car on a downhill slope. Speed (delta) is one thing, but how fast speed grows (gamma) decides how scary it gets.
Position gamma.forYou: As an option seller your gamma is negative, so watch it most in the last days before expiry.
Position gamma.goodBad: Closer to zero is calmer; more negative means faster-growing losses on a move.
Position gamma.impact: If gamma becomes more negative: small NIFTY moves cause bigger and faster changes in your loss. If it moves toward zero: the position is calmer.
Position gamma.readIt: When you see a negative position gamma, expect losses to grow faster than the move itself. Check it rises sharply near expiry.
Position gamma.simple: Gamma is how fast your position's delta changes when NIFTY moves. Delta is how many rupees you gain or lose per point. A seller usually has negative gamma, so losses speed up as NIFTY moves.

Position value.example: Like what it would cost to buy back something you sold.
Position value.forYou: Compare it with the credit each day.
Position value.impact: If it goes up: you are losing. If it goes down: you are gaining.
Position value.readIt: When you see it fall below your credit, you are in profit.
Position value.simple: This is what it would cost to close the position at that day's prices, in points per unit. Settled legs count at their intrinsic value.

Positioning decision log.example: Like a diary where you guess tomorrow's vegetable price from today's arrivals, then check if you were right.
Positioning decision log.forYou: Use it as a drill to train your reading of fund moves, not as a signal.
Positioning decision log.impact: Nothing here goes up or down. New rows change what you have practised on, and your guesses get better.
Positioning decision log.readIt: When you see a row, guess the next move from the context first. Then open the hindsight line to check.
Positioning decision log.simple: The last 20 weekly reports for one market. Each row shows what funds did and what else was true that week. Hindsight shows what price did next.

Positioning streak.example: If a family buys a bit of gold each month for 6 months, that is a 6-month streak. When they skip a month, the habit may be ending.
Positioning streak.forYou: A long streak breaking is a cue to reassess any position that leaned on that trend.
Positioning streak.goodBad: A long streak means persistent flow; a just-broken one means the flow may be tiring.
Positioning streak.impact: If it goes up: the flow is steady and the trend has support. If it resets to zero: the flow has paused or turned.
Positioning streak.readIt: When you see this number, a long streak means steady flow. It ignores size, so check the weekly change bars too.
Positioning streak.simple: It counts how many weeks in a row funds moved their net bet the same way. Trend-following funds add slowly over many weeks. A broken streak is often the first sign of tiredness.

Positioning summary.example: Like a scoreboard showing which team has more players on the field and what the crowd expects next over.
Positioning summary.forYou: It tells you who might be squeezed and whether the next event is priced fairly.
Positioning summary.impact: If big groups crowd onto one side: a fast unwind is more likely. If positions are balanced: moves tend to be calmer.
Positioning summary.readIt: When you see these tiles, start with who is short options and the event premium. They matter most for a seller.
Positioning summary.simple: Eight numbers that say who is carrying risk in index futures and options today. They also show what the next scheduled event is priced at. Each tile opens a card below.

Positioning swings.example: Think of a trader filling his godown with rice for 8 weeks and then emptying it over 5 weeks. Each fill and each emptying is one swing.
Positioning swings.forYou: Use past swings to judge how far a current fund build-up usually runs before it turns.
Positioning swings.goodBad: A swing far bigger than usual signals a stretched crowd; a small one is ordinary noise.
Positioning swings.impact: If a build-up swing grows larger than usual: the crowd is getting stretched. If an unwind runs long: selling pressure may be close to done.
Positioning swings.readIt: When you see a swing row, compare the size with past swings. Check price 4 weeks after the swing ended to see if the move kept going. Then look up news for that window.
Positioning swings.simple: A swing is one full build-up or unwind of fund bets, from one turning point to the next. Each row is one decision cycle. It shows how much funds added or cut and what prices did.

Positions vs price.example: Like a cricket highlight showing the ball and the batsman side by side, you see whether funds react to price or lead it.
Positions vs price.forYou: Learn whether funds in your market lead or follow before giving their moves weight.
Positions vs price.goodBad: There is no good or bad level; the timing pattern is what you learn.
Positions vs price.impact: If funds turn before price: their moves may lead. If funds turn after price: they are chasing and add little warning.
Positions vs price.readIt: When you see these charts, check if the fund line turns after the price line. If so, funds are following the trend. Hover for weekly numbers.
Positions vs price.simple: Price and fund positioning drawn on the same weekly time line in separate charts. Each chart has its own fair scale. Look at who turns first.

Practice on today's chain.example: Like solving today's newspaper sudoku: fresh numbers every day, same rules.
Practice on today's chain.forYou: Do a few each day rather than many once a week.
Practice on today's chain.impact: If your accuracy goes up: your calculation speed improves. If it drops: the mixed set is doing its job; keep going.
Practice on today's chain.readIt: When you see the mixed set, expect it to feel harder; mixing types helps you remember.
Practice on today's chain.simple: These are ten exercises built from today's option prices. They cover ranges, condor strikes, chance of profit, rupee maths and more. Grades use the same maths as the desk's cards. It trains calculation, not proof of an edge.

Pre-trade check.example: Like a packing list checked before a trip; deciding not to go is also allowed.
Pre-trade check.forYou: Write it fully for every paper trade.
Pre-trade check.impact: If more items pass: the trade fits your process. If fewer: it costs process points.
Pre-trade check.readIt: When you see a no on the checklist, think again before adding legs.
Pre-trade check.simple: This is the plan written before a paper trade. It holds your reason, chance of profit, chance of hitting the stop, exit plan and capital. A checklist reads today's market. Skipping the trade is a valid outcome.

Pre-trade gate.example: Like a pilot's checklist before take-off: fuel, flaps, doors; one red item and the plane waits.
Pre-trade gate.forYou: Run every new trade through it, even the ones you feel sure about.
Pre-trade gate.impact: If more hard rules fail: the trade breaks your own limits. If all pass: the trade fits your rules, which is not a promise of profit.
Pre-trade gate.readIt: When you see a red hard rule, stop and fix it, or write an honest reason if you override.
Pre-trade gate.simple: This is a checklist every new position must pass before it is saved. Hard rules block the trade unless you write why you override. Soft flags ask you to look twice. It also asks for a written if-then exit plan.

Previous close.example: Like the official closing mango price posted by the mandi, not the last random sale. If the NIFTY 25,500 call settled at Rs 40, today's change is measured from Rs 40.
Previous close.forYou: As a seller, check the previous close before reacting to a big change on a far strike.
Previous close.impact: If the previous close was stale: today's change can look falsely large. If it was clean: the change shows the real move.
Previous close.readIt: When you see a huge change on a quiet strike, check the previous close first. On thin strikes, it is often the stale previous close that is wrong. Margin was also set against it overnight.
Previous close.simple: The option's settlement price from the end of the last session. The exchange computes it over a closing window, not from the very last trade. All change numbers are measured from it.

Price and read.example: Like a short report card with marks and a teacher's comment.
Price and read.forYou: Use it as a quick summary for each farm series.
Price and read.impact: If price rises to the top of its range: it is near the year's high. If it drops: near the low.
Price and read.readIt: When you see this card, check where the price sits in its year range and the trend.
Price and read.simple: The latest price, its change, its place in the 12-month range, 1-year return, volatility and trend. A short paragraph reads it using only those figures.

Price history.example: Like a chart of onion prices over five years on a kitchen wall.
Price history.forYou: Check long history before judging today's price.
Price history.impact: If the line trends up: prices have risen. If down: fallen.
Price history.readIt: When you see this chart, ignore steps at roll dates.
Price history.simple: The price over the whole history held. For NCDEX futures, a dashed line shows the underlying spot price. Lines can step at contract rolls.

Pricer error.example: Like a scale that is usually off by 150 grams per kilo. You can still compare bags, but not trust exact weights.
Pricer error.forYou: Treat 18-year research numbers as rough because the prices are modelled.
Pricer error.impact: If error rises: model results are less reliable. If it falls: they are more reliable.
Pricer error.readIt: When you see pricer error, read it as typical error in % of premium. In the research region it is about 16%.
Pricer error.simple: How far the model's option prices are from real traded prices, as a median. It tells you how much to trust results priced by the model.

Pricer validation.example: Like checking a weighing scale against known weights before using it to sell rice.
Pricer validation.forYou: It tells you how much to trust the 18-year research numbers.
Pricer validation.goodBad: Smaller is better. Weekly short strikes stop at 2 sigma because the model underprices beyond that.
Pricer validation.impact: If errors are large in a region: results there are unreliable. If small: model prices there can be trusted more.
Pricer validation.readIt: When you see a cell, read it as typical error in points and in % of premium. Across the research region the median error is about 16%.
Pricer validation.simple: Checks how far the model's option price is from the price that really traded. It is shown by moneyness and days to expiry. Where the error is large, the research does not trade.

Primary source.example: Like keeping the original receipt, not just a friend's word about the price.
Primary source.forYou: Read the source for any rule that changes your rupees.
Primary source.impact: If a primary source is added: the row becomes more trustworthy. If missing: treat the row with care.
Primary source.readIt: When you see a circular number, you can look it up yourself.
Primary source.simple: This is the official SEBI or NSE document the row was checked against. Its number is shown. If only a secondary source was found, the row says so.

Prior 4-week price trend.example: Like checking whether people buy more umbrellas this week because it rained all last month. If gold rose 6% over the past 4 weeks and funds bought this week, that week agrees.
Prior 4-week price trend.forYou: As a seller, a strong link means a month-long trend often brings more fund flow the same way, so do not sell against it too close.
Prior 4-week price trend.goodBad: Neither. It explains fund behaviour; it does not forecast price.
Prior 4-week price trend.impact: If it goes up: funds chase older trends more, so a trend tends to keep getting fresh buying. If it goes down: funds react more to this week's move than to the past month.
Prior 4-week price trend.readIt: When you see this row, read the correlation and the same-direction share. A correlation near 0 and a share near 50% mean no link.
Prior 4-week price trend.simple: A test row: does the price trend of the 4 weeks before this week line up with how funds changed their position this week? The desk measures the correlation over all stored weeks. A strong link means funds follow trends that were already there.

Probability of overfitting.example: A class of 40 sits two exams. Suppose the topper of exam one usually lands in the bottom half of exam two. His first result was luck.
Probability of overfitting.forYou: A low PBO means the search's top picks tend to stay good, though it does not promise profit.
Probability of overfitting.goodBad: Under 25% is good; 25-50% is caution; above 50% means mostly noise. Current: 5.7%.
Probability of overfitting.impact: If PBO rises above 25%: treat the ranking with caution. Above 50%: the search mostly fits noise.
Probability of overfitting.readIt: When you see PBO, low is good. The desk's search shows 5.7% over 12,870 splits of 2,001 rules.
Probability of overfitting.simple: Also called PBO. It splits history into many halves, picks the best rule on one half, and checks it on the other. PBO is how often that best rule lands below the middle on the unseen half.

Process.example: Like grading a student's working in a maths answer, not just the final number.
Process.forYou: Aim for a steady 5 rather than a big profit.
Process.goodBad: High means rules were followed; low means the trade broke rules, whatever the profit.
Process.impact: If it goes up: your decisions follow the rules more. If it goes down: you are cutting corners.
Process.readIt: When you see 5 of 5, you followed every rule, win or lose.
Process.simple: This is the five-point process score of a closed paper trade: plan, defined risk, budget, conditions, exit as planned. It is scored apart from profit. One trade's result says little about the decision.

Process score.example: Like a driving test marking mirror checks and signals, not just whether you reached the end.
Process score.forYou: Keep it high while outcomes vary; that is the target.
Process score.goodBad: High means the rules were followed; low means the decision was poor, whatever the money.
Process score.impact: If it goes up: your decisions follow the rules more. If it goes down: you are breaking rules, even if you won.
Process score.readIt: When you see this score, read it before the profit. 80 percent over 5 replays earns Rules first.
Process score.simple: This is the share of the eight replay rules you followed. They cover price, risk, size, strikes, credit, exits, events and sticking to plan. It is decided before the outcome, so it is scored apart from profit.

Process vs outcome.example: Like a careful driver hit by another car versus a reckless driver who got home safe.
Process vs outcome.forYou: Read the four boxes together, never one trade alone.
Process vs outcome.impact: If good-process boxes grow: you build lasting habits. If bad-process boxes grow: results depend on luck.
Process vs outcome.readIt: When you see a run of bad-process wins, slow down; luck is not skill.
Process vs outcome.simple: This shows which box of the process-against-outcome grid a trade lands in. Good process with a loss is bad luck. Bad process with a win is a warning.

Producers & merchants.example: Like a farmer fixing the sale price of his crop with a mill before harvest. An oil producer that sells futures at 80 dollars knows what it will earn even if the price drops to 60.
Producers & merchants.forYou: As a seller, heavy hedger selling into a rally is protection, not a bearish forecast, so do not read it as a sell signal.
Producers & merchants.goodBad: Neither. Hedgers are not trying to forecast price.
Producers & merchants.impact: If it goes up: these businesses hold less short hedge, often after prices fall. If it goes down: they are selling more ahead, often into a rally to lock in good prices.
Producers & merchants.readIt: When you see this line on the positions chart, compare it with managed money. The two usually move in opposite directions.
Producers & merchants.simple: The CFTC group for real businesses that produce, trade, process or use the commodity, like oil companies, refiners and airlines. They use futures mainly to protect their business from price moves, not to bet. They are often on the opposite side of the funds.

Producers / merchants net.example: Like a cotton trader with 1,000 bales in the godown selling futures so a price fall does not hurt him. If this group holds 300,000 short and 100,000 long, the net is minus 200,000.
Producers / merchants net.forYou: As a seller, this is the other side of the funds, not a price forecast. Use it to understand who is selling, not to time trades.
Producers / merchants net.goodBad: Neither. A big short here is normal hedging.
Producers / merchants net.impact: If it goes up: hedgers are short less, often after prices have fallen. If it goes down: hedgers are selling more ahead, usually into a rally.
Producers / merchants net.readIt: When you see this number, check the weekly change under it and compare with managed money net. The two usually move in opposite directions.
Producers / merchants net.simple: The net position of farmers, grain traders, processors and other real businesses in this agri future: their longs minus their shorts. In most crops it is negative, because they sell futures to protect crops and stocks they own.

Profit captured.example: Like a mango seller who has sold 50 of his 100 mangoes by noon; waiting all day for the last few may not be worth it.
Profit captured.forYou: Use it to spot when a trade has done most of its job and holding on adds risk.
Profit captured.goodBad: Around 50 percent or more means most of the reward is banked. Low or negative means it has not paid yet.
Profit captured.impact: If it goes up: you are nearer the profit target and the rule may say close. If it goes down: the trade is giving back gains.
Profit captured.readIt: When you see this number near 50 percent, the take-profit rule is close. Check the exit rules row.
Profit captured.simple: This shows how much of the most you can make is already in your pocket. It is a percent. Sellers usually close well before 100 percent. The last part pays little for the risk you still carry.

Profit target.example: You sell mangoes on a hot day and 80 of 100 are gone by noon. Waiting till night for the last 20 risks the whole cart in a storm. If you sold a NIFTY call for Rs 40 and it is now Rs 20, a 50% target says buy it back and stop.
Profit target.forYou: As a seller, taking profit early banks real money and frees margin, instead of risking much for little.
Profit target.goodBad: A very high target means holding risk for crumbs; a middle target banks most money with less risk.
Profit target.impact: If it goes up: you hold longer for more money, but you stay exposed to gaps for longer. If it goes down: you take smaller wins sooner and spend less time at risk.
Profit target.readIt: When you see this number, read it as a share of your credit. For example, 50% means close when half is earned. Check how many days are left and how close spot is to your strike. Closing also frees your margin for the next trade.
Profit target.simple: The point where you close a trade early and keep the money. It is set as a share of the premium you collected. The last bit of premium comes in slowly but carries the same danger.

Progress signals.example: Like a report card for study habits, not for how many matches you played.
Progress signals.impact: If badges grow: your skills are proven over more tries. If they drop: recent work slipped.
Progress signals.readIt: When you see a badge, it means quality over a minimum sample.
Progress signals.simple: These are learning days and skill badges. Nothing rewards trading activity, profit or time spent. Streaks are avoided because more activity is a risk for a seller.

Projection cone.example: Like a parent saying the school bus is usually 5 minutes late, rarely 10. If gold is Rs 70,000, the one-sigma cone for a week might be Rs 68,600 to Rs 71,400.
Projection cone.forYou: As a seller, put short strikes outside the cone, ideally near or beyond the two-sigma edge.
Projection cone.impact: If the cone gets wider: bigger moves are normal now and strikes need more distance. If it gets narrower: moves are smaller, but sudden news can still break it.
Projection cone.readIt: When you see the cone, ask if your strike is outside the outer band. Price stays inside the inner band about 68% of the time, inside the outer band about 95%.
Projection cone.simple: The shaded band on each chart showing how far the price may travel. It is drawn at one and two standard deviations, which are measures of normal size of moves. It says nothing about direction.

Projection record.example: Like a teacher's register that cannot be erased. The inner band should hold about 68% of the time, the outer band about 95%.
Projection record.forYou: Trust the page's ranges only as far as this record shows they have held.
Projection record.goodBad: Near 68% for one sigma and 95% for two sigma is good; well below is bad for a seller.
Projection record.impact: If hit rates rise above target: ranges are a bit too wide. If they fall below: ranges are too narrow, which costs sellers money.
Projection record.readIt: When you see the record, compare hit rates with 68% and 95%. The lean's hit rate shows only after 20 leans resolve.
Projection record.simple: Every range and lean the page has published, scored once its date arrives. Rows are written once and never changed. That honesty is why the hit rates are worth reading.

Providers.example: Like a list of suppliers for a shop, with the last delivery date for each. If the news provider last worked 3 days ago, the headlines are old.
Providers.forYou: Before trusting an unusual number, check that its provider is working.
Providers.goodBad: All recent and no errors is good.
Providers.impact: If a provider starts failing: some numbers on the page stop updating. If it recovers: its data becomes current again.
Providers.readIt: When you see 'never' or a red error, the data from that provider is missing or old.
Providers.simple: A table of every data source the desk uses and when each one last worked. If a source fails, its error is shown here. It tells you which parts of the page are current.

Proxy 25d butterfly.example: If insurance for big floods costs much more than for a normal rain, people fear extremes.
Proxy 25d butterfly.forYou: Know that a rich butterfly means far-out options are pricey to buy and better paid to sell.
Proxy 25d butterfly.goodBad: High means tail fear; low means calm expectations.
Proxy 25d butterfly.impact: If it goes up: the market fears big surprises more. If it goes down: fear of extremes is easing.
Proxy 25d butterfly.readIt: When you see this number, higher means far strikes are rich. Lower means the middle is priced closer to the tails.
Proxy 25d butterfly.simple: It is the average volatility of the far call and far put minus the at-the-money volatility. It shows how much extra people pay for big moves. Higher means the tails are pricier.

Proxy 25d risk reversal.example: If people pay more for flood insurance than for drought insurance, they fear floods more.
Proxy 25d risk reversal.forYou: Use it to see which side of the market US holders fear more.
Proxy 25d risk reversal.goodBad: Strongly negative means fear of falls; strongly positive means a rush for upside.
Proxy 25d risk reversal.impact: If it goes up: demand for upside calls is rising. If it goes down: demand for downside protection is rising.
Proxy 25d risk reversal.readIt: When you see this number, negative means puts are dearer. Positive means calls are dearer.
Proxy 25d risk reversal.simple: It is an upside call's volatility minus an equally distant downside put's volatility. 25d means 25 delta, a standard distance. It shows which side people pay more to protect.

Proxy ATM IV.example: Like the going rate for insuring a car at today's value, not a scratched or brand new one.
Proxy ATM IV.forYou: Use it as a hint for MCX option prices, never as a trigger to sell.
Proxy ATM IV.goodBad: High means expensive options and nervous markets; low means calm.
Proxy ATM IV.impact: If it goes up: options on the ETF cost more and fear is rising. If it goes down: the market is calmer.
Proxy ATM IV.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with past readings and with the commodity's realised moves.
Proxy ATM IV.simple: ATM means at the money, the strike nearest today's price. ATM IV is the implied volatility there, for the ETF's main monthly expiry. It is the market's price for movement.

Proxy OI walls.example: Like speed bumps on a road: they slow cars down but do not stop them.
Proxy OI walls.forYou: Use walls as soft reference points, not as safe strikes.
Proxy OI walls.goodBad: Bigger walls may slow price more; small walls matter little.
Proxy OI walls.impact: If price nears a big wall: moves may slow there. If it breaks through: hedging can add to the move.
Proxy OI walls.readIt: When you see the walls, note their distance from spot. They are not barriers, only places where hedging may slow price.
Proxy OI walls.simple: The strikes with the most open calls above the price and open puts below it. They lie within 15% of today's price. Big positions there can slow price movement.

Proxy gamma flip.example: Above the flip, dealers act like shock absorbers on a bus. Below it, they act like a push on a swing.
Proxy gamma flip.forYou: Treat it as a rough hint about US market behaviour, not about MCX.
Proxy gamma flip.goodBad: Above the flip is usually calmer; below is usually wilder.
Proxy gamma flip.impact: If price falls below the flip: moves can get bigger. If price rises above it: moves can get calmer.
Proxy gamma flip.readIt: When you see this level, check if price is above or below it. Both conventions are shown, because who sold is not published.
Proxy gamma flip.simple: Gamma is how fast option risk changes as price moves. The flip is where dealer gamma changes sign. Above it, dealer hedging tends to calm moves; below it, to grow them.

Proxy put-call ratio.example: If more people buy home insurance than lottery tickets, they are cautious.
Proxy put-call ratio.forYou: Do not read a high ratio as a sell signal on its own.
Proxy put-call ratio.goodBad: Very high means heavy hedging; very low means heavy call buying.
Proxy put-call ratio.impact: If it goes up: more protection is held. If it goes down: more upside bets are held.
Proxy put-call ratio.readIt: When you see this ratio, remember ETF holders often buy puts to hedge. So a high ratio is not always a bearish bet.
Proxy put-call ratio.simple: Put open interest divided by call open interest on the ETF's main expiry. Open interest means options still open. Above 1 means more puts than calls.

Proxy term structure.example: Short-term umbrella hire costs more if a storm is due tomorrow.
Proxy term structure.forYou: A spiking front month is a warning before selling near-dated premium.
Proxy term structure.goodBad: Upward slope is normal; an inverted slope means stress.
Proxy term structure.impact: If the front rises above the back: a near event or panic is priced. If it slopes up again: calm has returned.
Proxy term structure.readIt: When you see this line, check if it slopes up. A front month higher than the back marks an event or stress.
Proxy term structure.simple: At-the-money volatility for each ETF expiry, nearest first. Normally later expiries cost a bit more. A front month above later ones signals near-term stress.

Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).example: Like asking 100 shopkeepers if business is better than last month. A PMI of 52 means slightly more say better.
Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).forYou: Treat PMI as slow background, not a reason for a short-term option trade.
Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).impact: If it goes up past 50: business is growing. If it falls below 50: business is shrinking.
Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).readIt: When you see a PMI, check the release date, provider and sector. Unavailable is shown when no verified feed exists.
Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI).simple: A survey of businesses about how conditions are going. 50 is the neutral line. Above 50 means things are growing; below means shrinking.

Put / call ratio.example: Like counting umbrellas and sunglasses sold: it does not tell you whether it will rain. A PCR of 1.3 means 130 puts open for every 100 calls.
Put / call ratio.forYou: Never sell or skip a trade on PCR alone; the desk found it no better than chance.
Put / call ratio.impact: If it goes up: more puts are open, often read as support below. If it goes down: more calls, often read as a ceiling above; neither predicts direction here.
Put / call ratio.readIt: When you see this number, above about 1.2 means the put side is crowded; below 0.8 the call side. Treat it as background only.
Put / call ratio.simple: Total put contracts open divided by total call contracts open. Every contract has a buyer and a seller. So it cannot tell who acted first, and the desk grades it as a coin flip.

Put OI.example: Like counting all umbrella rental slips still out: each slip has a renter and a shop. If put OI is 150 lakh, that many put contracts are open.
Put OI.forYou: Use put OI by strike to find the put wall, not to call direction.
Put OI.impact: If it goes up: more put positions are open, often read as support below. If it goes down: put positions are closing.
Put OI.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with call OI. Their ratio is the PCR.
Put OI.simple: The total number of put contracts still open. Each one has a buyer and a seller, so it belongs to both sides equally. It is shown in lakhs.

Put wall.example: Like a floor that usually holds but sometimes cracks in a storm. If the put wall is 24,500 and NIFTY is 25,000, it acts as a floor.
Put wall.forYou: Sell puts below the put wall and give them more room than calls, since this floor fails more often.
Put wall.impact: If the put wall moves up: the floor is closer to the price. If it moves down: the floor is further away.
Put wall.readIt: When you see this strike, note its distance below the price. It breaks more often than the call wall, usually on panic days.
Put wall.simple: The strike with the most put contracts open. Put sellers lose money below it, so they defend it. It held on 80.0% of graded sessions, less often than the call wall.

Put wall holds.example: Like a dam that is meant to hold back a flood. After each monsoon you check if the water crossed it. Floor walls are tested hardest on the days everything falls at once.
Put wall holds.forYou: As a seller, give short puts extra distance below the put wall, because falls come quickly.
Put wall holds.goodBad: Higher is better, but a put wall that holds less than the call wall is normal, not a fault.
Put wall holds.impact: If the hit rate goes up: the floor has been dependable. If it goes down: sharp falls have been breaking it, so short puts need more room.
Put wall holds.readIt: When you see this claim's hit rate, compare it with the call wall's. Markets fall faster than they rise, so the put wall usually holds less often.
Put wall holds.simple: Each day the desk writes down that NIFTY will not close below the put wall by expiry. The put wall is the put strike where sellers hold the most contracts. Later it checks if that came true.

Put wall test.example: Like testing if the most-watched floor of a building holds better than any other floor.
Put wall test.forYou: Do not treat the put wall as a guaranteed floor for your short puts.
Put wall test.impact: If the put wall beat the baseline clearly: it would be a useful floor. Since it did not: it is just a level.
Put wall test.readIt: When you see this test, compare hold rates. Put wall held 79%; any level held 78%; p = 0.43.
Put wall test.simple: Did NIFTY close above the strike with the most put open interest on every session until expiry? It is compared with any level the same distance below spot.

Questions.example: Like a practice set your teacher wrote herself.
Questions.forYou: Answer every question in weak units.
Questions.impact: If questions go up: more practice is available. If few: practise elsewhere too.
Questions.readIt: When you see a high count, that unit gets more practice.
Questions.simple: This is the number of original practice questions for this unit. None is copied from the NISM workbook or a question bank.

Questions answered.example: Like an odometer: it shows distance, not driving skill.
Questions answered.impact: If it goes up: more practice done. If it stays: no new practice.
Questions answered.readIt: When you see a big number, check accuracy too.
Questions answered.simple: This counts every practice answer you have submitted, across all sets. It is shown for context and earns nothing by itself.

RBI MPC decision.example: Like the bank telling you your home-loan EMI will go up or down. Because it is Indian, the desk measures NIFTY's move on the same session.
RBI MPC decision.forYou: As a seller, the rule only stands aside for an event that has measurably moved NIFTY, not just because the calendar calls it big.
RBI MPC decision.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: rate days have been moving NIFTY more. If it goes down: rate days have been quiet.
RBI MPC decision.readIt: When you see this row, look at Cases first: few cases means the number is not yet reliable. Then compare the move with an ordinary day.
RBI MPC decision.simple: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee decides India's repo rate, the base interest rate, about six times a year. The decision is announced during Indian market hours.

RBOB gasoline.example: Like the price of petrol compared with the crude that goes into it. If RBOB is 2.50 dollars a gallon, a 42-gallon barrel of it is worth 105 dollars.
RBOB gasoline.forYou: As a seller, there is no RBOB option on MCX, so use it as background for crude.
RBOB gasoline.goodBad: Neither. It is a market, not a score.
RBOB gasoline.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish on US petrol, often around the summer driving season. If it goes down: they are less bullish or adding shorts.
RBOB gasoline.readIt: When you see this row, compare its fund positioning with WTI. Strong petrol demand often shows up here before crude.
RBOB gasoline.simple: The US petrol future on NYMEX, in lots of 42,000 gallons. RBOB is the blend used to make the petrol sold at US pumps. Its price over crude shows how much refiners earn on petrol.

ROM (return on margin).example: A shop earning Rs 1,000 on Rs 10,000 stock beats one earning Rs 1,500 on Rs 50,000. If a NIFTY condor earns Rs 2,000 on Rs 50,000 margin, ROM is 4%.
ROM (return on margin).forYou: As a seller, judge strikes by ROM, not by how big the premium looks on screen.
ROM (return on margin).goodBad: Higher ROM means better use of capital for similar risk; below 0.80% is not worth the tail risk here.
ROM (return on margin).impact: If ROM goes up: you earn more per rupee locked, though check the risk shape. If it goes down below the floor: the premium does not pay for the risk.
ROM (return on margin).readIt: When you see ROM, compare it only between similar risk shapes. A defined-risk 26% and a naked 26% are not the same trade. Below the floor, the desk says no trade.
ROM (return on margin).simple: Credit divided by the margin blocked, for the life of the trade. It makes different strikes and setups comparable. This desk needs at least 0.80% before it suggests a trade.

RSI (14).example: Like a batsman's last 14 innings, mostly big scores. If NIFTY's RSI is 75, recent days were mostly up, but it can stay above 70 for weeks.
RSI (14).forYou: As a seller, do not move strikes on RSI alone, because the desk's record does not support it.
RSI (14).goodBad: Above 70 means strong recent gains; below 30 means strong recent losses; neither predicts reliably.
RSI (14).impact: If it goes up past 70: recent days were very one-sided up, and some traders may sell. If it goes down below 30: recent days were very one-sided down.
RSI (14).readIt: When you see RSI, treat 70 and 30 as popular lines, not proven signals. It is context only. Nothing the desk grades depends on it.
RSI (14).simple: RSI (relative strength index) compares average gains with average losses over 14 days. It runs from 0 to 100. Above 70 is called overbought; below 30, oversold.

RSI above 70 in an uptrend.example: Like a good student who already tops the class and then has an extra strong week. If NIFTY's 200-day average is 23,500, NIFTY at 25,400 with RSI 74 turns this on.
RSI above 70 in an uptrend.forYou: As a seller, short calls face the most pressure here, so check the table before selling calls close to spot.
RSI above 70 in an uptrend.goodBad: Neither; strength inside a strong trend.
RSI above 70 in an uptrend.impact: If this turns on: momentum is stretched up while the big trend is also up. If it turns off: either RSI cooled below 70 or NIFTY fell under its 200-day average.
RSI above 70 in an uptrend.readIt: When you see this state ON, a strong burst is happening inside a healthy long trend. The table shows how NIFTY behaved after such spells compared with an ordinary day.
RSI above 70 in an uptrend.simple: This is RSI(14) above 70 while NIFTY is also above its 200-day average. So the market is overbought inside a long-term rise.

RSI below 30 in a downtrend.example: Like a weak team losing even more heavily this week. If NIFTY's 200-day average is 25,000 and NIFTY is at 23,200 with RSI 25, this turns on.
RSI below 30 in a downtrend.forYou: As a seller, this is the riskiest backdrop for short puts, so keep them small, far and hedged.
RSI below 30 in a downtrend.impact: If this turns on: a fall is stretched inside a down market. If it turns off: the selling eased or NIFTY climbed back above its 200-day average.
RSI below 30 in a downtrend.readIt: When you see this state ON, selling is heavy and the big trend is also down. The table shows how NIFTY behaved after such spells.
RSI below 30 in a downtrend.simple: This is RSI(14) below 30 while NIFTY is also below its 200-day average. The market is oversold inside a longer-term fall.

RSI below 30 in an uptrend.example: Like a healthy person catching a short cold. If NIFTY's 200-day average is 23,500 and NIFTY drops quickly from 25,000 to 24,000 with RSI 28, this turns on.
RSI below 30 in an uptrend.forYou: As a seller, put premium is usually fatter after a sharp dip; the table tells you whether such dips tended to recover or keep falling.
RSI below 30 in an uptrend.goodBad: Neither; a dip, not yet a broken trend.
RSI below 30 in an uptrend.impact: If this turns on: a sharp pullback has hit an uptrend. If it turns off: either the dip eased or NIFTY fell below its 200-day average.
RSI below 30 in an uptrend.readIt: When you see this state ON, a fast fall is happening while the big trend is still up. The table shows how NIFTY moved after such dips.
RSI below 30 in an uptrend.simple: This is RSI(14) below 30 while NIFTY is still above its 200-day average. It is a sharp dip inside a longer-term rise.

RSI(14) above 70.example: Like a batsman who has hit boundaries on most of the last 14 balls. If NIFTY rose on 11 of the last 14 days, RSI is likely above 70.
RSI(14) above 70.forYou: As a seller, overbought is not a promise of a fall, so do not sell calls close to spot only because RSI is high.
RSI(14) above 70.goodBad: Neither; strong markets often stay overbought.
RSI(14) above 70.impact: If this turns on: upward momentum is stretched. If it turns off: the run of strong up days has cooled.
RSI(14) above 70.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY has had a strong run of up days. The table shows how long such spells lasted and how NIFTY moved over the next 5, 10 and 21 sessions.
RSI(14) above 70.simple: RSI measures how strong recent up days were compared with down days, on a 0 to 100 scale over 14 days. Above 70 is called overbought: buyers have been very strong.

RSI(14) below 30.example: Like a team that has lost most of its last 14 matches. If NIFTY fell on 11 of the last 14 days, RSI is likely below 30.
RSI(14) below 30.forYou: As a seller, oversold is not a promise of a bounce, so do not sell puts near spot just because RSI is low.
RSI(14) below 30.goodBad: Neither; weak markets can stay oversold.
RSI(14) below 30.impact: If this turns on: downward momentum is stretched. If it turns off: the selling has eased.
RSI(14) below 30.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY has had a hard run of down days. The table shows how long such spells lasted and what NIFTY did afterwards.
RSI(14) below 30.simple: RSI measures how strong recent up days were compared with down days, on a 0 to 100 scale over 14 days. Below 30 is called oversold: sellers have been very strong.

Ranked trades.example: Like a list of all the shops you could rent, sorted by profit per rupee of rent. The top shop is the best use of your money.
Ranked trades.forYou: It shows the best use of your risk money today, if any exists.
Ranked trades.goodBad: Higher EV per risk ranks higher; below zero means a loss on average after costs.
Ranked trades.impact: If the top rows turn positive: there are trades paid for their risk. If all stay negative: no trade is worth it today on the desk's numbers.
Ranked trades.readIt: When you see the list, look at the top rows and their EV per risk. A negative number means the trade loses on average after costs.
Ranked trades.simple: Every put spread, call spread and iron condor the scanner could price, sorted best first. Short strikes sit half a sigma to two sigma from NIFTY. Sigma here means one typical expected move.

Reading CFTC positioning.example: If 9 of 10 shoppers have already bought gold before Diwali, few buyers remain.
Reading CFTC positioning.forYou: Check the test result before betting against crowded funds.
Reading CFTC positioning.goodBad: Extremes mean crowding; near zero is normal.
Reading CFTC positioning.impact: If the z-score goes up: funds are more crowded long. If it goes down: more crowded short.
Reading CFTC positioning.readIt: When you see the z-score, above 2 or below -2 is extreme. Then check what followed past extremes.
Reading CFTC positioning.simple: Fund net long as a share of open interest, with a z-score against three years. A z-score shows how unusual a value is. It tests whether extremes predict the next four weeks.

Reading WASDE and crop reports.example: If the national grain stock left after a year shrinks, prices usually feel pressure upward.
Reading WASDE and crop reports.forYou: Avoid holding short options through WASDE days if they move your crop.
Reading WASDE and crop reports.goodBad: Low stocks-to-use means tight supply; high means plenty.
Reading WASDE and crop reports.impact: If stocks-to-use falls: supply is tighter and prices may rise. If it rises: supply is looser.
Reading WASDE and crop reports.readIt: When you see this report, check the change in stocks-to-use against the last report.
Reading WASDE and crop reports.simple: WASDE is the US farm department's monthly world crop report. It gives ending stocks, total use and stocks-to-use. The test checks if a stocks-to-use cut predicts a rise.

Reading inventory reports (EIA).example: If your kitchen rice tin usually drops 1 kg a week but dropped 3 kg, you are eating more.
Reading inventory reports (EIA).forYou: Check the test verdict before trading on an EIA surprise.
Reading inventory reports (EIA).goodBad: A big draw means tightness; a big build means surplus.
Reading inventory reports (EIA).impact: If stocks drop more than normal: crude prices tend to get support. If they rise more: prices tend to weaken.
Reading inventory reports (EIA).readIt: When you see the surprise, a big draw is bullish and a big build is bearish. Then check the test verdict.
Reading inventory reports (EIA).simple: The weekly EIA stock change compared with the usual change for that week over five years. The gap is the surprise. It is tested to see if it predicts the next five days.

Reading the carry.example: Like the line on a medicine strip that says how to read the dose chart. If a far contract shows no open interest, its carry is left blank on purpose, not by mistake.
Reading the carry.forYou: Trust carry numbers only on contracts marked liquid.
Reading the carry.goodBad: Neither; it is a reading guide, not a number.
Reading the carry.impact: If basis goes up across expiries: that is the normal cost of waiting. If it goes down below zero: the future is below the index, so the market is pricing a drop or a payout the index does not show yet.
Reading the carry.readIt: When you see a blank carry or an 'untraded' tag in the tables, read this note: the price there is an old stub, not a trade.
Reading the carry.simple: A short note explaining how to read the futures tables above it. It says why carry is hidden on contracts nobody trades, and what a negative basis means. It is the instructions for the carry numbers.

Real chain range.example: Like home videos that start only from the year you bought the camera.
Real chain range.forYou: Know which kind of day you are replaying.
Real chain range.impact: If the range grows: more real days to practise on. If not: synthetic days fill the gap.
Real chain range.readIt: When you see the start date, older days are synthetic, not real data.
Real chain range.simple: This is the first day with real stored option data that can be replayed. Real replays cover only the desk's own records, so they have few crisis days.

Real or paper.example: Like a practice net and a real match: the runs in the nets do not count on the scoreboard.
Real or paper.forYou: Use paper to rehearse rules, not to prove a strategy.
Real or paper.impact: If you switch to paper: nothing you do touches real P&L. If you switch to real: you see your actual trades.
Real or paper.readIt: When you see PAPER, the numbers are practice only.
Real or paper.simple: This switch moves My positions between real trades and paper trades, which are practice trades with no real money. They are stored apart and never mixed. Paper screens carry a PAPER badge.

Realised forecast.example: Like guessing tomorrow's crowd at a shop from yesterday, last week and last month together. If the forecast is 11% and options price 13%, sellers are being paid extra.
Realised forecast.forYou: Read it next to implied volatility; you want implied at least 1.10 times this forecast before selling.
Realised forecast.impact: If the forecast goes up: real moves are expected to grow, and selling gets less attractive. If it goes down: selling looks better paid.
Realised forecast.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with ATM implied volatility. Their ratio is the IV/RV number that drives the sell rule.
Realised forecast.simple: A forecast of how much NIFTY will actually move, built from yesterday, last week and last month. Each gets its own weight. The desk compares this with what options are charging.

Realised vol by gamma regime.example: Like plotting rainfall each week, grouped by whether the forecast said calm or stormy, with the forecast marked.
Realised vol by gamma regime.forYou: It shows whether calm gamma days actually paid you.
Realised vol by gamma regime.goodBad: Below the dashed tick favours sellers.
Realised vol by gamma regime.impact: If dots sit below the tick: sellers were overpaid. If above: sellers were underpaid.
Realised vol by gamma regime.readIt: When you see the dots, compare each group's middle with its dashed tick.
Realised vol by gamma regime.simple: Each session is a dot showing real volatility over the next five sessions. Dots are grouped by sellers' gamma then. A dashed tick shows what options implied. A group below its tick paid sellers.

Realised volatility (RV).example: An insurance company charges Rs 1,000; realised is how much it actually paid in claims. If NIFTY options charged for 1% daily moves but NIFTY moved 0.6%, sellers were well paid.
Realised volatility (RV).forYou: As a seller, you want implied volatility to stay above realised, because that gap is your pay.
Realised volatility (RV).goodBad: High RV means a rough market and more danger to short strikes; low RV means calm.
Realised volatility (RV).impact: If it goes up: moves are getting bigger, and short options face more risk. If it goes down: the market is calmer, and premium is easier to keep.
Realised volatility (RV).readIt: When you see this number, compare it with IV. The desk shows several windows and five methods. Short windows react fast and mislead more; long windows are steady but slow.
Realised volatility (RV).simple: How much NIFTY really moved, measured from past prices. Implied volatility is what options charge; realised is what actually happened. It is the bill the premium is judged against.

Recent extremes.example: If tomato prices ranged Rs 20 to Rs 80 this year and are Rs 70 now, they are near the top.
Recent extremes.forYou: Use it to spot stretched prices.
Recent extremes.impact: If price nears the high: it is stretched up. If it nears the low: stretched down.
Recent extremes.readIt: When you see this table, check position in range and the last move z-score.
Recent extremes.simple: The 12-month high and low, where today sits, the drop from the high and the year's largest moves. A z-score shows how unusual the latest move was.

Recommended rule.example: Like choosing a house where the whole street is good, not just one house in a bad street.
Recommended rule.forYou: It is the case for or against changing your rules, not an order to change them.
Recommended rule.goodBad: 'Same' means the research kept the desk's setting. Raw argmax is the single best training rule, before the neighbour check.
Recommended rule.impact: If the recommendation changes when new data arrives: it is less sturdy. If it stays stable: there is more reason to trust it.
Recommended rule.readIt: When you see this table, read each row where it differs from current. The current recommendation is a weekly 10-delta condor with 1-sigma wings, no take profit and a 1x intraday stop.
Recommended rule.simple: The research's sturdy choice of settings, shown next to the current playbook settings. It is chosen so that nearby settings also score well, not just one lucky one. Nothing changes until someone copies it into the playbook.

Recommended structure.example: A shopkeeper who only buys mangoes when they are ripe, cheap and plentiful; some days he buys none. If NIFTY is 25,000 and no strike pays enough for the risk, the desk says no trade.
Recommended structure.forYou: As a seller, the days you sit out often matter more than the days you trade.
Recommended structure.impact: If more filters pass: a trade appears, sized by the strictest limit. If fewer pass: the card shows none, and sitting out protects your capital.
Recommended structure.readIt: When you see this card, first check if it says none and why. If it suggests a trade, check strikes, credit and size. The size is the smallest of four limits, never an average.
Recommended structure.simple: The trade the desk's rules allow today, or a clear 'none'. Strikes must have enough buyers and sellers, be far enough from spot, and pay enough. 'None' is a real answer, not a failure.

Reliability of your forecasts.example: Like checking a forecaster: on days she said 80 percent rain, did it rain on 8 of 10?
Reliability of your forecasts.forYou: Look at the 70 to 90 percent bins most; that is where people are usually overconfident.
Reliability of your forecasts.goodBad: Dots on the diagonal are good; far below means you say sure too often.
Reliability of your forecasts.impact: If dots move toward the diagonal: you are better calibrated. If they drift below: you are more overconfident.
Reliability of your forecasts.readIt: When you see a dot, check how many forecasts sit in its bin. Under a dozen is mostly luck.
Reliability of your forecasts.simple: This chart groups your forecasts by the chance you gave, in 10 percent steps. Each dot shows how often those things really happened. Dots below the diagonal mean overconfidence. Dots above mean underconfidence.

Replay day.example: Like a newspaper from that morning: no future news inside.
Replay day.forYou: Choose a mix of calm and wild days.
Replay day.impact: If you pick a calm day: practice is routine. If you pick a crisis day: it tests your rules hard.
Replay day.readIt: When you see the date, imagine you know nothing beyond it.
Replay day.simple: This is the day you are replaying, as it looked at the close. Nothing after this close is shown until you commit.

Replay debrief.example: Like a coach's match review: the plan first, then the score.
Replay debrief.forYou: Write one lesson from each debrief.
Replay debrief.impact: If the process score goes up: your decisions improve, win or lose. If it goes down: a win is luck, and a warning.
Replay debrief.readIt: When you see it, read process before the money.
Replay debrief.simple: This shows the result, process score, forecast scores and what the desk did on the same day. Read the process score first.

Replay trainer.example: Like watching an old cricket match with the score hidden: you call the next move, then see what really happened.
Replay trainer.forYou: Replay crisis days too; they teach what calm days cannot.
Replay trainer.impact: If your process scores rise over replays: your decisions follow the rules better. If they fall: revisit the rules list.
Replay trainer.readIt: When you see a replay day, commit your trade before revealing anything.
Replay trainer.simple: You trade a past day using only what was known at its close. Then you watch what happened, one day at a time. Your decision is scored on the rules, apart from the money. It trains judgement, not order execution.

Replayable days.example: Like a library of old matches you can rewatch, except this week's.
Replayable days.forYou: Mix calm and crisis days in your practice.
Replayable days.impact: If it goes up: more days to practise on. If it stays the same: pick crisis days for variety.
Replayable days.readIt: When you see this count, more days mean more practice choices.
Replayable days.simple: This counts past days you can replay: real stored option data plus made-up crisis days. A real day needs its later expiry to have settled. So the most recent week is never listed.

Replays debriefed.example: Like counting matches you reviewed with the coach, including ones you chose not to play.
Replays debriefed.impact: If it goes up: your process figures become more reliable. If it stays low: scores are still early.
Replays debriefed.readIt: When you see this number grow, your sample of decisions is growing.
Replays debriefed.simple: This counts replays you finished and reviewed. Standing aside counts exactly like a trade. The score is about the decision, not about being active.

Research: how option sellers make money.example: Like a cookbook's list of tested recipes and who tested them. SEBI's study of about 1 crore traders is one source.
Research: how option sellers make money.forYou: Read the SEBI study summary to remember how most option traders lose money.
Research: how option sellers make money.impact: If a new rule is tested on stored NIFTY data and works: the desk uses it. If it fails: it is dropped.
Research: how option sellers make money.readIt: When you see this list, read what each source found. US results are a starting point, not proof for NIFTY.
Research: how option sellers make money.simple: A reading list behind the desk's rules. It covers the regulator's data on who wins in Indian options, academic studies and long-term results of option selling. Each line says what the desk uses from it.

Result a trade: filter pass vs fail.example: Like comparing your scores on days you slept well with days you did not.
Result a trade: filter pass vs fail.forYou: Use it to see the case for waiting in one picture.
Result a trade: filter pass vs fail.impact: If the gap widens: the filter mattered more in the test. If it narrows: less difference.
Result a trade: filter pass vs fail.readIt: When you see the two bars, check if the whiskers overlap; a big overlap means the gap is uncertain.
Result a trade: filter pass vs fail.simple: This chart compares the backtest's average trade on days the filter said sell with days it said stand aside. The whiskers are 90 percent ranges, showing how much results varied.

Retention.example: Like a weekly test at school: how many answers you still remember after a week. If you recalled 17 of 20 long-gap cards, retention is 85%.
Retention.forYou: As a seller, remembering your rules under pressure is what keeps a bad day from becoming a disaster.
Retention.impact: If it goes up: the rules are sticking in long-term memory. If it goes down: you are forgetting and should review more regularly.
Retention.readIt: When you see this, check how many reviews it is based on; under 30 is mostly noise.
Retention.simple: This is the share of cards you remembered correctly when they came back after a gap of 7 days or more. It shows how much really stays in your memory.

Retry ladder.example: Like calling the shop three times to check if the mangoes arrived. If they came on the first call, you skip the next two. For NIFTY, the exchange posts final numbers slowly after the close.
Retry ladder.forYou: As a seller, a failed ladder means today's numbers are not real yet, so wait before trading.
Retry ladder.impact: If all rungs fail: you see stale figures, clearly marked as old. If one rung succeeds: today's data is stored and the page is current.
Retry ladder.readIt: When you see this ladder, skipped on all rungs is the good state. Failed on all three means the page shows yesterday's numbers with an old stamp. Check the date before trading.
Retry ladder.simple: The same data fetch is tried three times in the evening: 6:00, 6:30 and 7:30 PM. Skipped means the data was already saved, not that it failed. Skipped on all three is healthy.

Return on margin.example: Like comparing shops by profit per rupee invested, not by total sales. Rs 800 credit on Rs 1,00,000 margin is 0.80%.
Return on margin.forYou: Skip trades below 0.80% return on margin.
Return on margin.goodBad: Higher is better; the desk wants at least 0.80%.
Return on margin.impact: If it goes up: more pay for the capital you tie up. If it goes down: the premium does not pay for the tail risk.
Return on margin.readIt: When you see this number, check it is at least 0.80%. The desk says no trade rather than lowering this bar.
Return on margin.simple: The credit divided by the margin blocked, for the trade's life. It lets you compare strikes fairly. The desk needs at least 0.80% or it suggests no trade.

Returns.example: Like checking how much rice prices rose in a week, a month and a year.
Returns.forYou: Use returns to see the speed of a move.
Returns.impact: If short returns beat long ones: momentum is recent. If they lag: the trend may be slowing.
Returns.readIt: When you see this table, compare short and long horizons.
Returns.simple: The price change over one week to five years and year to date. A horizon longer than the data shows a dash.

Revealed.example: Like a page counter in a book.
Revealed.forYou: Do not skip ahead; each day is a decision point.
Revealed.impact: If it goes up: you are closer to the end. If it stays: you have not moved forward.
Revealed.readIt: When you see it rise, more of the outcome is visible.
Revealed.simple: This counts how many days after the decision have been shown. The path ends when the second expiry settles.

Rich put wing.example: Like rain insurance in a flood zone costing extra. The seller earns more, but floods there are real.
Rich put wing.forYou: Extra premium on puts is real money, but it is paid for crash risk, so keep size small.
Rich put wing.goodBad: Flagged at 2 or more vol points above ATM IV.
Rich put wing.impact: If the put wing gets richer: sold puts pay more but fear of a fall is rising. If it cheapens: the extra pay disappears.
Rich put wing.readIt: When you see this flag, know you are paid extra for the risk the market fears most.
Rich put wing.simple: A put strike whose implied volatility is well above the at-the-money level. The market is paying extra for crash protection there. The desk flags it when the put's IV is 2 vol points or more above ATM.

Right answers.forYou: Focus on getting more right, not on answering all.
Right answers.impact: If it goes up: your score rises. If it goes down: your score falls.
Right answers.readIt: When you see this, compare with wrong answers.
Right answers.simple: This counts questions answered correctly in this set. Each adds one mark.

Risk budget.example: Like deciding you will spend at most Rs 2,000 on a gift, then picking the gift. Trading: budget Rs 20,000 and max loss Rs 6,000 a lot gives 3 lots.
Risk budget.forYou: Set the budget first, then work out the number of lots.
Risk budget.impact: If the budget goes up: bigger trades and bigger possible losses. If it goes down: smaller trades, smaller losses.
Risk budget.readIt: When you see a trade's max loss above it, the gate flags the trade.
Risk budget.simple: This is the most you agree to lose on one trade, in rupees. The desk uses Rs 20,000. Lots = budget divided by the worst loss per lot, rounded down. Size comes from the loss you can take, not broker margin.

Risk of ruin.example: Like the chance a shop loses half its savings and must close. Even 1 in 100 is too much.
Risk of ruin.forYou: Keep this under 1% always; ruin cannot be undone.
Risk of ruin.goodBad: Must stay under 1% for a size to count as safe.
Risk of ruin.impact: If it rises: your size is dangerous. If it falls: the account can survive bad luck.
Risk of ruin.readIt: When you see risk of ruin, it should be near zero. For the current rules it is about 0.1%.
Risk of ruin.simple: The share of two-year paths where the account fell to half its starting capital. That is the point where a desk stops trading.

Risk reversal history.example: Like comparing the price of rain insurance and drought insurance. If rain cover gets dearer, people fear rain more.
Risk reversal history.forYou: It tells you if crash fear is building, which matters most for your short puts.
Risk reversal history.goodBad: Below zero means puts dearer than calls, the normal state; a fast fall means fear is rising.
Risk reversal history.impact: If the risk reversal falls: crash protection gets dearer, so your short puts pay more but fear is rising. If it rises: fear of a fall eases.
Risk reversal history.readIt: When you see the risk reversal falling further below zero, puts are getting dearer. Check the put side of your trade next.
Risk reversal history.simple: Risk reversal is call IV minus put IV at the same distance from spot. Butterfly is how dear both far wings are versus the middle. This chart shows both every day.

Risk-budget book.example: A family spends at most Rs 20,000 on any one trip. So one bad trip never ruins the month.
Risk-budget book.forYou: It shows how fixed-risk sizing changes the same trades.
Risk-budget book.goodBad: Each trade risks about Rs 20,000 at its maximum loss.
Risk-budget book.impact: If the budget rises: profits and losses grow together. If it falls: everything shrinks, including the pain.
Risk-budget book.readIt: When you see the book line, compare it with the one-lot line. Results change because size changes with the trade's risk.
Risk-budget book.simple: A version of the backtest where each trade is sized so its maximum loss is about Rs 20,000. It shows results when size follows risk, not a fixed one lot.

Risk-neutral density.example: Like a crowd of cricket bettors whose bets show which scores they fear most. If NIFTY is 25,000, the chart may show more weight on a fall to 24,000 than a rise to 26,000.
Risk-neutral density.forYou: As a seller, a fat downside tail means your short put is riskier than a bell curve shows.
Risk-neutral density.impact: If the left tail gets fatter: the market fears a fall more, and puts get dearer. If the shape narrows: the market expects a calmer finish.
Risk-neutral density.readIt: When you see this chart, look at which tail is longer and fatter. The desk checks its average matches the forward price. About one day in five it fails, and the desk uses a simpler model.
Risk-neutral density.simple: A chart of where the market thinks NIFTY might finish, built from option prices at every strike. It shows a lopsided shape, not a perfect bell. Usually the downside tail is longer.

Rolled losers.example: Like paying one credit card with another: the bill does not go away, it just moves.
Rolled losers.forYou: Take the stop; open a new trade only if it passes the gate on its own.
Rolled losers.goodBad: Low is good; high means losses are being hidden.
Rolled losers.impact: If it goes up: more losses are being pushed forward. If it goes down: you take losses cleanly.
Rolled losers.readIt: When you see this count, ask whether each roll was planned or just avoiding the loss.
Rolled losers.simple: These are losing trades closed by moving them to another strike or expiry instead of taking the loss. Rolling turns a real loss into a hidden one.

Rough rice.example: Like the price paddy farmers get at the mandi before the husk is removed. If rough rice goes from 14 to 16 dollars, world rice is getting dearer.
Rough rice.forYou: Watch it with Indian rice-exporter stocks and with news of export curbs.
Rough rice.goodBad: Neither; good for exporters when high, good for consumers when low.
Rough rice.impact: If it goes up: Indian rice exporters earn more, but the government may limit exports to keep food cheap at home. If it goes down: exporters earn less and food inflation eases.
Rough rice.readIt: When you see rough rice, remember it is a thin US contract: it is a hint about world rice, not India's own price.
Rough rice.simple: The world price of unmilled rice, from the CBOT rough rice future in Chicago, in US dollars per hundred pounds. India is the world's biggest rice exporter. World rice prices affect Indian exports and food policy.

Rule.example: Like a road rule: stop at red, whatever happens at the next crossing.
Rule.forYou: Learn the eight replay rules by heart.
Rule.impact: If more rules pass: the process score rises. If more miss: it falls, whatever the money.
Rule.readIt: When you see a rule marked miss, read its detail to see what broke.
Rule.simple: This is a rule a seller can follow before knowing the outcome. Each rule counts once toward the process score. Rules that do not apply to a trade are left out.

Rule detail by model.example: Like testing a bicycle on a flat road, a hill and a muddy track. The weakest result shows where it fails.
Rule detail by model.forYou: It tells you which kind of market would hurt you most.
Rule detail by model.goodBad: The worst model's numbers are what the desk sizes on.
