Rule detail by model.impact: If one model shows much bigger losses: the rule is weak in that kind of market. If all agree: the result is sturdier.
Rule detail by model.readIt: When you see this table, find the worst model column. That is the market type to fear.
Rule detail by model.simple: Every statistic for the current rules and the leading variant, one model at a time. If one model is much worse, that kind of market is the one the rule cannot survive.

Rule research verdict.example: Like a coach picking a team on last season's matches, then judging it only on this season's matches.
Rule research verdict.forYou: Only the test years count as evidence, and even those are priced by a model.
Rule research verdict.goodBad: A rule that shines only in its training years is a fitted curve, not an edge.
Rule research verdict.impact: If the recommended rule keeps beating the current one in new years: switching has support. If the gap shrinks: the edge may have been luck.
Rule research verdict.readIt: When you see the verdict, read the out-of-sample numbers. Since 2020 the current rules made about Rs 32 a trade; the recommended rule made about Rs 674.
Rule research verdict.simple: Did any version of the desk's selling rules keep earning in years the search never saw? Rules are chosen on 2008-2019 only, then tested on 2020 onward. Option prices here come from a model, not real chains.

Rule-change timeline.example: Like a list of changes to cricket rules: old tactics may not work under new rules.
Rule-change timeline.forYou: Read it before trusting any old trading example.
Rule-change timeline.impact: If a new rule appears: old examples may give wrong rupee figures. If none: the current rules hold.
Rule-change timeline.readIt: When you see a row marked unverified, confirm it with the exchange before relying on it.
Rule-change timeline.simple: This lists SEBI and NSE rule changes since October 2024 that change a NIFTY seller's rupees. Examples are lot size, expiry day, margin, upfront premium and position limits. Each row is checked against the official circular.

Rule-set version.example: Like a recipe version: if you change the salt, old and new dishes cannot be judged together.
Rule-set version.forYou: Judge a rule set only after enough trades under the same version.
Rule-set version.impact: If it changes: older trades no longer test the current rules. If it stays: your sample keeps growing.
Rule-set version.readIt: When you see the version change, start judging results fresh from that date.
Rule-set version.simple: This is a fingerprint of the desk's rules: take profit, stop, risk budget and side-rule levels. When it changes, results before and after are different experiments.

Rules against benchmarks.example: Like comparing four routes to school on time taken and how often you were late.
Rules against benchmarks.forYou: It tells you whether following the rules is better than just selling every week.
Rules against benchmarks.goodBad: Expiries counts separate expiries, a truer sample size than the trade count.
Rules against benchmarks.impact: If the rules beat the plain condor: the extra steps earn their keep. If not: simpler is as good.
Rules against benchmarks.readIt: When you see this table, compare expectancy and max drawdown across rows. All four lost money on the stored sample; the monthly version lost least, about Rs 24 a trade.
Rules against benchmarks.simple: The same numbers for four lines. They are the weekly rules, a monthly version, the rules never standing aside, and a plain condor every time. It shows if the rules add value.

Rules first.example: Like a safe-driver award for 5 trips without breaking a rule.
Rules first.forYou: Earn it by following rules, not by trading more.
Rules first.impact: If your average rises above 80 percent: you earn it. If it falls below: you can lose it.
Rules first.readIt: When you see not yet, check your average over the last 5 debriefs.
Rules first.simple: This badge needs a process score of 80 percent or more, averaged over your last 5 replay debriefs. Standing aside counts the same as trading.

Rules in force.example: Like train fares: a trip last year must use last year's fare chart, not today's.
Rules in force.forYou: It keeps your cost and margin numbers correct for the date you trade.
Rules in force.goodBad: Every rule is looked up by date.
Rules in force.impact: If a rule changes: costs, margin or timing of your trades change from that date. If none change: the cost stack stays the same.
Rules in force.readIt: When you see this table, check the 'from' dates and any upcoming changes.
Rules in force.simple: The Indian exchange and tax rules the desk uses, each with the date it began and its circular. Costs, expiry day, lot size, settlement and margin all changed in 2024-2026. A backtest using today's rates for last year would be wrong.

Rules vs always-sell.example: Like comparing a chef's special recipe with plain dal and rice. If the special loses less, the recipe added something.
Rules vs always-sell.forYou: Losing less than the benchmark is not the same as making money.
Rules vs always-sell.goodBad: Positive means the rules beat the plain condor on this sample.
Rules vs always-sell.impact: If it rises: the rules' strike choice and standing aside add value. If it turns negative: plain selling would have done better.
Rules vs always-sell.readIt: When you see this number, check its sign. On the stored sample both lost. The rules lost Rs 17,026 and plain selling lost Rs 23,553. So the rules were about Rs 6,500 better.
Rules vs always-sell.simple: The desk rules' total profit minus the profit of simply selling a 1-sigma iron condor every week. It shows if the rules' choices added money over the plain version.

Rupee.example: Like an imported phone getting dearer when the rupee weakens. If the rupee weakens 1%, MCX gold rises about 1% with no change abroad.
Rupee.forYou: In weeks when the rupee is in the news, check it before selling MCX calls.
Rupee.impact: If USD/INR goes up (rupee weaker): MCX prices rise. If it goes down (rupee stronger): MCX prices fall.
Rupee.readIt: When you see this row, read the percentile. 70 or above votes up for MCX gold, silver and crude; 30 or below votes down.
Rupee.simple: The rupee's rate against the US dollar, as a 20-day move and its rank. A weaker rupee lifts every MCX price even if world prices stay flat. It votes only for the MCX markets, not WTI or Brent.

Rupees.example: Like a bill split among friends who shared the meal.
Rupees.forYou: Fix the habit with the most rupees first.
Rupees.impact: If it goes up: the habit is costing more. If it goes down: it is costing less.
Rupees.readIt: When you see a large figure, this habit has cost you the most.
Rupees.simple: These are the rupees you linked to this habit. A paper or real loss is split across the habits tagged in its review. Lesson and test misses carry no rupee cost.

SEBI turnover fee.example: Like a one-paisa stamp on a big letter. It is there but hardly noticed.
SEBI turnover fee.forYou: You can ignore it for decisions.
SEBI turnover fee.impact: If it changes: costs move by paise. It does not matter in practice.
SEBI turnover fee.readIt: When you see this, know it never changes a decision. It is listed so the costs add up.
SEBI turnover fee.simple: The regulator's fee: Rs 10 per crore of premium turnover, on both sides. At option premium sizes it rounds to paise per order.

STT on options exercised.example: Like a toll paid only if you drive through the gate yourself. Sell the car before the gate and you pay none.
STT on options exercised.forYou: Close an in-the-money long leg before expiry when this tax would be larger.
STT on options exercised.impact: If your long leg ends deep in the money: this tax grows. If it ends worthless: there is no tax.
STT on options exercised.readIt: When you see this, check if your long leg will be in the money at expiry. If so, compare this tax with the cost of closing it.
STT on options exercised.simple: STT charged on the in-the-money value when a bought option is exercised at expiry. A seller who is assigned pays none. On a spread, it can cost more than closing the long leg before 15:30.

STT on options sold.example: Like a sales tax charged every time you sell goods at the market.
STT on options sold.forYou: As a seller you pay it on every trade, so it matters on many small credits.
STT on options sold.impact: If STT rises: each sale costs more. If it falls: selling costs less.
STT on options sold.readIt: When you see this rate, apply it to the premium of each sale. At 0.15%, selling Rs 2,000 of premium costs Rs 3 of STT.
STT on options sold.simple: STT means Securities Transaction Tax, a government tax. It is charged on the premium each time you sell an option. That includes opening a short or closing a long.

Safe position size.example: Like the safe load for a bridge: tested on the worst day, not the average day.
Safe position size.forYou: The desk's own numbers say the current size is a bit too large.
Safe position size.goodBad: Use the lower of this limit and half of Kelly. For the current rules Kelly is zero, so no size is recommended.
Safe position size.impact: If the safe size rises: you can take more risk. If it falls: cut your size.
Safe position size.readIt: When you see this, compare it with your current size. For the current rules it is about 3.6% of capital per trade, below the 4% used.
Safe position size.simple: The biggest loss per trade, as a share of capital, that passes two tests. A 30% drawdown stays under 5% likely, and ruin under 1%. It must pass on every model and crisis. Never size above it or half of Kelly.

Same-week price change.example: Like noticing that more people buy gold in the same week the TV says gold is rising. If copper rose 3% this week and funds added 10,000 net contracts, that week agrees.
Same-week price change.forYou: As a seller, do not treat a fund-buying headline as a forecast. It usually just repeats what price already did.
Same-week price change.goodBad: Neither. A high value is normal and is not a trade signal.
Same-week price change.impact: If it goes up: funds are more clearly trend followers, so their buying describes the rally rather than predicting it. If it goes down: fund flows are closer to independent of price.
Same-week price change.readIt: When you see this row, read the correlation and the same-direction share. A high share, like 70%, means funds mostly move with price.
Same-week price change.simple: A test row: when price rose in a week, did funds also add to their net position in that same week? The desk measures the correlation over all stored weeks. It is usually the strongest link, because funds mostly follow price.

Scenario simulator.example: Like a farmer asking: what if it rains a little, a lot, or not at all? He sees his crop in each case before planting.
Scenario simulator.forYou: It shows your possible loss before you trade, so you can choose strikes and size calmly.
Scenario simulator.goodBad: No costs, slippage or early exits are included, so real results are a bit worse.
Scenario simulator.impact: If NIFTY moves toward your short strikes: cells turn orange and losses grow. If IV rises: the position loses value before expiry even if NIFTY stays put.
Scenario simulator.readIt: When you see the grid, find the orange cells. Note how far NIFTY must move to reach them and how big the loss is in rupees per lot.
Scenario simulator.simple: A grid that reprices the playbook's trade if NIFTY moves up or down by up to 4%. It shows after one day, halfway and at expiry. You can also shift IV up or down.

Scheduled check.example: Like a sealed envelope you open only at 3 pm.
Scheduled check.forYou: Use the waiting time for something other than the market.
Scheduled check.impact: If a rule fires before the check: you are told anyway. If not: wait for the set time.
Scheduled check.readIt: When you see this, trust the exit-rule status; if nothing fired, there is nothing to do.
Scheduled check.simple: Live profit and loss is hidden until the next check time. Exit-rule status is still shown.

Scheduled checks.example: Like checking exam results once on result day instead of refreshing the site every minute.
Scheduled checks.forYou: Try it for a few weeks and compare your stop-to-close and overrides.
Scheduled checks.impact: If you turn it on: fewer emotional looks and reactions. If off: you see every move.
Scheduled checks.readIt: When you see it on, live P&L stays hidden until the next check time.
Scheduled checks.simple: This option hides live profit and loss except at set times or when a target or stop fires. Watching every price tick invites panicky exits. It is experimental for sellers.

Scheduled events.example: Like a cricket match with rain forecast for the afternoon: plan for it before you start. Inflation data on the 12th could move NIFTY 200 points.
Scheduled events.forYou: Before selling, check for big events before expiry and widen or skip trades around them.
Scheduled events.impact: If more events fall inside expiry: risk to short options rises. If none: the range is cleaner.
Scheduled events.readIt: When you see this list, check which events fall before your expiry. Monthly dates are by convention and can shift for holidays.
Scheduled events.simple: Data releases and policy decisions already booked before expiry. The option range does not include them. An event inside expiry is risk the band was not built for.

Score.example: Like one ball's result in a long innings.
Score.forYou: Look at the trend over many replays.
Score.impact: If running scores improve: your forecasts improve. If they worsen: adjust your confidence.
Score.readIt: When you see a single score, do not judge yourself on it.
Score.simple: For your chance of profit, this is the Brier score, where lower is better. For your range, it says inside or outside. One forecast is noise. Read the running figures.

Scored.example: Like the number of exam papers already marked. If 300 claims are scored, the hit rates rest on 300 checks.
Scored.forYou: Give a hit rate weight only when enough claims have been scored.
Scored.impact: If it goes up: the record becomes more reliable. If it is small: hit rates are shaky.
Scored.readIt: When you see this number, check it is large before trusting any hit rate.
Scored.simple: How many of the desk's claims have been graded. A claim is written down before the result and never changed. More scored claims make the record more trustworthy.

Seasonal out-of-sample check.example: Like learning from old years' weather and testing on the last three years.
Seasonal out-of-sample check.forYou: Trust patterns that pass this check more.
Seasonal out-of-sample check.goodBad: Well above 50% is good; near 50% is a coin flip.
Seasonal out-of-sample check.impact: If it goes up: the pattern held on new years. If near 50%: it did not.
Seasonal out-of-sample check.readIt: When you see the sign right share, compare with 50%.
Seasonal out-of-sample check.simple: Month patterns learned on all years but the last three, then graded on those three. Well above 50% means the pattern carries forward.

Seasonality.example: Like gold demand rising every Diwali. It votes up only at 65% or better with 7 or more years, and down at 35% or worse.
Seasonality.forYou: Treat seasonality as a small hint at most, never as a reason to sell or skip a trade.
Seasonality.impact: If the hit rate rises past 65%: it votes up. If it falls below 35%: it votes down; otherwise nothing.
Seasonality.readIt: When you see this row, read the hit rate and the number of years. 60% over ten years can happen by luck alone.
Seasonality.simple: Checks whether the price was higher about one month later, from this same date, in each past year. It votes only when the result is clearly lopsided. Most of the time it rightly votes nothing.

Seasonality by month.example: If onions always rise in September across many years, that is seasonal.
Seasonality by month.forYou: Use seasonal patterns as context, never as a sure bet.
Seasonality by month.goodBad: Seasonal is a useful tendency; noise is not.
Seasonality by month.impact: If a month is truly seasonal: it has a tendency. If noise: no lean.
Seasonality by month.readIt: When you see the verdict, trust only seasonal or strongly seasonal. About 1 in 20 passes by luck.
Seasonality by month.simple: Average return in each calendar month. The month labels are shuffled 1,000 times to test chance. It is seasonal only if it passes and both halves of years agree.

Seasonality by week of year.example: Like checking prices for each week of the year instead of each month.
Seasonality by week of year.forYou: Rely on monthly patterns more than weekly ones.
Seasonality by week of year.impact: If a week pattern passes: it is a tendency. If not: noise.
Seasonality by week of year.readIt: When you see this chart, prefer the monthly view if the weekly test fails.
Seasonality by week of year.simple: Average return in each week of the year, tested like the months. Fifty-two small groups are noisy.

Seasonality evidence.example: If onion prices swung most in October in old years and still do in new years, the pattern is real.
Seasonality evidence.forYou: Avoid selling premium into months with proven high volatility.
Seasonality evidence.goodBad: A confirmed pattern is useful; noise is not.
Seasonality evidence.impact: If a month's volatility is truly high: sellers face more risk then. If low: calmer months.
Seasonality evidence.readIt: When you see the verdict, trust real only when both tests pass. Price direction is tested separately.
Seasonality evidence.simple: Tests whether volatility really changes by calendar month. A pattern found in 2000-2012 is checked on 2013 on. It is real only if both tests hold.

Seasonality: what is real.example: Like checking if the rain-in-June pattern still holds in recent years.
Seasonality: what is real.forYou: Rely only on patterns that held out of sample.
Seasonality: what is real.impact: If a pattern held: it is useful context. If not: treat it as noise.
Seasonality: what is real.readIt: When you see this table, check held 2013 on and the Friedman p value.
Seasonality: what is real.simple: Which farm markets have a calendar pattern in volatility that held on new years. It also checks if seasonal price direction predicts anything.

Sector effect.example: Like rain: bad for the umbrella-less walker, good for the umbrella seller. A strong dollar hurts NIFTY but helps IT and pharma exporters.
Sector effect.forYou: If you sell options on stocks, check the sector effect, not just the index view.
Sector effect.impact: If the driver rises: sectors marked ++ tend to gain, -- tend to lose. If it falls: the reverse.
Sector effect.readIt: When you see this column, check if a driver splits the market. The dollar is the classic case.
Sector effect.simple: What a rise in a driver does to each sector, which can differ from the index. ++ is strongly good, ~ no clear effect, -- strongly bad. These are directions, not sizes.

Sell threshold.example: Like selling umbrellas only when people pay more than the rain usually costs you.
Sell threshold.forYou: Use it to understand why the side rule said sell or stand aside today.
Sell threshold.impact: If the threshold goes up: fewer sell days, stricter rule. If it goes down: more sell days, looser rule.
Sell threshold.readIt: When you see the threshold, compare today's IV to RV ratio with it.
Sell threshold.simple: Implied volatility is the market's priced-in fear; realised volatility is how much NIFTY actually moves. The side rule says sell only when implied is at least this many times the realised forecast.

Seller edge.example: Like a tiffin service collecting Rs 100 a week for meals that cost Rs 90. The Rs 10 left is the edge.
Seller edge.forYou: It is the plainest test of whether selling straddles has paid at all.
Seller edge.goodBad: Positive helps sellers; negative means sellers were underpaid. Costs come off this too.
Seller edge.impact: If the edge rises: selling has paid more than it cost. If it falls below zero: buyers have been winning.
Seller edge.readIt: When you see the average edge, check its sign and how many cases it covers. Over 311 cases it was about minus 4 points, roughly break-even before costs.
Seller edge.simple: Premium collected minus what the option paid out at expiry, in points. Positive means the seller kept money. It is averaged over many past straddles.

Seller paid.example: Like an insurer selling cover only when premiums exceed typical claims.
Seller paid.forYou: Check this first in every replay.
Seller paid.impact: If the ratio goes up: selling pays better. If it goes down below 1: selling underpays.
Seller paid.readIt: When you see this rule missed, you sold cheap premium.
Seller paid.simple: This rule says sell only when implied volatility is at least realised volatility. That is an IV/RV ratio of 1 or more. Below 1, the seller is paid less than the risk has been costing.

Seller&rsquo;s math today.example: Like re-calculating a recipe after the packet size changed from 500 g to 400 g.
Seller&rsquo;s math today.forYou: Use today's figures, never old examples.
Seller&rsquo;s math today.impact: If the lot size goes up: each point is worth more rupees, both ways. If it goes down: each point is worth less.
Seller&rsquo;s math today.readIt: When you see this, compare the new rupee figure with what older examples said.
Seller&rsquo;s math today.simple: This shows what a rule change does to a seller's rupees. It uses today's spot, lot size and playbook spread. Old examples built on lot 75 or Thursday expiry give wrong figures today.

Settlement.example: Like the final whistle score of a match.
Settlement.forYou: Compare it with your range after every replay.
Settlement.impact: If it lands outside your range often: your ranges are too narrow. If inside about 80 percent of the time: well calibrated.
Settlement.readIt: When you see it, check whether it fell inside your forecast range.
Settlement.simple: This is the exchange's final price for the first expiry, the index close on expiry day. Your 80 percent range is checked against it.

Settlement price.example: Like grading a runner on his average speed over the last lap instead of his final step.
Settlement price.forYou: From December, the last half hour matters more than the final tick for your short strikes.
Settlement price.impact: If NIFTY moves late in the day: under the new rule it moves the settlement less. If it moves before 15:00: it counts more.
Settlement price.readIt: When you see this, remember an average is harder to push at the last second. A strike near spot at 15:00 settles near where the half hour traded.
Settlement price.simple: The NIFTY level expiring contracts are settled at in cash. Until 2-Aug-2026 it was the closing index value. From 3-Aug it is the closing-auction close. From 7-Dec-2026 it is an average price over the last 30 minutes, 15:00 to 15:30.

Shading.example: Like a coupon that is already worth money today versus one that only might be worth something later. With NIFTY at 25,000, the 24,800 call is shaded because it is already 200 points in the money.
Shading.forYou: As a seller, sell from the unshaded (out-of-the-money) side; selling shaded options means you start already losing the intrinsic value.
Shading.goodBad: Neither; shading only marks where the money already is.
Shading.impact: If NIFTY goes up: more call strikes become shaded and fewer puts. If it goes down: more put strikes become shaded.
Shading.readIt: When you see shading, know those premiums are big because they already hold value. The unshaded side is where premium sellers usually work.
Shading.simple: Shaded cells in the option chain are in-the-money options. That means calls with strikes below the current price and puts with strikes above it. Their price is mostly real value, not time value.

Share of capital.example: Like saying a Rs 2,000 phone bill is 4 percent of a Rs 50,000 salary; the percent shows how much it really bites.
Share of capital.forYou: Keep it under your cap on every trade.
Share of capital.goodBad: Low (around 2 percent or less) is small; high means one trade is a big bet.
Share of capital.impact: If it goes up: the trade risks more of your account. If it goes down: the trade is a smaller bite.
Share of capital.readIt: When you see this percent, compare it with your per-trade cap, 2 percent by default.
Share of capital.simple: This is the max loss if gapped, shown as a percent of the capital you entered. The per-trade and book caps use the same units.

Share of cost.example: Like a bar chart of monthly spending by category.
Share of cost.forYou: Use it to choose which habit to fix first.
Share of cost.impact: If a bar grows: that habit takes more of your losses. If it shrinks: you are improving.
Share of cost.readIt: When you see a short bar with a high count, the habit is frequent but cheap.
Share of cost.simple: This bar shows the habit's rupees against your costliest habit. The biggest leak reads at a glance. Check the count column too.

Sharpe.example: Two students both average 70 marks. One scores 68 to 72; the other swings from 40 to 100. The steady one has the higher Sharpe.
Sharpe.forYou: Sharpe hides rare crashes, which matter a lot for sellers, so read it with the tail numbers.
Sharpe.goodBad: Higher is better; option selling can show a fine Sharpe until a crash.
Sharpe.impact: If Sharpe rises: returns are steadier for the same average. If it falls below zero: the rule lost money.
Sharpe.readIt: When you see Sharpe, under 0.5 is weak, around 1 is decent. Out-of-sample: recommended 0.96, current rules 0.07.
Sharpe.simple: Sharpe ratio is average return divided by how bumpy the returns are. It asks: how much do you earn for each unit of ups and downs? Here it uses monthly returns, yearly scale.

Short call holds.example: Like a shopkeeper promising the price will not go above Rs 100 this week, then checking on Sunday. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the short call is 25,500, the claim holds if NIFTY stays under 25,500.
Short call holds.forYou: Use this record to judge how far above NIFTY your short calls should sit.
Short call holds.goodBad: Higher is better, as long as it is at least the probability the desk claimed.
Short call holds.impact: If the hit rate goes up: the suggested short calls have been safe. If it goes down: calls have been tested, so place them further away.
Short call holds.readIt: When you see its hit rate, compare it with the chance the desk stated. Lower than stated means rallies have been stronger than expected.
Short call holds.simple: The desk writes down that NIFTY will stay below the short call strike of its suggested trade until expiry. Later it checks if that came true. It shows how safe the suggested ceiling has been.

Short leg.example: Like selling a warranty on a phone for Rs 200: you keep the Rs 200 if the phone works, but you pay if it breaks.
Short leg.forYou: Always pair a short leg with a bought leg behind it so its loss has a limit.
Short leg.impact: If NIFTY moves toward its strike: the leg costs more to buy back and you lose. If NIFTY moves away: it shrinks and you gain.
Short leg.readIt: When you see a short leg, read its sigma-away column to see how close the danger is.
Short leg.simple: A short leg is an option you sold. You took its price in cash and keep it if the option expires worthless. Its danger is NIFTY moving past its strike.

Short put holds.example: Like a promise that the river will not fall below a mark on the bridge this week. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the short put is 24,500, the claim holds if NIFTY stays above 24,500.
Short put holds.forYou: As a seller, give short puts more room than short calls.
Short put holds.goodBad: Higher is better; a lower rate than the call side is normal in falling markets.
Short put holds.impact: If the hit rate goes up: the suggested floors have held. If it goes down: falls have been sharp, so keep short puts further away and smaller.
Short put holds.readIt: When you see its hit rate, compare it with the call side. Falls come faster than rallies, so puts are usually tested more.
Short put holds.simple: The desk writes down that NIFTY will stay above the short put strike of its suggested trade until expiry. Later it checks if that came true. It shows how safe the suggested floor has been.

Short strangles.example: Like selling flood insurance with no reinsurance. You keep more premium, but one big flood can wipe you out.
Short strangles.forYou: They show what a condor's protection costs you; they are not for trading.
Short strangles.goodBad: Shown for comparison only; unlimited risk.
Short strangles.impact: If NIFTY makes a big move: losses grow without limit. If it stays quiet: you keep a larger premium than a condor.
Short strangles.readIt: When you see strangles, read them only as a comparison. The desk never ranks or offers them.
Short strangles.simple: Selling an out-of-the-money put and call with nothing bought for protection. The premium is bigger than a condor's. But the possible loss has no ceiling.

Short strike holds claim.example: Like grading only the days you actually batted. If the range held but your strike broke, the strike choice was wrong, not the volatility.
Short strike holds claim.forYou: This is the claim closest to your money, so check it before trusting suggested strikes.
Short strike holds claim.impact: If it goes up: strike choice is working. If it goes down while range claims hold: strike selection needs fixing.
Short strike holds claim.readIt: When you see this, compare it with the range claim on the same day.
Short strike holds claim.simple: A claim that the strike the desk suggested selling would not be crossed. It is made only on days a trade passed the filters. So it has fewer results than other claims.

Short strike tested.example: Like flood water reaching the doorstep: not inside yet, but now you must choose to move things or not.
Short strike tested.forYou: Decide using the plan you wrote at entry, not the P&L you see now.
Short strike tested.impact: If NIFTY moves further toward the strike: losses grow fast. If it moves back: the flag clears.
Short strike tested.readIt: When you see this flag, check your written plan for what you said you would do here.
Short strike tested.simple: A strike is tested when NIFTY comes within half a sigma of a strike you sold. Sigma is a normal move. It is the moment to decide. Close, roll, or accept the risk on purpose.

Shorts outside 1 sigma.example: Like parking your car outside the usual flood line.
Shorts outside 1 sigma.impact: If strikes move further out: safer, less credit. If closer: more credit, more risk.
Shorts outside 1 sigma.readIt: When you see this rule missed, a short strike is too close.
Shorts outside 1 sigma.simple: This rule says every sold strike must be at least one expected move away from the forward price. Inside that band, the strike is more likely than not to be reached.

Side rule.example: Like a mango trader buying only if the selling price is at least 10% above his cost. Below that, he waits.
Side rule.forYou: It is the desk's first filter; in the stored backtest, sell days did better than stand-aside days.
Side rule.goodBad: 1.10 or more says sell. In the backtest, sell-day trades averaged Rs 113. Stand-aside-day trades averaged minus Rs 1,164.
Side rule.impact: If the ratio rises above 1.10: the rule says sell. If it falls below: it says stand aside.
Side rule.readIt: When you see the side rule, read the ratio. On 13-Nov-2026 implied was only 0.84 times the forecast, so it said stand aside.
Side rule.simple: The desk's gate that says sell or stand aside. It compares implied volatility with the desk's forecast of real volatility. Sell only if implied is at least 1.10 times the forecast.

Side rule backtest.example: Like checking your old cricket bets using only the team news known before each match. If the rule's sells won 70% while selling every day won 60%, the rule helped.
Side rule backtest.forYou: Trust the rule more when it beats always-selling on both average and worst loss.
Side rule backtest.impact: If the rule's results rise above always-selling: the rule is adding value. If they fall below: the rule is not helping yet.
Side rule backtest.readIt: When you see this, compare the rule's win rate, average and worst loss with selling every day. Days sharing an expiry are linked, so count expiries too.
Side rule backtest.simple: The buy-or-sell rule replayed on every stored day, using only what was known that day. It tests whether the rule would have made money. If a buy reason never paid, the rule does not use it.

Sigma (&sigma;).example: If a bus is usually 5 minutes late give or take 3, the 3 minutes is sigma. If NIFTY's one sigma is 300 points at 25,000, most finishes land between 24,700 and 25,300.
Sigma (&sigma;).forYou: As a seller, think of strike distance in sigma, not just points.
Sigma (&sigma;).goodBad: A big sigma means a rough market; a small sigma means a calm one.
Sigma (&sigma;).impact: If sigma goes up: normal moves are bigger, so strikes need more distance. If it goes down: moves are smaller, and premium is thinner.
Sigma (&sigma;).readIt: When you see a sigma number, read it as the size of a normal move. A 2-sigma move is rare but happens. Real big moves come in clusters and are larger than the model expects.
Sigma (&sigma;).simple: Sigma is one standard step of how far the market usually moves. About 2 days in 3 stay inside one sigma. About 19 in 20 stay inside two sigma.

Sigma away.example: Like a batsman's distance from the boundary rope measured in average shots: 2 shots away is safe, half a shot away is danger.
Sigma away.forYou: Check it each scheduled look; it is the quickest danger gauge for a short leg.
Sigma away.goodBad: High (over 1.5) is comfortable; low (under 0.5) means the strike is tested.
Sigma away.impact: If it goes up: your strike is safer. If it goes down: NIFTY is getting close and the trade is at risk.
Sigma away.readIt: When you see a number under 0.5, the short strike is tested. Decide to close, roll or accept.
Sigma away.simple: Sigma is the size of a normal move up to expiry. This shows how many such moves NIFTY is from your sold strike. Under 0.5 means the strike is under attack. Over 1.5 means it is comfortably far.

Sigma from spot.example: Like measuring how far a house is from a river in flood heights, not metres.
Sigma from spot.forYou: Use sigma, not points, to compare strikes across days.
Sigma from spot.goodBad: Above 1 is outside the normal range; under 1 is inside it.
Sigma from spot.impact: If it goes up: the strike is safer. If it goes down: the strike is more at risk.
Sigma from spot.readIt: When you see under 1 on a sold strike, an ordinary move can reach it.
Sigma from spot.simple: This shows how many one-sigma moves a strike is from the current NIFTY level. Under 1 means inside the expected range. The desk's condor sells just outside it.

Sigma used.example: Like averaging two weather forecasts to plan your umbrella. If sigma is 16% a year, a normal day moves about 1%.
Sigma used.forYou: A higher sigma means your strikes need more distance for the same safety.
Sigma used.impact: If it goes up: every range on the page widens. If it goes down: ranges narrow.
Sigma used.readIt: When you see this number, compare it across markets. Crude's will be much higher than gold's.
Sigma used.simple: The yearly volatility figure each cone is built on. It is the average of two estimates: a forecast and a recent measure. Divided by about 16, it becomes the daily move size.

Signal grading.example: Like checking if a fortune teller does better than flipping a coin over 300 days.
Signal grading.forYou: Do not trade on pin, walls, flip or cone signals alone; the desk could not show they beat chance.
Signal grading.goodBad: Works = p under 0.05; weak = p under 0.25; too few = under 20 cases.
Signal grading.impact: If a signal later moves to 'works': it is worth using. If it stays 'does not work': ignore it for decisions.
Signal grading.readIt: When you see verdicts, most signals said 'does not work' on 315 stored sessions. Only the gamma regime was 'weak'.
Signal grading.simple: Checks if the newer signals on the Volatility and Gamma tab actually help a seller. Each is tested against a fair stand-in on every stored session. It is a study done after the fact, not a live record.

Signal scorecard.example: A weather man who says 'no snow in Chennai' is right 100% of the time. That is not skill, since anyone would be right.
Signal scorecard.forYou: A high hit rate alone can fool you; always look at the edge.
Signal scorecard.impact: If edge grows and p falls under 0.05: the signal works. If edge is near zero: it does not.
Signal scorecard.readIt: When you see the scorecard, look at edge over baseline and p-value, not the hit rate alone.
Signal scorecard.simple: Each signal, what it claims, how often it was right and how often a fair stand-in was right. Only the edge over the stand-in is evidence.

Signal verdicts.example: Like report-card stamps: pass, weak, fail or absent.
Signal verdicts.forYou: It is the quickest way to know which signals to trust.
Signal verdicts.goodBad: Works, weak, does not work, too few.
Signal verdicts.impact: If a tile turns to 'works': consider using that signal. If it stays 'does not work': ignore it.
Signal verdicts.readIt: When you see the tiles, count how many say 'works'. Now none do; one says weak.
Signal verdicts.simple: One tile per signal, showing its verdict and its rate against the baseline. Open a tile for the numbers behind it.

Silver (MCX).example: Like a younger brother who copies his elder brother but runs twice as fast. If gold moves 1%, silver may move 2%.
Silver (MCX).forYou: If you sell silver options, keep strikes further away than you would for gold.
Silver (MCX).impact: If it goes up: long silver gains and short calls are pressured. If it goes down: short puts are pressured, and moves can be sharp.
Silver (MCX).readIt: When you see this number, look at its range: it will be wider than gold's for the same time. Check the gold/silver ratio to see if silver is cheap or dear.
Silver (MCX).simple: The price of silver in India on MCX, in rupees per kilogram. It swings more than gold, so its ranges are wider. It is also used in factories, which gold mostly is not.

Simulated P&L per trade.example: Like a bakery that earns a little most days and loses a lot when the oven breaks.
Simulated P&L per trade.forYou: Your result depends on the rare far-left trades, so plan for them.
Simulated P&L per trade.goodBad: Each trade sized to a Rs 20,000 maximum loss.
Simulated P&L per trade.impact: If the left tail grows: rare big losses dominate. If it shrinks: losses are smaller and rarer.
Simulated P&L per trade.readIt: When you see this chart, look past the tall bars near zero to the small bars far left.
Simulated P&L per trade.simple: P&L means profit and loss. This bar chart shows how single simulated trades ended, after costs. Most sit just above zero; the left tail is where the account is decided.

Simulated expectancy.example: Like averaging a batsman's score over thousands of imaginary matches on three kinds of pitch.
Simulated expectancy.forYou: Here too the current rules lose a little on average, so do not expect steady income from them.
Simulated expectancy.goodBad: Positive is good; it is partly an input because the models build implied vol from history.
Simulated expectancy.impact: If it rises above zero: the rule earns on average in the model worlds. If it stays below zero: it loses on average.
Simulated expectancy.readIt: When you see this number, check its sign. For the current weekly rules it was about minus Rs 156 per lot.
Simulated expectancy.simple: The average result of one simulated trade after all costs, at the desk's Rs 20,000 maximum loss. It is averaged across the three models.

Size step-down.example: Like a batsman out of form who plays safer shots until he scores again.
Size step-down.forYou: Accept it; it limits damage during a bad patch.
Size step-down.impact: If it switches on: each trade risks half as much. If it switches off: normal size returns.
Size step-down.readIt: When you see step-down on, your cap is half; size new trades to match.
Size step-down.simple: After two stops in a row or a 5 percent fall from your peak, the per-trade cap halves. It returns when a winner closes and the fall is under 2 percent. Trade smallest when trading worst.

Sizing schemes.example: Like testing how much load a truck can carry on the same road before it tips.
Sizing schemes.forYou: It shows how much size you can afford with these rules.
Sizing schemes.goodBad: Under 5% chance of a 30% drawdown and under 1% ruin is the desk's line.
Sizing schemes.impact: If you risk more per trade: drawdown and ruin chances rise fast. If less: both fall.
Sizing schemes.readIt: When you see this, find the biggest risk where the chance of a 30% drawdown stays under 5%.
Sizing schemes.simple: The same rules with different ways of choosing size. It tests risking 1, 2 or 3% of capital, sizing to a stress loss, and sizing to forecast volatility. Each cell shows drawdown and ruin chances.

Skew.example: Like a hill that is steep on one side and gentle on the other. If skew is -0.5, the fall side is the steep one.
Skew.forYou: When skew is very negative, sell puts further away than calls.
Skew.impact: If it goes more negative: falls are feared more, so short puts carry more risk. If it moves toward zero: fear is easing.
Skew.readIt: When you see this number, expect it below zero. More negative means more fear of falls.
Skew.simple: The lean in the shape of expected moves, read from option prices. Negative skew means big falls are priced as more likely than big rises. For stock indexes it is usually negative.

Skew history.example: Like a mango seller's price diary for the past year. You can see if today's price is high or low for the season.
Skew history.forYou: It shows if today's premium is high or low against recent history.
Skew history.goodBad: The front expiry is the nearest one at least 2 days away. So an expiry-day drop does not look like a crash.
Skew history.impact: If the line rises: options get dearer, sellers collect more but the market expects bigger moves. If it falls: premium shrinks.
Skew history.readIt: When you see this chart, check where today's dot sits against the past months. Then check IV rank and percentile for the number.
Skew history.simple: A chart of the front expiry's at-the-money IV on every stored day. It also shows the steadier 30-day IV and India VIX. It tells you if option prices have been rising or falling.

Skill badges.example: Like a scout badge earned by skill, not attendance.
Skill badges.forYou: Work on the badge closest to its condition.
Skill badges.impact: If you earn more: your skills are proven. If you lose one: recent figures dropped.
Skill badges.readIt: When you see a badge earned, check that it still holds next month.
Skill badges.simple: These are badges for process, calibration, crisis replays and exam readiness. Each needs quality over a minimum sample. None counts trades.

Slippage.example: Like a vegetable seller quoting Rs 40 but you end up paying Rs 41 after bargaining fails.
Slippage.forYou: Trade liquid strikes so slippage stays small.
Slippage.goodBad: Smaller is better; half the bid-ask per leg each way.
Slippage.impact: If spreads widen: slippage grows and eats your edge. If they narrow: you keep more.
Slippage.readIt: When you see slippage, check bid-ask spreads on your legs. Wide spreads mean big slippage.
Slippage.simple: The gap between the fair middle price and the price you actually get. The desk charges half the bid-ask gap on each leg, each way. Where there is no quote, it uses 3% of the price.

Smile sensitivity.example: If your cake only works with one exact oven temperature, the recipe is fragile.
Smile sensitivity.forYou: Trust a rule more if its result does not depend on the assumed smile.
Smile sensitivity.goodBad: Stable across smiles is good; flipping is a warning.
Smile sensitivity.impact: If the verdict flips with the smile: the result rests on the assumption. If it holds: it is sturdier.
Smile sensitivity.readIt: When you see this table, check if the verdict stays the same in all runs.
Smile sensitivity.simple: The smile is how option volatility changes across strikes. It is assumed here. So the rules are re-run with no smile and with twice the skew.

Soft flags (worth a second look).example: Like a weather warning before a trip: you may still go, but you pack an umbrella and drive slower.
Soft flags (worth a second look).forYou: Pause for one minute on each flag before you save the trade.
Soft flags (worth a second look).impact: If more flags show: the trade carries extra risks worth thinking about. If none show: no extra warnings today.
Soft flags (worth a second look).readIt: When you see a soft flag, read it and decide on purpose whether to go ahead.
Soft flags (worth a second look).simple: These are warnings in the pre-trade gate that do not block. Examples: an event inside the trade, 0-1 day to expiry, soon after a stop, big size, strong emotion. They ask you to look twice.

Softs: sugar, coffee and cocoa supply sh.example: If a bad monsoon ruins cane, sugar prices can jump overnight.
Softs: sugar, coffee and cocoa supply sh.forYou: Be extra careful with short calls in softs.
Softs: sugar, coffee and cocoa supply sh.impact: If supply fails: prices jump and short calls lose. If supply is fine: prices stay calmer.
Softs: sugar, coffee and cocoa supply sh.readIt: When you see this case, note that the short call is the leg that breaks.
Softs: sugar, coffee and cocoa supply sh.simple: Softs are crops like sugar, coffee and cocoa. This replays the 2023-24 cocoa spike, 2024 coffee spike and 2010-11 sugar rally for an option seller. Supply shocks make prices gap up.

Sources and freshness.example: Like checking the 'best before' date on a milk packet. If the CFTC positions are 10 days old and the limit is 10 days, they are just about to expire.
Sources and freshness.forYou: If key inputs are stale, give the analysis less weight that day.
Sources and freshness.goodBad: All fresh is good; stale inputs are a warning.
Sources and freshness.impact: If more inputs turn stale: the analysis is less reliable. If all are fresh: the explanation rests on current data.
Sources and freshness.readIt: When you see this table, look for any input marked stale before you trust the analysis above it.
Sources and freshness.simple: A table showing where each input came from and how old it is. Prices, fund positions and headlines each have an age limit. Anything older is marked so you know not to trust it.

Sovereign yield.example: Like the interest a bank pays on a fixed deposit. If the 10-year US yield rises from 4% to 4.5%, bond prices fall.
Sovereign yield.forYou: Watch big jumps in US yields as a possible source of a NIFTY gap.
Sovereign yield.impact: If yields go up: borrowing gets dearer, often a weight on stocks. If they go down: borrowing is cheaper.
Sovereign yield.readIt: When you see a yield, check its maturity, source and date. Changes are often shown in basis points, 100 to 1%.
Sovereign yield.simple: The interest rate on government debt for a given length of time. Yields and bond prices usually move opposite ways. A yield is not a bond price.

Spaced review.example: Like revising a times table: today, then in 3 days, then a week later, until it sticks for good.
Spaced review.forYou: Do your due cards daily; testing yourself beats rereading.
Spaced review.impact: If you recall more cards: they move to longer gaps and you review less. If you miss: they return tomorrow.
Spaced review.readIt: When you see cards due today, clear them before starting new lessons.
Spaced review.simple: These are short daily reviews of terms, live cards and your own habits. Each card comes back just before you would forget it. Each correct recall stretches the gap: 1, 3, 7, 16, 35, 80 days. A miss sends it back to tomorrow.

Spot.example: Like today's mandi price board for mangoes, which every deal is compared with. If NIFTY spot is 25,000, the 25,500 call is 500 points away.
Spot.forYou: As a seller, watch where spot sits between your two short strikes, not the number itself.
Spot.impact: If spot goes up: your short call gets closer and your short put further. If it goes down: the put gets closer and the call further.
Spot.readIt: When you see spot, compare it with the walls and the expected range. On expiry day, settlement uses the last half-hour average, not the last tick.
Spot.simple: The current NIFTY level. It is an average of 50 stock prices, so you cannot buy it directly. Every strike, range and probability is measured from it.

Spread.example: Like saying the shop charges Rs 10 above cost instead of 10% above cost. If implied is 13% and forecast 11%, the spread is +2 points.
Spread.forYou: Use IV/RV as your main check; this is the same information.
Spread.impact: If it goes up: more premium per unit of risk. If it goes down or negative: selling is not paid.
Spread.readIt: When you see this number, treat it as a copy of IV/RV. Positive means options are priced above expected moves.
Spread.simple: Implied volatility minus the forecast of real movement, in volatility points. It is the same idea as IV/RV, but as a difference. The desk found the two move almost exactly together.

Stamp duty.example: Like a small registration fee when you buy a plot, paid only by the buyer.
Stamp duty.forYou: It hardly affects you, but you pay it on your protective wings.
Stamp duty.impact: If it rises: buying legs costs slightly more. If it falls: slightly less.
Stamp duty.readIt: When you see stamp duty, know it is tiny: on Rs 2,000 of premium it is 6 paise.
Stamp duty.simple: A government tax on buying options, 0.003% of premium. It is charged only on buys, not on sells.

Stand-down.example: Like a cook who says if the milk drops below this mark, I stop cooking and rethink. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the one-session 1-sigma move is 160 points, the stand-down is 24,840.
Stand-down.forYou: As a seller, if NIFTY keeps trading below this, do not add shorts; the note says to size for it rather than widen the stop.
Stand-down.goodBad: Neither; it is a safety line, not a prediction.
Stand-down.impact: If it goes up: NIFTY rose or daily swings are expected to shrink. If it goes down: NIFTY fell or bigger daily swings are expected.
Stand-down.readIt: When you see this level, read it as the line below which the day's selling plan should be paused.
Stand-down.simple: This is NIFTY's spot minus a 1-sigma move for just the next trading session. The desk's note calls a sustained trade below it the hard stand-down: its view is wrong and it stops trusting the range.

Starting position.example: Like setting up your shop stall before customers arrive, on the side of the street with more traffic. In a lean-up plan it is a bull put spread under the first floor.
Starting position.forYou: Enter this position first, then apply the profit-take and stop rules from day one.
Starting position.impact: If the lean is up: it sells puts below the first floor. If down: it sells calls above the first ceiling.
Starting position.readIt: When you see it, read the strikes, credit, max loss and breakeven per lot.
Starting position.simple: The spread to put on now, before any branch plays out. It is sold beyond the nearest wall on the side history favours. With no lean it is an iron condor across both walls.

Stochastic above 80.example: Like a student scoring near his best marks of the last two weeks. If NIFTY's 14-day range is 24,400 to 25,000 and it closes at 24,950, stochastic is above 80.
Stochastic above 80.forYou: As a seller, a strong market can stay above 80 for many days, so this is not a safe signal to sell calls close to the money.
Stochastic above 80.goodBad: Neither; overbought is a description, not a sell signal.
Stochastic above 80.impact: If this turns on: price is pressing the top of its 2-week range. If it turns off: price has slipped back toward the middle of the range.
Stochastic above 80.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY is closing near its recent highs. The table shows how long it usually stays there and what NIFTY did afterwards.
Stochastic above 80.simple: Stochastic shows where today's close sits inside the last 14 days' high-to-low range, from 0 to 100 (smoothed over 3 days). Above 80 means NIFTY is closing near the top of its recent range.

Stochastic below 20.example: Like a shop's sales being near the lowest of the last two weeks. If NIFTY's 14-day range is 24,400 to 25,000 and it closes at 24,450, stochastic is below 20.
Stochastic below 20.forYou: As a seller, do not assume a bounce is due and sell puts close to spot; falling markets can stay low for a while.
Stochastic below 20.goodBad: Neither; oversold is a description, not a buy signal.
Stochastic below 20.impact: If this turns on: price is pressing the floor of its 2-week range. If it turns off: price has bounced back up into the range.
Stochastic below 20.readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY is closing near its recent lows. The table shows how long such spells last and how NIFTY moved after them.
Stochastic below 20.simple: Stochastic shows where today's close sits inside the last 14 days' high-to-low range, from 0 to 100. Below 20 means NIFTY is closing near the bottom of its recent range.

Stood aside.example: Like a fisherman who stays home on a stormy day: that is a decision, not a failure. If 20 of 100 sessions stood aside, those were no-trade days.
Stood aside.forYou: On a stood-aside day, do not force a trade.
Stood aside.impact: If it goes up: fewer days offered a good trade. If it goes down: more days passed the filters.
Stood aside.readIt: When you see this number, remember that not trading is a scored choice. It is not a miss.
Stood aside.simple: Sessions where no strike passed the desk's filters, so no trade was suggested. The filters check easy trading, distance and premium. For a seller this is a valid answer, scored as one.

Stop at 1.5x credit.example: Like a fixed rule for a bad cricket over: if it costs 15 runs, change the bowler. Trading: credit Rs 4,000, so stop at a Rs 6,000 loss.
Stop at 1.5x credit.forYou: Write the rupee stop level in your plan the day you open the trade.
Stop at 1.5x credit.goodBad: Hitting the stop is a planned, normal cost; skipping it is the expensive mistake.
Stop at 1.5x credit.impact: If the loss reaches it: close the trade. If you skip it: one loss can wipe out several winners.
Stop at 1.5x credit.readIt: When you see the loss near this level, get ready to close, not to hope.
Stop at 1.5x credit.simple: This rule says close the trade when its loss reaches 1.5 times the credit. It applies whatever day that is. It caps how much one trade can give back.

Stop checked intraday.example: Like a guard who checks the gate all day instead of only at night. Thieves have less time.
Stop checked intraday.forYou: The 18-year research and stress lab both favoured intraday stops for limiting tail losses.
Stop checked intraday.goodBad: Intraday checking shrinks stop slippage; close checking showed about 1.5x on average.
Stop checked intraday.impact: If stops are checked intraday: losses stay nearer the planned level. If only on the close: losses can run well past it.
Stop checked intraday.readIt: When you see this row, compare its tail and drawdown with the close-checked stop.
Stop checked intraday.simple: A stop watched during the day, not just at the close. It fills near the stop level unless the market gaps through overnight. Close-only stops are often hit far beyond the level.

Stop loss.example: At a cricket betting crowd, a smart friend says: I stop when I have lost twice my usual win. If you sold a NIFTY put for Rs 30, a 2x stop means you buy it back when the loss reaches Rs 60.
Stop loss.forYou: As a seller, decide your stop before you enter, because short options lose faster than they gain.
Stop loss.goodBad: A low multiple like 2x keeps a loss survivable; 5x lets one loss eat weeks of wins.
Stop loss.impact: If it goes up: each loss gets bigger and can erase many wins. If it goes down: losses stay small, but you get stopped out more often on normal wiggles.
Stop loss.readIt: When you see this number, read it as how many winning trades one loss can undo. 2x is something this hit rate can carry; 5x is not. Next, compare it with the gap scenarios, because a gap can jump past your stop.
Stop loss.simple: The loss at which you close the trade, no arguing. On this desk it is a multiple of the premium you collected. A stop at 2 times the credit means one loss wipes out two wins.

Stop slippage.example: You set an alarm for 6 am but wake at 7 because of a power cut. The alarm level was 6; the fill was 7.
Stop slippage.forYou: Your stop is not a guarantee; plan for losses beyond it.
Stop slippage.goodBad: Near 1.00x is good; checking stops intraday misses only on overnight gaps.
Stop slippage.impact: If slippage rises: stops protect less than you think. If it falls toward 1.0x: stops work as planned.
Stop slippage.readIt: When you see this, read the average and the 95th percentile. The current close-checked stop averaged about 1.5x and was 2.3x at the 95th percentile.
Stop slippage.simple: How much a stop really lost compared with the loss it was meant to cap. 1.00x means it filled exactly at the level. Stops checked only on the close are often gapped through.

Stop to close.example: Like a fire alarm: the faster you leave, the less harm.
Stop to close.forYou: Close as soon as the stop shows; decide nothing else first.
Stop to close.goodBad: Near zero minutes is good; long delays mean hoping instead of acting.
Stop to close.impact: If it goes up: you hesitate more, and losses can grow. If it goes down: you act on stops quickly.
Stop to close.readIt: When you see a large number, you waited after the stop fired.
Stop to close.simple: This is the minutes between a stop first showing in this browser and you closing the trade. Successful professionals take losses fast. The target is about zero.

Stop vs winners.example: Like three days of savings gone with one expensive meal: Rs 500 saved over three days, Rs 1,500 spent in one night.
Stop vs winners.forYou: Remember it when you are tempted to hold past a stop.
Stop vs winners.goodBad: Lower means stops are cheaper relative to wins; higher means one loss undoes a lot of work.
Stop vs winners.impact: If it goes up: each stop hurts more, so you need more winners. If it goes down: a stop costs fewer winners.
Stop vs winners.readIt: When you see 3, read it as: one stop equals three take-profit wins.
Stop vs winners.simple: This shows how many winning trades one stopped loss wipes out. With these rules one stop erases about three winners. That is why skipping a stop is so costly.

Storage, carry and the cost of holding.example: Keeping potatoes in cold storage for 3 months costs rent, so the 3-month price is higher.
Storage, carry and the cost of holding.forYou: Ignore roll-day jumps on continuous charts.
Storage, carry and the cost of holding.goodBad: Normal carry is calm; an inverted curve signals shortage.
Storage, carry and the cost of holding.impact: If carry grows: supply is plentiful. If the curve inverts: supply is tight.
Storage, carry and the cost of holding.readIt: When you see this table, check roll gaps and whether the curve slopes up or down.
Storage, carry and the cost of holding.simple: Later futures months usually cost more than the nearest, because storage and interest cost money. This is called carry. An inverted curve means supply is tight now.

Store.example: Like a shop's ledger book that keeps every day's sales, so you can check any old day. A NIFTY claim from four months ago can be graded against the real numbers of that day.
Store.forYou: As a seller, a healthy store means the track record you rely on is complete.
Store.impact: If the size grows normally: new sessions are landing safely. If it stays flat on trading days: the fetch is skipping for an unreported reason.
Store.readIt: When you see the size, it should grow steadily each trading day. A flat size across several trading days means sessions are not being saved. Check the fetch pipeline next.
Store.simple: The database file where every fetched session is saved. It holds option chains, index history, positions and the claims record. The page rebuilds its numbers from it.

Straddle expected move.example: If a betting crowd pays Rs 170 for a bet that wins on any big score swing, they expect a swing of about 170. If the NIFTY 25,000 call and put cost 170 together, the market expects about 170 points.
Straddle expected move.forYou: As a seller, keep short strikes outside this move, or you are underpaid for the range.
Straddle expected move.goodBad: A big straddle means big expected moves; a small one means a calm expected week.
Straddle expected move.impact: If it goes up: the market expects bigger moves, so strikes should sit further away. If it goes down: a calmer week is priced, and premium shrinks.
Straddle expected move.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with your short strike distance. If the straddle says 170 and your strikes are 120 away, you are inside the expected move. It says nothing about direction.
Straddle expected move.simple: Add the price of the at-the-money call and put. That total is roughly the move the market expects by expiry. It is shown in points.

Straddle hit rate.example: Like a goalkeeper who saves 53 of 100 penalties. Good to know, but one missed big shot can cost the match.
Straddle hit rate.forYou: It shows how often a sold straddle survived, but always check the size of the losses too.
Straddle hit rate.goodBad: Above 50% is better for sellers, but a high hit rate with big losses can still lose money.
Straddle hit rate.impact: If the hit rate rises: more expiries end inside the range. If it falls: more expiries break out and sellers lose.
Straddle hit rate.readIt: When you see the hit rate, read it with the edge. Over 311 cases it was 53%; the last 20 cases kept only 40%.
Straddle hit rate.simple: How often NIFTY finished inside the at-the-money straddle's price range at expiry. Inside means the seller kept some money. It is a count of wins, not of rupees.

Straddle kept by premium signal.example: Like comparing how often an umbrella seller profited on days his helper said 'prices are good'.
Straddle kept by premium signal.forYou: On stored data, rich rows did not keep more, so do not sell on that label alone.
Straddle kept by premium signal.goodBad: Higher survival and edge on rich rows means a useful signal.
Straddle kept by premium signal.impact: If rich rows keep more: the signal helps. If not: it does not.
Straddle kept by premium signal.readIt: When you see this table, compare rich rows with thin and cheap rows, and the average seller edge.
Straddle kept by premium signal.simple: How often a sold at-the-money straddle survived to expiry, split by what the premium signals said. A useful signal shows clearly better survival on its rich rows.

Straddle move.example: Like saying the bus is expected to be 2% late on a 50 minute trip. A 200 point straddle at NIFTY 25,000 is 0.8%.
Straddle move.forYou: Use it as a quick check that your strikes are beyond the expected move.
Straddle move.impact: If it goes up: bigger moves are priced. If it goes down: smaller moves are priced.
Straddle move.readIt: When you see this percent, cross-check it with the sigma band. A big gap usually means the volatility input is off.
Straddle move.simple: The ATM straddle cost as a share of the NIFTY price. It is the expected move in percent. It should roughly agree with the sigma band.

Strategy builder.example: Like cooking your own recipe, then a judge tastes it by the same rules as the restaurant's menu.
Strategy builder.forYou: It lets you test your own idea before risking money.
Strategy builder.goodBad: Judge a build by EV after costs and max loss, not by credit alone.
Strategy builder.impact: If you widen strikes: POP rises and credit falls. If you add lots: every number, gain and loss, grows the same way.
Strategy builder.readIt: When you see a built trade, compare its EV per risk with the best scanner row. If it is worse, the scanner already found something better.
Strategy builder.simple: A tool to put any legs together on any expiry. It shows the payoff, Greeks, odds and EV after costs, using the same numbers as the scanner. Legs are saved only in your browser.

Strategy by expiry.example: Like planning separate tiffins for each day of the week. A spread is shown only if it kept its credit in 70% or more of past cases. About Rs 120 of costs is taken off.
Strategy by expiry.forYou: Prefer the pick with the best expected profit per rupee at risk, and skip expiries showing no trade.
Strategy by expiry.impact: If volatility goes up: picks move further out and credits grow. If no spread passes 70%: that expiry shows no trade.
Strategy by expiry.readIt: When you see this, read each expiry's pick and its expected rupees. Prices use the bid for legs sold and the ask for legs bought.
Strategy by expiry.simple: One suggested trade for each expiry: this week, next week, this month and next month. Each is judged separately. Standing aside on one expiry is a valid answer.

Strategy lab summary.example: Like a weather board at a fishing jetty. Is it safe to go out, and how big might the best catch be?
Strategy lab summary.forYou: It tells you in one glance whether today is a day to sell at all.
Strategy lab summary.goodBad: On 13-Nov-2026 the side rule said stand aside and none of 3,388 ranked trades had positive EV after costs.
Strategy lab summary.impact: If the side rule turns to sell and some trades show positive EV: there may be a paid trade. If EV stays negative everywhere: no trade is paid after costs.
Strategy lab summary.readIt: When you see these tiles, read the side rule first. If it does not say sell, the trades below are for reference only.
Strategy lab summary.simple: Six numbers that frame every trade on the Strategy lab tab. They show the side rule, the best expected profit after costs, and how many trades clear their costs. They also show how far the desk expects NIFTY to move.

Stress lab.example: Like testing a bridge with heavy fake trucks before opening it.
Stress lab.forYou: Never trade more lots than the tail-safe size.
Stress lab.goodBad: A small safe size means risky tails; zero means even one lot is too much.
Stress lab.impact: If tail losses grow: the safe size shrinks. If they shrink: the safe size grows.
Stress lab.readIt: When you see the tail-safe size, it is the most lots with ruin at most 1% under every model.
Stress lab.simple: The rules tested on thousands of made-up two-year markets, built from this commodity's own behaviour. It measures how bad the tails get. It sets the tail-safe size.

Stress test summary.example: Like a car crash-test lab running many crashes on dummies, so real passengers know the risk.
Stress test summary.forYou: It tells you how much pain to be ready for, not how much you will earn.
Stress test summary.goodBad: Each trade is sized to a Rs 20,000 maximum loss on Rs 5 lakh. Tails come from the worst model.
Stress test summary.impact: If tail numbers get worse: the rule is more dangerous at this size. If they shrink: it is safer.
Stress test summary.readIt: When you see this, focus on the tail numbers: CVaR, drawdown and ruin. About 80 million trade paths were simulated.
Stress test summary.simple: The desk's rules run through millions of made-up market paths from three kinds of model. It shows how bad things can get at the desk's size. It is not a forecast of profit.

Stress-lab candidates.example: Like a new medicine that worked in the lab now being tried on real patients.
Stress-lab candidates.forYou: It joins the safety lab with the real record before any rule changes.
Stress-lab candidates.goodBad: More positive windows and a positive test expectancy is better.
Stress-lab candidates.impact: If a candidate also wins on real history: it has stronger support. If it only wins in simulation: it has not met the real market yet.
Stress-lab candidates.readIt: When you see this table, read the out-of-sample rows and how many walk-forward windows were positive.
Stress-lab candidates.simple: Rules the stress lab picked from about 80 million simulated paths. Here each is run on real NIFTY history since 2008. Adoption depends on these real-history results, not on the simulation.

Strike.example: Like betting a batsman will not cross 50 runs; 50 is your strike. If NIFTY is 25,000, you could sell the 25,500 call, betting NIFTY stays below 25,500.
Strike.forYou: As a seller, choosing the strike is most of the trade, so use the filters, not the richest-looking price.
Strike.impact: If you pick a strike further away: less premium, less chance of a loss. If you pick a closer one: more premium, more chance of being tested.
Strike.readIt: When you see the strike list, check how far each strike is from spot. Far strikes pay less but are safer. Strikes near a big OI wall have writers defending them.
Strike.simple: The price level an option is about. NIFTY strikes come every 50 points. Choosing a strike is choosing your chance of being hit.

Strong downtrend (ADX > 25, -DI on top).example: Like a cricket team losing wicket after wicket in a steady collapse. If NIFTY falls most days from 25,000 to 23,800 over a month, ADX rises above 25 with -DI on top.
Strong downtrend (ADX > 25, -DI on top).forYou: As a seller, short puts are the side at risk here, and falls come fast, so give puts extra room and keep wings on.
Strong downtrend (ADX > 25, -DI on top).goodBad: Bad for put sellers; neither for the market as a whole.
Strong downtrend (ADX > 25, -DI on top).impact: If this turns on: a strong downward trend has formed. If it turns off: the selling has lost its force.
Strong downtrend (ADX > 25, -DI on top).readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY is in a clear, strong fall. The table shows how long such spells lasted and how NIFTY moved after them.
Strong downtrend (ADX > 25, -DI on top).simple: ADX measures how strong a trend is on a 0 to 100 scale (14 days). Above 25 counts as strong. -DI on top of +DI means the strong trend is downward.

Strong uptrend (ADX > 25, +DI on top).example: Like a river flowing fast in one direction instead of swirling. If NIFTY climbs most days from 24,000 to 25,200 over a month, ADX rises above 25 with +DI on top.
Strong uptrend (ADX > 25, +DI on top).forYou: As a seller, short calls are the side at risk in a strong uptrend, so keep them further away or smaller.
Strong uptrend (ADX > 25, +DI on top).goodBad: Neither; good for put sellers, harder for call sellers.
Strong uptrend (ADX > 25, +DI on top).impact: If this turns on: a strong upward trend has formed. If it turns off: the trend has lost strength or turned sideways.
Strong uptrend (ADX > 25, +DI on top).readIt: When you see this state ON, NIFTY is in a clear, strong rise. The table shows how long such spells lasted and what came next.
Strong uptrend (ADX > 25, +DI on top).simple: ADX measures how strong a trend is, whatever its direction, on a 0 to 100 scale (14 days). Above 25 counts as a strong trend. +DI on top of -DI means the strong trend is upward.

Swing turning point.example: Like a cricket team's run rate that keeps rising and then clearly turns down for several overs. If funds built up to 200,000 net long and then cut by more than the threshold, the 200,000 week gets the dot.
Swing turning point.forYou: As a seller, a fresh turning point after a big build-up is a reason to be more careful on the side the funds were pushing.
Swing turning point.goodBad: Neither. It is a marker, and it is seen only after the fact.
Swing turning point.impact: If this happens again: a turning point after a long build-up often means the trend has lost its fuel, but it is confirmed only after the turn.
Swing turning point.readIt: When you see a dot, check what price did around it. Most turning points come with price turning too, because funds mostly follow price.
Swing turning point.simple: A dot on the managed money chart where funds stopped building their position and started cutting it, or the other way round. The desk marks it only when the net turns back by more than 0.6 standard deviations, so small wiggles do not count.

Symbol.example: Like a train number: 12951 is always the same train even if people call it by different names. GC=F is gold futures on COMEX, and NIFTY is the NSE index.
Symbol.forYou: Copy the symbol when you want to check a price yourself.
Symbol.impact: If it changes: the desk is now reading a different contract or source, so compare prices with care. If it stays the same: you are looking at the same instrument as before.
Symbol.readIt: When you see a symbol, use it to look the instrument up in your broker or on a chart site.
Symbol.simple: The short code the exchange or data provider uses for an instrument. It lets you find the same thing on any trading app. It is a name tag, not a number to judge.

Synthetic pricer error.example: Like a sketch artist's drawing compared with a photo: close enough to recognise, not exact.
Synthetic pricer error.forYou: Treat synthetic crisis prices as rough.
Synthetic pricer error.impact: If the error goes up: trust synthetic prices less. If it goes down: they are closer to real.
Synthetic pricer error.readIt: When you see the error, judge how much to trust a synthetic price.
Synthetic pricer error.simple: Old crisis days have no stored option prices. The desk builds prices from NIFTY and India VIX, the fear index. This shows how far those made-up prices are from real ones. Use crisis replays to rehearse maths, not exact prices.

Synthetic vs real chains.example: Like comparing a map with the real road. If the map is off, every route planned on it is off too.
Synthetic vs real chains.forYou: It warns you when the long model history may be misleading.
Synthetic vs real chains.goodBad: Same sign and close numbers is good.
Synthetic vs real chains.impact: If the gap grows: model results are less trustworthy. If they agree: model results are more believable.
Synthetic vs real chains.readIt: When you see this table, check if real and synthetic agree on the sign. Then check by how much they differ.
Synthetic vs real chains.simple: The real backtest's trades priced again by the model, compared with the real results. If the two disagree on profit or loss, every model figure carries that error.

Tags.example: Like labels on photo albums: wedding, holiday, birthday. A day tagged crash and event, like an election result day, was a big-move day.
Tags.forYou: As a seller, practise crash and gap days on paper so you know how your positions behave before it happens for real.
Tags.impact: If this turns on (a tag like crash): that day had a big, sharp move. If it turns off: the day was more ordinary.
Tags.readIt: When you see tags, use them to pick the kind of day you want to practise. A blind random pick hides them so you cannot cheat.
Tags.simple: Tags are short labels on each replay day that say what kind of day it was, such as crash, gap, event, budget, synthetic, desk loss or desk trade.

Tail exposure.example: Like a house in a flood zone: a smoke alarm will not help, only height and insurance do.
Tail exposure.forYou: Check it before adding any position.
Tail exposure.goodBad: Small means a gap would hurt but not ruin; large means one bad morning could do serious damage.
Tail exposure.impact: If it goes up: a bad gap costs more, so trim size. If it goes down: the book is safer against shocks.
Tail exposure.readIt: When you see these figures, find the worst gap row. Ask if you could take that loss calmly.
Tail exposure.simple: This shows what your trades lose in a tail, a rare huge move, if NIFTY gaps. A gap means it opens far from yesterday's close. A stop cannot protect you in a gap. Only the bought wing and a small size do.

Tail sessions.example: Like judging a bowler on only 3 matches. If tail sessions is 8, expected shortfall is a rough guess.
Tail sessions.forYou: When tail sessions are few, size smaller than the risk numbers suggest.
Tail sessions.impact: If it goes up: tail estimates become more reliable. If it is small: they may be badly off.
Tail sessions.readIt: When you see this number, a small value means VaR and expected shortfall are uncertain.
Tail sessions.simple: The count of very bad sessions the risk numbers are built from. A small count means the tail numbers rest on few examples. Read them as rough then.

Take profit.example: Like selling half your mangoes early at a good price, instead of waiting and risking rain.
Take profit.forYou: Early profit-taking helped on real chains. The 18-year research instead preferred holding the condor with a tight stop.
Take profit.goodBad: The current rule takes profit at 50% of the credit.
Take profit.impact: If you take profit sooner: more small wins, more orders and costs. If later or never: bigger wins but more time exposed to a crash.
Take profit.readIt: When you see take profit in the rules, note the level. On the real-chain test, taking profit at 50% lost less than holding to expiry.
Take profit.simple: Closing a trade early once you have kept part of the credit. The desk's rule closes at half the credit. It locks in small wins and frees capital.

Technicals &amp; valuation.example: Like a doctor checking pulse, blood pressure and weight before giving advice. Indicators like RSI and averages tell you if NIFTY has run too far or fallen too far.
Technicals &amp; valuation.forYou: As a seller, use these levels to choose strike distances, not to bet on direction.
Technicals &amp; valuation.goodBad: Neither; a set of readings to understand the market.
Technicals &amp; valuation.impact: If the readings go up (stronger): the chart backdrop supports the market. If it goes down (weaker): the backdrop is fragile.
Technicals &amp; valuation.readIt: When you see this section, use it to understand the backdrop, then open the full note for the levels and kill switches.
Technicals &amp; valuation.simple: This section holds the chart indicators, pivot levels, option levels and today's full note. It shows where NIFTY stands on its chart and how expensive it is.

Term structure.example: Like mangoes costing more today than next week because everyone wants them now. For crude, backwardation beyond -0.5% votes +1, contango beyond +1% votes -1.
Term structure.forYou: For crude options, a deep backwardation is a reason to respect upside risk on short calls.
Term structure.impact: If backwardation deepens: crude supply is tight, a support for prices. If contango widens: supply is loose, a weight on prices.
Term structure.readIt: When you see this row, read the spread. For crude it means something; for gold and silver, contango is just storage and interest cost and never votes.
Term structure.simple: Compares the next month's futures price with this month's. Next month cheaper is called backwardation. Next month dearer is called contango.

The 27 and the 6.example: Like a shop that earns Rs 100 on 27 days but loses Rs 600 on 6 days: Rs 2,700 earned, Rs 3,600 lost.
The 27 and the 6.forYou: Look at it whenever a long run of wins makes you feel safe.
The 27 and the 6.impact: If stops become bigger or more frequent: total results fall fast. If fewer: the many small wins can show through.
The 27 and the 6.readIt: When you see it, notice that the losses are few but large.
