The 27 and the 6.simple: This shows the desk's own backtest in one picture. Every profit-take won and every stop lost. The few stops erased the many wins. A strategy can win three trades in four and still lose money.

The clear picture.example: Like asking how 150 past patients like you recovered. Strike levels are the edges of the 8-in-10 range, rounded outward to the nearest 50.
The clear picture.forYou: Place short strikes at or beyond the 8-in-10 edges for the expiry you trade.
The clear picture.impact: If the walk-forward tests hold up: the ranges deserve trust. If not: treat them carefully.
The clear picture.readIt: When you see this, read the 8-in-10 range edges and whether the band held in past tests.
The clear picture.simple: The study in plain words. It says whether direction can be called and where NIFTY tended to settle by each expiry. It also says what would change the view. It uses the 150 past days most like today.

The positioning read.example: Like seeing where shopkeepers have stacked the most stock: they expect buyers there. If call sellers crowd at 25,500 and put sellers at 24,500, the market expects to stay between.
The positioning read.forYou: Use the edges it names to place short strikes outside them, not the direction to bet on.
The positioning read.impact: If sellers move their money: the read changes the same day. If the named strikes break: the read was wrong and should be dropped.
The positioning read.readIt: When you see this line, look for the edges it names. Those are the strikes that must break for the read to be wrong. Each read is recorded and graded later.
The positioning read.simple: The desk's one-line summary of where the market leans today. It is read from where option sellers have put real money. It is not a forecast and has no target.

The trade.example: Like a recipe card: ingredients, steps and when to switch off the gas. It holds the expected range, buy or sell today, the recommended structure, the exit plan and gap scenarios.
The trade.forYou: As a seller, follow the exit plan as written; the plan is part of the trade.
The trade.goodBad: Neither; standing aside is also a valid answer.
The trade.impact: If this turns on (side call is sell): premium is rich and no measured event is ahead. If it turns off (stand aside): the rule sees no paid edge today.
The trade.readIt: When you see this section, read the side call first, then the structure and exit plan before entering anything.
The trade.simple: This section on the Today page puts the trade together: how far NIFTY can move by expiry, which side to take, what to sell and when to get out.

Theta / day.example: Like ice in a cold-drink shop melting a little every hour. The seller of ice is happy each hour it melts.
Theta / day.forYou: Theta is your daily pay as a seller, but it comes with negative gamma risk.
Theta / day.goodBad: Higher positive theta is more daily income, usually with more gamma risk.
Theta / day.impact: If theta rises: you earn more each quiet day. If it falls: time pays you less, so a move hurts more than time helps.
Theta / day.readIt: When you see theta per day, read it in rupees per lot. Compare it with the possible loss in the scenario grid.
Theta / day.simple: Theta is how much an option's price melts away each day as time passes. For a seller it is the daily income if nothing else changes. It grows faster near expiry.

Theta/day.example: Like a parking lot owner earning Rs 100 a day per car parked, while the car owner pays that Rs 100.
Theta/day.forYou: Use it to see which leg earns the most and which costs you.
Theta/day.impact: If it goes up on a sold leg: more daily pay, usually with more risk. If it goes down: less pay.
Theta/day.readIt: When you see this number, add it across legs to see the daily pay of the whole trade.
Theta/day.simple: This is what one day of time passing is worth on this one leg, in rupees. Sold legs earn it. Bought legs pay it.

Time exit.example: You leave the cinema before the last 5 minutes to beat the parking rush, even if the movie is good. If your NIFTY 25,500 call is worth only Rs 3 the day before expiry, you still buy it back and exit.
Time exit.forYou: As a seller, exiting before expiry day avoids the hours when safe strikes turn into big losses.
Time exit.impact: If the exit moves closer to expiry: you collect a little more premium but carry expiry-day danger. If it moves earlier: you give up a little premium and avoid the fastest, riskiest hours.
Time exit.readIt: When you see this date, treat it as a hard rule, not a suggestion. Check how many sessions remain before it. When it fires, the trade is usually winning, and that is exactly when people ignore it.
Time exit.simple: A fixed day when you must be out of the trade, win or lose. On this desk, that day is before expiry day. On the last day, risk is huge compared to the little premium left.

Times.example: Like counting how many times you forgot your keys this month.
Times.forYou: Watch frequent habits; cheap ones can turn costly.
Times.impact: If it goes up: the habit is growing. If it goes down: you are breaking it.
Times.readIt: When you see a high count with low rupees, the habit is frequent but cheap so far.
Times.simple: This is how many entries in your mistake log carry this habit. It breaks ties when two habits cost the same rupees.

Today&rsquo;s lesson.example: Like a teacher who uses today's newspaper headline as the class topic.
Today&rsquo;s lesson.forYou: Do it daily; answers change, so they cannot be memorised.
Today&rsquo;s lesson.impact: If the market changes: a different lesson is chosen. If nothing unusual happens: your costliest habit decides.
Today&rsquo;s lesson.readIt: When you see today's lesson, check which trigger chose it.
Today&rsquo;s lesson.simple: This is one short lesson a day, chosen by what the market is doing. It could be cheap premium, an event, a fear spike, a broken range or expiry day. Else a rule change or your costliest habit. Its questions use today's numbers.

Topic.forYou: Check the official syllabus before the exam.
Topic.impact: If NISM revises it: the topic list may change. If not: the summary holds.
Topic.readIt: When you see a topic, decide if you know it well.
Topic.simple: This says what the unit's test covers. The wording is the desk's summary, not NISM's. Check NISM's current objectives before the exam.

Touch probability.example: A batsman may cross the line during a run even if he ends safe. Touching the line is more common than being run out.
Touch probability.forYou: Touches trigger stops and fear, so this number tells you how often you may need to act.
Touch probability.goodBad: Lower is calmer; about twice the chance of finishing beyond the strike.
Touch probability.impact: If it rises: your stop or adjustment is more likely to be triggered. If it falls: the strike is safer from a scare.
Touch probability.readIt: When you see touch probability, use it to plan stops. A 30% touch means a stop near the strike may be hit about 3 times in 10.
Touch probability.simple: The chance NIFTY trades through your short strike at some time before expiry. Not just at the end, but any time. It is roughly double the chance of finishing beyond the strike.

Trade journal.example: Like a shop's diary of sales: what sold, why, and what profit, so patterns show over months.
Trade journal.forYou: Export it often so a browser reset does not erase it.
Trade journal.impact: If you fill it fully: your metrics become trustworthy. If you skip entries: the metrics mislead you.
Trade journal.readIt: When you see the journal, sort by exit or emotion to find patterns.
Trade journal.simple: This is a diary of every trade. It holds the edge you named, confidence, emotion, gate result, exit and profit or loss. It stays only in this browser, so export it to keep a copy.

Trades a week.example: Like eating 5 meals a day when you are hungry only 3 times.
Trades a week.forYou: Aim to match your trades to the filter's sell days.
Trades a week.goodBad: At or below the edge count is good; well above means overtrading.
Trades a week.impact: If your count goes up past the edge count: more no-edge trades. If it falls to match: you trade only when paid.
Trades a week.readIt: When you see your count above the edge count, some trades were not backed by the filter.
Trades a week.simple: This shows how often you open a trade. Beside it is how often the desk's filter saw an edge. More trades than edge days means trading on no-edge days.

Trading-day basis.example: A shop open 5 days a week sells mangoes on 5 days, not 7. If NIFTY expiry is 4 trading days away but 6 calendar days, the trading-day band is about 18% narrower.
Trading-day basis.forYou: As a seller, holiday weekends are when this matters, as you decide whether to hold through.
Trading-day basis.impact: If holidays add calendar days: premium decays more than risk grows. If trading days are added: the range gets wider.
Trading-day basis.readIt: When you see this note, know the range uses market days only. It matters most across long weekends and holidays. Options lose value by calendar time, but risk comes on trading days.
Trading-day basis.simple: A note that a number counts only market-open days, not calendar days. A weekend adds two calendar days but zero trading days. This changes the width of every range.

Train objective.example: Like ranking drivers by distance covered per accident, with a penalty for any very bad crash.
Train objective.forYou: It explains why the research picks safer rules over the highest-return ones.
Train objective.goodBad: Higher is better; the test score matters more.
Train objective.impact: If test objective stays near train: the rule held up. If it collapses: it was fitted.
Train objective.readIt: When you see train and test objective, compare them. A big drop from train to test signals luck.
Train objective.simple: The score used to rank rules in the training years. It is yearly return divided by the average worst-5% trade loss, minus a penalty if drawdown passes 20%. Higher means more return per unit of tail risk.

Train-test rank correlation.example: If mock-exam toppers are mostly board-exam toppers too, the mock was a good guide.
Train-test rank correlation.forYou: A high value means the research's ranking is a useful guide.
Train-test rank correlation.goodBad: Closer to 1 is better; near 0 means the search is guessing.
Train-test rank correlation.impact: If it rises: good training rules stay good in testing. If it falls toward zero: training ranks mean nothing.
Train-test rank correlation.readIt: When you see this, above 0.5 is a strong match. The desk's search shows 0.68.
Train-test rank correlation.simple: Rank all rules by their training score, then by their test score. This number says how well the two orders match, from minus 1 to 1.

Treasury futures position.example: Like a booking for a future purchase, not goods already in the shop. A net short in 10-year futures does not prove a view on yields.
Treasury futures position.forYou: Use it only as delayed world background.
Treasury futures position.impact: If the net goes up: the group is more long those futures. If it goes down: more short.
Treasury futures position.readIt: When you see this row, check the contract, category and date.
Treasury futures position.simple: A reported group position in a named US government bond futures contract. It is not the same as owning bonds. 2-year and 10-year contracts are separate markets.

Treasury tenor.example: Like fixed deposits of different lengths paying different rates. The 10Y might pay 4.3% while the 2M pays 5%.
Treasury tenor.forYou: Use tenors as world background; a sharp move in the 10Y can affect global risk mood.
Treasury tenor.impact: If a tenor's yield goes up: money for that length is dearer. If it goes down: cheaper.
Treasury tenor.readIt: When you see a tenor, its level is a yield and its change is in basis points. They are different readings.
Treasury tenor.simple: The length of time for a point on the US government yield curve. 2M is two months, 10Y is ten years. The page shows 2M, 6M, 1Y, 2Y, 10Y and 30Y.

Trend.example: Like a student scoring above his weekly, monthly and yearly average marks: he is in good form. If gold is above all three averages, trend votes +1.
Trend.forYou: If trend is strongly up, be careful selling calls close to the price.
Trend.impact: If price climbs above all three: the vote becomes +1. If it falls below all three: the vote becomes -1; averages turn late, after price does.
Trend.readIt: When you see this row, count how many averages the price is above. 3 of 3 means a clear up trend; 0 of 3 a clear down trend.
Trend.simple: Where the price sits against its 20, 50 and 200 day averages. Above all three votes for up. Below all three votes for down. Mixed votes nothing.

Trend and range read.example: If onion prices have been above last month's and last season's average, the trend is up.
Trend and range read.forYou: Use it to know which way the plan leans and why.
Trend and range read.goodBad: A clear trend tells you which side is riskier; sideways suits two-sided strategies.
Trend and range read.impact: If the trend turns up: the plan leans up. If it turns sideways: the plan sells both sides.
Trend and range read.readIt: When you see this read, check up, down or sideways. ADX above 25 is trending; below 20 is sideways. Where no implied vol exists, this and the range are all you get.
Trend and range read.simple: The direction and strength of the trend, and what history says about moves like today's. The plan leans on this reading. Trend is up when price is above its 50 and 200-day averages.

Trend regime.example: Like noting whether prices have been rising, falling or flat this season.
Trend regime.forYou: Use it as context for tier 1 trades.
Trend regime.impact: If it turns up: rising prices are favoured. If it turns down: falling.
Trend regime.readIt: When you see this state, check the odds it lasts.
Trend regime.simple: Up, down or range, using price against a fast and slow moving average. It shows the state over two years. It shows odds that a spell this old lasts longer.

Trend state base rates.example: If rice rose more often after up months than after any month, and in both decades, that is real.
Trend state base rates.impact: If reliable: the state has a real lean. If not: treat as noise.
Trend state base rates.readIt: When you see this table, check the reliable column.
Trend state base rates.simple: What the series did after each trend state, compared with any period. It counts as reliable only if the gap is big and holds in both halves of history.

Type.example: Like choosing between insurance against rain and insurance against drought. A NIFTY 25,500 CE pays if NIFTY goes above 25,500; a 24,500 PE pays if it goes below 24,500.
Type.forYou: As a seller, always check the Type before placing an order; a CE and PE mix-up turns a safe leg into a risky one.
Type.impact: If this turns on (CE chosen): the leg is tied to rises above its strike. If it turns off (PE chosen): the leg is tied to falls below its strike.
Type.readIt: When you see CE or PE, read it with the Action column: SELL CE means you lose if NIFTY rises a lot; SELL PE means you lose if NIFTY falls a lot.
Type.simple: In a leg table, Type tells you whether the option is a call (CE) or a put (PE). A call gains when NIFTY rises; a put gains when NIFTY falls. In the Replay trainer list, Type tells you whether the day is a real stored chain or a synthetic crisis day.

ULSD / heating oil.example: Like diesel for lorries and generators getting dearer in winter. If ULSD is 3.00 dollars a gallon, a 42-gallon barrel is worth 126 dollars.
ULSD / heating oil.forYou: As a seller, there is no diesel option on MCX, so use it as background for crude.
ULSD / heating oil.goodBad: Neither. It is a market, not a score.
ULSD / heating oil.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish on diesel. If it goes down: they are less bullish or adding shorts.
ULSD / heating oil.readIt: When you see this row, compare it with WTI. Funds buying diesel while selling crude can mean tight diesel supply rather than a broad oil view.
ULSD / heating oil.simple: The New York Harbor ultra-low sulphur diesel future on NYMEX, in lots of 42,000 gallons. It used to be called heating oil, which is why both names are shown. It tracks diesel for trucks and heating fuel.

US 13-week Treasury bill.example: Like the interest on a three-month fixed deposit, but for the US government. If it is 4.0% and falls to 3.7%, markets expect the Fed to cut rates soon.
US 13-week Treasury bill.forYou: A falling short-term US rate is usually a tailwind for NIFTY; a rising one is a headwind.
US 13-week Treasury bill.goodBad: For Indian stocks, lower is usually better.
US 13-week Treasury bill.impact: If it goes up: dollar cash pays more, which can pull money out of markets like India. If it goes down: cheaper dollar money tends to help emerging markets.
US 13-week Treasury bill.readIt: When you see this yield, compare it with the Fed's policy rate. If it is below it, markets expect a cut.
US 13-week Treasury bill.simple: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow money for about three months. It closely follows what the US central bank (the Fed) has set or is about to set. It is the world's main short-term rate.

US 30-year.example: Like the rate on a 30-year home loan, set by what lenders expect over decades. If it rises from 4.5% to 5%, long-term money got costlier for everyone.
US 30-year.forYou: A sharp jump in long US yields often brings volatility to NIFTY too; widen short strikes on such days.
US 30-year.goodBad: For stocks, a calm or falling long yield is better.
US 30-year.impact: If it goes up: borrowing gets costlier and stock values worldwide come under pressure. If it goes down: long-term money gets cheaper, usually supportive for stocks.
US 30-year.readIt: When you see the 30-year yield, compare it with the 13-week bill. Long rates far above short rates often mean investors worry about inflation or debt.
US 30-year.simple: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow for 30 years. It shows what investors expect for inflation and growth over a very long time. It moves slower than the short rates but matters for all long-term borrowing.

US CPI.example: Like checking how much your monthly grocery bill went up versus last year. It comes out in the US evening, so NIFTY reacts on the next Indian session.
US CPI.forYou: As a seller, if this counts and falls before expiry, the side rule stands aside rather than selling.
US CPI.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: inflation news has been hitting NIFTY harder. If it goes down: NIFTY has been shrugging it off.
US CPI.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with an ordinary day's move and check whether Counts says yes.
US CPI.simple: US CPI is the monthly measure of how fast prices are rising in America. It shapes what the US central bank will do with rates, which moves world markets.

US Dollar Index.example: Like a class average, not one student's marks. If the index rises, the dollar is stronger against the basket overall.
US Dollar Index.forYou: A sharp dollar rise can mean foreign money leaving India, so watch your short puts.
US Dollar Index.impact: If it goes up: commodities in dollars and emerging markets often feel pressure. If it goes down: they often get relief.
US Dollar Index.readIt: When you see this number, compare its date with the currency pairs before drawing conclusions.
US Dollar Index.simple: A measure of the US dollar against a basket of 6 major currencies. It is not the rate against any single currency. A 1-point change is not a 1% move.

US ETF options proxy.example: If you cannot see the price list at your own mandi, you look at the next town's list. It is close, but not the same.
US ETF options proxy.forYou: Remember this is not the Indian order book, and a proxy never triggers a sale.
US ETF options proxy.goodBad: There is no good level; it is context about US holders.
US ETF options proxy.impact: If US holders buy more puts: fear is rising abroad. If they buy more calls: the upside chase is growing.
US ETF options proxy.readIt: When you see this card, use its shape, like skew and walls relative to spot. Do not use its dollar levels for MCX.
US ETF options proxy.simple: An ETF is a fund traded like a share. US ETFs like GLD hold gold, and their options are free to see. The desk uses them as a stand-in, a proxy, for MCX options.

US nonfarm payrolls.example: Like a report card on whether America's businesses are hiring. It lands at about 6 pm India time, after NIFTY closes, so NIFTY reacts on the next session.
US nonfarm payrolls.forYou: As a seller, a Friday release means a weekend and a gap open on Monday, so short positions carry it over two days off.
US nonfarm payrolls.impact: If its move versus a normal day goes up: jobs reports have been shaking NIFTY more. If it goes down: NIFTY has been ignoring them.
US nonfarm payrolls.readIt: When you see this row, compare its move with an ordinary day's move and check whether Counts says yes.
US nonfarm payrolls.simple: Nonfarm payrolls is the monthly count of new jobs in America, usually out on the first Friday. A surprise moves the dollar and US bond yields in one go.

Unanswered.example: Like skipping a ball: no runs but no wicket.
Unanswered.forYou: Guess if you can rule out even one option.
Unanswered.impact: If blanks go up: fewer marks scored. If they go down: more chances to score.
Unanswered.readIt: When you see many blanks, consider guessing if you can rule out one option.
Unanswered.simple: This counts questions left blank. A blank costs nothing. With four options, a random guess still gains a little on average.

Unit.example: Like a chapter number in a textbook.
Unit.forYou: Use it to plan study order.
Unit.impact: If you move up the units: topics shift from products to rules. If you stay low: rules units stay weak.
Unit.readIt: When you see the number, it tells you which part of the syllabus it is.
Unit.simple: This is the NISM Series VIII unit number from the published test plan. Units 1 to 5 are product knowledge. Units 6 to 10 are mechanics, rules, tax and conduct.

Unscheduled looks.example: Like opening the fridge again and again when not hungry.
Unscheduled looks.forYou: Track it for a week to see your peeking habit.
Unscheduled looks.goodBad: Zero is ideal; many means the urge to watch is strong.
Unscheduled looks.impact: If it goes up: more urges to peek. If it goes down: better patience.
Unscheduled looks.readIt: When you see this above zero, note what made you look.
Unscheduled looks.simple: This counts times you opened live profit and loss outside a scheduled check. It is a measure of peeking.

Upcoming rule changes.example: Like a notice that the school timing changes next month. You plan ahead.
Upcoming rule changes.forYou: It warns you before a rule change catches you by surprise.
Upcoming rule changes.goodBad: Check this list before each new month.
Upcoming rule changes.impact: If a change raises costs or margin: plan for smaller size. If it changes settlement: plan your expiry-day exits.
Upcoming rule changes.readIt: When you see this, note the date and how it affects your trades.
Upcoming rule changes.simple: Rules and rates already announced with a future start date. The desk switches on that date by itself. The big one now is average-price settlement from 7-Dec-2026.

Upper 1 sigma.example: Like a weather forecaster saying the high will probably not cross 34 degrees. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the 1-sigma move to expiry is 500 points, the upper 1 sigma is 25,500.
Upper 1 sigma.forYou: As a seller, a short call at or beyond this line has roughly a 1 in 6 chance of finishing in the money, by the option market's own pricing.
Upper 1 sigma.goodBad: Neither; a guide for where to place short calls.
Upper 1 sigma.impact: If it goes up: options are charging for bigger moves, or NIFTY has risen. If it goes down: expected moves have shrunk or NIFTY has fallen.
Upper 1 sigma.readIt: When you see this level, read it as a ceiling that holds about 2 times in 3, not a wall. The table sorts it among the other levels from highest to lowest.
Upper 1 sigma.simple: This is the top edge of the range NIFTY is expected to stay inside by expiry about 68 times out of 100. It comes from today's implied volatility, the move option prices are charging for.

Upper 2 sigma.example: Like saying the summer high will almost surely stay under 40 degrees. If NIFTY is 25,000 and 1 sigma is 500 points, the upper 2 sigma is 26,000.
Upper 2 sigma.forYou: As a seller, this is a natural place for the protective long call (the wing) of an iron condor.
Upper 2 sigma.goodBad: Neither; an outer guide, and real markets cross it more often than 5 in 100.
Upper 2 sigma.impact: If it goes up: options are pricing bigger possible moves, or NIFTY has risen. If it goes down: the market expects calmer moves or NIFTY has fallen.
Upper 2 sigma.readIt: When you see this level, read it as an outer limit that should rarely be crossed by expiry.
Upper 2 sigma.simple: This is the top edge of the wider range NIFTY should stay inside by expiry about 95 times out of 100. It is twice the 1-sigma distance above spot.

VIX in its top 20% in a downtrend.example: Like heavy rain falling on a road that is already flooded. If NIFTY is below its 200-day average and VIX is 22 when it usually sits near 14, this turns on.
VIX in its top 20% in a downtrend.forYou: As a seller, premium is rich but moves are big, so sell only with wings and smaller size.
VIX in its top 20% in a downtrend.goodBad: Rich premium for sellers, but the riskiest time to be short without protection.
VIX in its top 20% in a downtrend.impact: If this turns on: fear is high in a weak market. If it turns off: VIX has cooled or NIFTY has climbed back above its 200-day average.
VIX in its top 20% in a downtrend.readIt: When you see this state ON, fear and a falling market are together. The table shows how NIFTY behaved after such spells.
VIX in its top 20% in a downtrend.simple: This is on when India VIX is higher than on 80% of days in its past year and NIFTY is below its 200-day average. Fear is high while the market is weak.

VIX in its top 20% while NIFTY rallies i.example: Like a family still buying insurance in a hurry while their business is doing well. If NIFTY rises from 24,800 to 25,100 this week, is above its 200-day average, and VIX is 19 when it usually sits near 13, this turns on.
VIX in its top 20% while NIFTY rallies i.forYou: As a seller, premium is rich here, but check the table before assuming the rally is safe.
VIX in its top 20% while NIFTY rallies i.goodBad: Neither; a mixed signal worth a second look.
VIX in its top 20% while NIFTY rallies i.impact: If this turns on: the rally has nervous buyers paying for protection. If it turns off: VIX has cooled, the rally stalled, or NIFTY fell below its 200-day average.
VIX in its top 20% while NIFTY rallies i.readIt: When you see this state ON, traders are hedging into a rally. The table shows how NIFTY moved after such spells.
VIX in its top 20% while NIFTY rallies i.simple: This is on when India VIX is in the top 20% of its year, NIFTY is above its 200-day average, and NIFTY is up over the last 5 sessions. Fear stays high even while prices rise.

VIX up 15%+ in 5 sessions.example: Like onion prices jumping from 40 rupees to 47 rupees in a single week. If VIX goes from 13 to 15.2 in 5 sessions, this turns on.
VIX up 15%+ in 5 sessions.forYou: As a seller, a fast VIX jump hurts open short options even before NIFTY moves much; the desk's note says to close short premium if VIX gains more than 15% in one session.
VIX up 15%+ in 5 sessions.impact: If this turns on: fear is rising fast and option prices are climbing. If it turns off: the jump has slowed or reversed.
VIX up 15%+ in 5 sessions.readIt: When you see this state ON, option prices have jumped quickly. The table shows how NIFTY moved after such jumps.
VIX up 15%+ in 5 sessions.simple: This is on when India VIX is more than 15% higher than it was 5 sessions ago. Fear has risen fast.

VWAP.example: Like the average price paid for mangoes at the mandi, counting big buyers more. If most trading happened near 25,000, VWAP sits near 25,000.
VWAP.forYou: Use VWAP as a fair-price marker for the day, not as a trading signal.
VWAP.impact: If price stays above it: buyers had the upper hand. If below: sellers did.
VWAP.readIt: When you see this number, compare the close with it. A close above VWAP means buyers were stronger through the day.
VWAP.simple: Volume-weighted average price for the day. Prices where more trading happened count more. The desk builds it exactly from each stock's trading.

VaR 95%.example: Like saying only 1 day in 20 does the shop lose more than Rs 2,000. It does not say whether that day loses Rs 2,100 or Rs 20,000.
VaR 95%.forYou: Never size on VaR alone; use expected shortfall.
VaR 95%.impact: If it goes up: bad days start at a bigger loss. If it goes down: bad days start at a smaller loss.
VaR 95%.readIt: When you see this number, always read expected shortfall next to it. VaR alone hides the tail.
VaR 95%.simple: The loss that is beaten only on the worst 5% of days. It says where bad days start. It ignores how bad those worst days get.

VaR and expected shortfall.example: VaR says floods start above the third step; expected shortfall says floods average up to the sixth. If NIFTY VaR is Rs 5,000 but expected shortfall is Rs 20,000, bad days are very bad.
VaR and expected shortfall.forYou: As a seller, size your trade against expected shortfall, not against VaR or POP.
VaR and expected shortfall.goodBad: Low expected shortfall means survivable bad days; high means a single bad day can hurt a lot.
VaR and expected shortfall.impact: If expected shortfall goes up: your bad days get worse, so cut size or add a wing. If it goes down: tail losses are smaller and easier to survive.
VaR and expected shortfall.readIt: When you see these, read expected shortfall first. Put it next to POP. High POP with large expected shortfall is a trade that wins often and loses badly.
VaR and expected shortfall.simple: VaR (value at risk) is the loss that only the worst few days go past. Expected shortfall is the average loss on those worst days. For sellers, the second number matters more.

Variance premium sensitivity.example: If your shop only profits when customers pay 25% extra, the business is shaky.
Variance premium sensitivity.forYou: Distrust agri edges that only work with an assumed premium.
Variance premium sensitivity.goodBad: Positive at x1.00 is good; needing x1.25 is a warning.
Variance premium sensitivity.impact: If results stay positive with no premium: the edge is sturdier. If they need a high premium: it is not proven.
Variance premium sensitivity.readIt: When you see this table, check the no-premium run. It must be positive for the gate.
Variance premium sensitivity.simple: The rules re-priced with no extra premium, the assumed 1.10 times, and 1.25 times. The premium a seller collects is only an assumption here. An edge that needs 1.25 times is not evidence.

Variance ratio.example: A rubber band snaps back (below 1), while a rolling ball keeps rolling (above 1). If NIFTY's ratio is 1.3, a 200-point rise may extend further toward your call.
Variance ratio.forYou: As a seller, below 1 is the friendlier condition for your range to hold.
Variance ratio.goodBad: Above 1 is harder for range sellers; below 1 is easier; near 1 is neutral.
Variance ratio.impact: If it goes up above 1: trends extend, and ranges are less likely to hold. If it goes down below 1: moves reverse, which helps range sellers.
Variance ratio.readIt: When you see this number, near 1 is the usual state. The desk only adjusts bands when the test clearly rejects randomness. It says nothing about direction.
Variance ratio.simple: It checks if moves keep going or tend to turn back. Near 1 means no pattern, like random steps. Above 1 means moves extend; below 1 means moves reverse.

Variance risk premium.example: An umbrella insurer charges Rs 100 a month and usually pays Rs 70; the Rs 30 pays for the rare flood. If NIFTY IV is 14 and realised turns out 11, the premium is about 3 points.
Variance risk premium.forYou: As a seller, when this gap is thin, stand aside rather than trying harder.
Variance risk premium.goodBad: Wide and positive means you are paid well for risk; thin or negative is a warning sign.
Variance risk premium.impact: If it goes up: selling is paid more for its risk. If it goes down toward zero or below: the pay no longer covers the risk. Big moves often follow.
Variance risk premium.readIt: When you see this number, positive and wide is the seller's good condition. Thin or negative means you are not being paid for the risk. Check IV / RV next.
Variance risk premium.simple: The gap between what options charge for movement and the movement that actually comes. Most of the time it is positive. It is the seller's pay for taking on rare big losses.

Vega.example: Like an umbrella seller who promised umbrellas at a fixed price. If clouds gather, umbrellas get dearer and his promise costs him more.
Vega.forYou: As a seller you lose when fear rises, so vega tells you how much one jump in fear costs.
Vega.goodBad: Smaller negative vega means less damage from a jump in IV.
Vega.impact: If IV rises: a short-vega position loses even if NIFTY stays still. If IV falls: it gains.
Vega.readIt: When you see vega, read it as rupees per 1 point of IV. Ask what happens if India VIX jumps 3 points.
Vega.simple: Vega is how much an option's price changes when implied volatility moves by one point. A seller has negative vega. So if fear rises, the sold options get dearer and the seller loses.

Version.example: Like a phone software version number: a new number means something inside changed.
Version.forYou: Note the code in your weekly review.
Version.impact: If the code changes: start counting trades again for judging. If it stays: keep adding to the same sample.
Version.readIt: When you see a new code, older results belong to the old rules.
Version.simple: This is a short code made from the desk's rules. Any change to any rule gives a new code. The date it first appeared starts a new sample of trades.

Vol clustering, lag 1.example: Like rain: a rainy day is often followed by another rainy day.
Vol clustering, lag 1.forYou: Big moves come in bunches, so one stop-out may be followed by another.
Vol clustering, lag 1.goodBad: Closer to the real figure is better for a model.
Vol clustering, lag 1.impact: If clustering is higher: bad days come in groups, deepening drawdowns. If lower: bad days are spread out.
Vol clustering, lag 1.readIt: When you see this, compare each model with real NIFTY. A model with too little clustering is too gentle.
Vol clustering, lag 1.simple: How much a wild day tends to be followed by another wild day. It is a correlation between today's squared move and yesterday's. Real NIFTY shows about 0.16.

Vol premium call.example: An insurance company charged Rs 1,000 and paid out only Rs 700 in claims; it was paid well. If NIFTY options priced a 1% daily move but NIFTY moved only 0.7%, the call was right.
Vol premium call.forYou: As a seller, this is the score that says whether selling options is worth doing at all.
Vol premium call.goodBad: Around 60% or more is a real edge; near 50% is a coin flip and no edge.
Vol premium call.impact: If the hit rate goes up: selling has been fairly paid more often. If it goes down toward 50%: the edge is gone. The honest move is to stop selling until it returns.
Vol premium call.readIt: When you see this hit rate, about 60% means a real but small edge. Near 50% means the desk cannot tell rich prices from cheap ones. Then check the IV / RV ratio for today.
Vol premium call.simple: A claim that options were priced higher than the moves that actually came. Volatility means how much prices jump around. If the claim holds, sellers were paid fairly for their risk.

Vol-scaled size (HAR).example: Like a driver who goes slower in heavy rain and faster on a clear road.
Vol-scaled size (HAR).forYou: It cuts size when danger rises, though a sudden crash from calm can still hurt.
Vol-scaled size (HAR).goodBad: The 18-year research's recommended rule uses vol-scaled size.
Vol-scaled size (HAR).impact: If forecast vol rises: size shrinks. If it falls: size grows.
Vol-scaled size (HAR).readIt: When you see this, compare its tail numbers with fixed size. The desk scales between 0.5x and 1.5x of normal size.
Vol-scaled size (HAR).simple: Choosing size by forecast volatility. Trade more when markets are calm and less when they are wild. HAR is a simple forecast model built from past daily, weekly and monthly swings.

Volatility by year.example: Like comparing this year's rainfall with past years.
Volatility by year.forYou: Use it to judge if current swings are unusual.
Volatility by year.impact: If this year's bar is high: moves are wild. If low: calm.
Volatility by year.readIt: When you see this chart, compare today's level with past years.
Volatility by year.simple: Real volatility in each calendar year. It shows whether today's movement is normal or belongs to a calm or a wild year.

Volatility cone.example: Like knowing a cricket ground's scores over 20 years: lowest 120, typical 160, highest 220. If bookies expect 200 today, they expect a big day.
Volatility cone.forYou: It tells you if the premium you sell is big enough for how much NIFTY usually moves.
Volatility cone.goodBad: Desk verdicts: 75th percentile or more is rich, 50-75 fair to rich, 25-50 thin, under 25 cheap. The desk's test of this verdict did not beat chance.
Volatility cone.impact: If implied moves up the cone: premium is richer than usual. If it moves down: you are paid less than NIFTY usually moves.
Volatility cone.readIt: When you see the cone, find where today's implied dot sits. Near the top is rich, near the bottom is cheap.
Volatility cone.simple: It shows how much NIFTY really moved over 5 to 63 sessions since 2007. It marks the lowest, typical and highest. Today's implied volatility is marked on it. That tells you if premium is rich or cheap.

Volatility desk summary.example: Like a cricket captain checking pitch, weather and dew before choosing to bowl first. One look, then he decides.
Volatility desk summary.forYou: It is your morning checklist before you sell any NIFTY premium.
Volatility desk summary.impact: If the tiles turn favourable (rich premium, writers long gamma, straddles paying): selling looks better paid. If they turn against you: premium is thin or price may run, so size down or wait.
Volatility desk summary.readIt: When you see these tiles, read them as a checklist, not as one signal. Check the gamma flip, the IV percentile and the straddle hit rate first.
Volatility desk summary.simple: Eight small boxes at the top of the Volatility and Gamma tab. Together they say if selling options looks paid today. Each box opens a longer card below it.

Volatility regime.example: Like the noise level in a classroom: it tells you how loud, not which way the children will run. Crude at 50% yearly volatility moves about 7% in a week.
Volatility regime.forYou: When the percentile is low, do not shrink your strike distance too much; quiet spells end.
Volatility regime.impact: If volatility goes up: ranges widen and option prices rise. If it goes down: ranges shrink and premiums fall, but the calm may not last.
Volatility regime.readIt: When you see this row, read the percentile. A low percentile means a quiet spell, which can end suddenly.
Volatility regime.simple: How jumpy the market is now compared with its past year. It sets how wide every range is. It never votes for up or down.

Volatility rising.example: Like a road that had light traffic all month suddenly getting jams this week. If NIFTY's 5-day realised volatility is 16% against 12% over 21 days and implied 14%, this turns on.
Volatility rising.forYou: As a seller, rising real moves eat into your edge, so sell smaller or further out.
Volatility rising.goodBad: Bad for sellers while it lasts.
Volatility rising.impact: If this turns on: recent moves are outrunning what options price. If it turns off: the market has calmed back toward normal.
Volatility rising.readIt: When you see this row, it shows what buying the at-the-money straddle on such days would have earned, held to expiry.
Volatility rising.simple: This buy reason is present when NIFTY's last 5 sessions moved more than 1.10 times its last 21 sessions, and also more than implied volatility. Real moves are speeding up faster than options charge for.

Volatility smile.example: Like flood insurance costing more in a low-lying area than on a hill. People pay more to protect against a fall.
Volatility smile.forYou: It shows where along the strikes you are being paid extra, and why.
Volatility smile.goodBad: A steeper put side means more fear is priced. A put 2 vol points above ATM is flagged as a rich put wing.
Volatility smile.impact: If the put side steepens: protection costs more and sold puts pay more, but the market fears a drop. If it flattens: puts are cheaper and fear is lower.
Volatility smile.readIt: When you see the smile, check how steep the left side is. A steep left side means puts are dear and fear of a fall is high.
Volatility smile.simple: Implied volatility for each strike of one expiry. For NIFTY, low strikes (puts) usually carry a higher IV than high strikes. So the line slopes down to the right.

Volume.example: Like the number of customers who walked into a shop today, not how many bought a yearly membership. If 10 lakh traded but OI barely changed, it was churn.
Volume.forYou: Prefer strikes with good volume so you can get in and out at fair prices.
Volume.impact: If it goes up with OI: new positions are building. If it goes up without OI: it is same-day churn.
Volume.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with the change in OI. Volume without OI change is churn.
Volume.simple: The number of contracts traded today. High volume with little change in open contracts means quick in-and-out trading. It does not show lasting commitment by itself.

WTI.example: Like the wholesale mandi price that your local shop's price follows. If WTI goes from $70 to $73, MCX crude rises by a similar share.
WTI.forYou: If you hold MCX crude options, watch WTI overnight, because it moves your position before India opens.
WTI.impact: If it goes up: MCX crude rises too and India's import costs grow. If it goes down: MCX crude falls and oil-hit Indian costs ease.
WTI.readIt: When you see this number, compare its move with MCX crude. Any difference comes from the rupee.
WTI.simple: WTI is the American crude oil price, in dollars per barrel. MCX crude in India settles to this price. It is kept in dollars so the world price stays visible.

WTI crude.example: Like the main wholesale mandi rate that every local shop follows. If WTI goes from 70 to 77 dollars, MCX crude rises about 10% too, plus or minus any rupee move.
WTI crude.forYou: As a seller of MCX crude options, this row is the closest positioning read for your contract.
WTI crude.goodBad: Neither. It is a market, not a score.
WTI crude.impact: If it goes up: funds are more bullish on US crude, which usually goes with a rising price. If it goes down: funds are cutting longs or adding shorts.
WTI crude.readIt: When you see this row, read the funds' net, its weekly change and the 3-year percentile. A high percentile means funds are already heavily long.
WTI crude.simple: West Texas Intermediate, the main US crude oil future, traded on NYMEX in lots of 1,000 barrels. MCX crude oil is priced from it, so its moves show up on MCX.

Walk forward.example: Like watching a series one episode a day, with no spoilers.
Walk forward.forYou: Reveal one day at a time and decide honestly.
Walk forward.impact: If NIFTY moves toward a short strike: the position value rises and you lose. If it moves away: you gain.
Walk forward.readIt: When you see each new day, check if any exit rule fired.
Walk forward.simple: This shows the days after your decision, one at a time, with the position valued at each close. Exit rules are checked at each close. A move during the day that reversed is invisible.

Walk-forward Sharpe.example: Like a farmer choosing seeds using the last six harvests, then planting for two years, then choosing again.
Walk-forward Sharpe.forYou: It is the most realistic test of whether research helps you going forward.
Walk-forward Sharpe.goodBad: Above zero is the minimum; higher is better.
Walk-forward Sharpe.impact: If it rises: re-choosing rules with fresh data keeps working. If it falls toward zero: the edge fades in real use.
Walk-forward Sharpe.readIt: When you see this, compare it with the current rules on the same years. Walk-forward gave 0.74.
Walk-forward Sharpe.simple: Walk-forward means: choose the rule on 6 past years, trade it for the next 2 years, then repeat. The Sharpe of all those stitched test periods is this number. It copies how you would really use research.

Wall holds claim.example: Like a dam that holds water better than the riverbank downstream. Call wall held 92.9%, put wall 80.0%.
Wall holds claim.forYou: Trust the call wall more than the put wall when placing strikes.
Wall holds claim.impact: If a wall's hit rate goes up: that edge is more reliable. If it goes down: it is less reliable.
Wall holds claim.readIt: When you see this, compare the two hit rates. The put wall breaks on days when everything falls together.
Wall holds claim.simple: A claim that NIFTY will not close beyond the call wall above or the put wall below. It rests on where money is really committed. The call wall holds more often than the put wall.

Weather, monsoon and the Indian crop cal.example: Rice is sown with the June monsoon and harvested in autumn; wheat is sown in winter.
Weather, monsoon and the Indian crop cal.forYou: Be careful selling premium during sowing and weather-scare months.
Weather, monsoon and the Indian crop cal.goodBad: Volatile months mean higher risk; calm months mean lower.
Weather, monsoon and the Indian crop cal.impact: If the monsoon fails: kharif prices can jump. If it is good: prices can ease.
Weather, monsoon and the Indian crop cal.readIt: When you see this calendar, note the most volatile month for your crop.
Weather, monsoon and the Indian crop cal.simple: When each crop is sown and harvested in India, the US, Brazil and West Africa. Kharif crops grow with the monsoon; rabi crops after it. It shows which months each market swings most.

Weekly change in managed money.example: Last week a sweet shop had booked 10 kg of gold jewellery buys and 4 kg of sells. This week it is 12 kg buys and 3 kg sells. Net went from 6 to 9: up 3, from both new buying and fewer sellers.
Weekly change in managed money.forYou: A big unusual change is a cue to check the news and your open positions.
Weekly change in managed money.goodBad: A large change shows strong fresh action by funds; a small change means they mostly sat still that week.
Weekly change in managed money.impact: If it goes up: funds added longs or covered shorts, which pushes price support. If it goes down: funds sold longs or added shorts, which adds pressure on price.
Weekly change in managed money.readIt: When you see this number, compare it with a typical week shown beside it. A change more than about 2 times typical is unusual. Then check which leg, longs or shorts, did the moving.
Weekly change in managed money.simple: This is how much the funds' net bet changed since last week's report. It is split into change in buy bets and change in sell bets. The split tells you why the net moved.

Weekly loss limit.example: Like a weekly cap on eating out: hit Rs 1,000 by Thursday and you cook at home till Monday.
Weekly loss limit.forYou: Use the break to review the week's trades.
Weekly loss limit.impact: If you hit it: no new entries until Monday. If you stay under: trading stays open.
Weekly loss limit.readIt: When you see this hit, take the rest of the week off new trades.
Weekly loss limit.simple: Once your booked losses this week reach this, new trades are locked until next Monday. The default is 2.5 percent of capital.

Weekly market context.example: If you sold gold jewellery in a week when the rupee fell and gold jumped, you would remember that week's backdrop. In the same way, a gold fund sale next to a dollar rise tells a story.
Weekly market context.forYou: Use it to see if a fund move was just a reaction to the dollar or yields.
Weekly market context.goodBad: There is no good or bad level here; it is background that explains fund moves.
Weekly market context.impact: If the dollar or yields go up: gold and silver often face pressure. If they go down: metals often get support.
Weekly market context.readIt: When you see these figures, line them up with the fund change. A dollar up and gold down week with fund selling fits the usual pattern. Then check dated news, like Fed or US jobs data, before naming a cause.
Weekly market context.simple: This shows the metal price, the US dollar index and the US 10-year bond yield for the same week. Each is measured Tuesday to Tuesday, like the CFTC report. It shows what the market did while funds traded.

Weekly net change.example: Like your savings going from Rs 10 to Rs 15: up Rs 5, but you do not know why. From 10 to 15 contracts is +5.
Weekly net change.forYou: Use it only as one clue among several.
Weekly net change.impact: If it goes up: the group moved toward long. If it goes down: it moved toward short.
Weekly net change.readIt: When you see this number, do not read it as proof of new buying or covering. Check gross longs and shorts too.
Weekly net change.simple: The latest net position minus last week's. Positive means the group became more long or less short. It does not show which trades caused it.

Weekly review.example: Like a coach reviewing a match: a good shot caught on the boundary is still a good shot.
Weekly review.forYou: Do it once a week, same day, same time.
Weekly review.impact: If good-process trades go up: your habits improve. If bad-process trades go up: luck is covering mistakes.
Weekly review.readIt: When you see trades in the bad-process-profit box, treat them as warnings, not wins.
Weekly review.simple: This sorts the week's closed trades by process (rules kept or not) and outcome (profit or loss). Good process with a loss is a normal cost. Bad process with a profit is luck.

Weekly vs monthly OI.example: Like comparing daily wage workers with permanent staff. If the weekly put wall is 24,800 and the monthly is 24,500, the slow money sits lower.
Weekly vs monthly OI.forYou: Use the walls of the expiry you are trading, not the other one.
Weekly vs monthly OI.impact: If walls on both expiries agree: the levels are stronger. If they differ: fast and slow money disagree.
Weekly vs monthly OI.readIt: When you see this, compare PCR, put wall and call wall for each expiry.
Weekly vs monthly OI.simple: Open interest is how many option contracts are still open at each strike. This compares the weekly expiry with the monthly one. Weekly shows fast money; monthly shows bigger, slower positions.

Weight.example: In a class of 50, the class captain's vote counts as 13 and a new student's as 0.3. A 2% jump in a 0.3% weight stock barely moves NIFTY; the same jump in the biggest stock moves it a lot.
Weight.forYou: As a seller, watch the heaviest stocks, because their big moves can push NIFTY toward your strike.
Weight.goodBad: A high weight means the stock can move the index; a low weight means it hardly can.
Weight.impact: If a stock's weight goes up: its moves push NIFTY more. If it goes down: its moves matter less to the index.
Weight.readIt: When you see this number, use it to judge which stock moves really matter. Big weights drive the index. Small weights are mostly noise, however loud the headline.
Weight.simple: A stock's share of the NIFTY index. The exchange lists the members but not their weights. The desk works out the weights from daily price moves.

What can be graded.example: Like a teacher who grades only the subjects actually taught.
What can be graded.forYou: Do not expect trade grades on tier 2 or 3.
What can be graded.impact: Nothing moves here. If a series moves to tier 1: it gets graded plans.
What can be graded.readIt: When you see this card, note that no live grading exists for these series.
What can be graded.simple: What on this series can be checked against what happened, and what cannot. No desk calls exist on tier 2 or 3. Only the seasonal claim is graded.

What could happen.example: Like a weather report that says if the clouds stay, it rains; if the wind turns, it clears. If the Fed cuts rates next week, gold may rise; if it holds, gold may fall.
What could happen.forYou: Plan your trade for each path before the event, so you are not deciding in a panic.
What could happen.goodBad: Neither; it is a plan, not a prediction.
What could happen.impact: If an event on the list comes closer: the chance of a sharp move rises. If it passes quietly: the market often calms down.
What could happen.readIt: When you see this section, note the trigger for each path and the dates in Events ahead.
What could happen.simple: The desk's list of possible next moves for this market, with what would cause each one. It is a set of if-then paths, not a single forecast. It also lists the events coming up that could trigger a move.

What could happen by each expiry.example: Like a weather table for each day of the week, with normal values beside. 8 in 10 is the 10th to 90th percentile range.
What could happen by each expiry.forYou: Use the ranges and wall-break odds for strikes; trust the up chance only with positive skill.
What could happen by each expiry.impact: If the up chance rises above its bracket: today's setup leans up. If skill is negative: ignore the up chance.
What could happen by each expiry.readIt: When you see this, compare each number with its bracket. Check skill: negative means the base rate did better.
What could happen by each expiry.simple: For each expiry it shows the chance NIFTY ends higher and its likely settle range. It also shows odds of big moves and wall breaks. Bracketed numbers are for any day. That shows what today's setup changes.

What each choice does on average.example: Like checking if extra tuition helps the average student in a whole school, not just the topper.
What each choice does on average.forYou: It tells you which settings help in general, not just in one lucky rule.
What each choice does on average.goodBad: Medians are used so a few extreme rules cannot move a row.
What each choice does on average.impact: If a choice lifts the median: it helps broadly. If it only helps the single best rule: it may be luck.
What each choice does on average.readIt: When you see this table, compare the test median across choices in one group.
What each choice does on average.simple: Every searched rule grouped by one setting at a time. It shows the median training and test score and the share of rules with a positive test Sharpe. A setting that helps thousands of random rules is real evidence.

What happened.impact: If it often differs from your forecast: you may be overconfident. If it often matches: good calibration.
What happened.readIt: When you see it, compare with what you said.
What happened.simple: This is the real outcome the forecast is scored against. It comes from the revealed days only.

What it takes.example: Like the rule for a swimming certificate: swim 50 metres without help.
What it takes.forYou: Read it before chasing a badge.
What it takes.impact: If the condition is met: you earn it. If not: keep practising.
What it takes.readIt: When you see it, compare with where you are.
What it takes.simple: This states the exact condition for the badge. No badge depends on the number of trades or on profit. Minimum samples stop one lucky answer from earning it.

What kept spells going.example: Like checking what long monsoon spells had on day one that short ones did not. If none shows, nothing on day one predicted length.
What kept spells going.forYou: Use it as a soft hint about how long a trend might stay.
What kept spells going.impact: If today's reading matches long spells: the state may run on. If it matches short ones: it may fade soon.
What kept spells going.readIt: When you see this, a listed condition hints a spell may last. An empty list means no clear clue was found.
What kept spells going.simple: Compares day-one readings of long spells with short ones. It shows what tends to keep a state alive. A condition is listed only if the gap is clearly large.

What the desk did.example: Like comparing your answer with the teacher's and with a simple rule of thumb.
What the desk did.forYou: Use it as a reference, not a target.
What the desk did.impact: If the desk did better: study why. If you did better: check it was not luck.
What the desk did.readIt: When you see it, compare your process with the desk's, not just the money.
What the desk did.simple: This shows the desk's own side rule and backtest trade on the same day. It also shows a benchmark that always sells a 1-sigma condor. The backtest is in-sample, meaning the rules were made after seeing that period.

What the news says.example: Like hearing the same story from a newspaper and from a neighbour: both count, but you trust them differently. A headline from a major wire service carries more weight than an unknown blog.
What the news says.forYou: Never trade on a headline alone; check whether the desk's numbers agree with it.
What the news says.goodBad: Neither; news is context, not a signal.
What the news says.impact: If many fresh headlines point the same way: the market mood is strong. If headlines conflict: expect choppy, uncertain moves.
What the news says.readIt: When you see a headline, check its time and source. Headlines older than the freshness limit are dropped.
What the news says.simple: The latest headlines about this market from news sources, with each publisher's reputation tier. The tier is a label, not a filter. Always read the article before relying on it.

What the record says so far.example: Your cricket club checks its season record: great at defending, poor at guessing tosses. The NIFTY record shows the 2-sigma range held 96.5%, the call wall 92.9%, and direction only 49.2%.
What the record says so far.forYou: As a seller, use this record to trust the range parts of the note and ignore the direction call.
What the record says so far.impact: If a strong claim's score drops: trust it less and investigate. If a weak claim's score rises over many sessions: it may deserve more attention, slowly.
What the record says so far.readIt: When you see this summary, take the ranges, walls and volatility parts seriously. Treat any direction line as a guess. Read it before changing any rule, not after a bad day.
What the record says so far.simple: The overall result from every stored session so far. Ranges and walls have held up well. Direction calls have been right about half the time, like a coin.

When premium is too cheap to sell.example: Like an umbrella seller in a dry week: he does not start buying umbrellas, he sells fewer. Sell smaller and further out, or not at all.
When premium is too cheap to sell.forYou: On cheap days, cut size or skip, and park unused margin where it earns safely.
When premium is too cheap to sell.goodBad: The desk wants implied at least 1.10 times forecast; below that premium is too cheap.
When premium is too cheap to sell.impact: If the ratio rises above 1.10: normal selling resumes. If it stays below: sell small and far, or stand aside, and keep idle margin earning.
When premium is too cheap to sell.readIt: When you see this, compare selling-when-cheap results with selling-when-rich. Count expiries, since days share expiries.
When premium is too cheap to sell.simple: What to do when options are not priced above the moves that usually follow. The sell bar is implied at 1.10 times the forecast. The desk's replay says do not switch to buying.

Where NIFTY stands.example: Like a health check-up card: pulse, temperature, weight together. If RSI is 72 and ADX 28, NIFTY is in a strong, stretched up trend.
Where NIFTY stands.forYou: Use these readings mainly to judge the size of coming moves, not to pick a direction.
Where NIFTY stands.impact: If VIX percentile goes up: bigger moves have tended to follow. If ADX goes up: a trend is getting stronger.
Where NIFTY stands.readIt: When you see these readings, look at the box under them. It says if history found a reliable direction or just bigger or smaller moves.
Where NIFTY stands.simple: Trend, momentum, trend strength and fear readings in one place, from the daily chart. RSI above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold. ADX below 20 means sideways, above 25 trending.

Where on the desk.example: Like a map showing where in the city you can see a thing you studied.
Where on the desk.forYou: Visit the tab after studying the unit.
Where on the desk.impact: If a unit has tabs: you can practise live. If none: rely on the question bank.
Where on the desk.readIt: When you see a tab name, open it to see the idea live.
Where on the desk.simple: This shows the tabs where the unit's ideas appear with live numbers. Practise there to see the idea on today's prices.

Where you are.example: Like a progress bar on a download.
Where you are.forYou: Read it as direction, not verdict.
Where you are.impact: If it goes up: you get closer. If it goes down: you move away.
Where you are.readIt: When you see it near the condition, a bit more good work earns it.
Where you are.simple: This is your current figure against the badge condition. It is worked out in this browser from your saved history. Small samples move it a lot.

Which claims hold up.example: A school report card with marks per subject, not one total. If NIFTY range claims score 96% and direction scores 49%, you trust the range and ignore the direction call.
Which claims hold up.forYou: As a seller, size trades only on the claims at the top of this table, like ranges and walls.
Which claims hold up.goodBad: High scores in the nineties mean trustworthy; scores near 50% mean no better than a coin flip.
Which claims hold up.impact: If a claim's score goes up: it earns more trust for your decisions. If it goes down: rely on it less and find out what broke.
Which claims hold up.readIt: When you see this table, read it top to bottom. The gap between top and bottom is the lesson. Trust claims near the top. Only use the top rows for sizing trades.
Which claims hold up.simple: A table of every kind of claim the desk makes, each scored on its own. It shows which parts of the model work. Range and wall claims score high; direction claims score about 50%.

Who.example: Like a scoreboard column for each team.
Who.impact: If a different row did better: study its choice. If yours did: check it was not luck.
Who.readIt: When you see a row, read whose choice it was before comparing.
Who.simple: This says whose decision the row shows: the desk rule, its backtest trade or the benchmark. All use the same day's data.

Who is short options.example: Like knowing which shops promised fixed prices on umbrellas. If it pours, they rush to buy stock.
Who is short options.forYou: You are on the same side as these groups, so their pain can become yours.
Who is short options.goodBad: A large net short with a fast move is the classic squeeze.
Who is short options.impact: If sellers grow and NIFTY runs toward sold strikes: their hedging can speed the move. If they shrink: less squeeze risk.
Who is short options.readIt: When you see this table, note who is short. On 13-Nov-2026 FIIs were net short calls; Clients and Pros were net short puts.
Who is short options.simple: Which groups have sold more index options than they bought, for calls and for puts. Sellers are short gamma, so they may chase the market to stay hedged. It does not say at which strike.

Whole book.example: Like a family's total monthly bills, not just one person's.
Whole book.forYou: Check it before adding a trade, since each new one adds to it.
Whole book.impact: If it goes up: all trades together risk more. If it goes down: your total risk shrinks.
Whole book.readIt: When you see this row, compare its max loss with the book cap.
Whole book.simple: The book is all your open trades together. This row adds them all up. The book cap applies to its max loss.

Why POP understates risk.example: A cricket bet with 85% odds wins Rs 10 most days, then loses Rs 200 once. If you sell a far NIFTY strike with 85% POP, the 15% losing days can be very large.
Why POP understates risk.forYou: As a seller, treat high POP as small frequent wins with rare big losses, not as safety.
Why POP understates risk.impact: If IV goes down: the model's tails shrink but real ones do not, so POP looks too safe. If IV goes up: the gap narrows, but losses still come in big lumps.
Why POP understates risk.readIt: When you see a POP number, mentally lower it, especially when IV is low. Check expected shortfall next, which shows how big the bad days are.
Why POP understates risk.simple: POP comes from a model that expects smooth, normal moves. Real markets jump on budget days, results and world shocks. So big losses happen more often than POP suggests.

Why a wing (defined risk).example: Like paying for helmet and insurance on your scooter ride. If you sell the NIFTY 25,500 call, buying the 25,700 call means your loss stops growing past 25,700.
Why a wing (defined risk).forYou: As a seller, a wing is the cheapest protection you can buy against a gap you cannot stop.
Why a wing (defined risk).impact: If the wing is closer: the loss cap is tighter, but more premium is spent. If it is further: you keep more premium, but the worst case is larger.
Why a wing (defined risk).readIt: When you see the wing cost, compare it with the loss it caps. In one session, wings cost 33 of 53 points of credit but kept the loss under 4 times credit. Below VIX 12.5, this desk requires them.
Why a wing (defined risk).simple: A wing is an option you buy beyond your short strike. It caps how much you can lose. It costs part of your premium, but your worst case becomes a known number.

Why five RV estimators.example: A cricket score of 150 hides whether wickets fell in a scary collapse. A NIFTY day that closed flat after a 300-point swing looks calm on close-to-close but wild on the others.
Why five RV estimators.forYou: As a seller, trust the higher estimators when they disagree, because your strike felt those swings.
Why five RV estimators.impact: If the five spread apart: risk is hiding inside the day or overnight. If they agree: the volatility reading is more solid.
Why five RV estimators.readIt: When you see these five numbers, check if they agree. Yang-Zhang is the main reference here. If close-to-close is calm but the others are high, the closing price is hiding big swings.
Why five RV estimators.simple: There are five ways to measure how wild the market was. Some use only the closing price; others use the high, low, open and overnight gaps. When they disagree, the disagreement itself is a clue.

Why it moved.example: Like a cricket commentator explaining why the score jumped: two sixes and a dropped catch. If gold rose 1.5% and the dollar fell 0.8% the same day, the dollar is one stated reason.
Why it moved.forYou: Use it to understand, not to predict: a reason for yesterday's move is not a promise about tomorrow.
Why it moved.impact: If more of the move is explained: the cause is clear and easier to follow. If less is explained: the move may be driven by something not yet in the news, so be more careful.
Why it moved.readIt: When you see this section, read the reasons and check the tags: blue tags are the desk's own numbers, grey tags are headlines.
Why it moved.simple: The desk's short explanation of why each market moved, built from the day's price data, fund positions and news. Each reason links to the numbers or articles behind it. Any part of a move it cannot explain is said plainly, not filled in.

Why the desk stands aside.example: A ticket booking app says 'housefull', 'price too high' or 'seat too close to the screen'. If NIFTY is 25,000 and the only paying call is 25,100, the tag says too close.
Why the desk stands aside.forYou: As a seller, respect this tag, because one badly priced strangle can undo weeks of premium.
Why the desk stands aside.impact: If the reason clears, like premium rising or liquidity improving: a trade may be proposed. If the reason stays: standing aside saves you from trades the record says lose.
Why the desk stands aside.readIt: When you see this tag, read it as a decision, not an error. Marginal means it barely passed the rules. Needs history means there is not enough past data yet to rank it.
Why the desk stands aside.simple: A tag that explains why no trade was suggested. Illiquid means hard to trade at the shown price. Thin premium means too little pay. Too close means the strike sits inside the expected range.

Win rate.example: A shopkeeper who profits on 77 days out of 100 sounds great. But if the 23 bad days lose more, he is still behind.
Win rate.forYou: A high win rate is normal for a seller and is not proof of profit.
Win rate.goodBad: Higher is nicer, but expectancy decides. Desk rules: 77% wins, minus Rs 437 average.
Win rate.impact: If it rises with the same loss size: results improve. If it rises only because losses got bigger: nothing improved.
Win rate.readIt: When you see win rate, always look at average win and average loss next. The weekly rules won 77% but lost money overall.
Win rate.simple: The share of trades that made money after costs. It counts wins, not rupees. Option selling usually has a high win rate and a few big losses.

Within risk budget.example: Like keeping a gift within the Rs 2,000 you set aside.
Within risk budget.forYou: Work out lots from the budget.
Within risk budget.impact: If max loss goes up past the budget: the rule fails. If it stays under: it passes.
Within risk budget.readIt: When you see this rule missed, cut the lots.
Within risk budget.simple: This rule says the worst loss at expiry, in rupees, must fit the desk's per-trade budget. Size by risk, not by available margin.

Worked cost example.example: Like a taxi ride: going and coming back costs two fares; staying overnight costs one.
Worked cost example.forYou: Closing early costs about 14% of the credit here, so very thin trades are hardly worth it.
Worked cost example.goodBad: Lower share of credit is better; brokerage is the biggest part.
Worked cost example.impact: If the credit is thin: costs eat a big share. If the credit is larger: costs matter less.
Worked cost example.readIt: When you see this, compare the cost with the credit. On 13-Nov-2026: Rs 227 closed early versus Rs 117 held, on a Rs 1,586 credit.
Worked cost example.simple: What one lot of today's playbook condor costs to trade. It compares closing early at the profit-take with holding to expiry. Closing early doubles the orders and the slippage.

Worst 5% of trades.example: Of 100 cricket matches, average the scores of the 5 worst. That tells you how badly a bad day goes.
Worst 5% of trades.forYou: It is the loss you must be ready to take several times a year.
Worst 5% of trades.impact: If it grows more negative: bad trades hurt more. If it shrinks: the tail is thinner.
Worst 5% of trades.readIt: When you see this, compare it with average win. The recommended rule's worst 5% average about minus Rs 7,260 since 2020; current about minus Rs 9,540.
Worst 5% of trades.simple: The average loss of the worst 5 in every 100 trades, per lot. It is the same idea as CVaR 95. It shows how bad the bad trades are.

Worst path.example: Like the one time your auto took two hours in a flood. It shows what is possible, not what is normal.
Worst path.forYou: Ask yourself if you could survive the worst path before sizing up.
Worst path.impact: If it goes up (more negative): the worst simulated case is uglier. If it shrinks: the worst case is milder.
Worst path.readIt: When you see this number, use it to feel the shape of the worst case. Plan with expected shortfall instead.
Worst path.simple: The worst result among all the simulated paths. It is just one draw, not an average. Use it as a reminder, not a plan.

Writer gamma by strike.example: Think of a shopkeeper who sells more when prices rise and buys more when they fall. He keeps prices steady. A panicking shopkeeper does the opposite and makes swings bigger. Bars above zero are the calm shopkeeper.
Writer gamma by strike.forYou: It tells you where NIFTY may stick and where it may run through your short strikes.
Writer gamma by strike.goodBad: Above zero (long gamma) calms price; below zero (short gamma) speeds it up. The desk's grading found the pin effect did not beat chance on its stored data.
Writer gamma by strike.impact: If bars near spot grow above zero: moves tend to be absorbed, good for a seller's range. If they turn below zero: hedging chases moves, so your short strikes are at more risk.
Writer gamma by strike.readIt: When you see a tall bar above zero near spot, expect price to stick around that strike. Tall bars below zero mean moves there can run. Remember the desk guesses who the sellers are from NSE's participant data.
Writer gamma by strike.simple: Gamma is how fast an option's risk grows when NIFTY moves. This chart shows, strike by strike, how much option sellers must re-hedge if NIFTY moves 1%. Bars above zero calm price; bars below zero can push it.

Wrong answers.example: Like losing a quarter run for each dropped catch.
Wrong answers.impact: If it goes up: your score falls. If it goes down: your score rises.
Wrong answers.readIt: When you see many wrong answers, you may be guessing too much.
Wrong answers.simple: This counts questions answered incorrectly in this set. Each costs a quarter mark.

Year by year results.example: Like a shop that makes all its yearly profit in Diwali week. One bad Diwali and the year is lost.
Year by year results.forYou: Steady small years are worth more than one great year.
Year by year results.goodBad: More positive years with small losing years is better.
Year by year results.impact: If returns spread across many years: the edge is steadier. If they bunch in a few years: one bad year can undo it.
Year by year results.readIt: When you see this table, count the losing years and how big they were.
Year by year results.simple: Each line's return on Rs 10 lakh within each calendar year. A rule that earns its whole record in two or three years is fragile.

You said.example: Like a sealed prediction opened after the match.
You said.impact: If it matches outcomes often: you are calibrated. If it misses often: adjust.
You said.readIt: When you see it, compare with what happened.
You said.simple: This is your committed forecast. It was locked before the reveal.

You vs the desk vs the base rate.example: Like comparing your cricket predictions with an expert's and with simply saying the home team wins.
You vs the desk vs the base rate.forYou: Trust the direction only after many dozens of forecasts.
You vs the desk vs the base rate.goodBad: Positive skill means you beat that reference; negative means you would do better copying it.
You vs the desk vs the base rate.impact: If your skill goes up: your forecasts add real information. If it goes below zero: quoting their number would have done better.
You vs the desk vs the base rate.readIt: When you see your skill against each, above zero beats them and below zero loses to them.
You vs the desk vs the base rate.simple: This compares your Brier score with the desk model's and the base rate's on the same questions. The base rate is how often the thing happens anyway. Skill above zero means you beat that forecaster.

Your Brier score.example: Like a weather forecaster's report card: saying 90 percent and it rains scores well; saying 90 percent and it stays dry scores badly.
Your Brier score.forYou: Compare it only with references on the same questions, never alone.
Your Brier score.goodBad: Lower is better; under the base rate's score means real skill, near 0.25 means coin-flip quality.
Your Brier score.impact: If it goes down: your forecasts are better. If it goes up: they are worse or more overconfident.
Your Brier score.readIt: When you see a value, compare it with the desk and base rate. Quoting the base rate scores about 0.21 on range questions.
Your Brier score.simple: This scores your yes-or-no forecasts. For each, take your chance minus the outcome, square it, and average. Zero is perfect. Always saying 50 percent scores 0.25.

Your accuracy.example: Like a batting average after only 3 innings: very jumpy.
Your accuracy.forYou: Answer at least 10 per unit before judging.
Your accuracy.goodBad: 70 percent or more counts toward the All ten units badge; low means revise.
Your accuracy.impact: If it goes up: you know the unit better. If it goes down: revise it.
Your accuracy.readIt: When you see few answers, do not trust the percent yet.
Your accuracy.simple: This is the share of your answers in this unit that were right. Under about 10 answers, it moves a lot with each question.

Your confidence.example: Like a batsman who says he has a 70% chance of scoring 30 runs. Over 20 innings you see if he really scored 30 about 14 times.
Your confidence.forYou: Write an honest number on every trade, even when you feel very sure.
Your confidence.goodBad: Good is when your stated chances match how often trades actually win.
Your confidence.impact: If your average confidence goes up but results do not: you are becoming overconfident. If it matches your real win rate: your sense of the odds is good.
Your confidence.readIt: When you see this column, compare each number with the result. Your calibration score on the Discipline tab sums this up over many trades.
Your confidence.simple: This is the chance you wrote down, before the trade, that it would end in profit. The desk later checks your numbers against what happened. That shows whether your feeling is too sure or too unsure.

Your forecast.example: Like predicting both who wins and the likely run range before the match.
Your forecast.forYou: Make a real forecast every replay.
Your forecast.impact: If your forecasts are honest: your calibration scores are useful. If they are guesses: the scores mislead.
Your forecast.readIt: When you see it, write numbers you really believe.
Your forecast.simple: This is your chance of profit and your 80 percent range for NIFTY at the first expiry. You commit them with the trade. Both are scored after the reveal.

Your next step.example: Like a coach who sees rain clouds and says: today we practise playing on a wet pitch.
Your next step.forYou: Start here on busy days; it is a suggestion, not a gate.
Your next step.impact: If the market changes: the pick changes to match. If you master a lesson: it is skipped for the next one.
Your next step.readIt: When you see the pick, read the reason line to learn what in today's market chose it.
Your next step.simple: This picks one lesson from today's market, like thin premium, an event, a fear jump or expiry day. If nothing stands out, it gives your next unfinished lesson. It also shows today's forecasts and your weakest exercise.
