Your process.example: Like a cricketer's net practice diary: how many balls faced, mistakes made and what to fix next week. It is about how you trade, not whether one trade won.
Your process.forYou: As a seller, steady rule-following matters more than any single month's profit, because one broken rule can undo many winning trades.
Your process.impact: If your process score goes up: you are following your own rules more often. If it goes down: habits are slipping, whatever the P&L says.
Your process.readIt: When you see this section, check your limits first, then your metrics and the weekly review.
Your process.simple: This section holds your limits, discipline metrics, weekly review and trade journal. It is saved only in this browser.

Your progress.example: Like a report card that grades study, not how many matches you played.
Your progress.impact: If these numbers rise: your skills are growing. If they stall: change what you practise.
Your progress.readIt: When you see your frequent misses, those are the skills to revisit next.
Your progress.simple: This shows lessons done and mastered, exercise accuracy, forecasts resolved, your Brier score, learning days and frequent misses. It counts skills and judgement, never trading. There are no streaks to protect.

Your result.example: Like a match scorecard that shows both the runs and how well you followed the coach's plan. A small loss with process 90% is a good replay; a big win with process 30% is a lucky one.
Your result.forYou: As a seller, a high process score repeated over many days matters more than one lucky win.
Your result.goodBad: Higher process is better; the rupee result alone can mislead.
Your result.impact: If it goes up: you are trading past days better and following your rules. If it goes down: check the debrief to see which rule slipped.
Your result.readIt: When you see this, look at the process score first, then the money.
Your result.simple: This shows how your replay of that day ended: the rupee profit or loss, or stood aside, plus your process score. Process score measures how well you followed rules you could have known that day.

Your trade.example: Like sealing your exam answer sheet: no changes after handing in.
Your trade.forYou: Write the plan as you would for a real trade.
Your trade.impact: If your plan is clear: the replay scores it fairly. If it is vague: exits get messy.
Your trade.readIt: When you see it locked, the replay will now test your plan.
Your trade.simple: This is the legs, size, exit plan and forecast you commit before anything is revealed. Once committed it cannot change. Only the exit rules or a written override can close it.

Z-score of the move.example: If you usually walk 1 km and today you walked 2.5 km, that is a Z of 2.5. If NIFTY was expected to move 100 points and moved 250, Z is 2.5.
Z-score of the move.forYou: As a seller, a run of high Z days means the ranges you sell are too tight right now.
Z-score of the move.goodBad: Z below 1 is a normal day; Z above 2 is a real shock.
Z-score of the move.impact: If Z goes up: the day was a bigger surprise than expected, and short strikes felt more stress. If Z stays low on most days: bands may be wider than needed.
Z-score of the move.readIt: When you see Z values, look at many days, not one. About one day in three should be above 1. If far fewer are, the bands are too wide.
Z-score of the move.simple: The actual move divided by the move the model expected. A Z of 1 means NIFTY moved exactly one expected step. A Z of 2.5 means two and a half times that.

mean-reverting.example: Like a swing that keeps coming back to the middle. NIFTY may move 1% on most days, yet after a week it is still near 25,000.
mean-reverting.forYou: As a seller, this helps range trades at expiry, but daily swings can still hit intraday stops.
mean-reverting.goodBad: Good for range sellers, as long as it holds.
mean-reverting.impact: If this turns on: price keeps snapping back, so expiry ranges are tighter than usual math expects. If it turns off: moves are behaving more like a random walk again.
mean-reverting.readIt: When you see this pill, the expected range built from daily volatility may be too wide for that horizon. Check the Z column: above 1.96 in size means the result is strong enough to trust.
mean-reverting.simple: This regime means NIFTY's moves over several days have been smaller than its daily moves would suggest: up days tend to be undone by down days. The desk calls it mean-reverting when the variance ratio is below 0.9.

p-value.example: If a coin lands heads 9 times in 10, the p-value is about 1%. It is unlikely to be a fair coin.
p-value.forYou: Only trust signals with a small p and enough cases.
p-value.goodBad: Under 0.05 = works; under 0.25 = weak; above = does not work.
p-value.impact: If p falls below 0.05: the signal likely works. If it rises above 0.25: it looks like luck.
p-value.readIt: When you see p, small is good. Pin p = 0.40 means a result like that happens by luck 40% of the time.
p-value.simple: The chance of seeing a result this good by pure luck if the signal did nothing. Small means luck is an unlikely explanation. The desk calls under 0.05 'works'.

trending.example: Like a snowball rolling downhill, getting bigger as it goes. If NIFTY moves 1% a day and each day goes the same way, a 5-day move can be much more than the usual math expects.
trending.forYou: As a seller, put short strikes further away when this regime is on, because your range is likely too tight.
trending.impact: If this turns on: moves are compounding, so price ranges are wider than usual math expects. If it turns off: moves are behaving more like a random walk again.
trending.readIt: When you see this pill, the expected range built from daily volatility may be too narrow for that horizon. Check the Z column: above 1.96 means the result is strong enough to trust.
trending.simple: This regime means NIFTY's moves over several days have been bigger than its daily moves would suggest: moves keep adding up in one direction. The desk calls it trending when the variance ratio is above 1.1.

untraded.example: Like a shop's price tag on an item nobody has bought in months: the tag says Rs 500, but no one has paid that. NIFTYFPI far contracts often show this.
untraded.forYou: Never place a trade in an untraded contract: you may not find anyone to close it with.
untraded.goodBad: Bad for trading; it means there is no market there.
untraded.impact: If a contract goes from untraded to liquid: real trades are happening, so its numbers become meaningful. If it goes from liquid to untraded: interest dried up, so its price is stale.
untraded.readIt: When you see 'untraded', ignore that row's price, basis and carry. Read the 'liquid' rows instead.
untraded.simple: This futures contract had no real trading, so its price is a carried-forward placeholder. The desk marks it so you do not trust a price nobody paid. Its carry is left blank for the same reason.
